stories.Headline: Chamath: SpaceX’s Revenue From Anthropic “Could 2 to 3x” as the Data Center Freeze Bites
stories.Summary:
Chamath Palihapitiya said on this weekend's All-In podcast that SpaceX's revenue from Anthropic "could 2 to 3x" if a freeze on new US data centers takes hold. His argument was that a slowdown helps whoever already owns compute capacity, and he counted SpaceX among the hyperscalers that do. He said the freeze is bad news for the AI labs, which he described as short of this capacity and needing to grow. The comments came after SpaceX stock slid for two days following the midterm elections, then bounced 6% on Friday.

On the contract itself, Anthropic's S-1 puts its SpaceX deals at up to $120.5 billion over terms running into 2029. That works out to about $3.1 billion a month, or roughly $37 billion a year, once all the capacity is delivered, which Anthropic expects in December. The first periods of the deals end in January and March 2027, and after that either side can cancel on 90 days' notice. Chamath said SpaceX could use that exit to reprice the compute at the spot rate, which he put at probably double. Doubling the annual figure gives about $74 billion, and tripling it gives about $112 billion.

TIKR's writer treated Chamath's 2 to 3x as the best case, since it would require Musk to walk away from a customer worth about $37 billion a year at full capacity. Analysts expect SpaceX's total revenue to jump from $48.9 billion this year to $180 billion in 2027, and at today's rates Anthropic alone would be about a fifth of next year's revenue. SpaceX is already getting paid more for scarce compute without a showdown. Its Super Intelligence segment brought in $7.56 billion in the third quarter, up from $2.56 billion in the second, and Musk has said on earnings calls that renewals are coming in at higher dollars per watt. Anthropic could use the same exit, and its S-1 lists large compute commitments to several other suppliers.

The political background is that Democrats won both the House and the Senate last week, and investors read that as bad news for SpaceX, whose compute business now brings in about half of its revenue. Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor's race on a promise of an immediate moratorium on data centers, and Simply Wall St reported that she plans to freeze new data center approvals. Simply Wall St also said incoming Senator James Talarico supports rules that would make AI infrastructure operators such as SpaceX fund local infrastructure and address environmental impact. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of the gigawatts of US data centers in the works are planned for Texas, where SpaceX has projects. Republicans look set to keep the state Senate, so a moratorium would still need lawmakers to approve it.

SpaceX can only charge for compute it actually builds, and its capital spending nearly tripled from a year earlier to $19.6 billion in the third quarter. Management expects $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone, and the company ran about 2.2 gigawatts at the end of October. Simply Wall St said the planned pause targets the facilities behind SpaceX's Anthropic and Google compute deals, which it reported at up to $45 billion and $920 million a month respectively. Sequoia's Shaun Maguire replied "Fully agree" to a post calling SpaceX the biggest beneficiary of tighter regulation on ground-based data centers, though his own model assumes only about a 20% slowdown from the last two years. TIKR's writer concluded that the freeze helps SpaceX more than it hurts over the next year, but that 2027 growth would depend far more on price than on new gigawatts if Texas passes a moratorium.

On what comes next, the first window to exit the Anthropic deals opens in January. Fourth-quarter results early next year will show how close December revenue came to management's $100 billion run-rate goal. Simply Wall St said investors should watch whether SpaceX revises its internal target of more than 2 gigawatts of AI compute online by the end of 2026, or shifts its buildout toward sites outside Texas. Any change in disclosed AI capex timing or utilization against the Anthropic and Google commitments would show how much the new rules are affecting the company.

stories.Headline: The AI Regulation Fight Is About Speed. It Should Be About Measurement
stories.Summary:
Washington is split between those who want AI development slowed and those who want the United States to stay ahead of China, but two Wharton-affiliated scholars, Burcu Esmer and N. Bugra Ozel, argue the more pressing need is measurement. They say the core problem is that firms, regulators, investors, and the public lack a reliable system for identifying, comparing, and tracing AI's consequences. In September, Anthropic and Accenture each said they expect to invest at least $1 billion over five years in embedded evaluation, but Anthropic acknowledged that no standards govern what outside evaluators may see or how they report. Google DeepMind's CEO, Demis Hassabis, has proposed a U.S. oversight body modeled on FINRA, though the authors note that such a body would be toothless without reporting authority and direct access. Labs currently choose their own benchmarks and hold most of the underlying data.

The authors propose a narrower first federal step: a standardized harm ledger with a common reporting architecture for recording what AI systems do, whom they affect, and how often consequential failures occur. Duties would scale with size and risk, leaving most startups and research labs outside the regime. They urge Congress to pass an AI Measurement and Incident Reporting Act before the current session ends. Under that proposal, NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation would publish common definitions and reporting forms within a year. Frontier developers above a capability threshold would file standardized pre-release evaluations and serious-incident reports, while large hospitals, employers, and lenders would report consequential errors and outcome disparities to their existing regulators.

Independent auditors would verify the reports, and aggregate results would be public. The authors argue that delay carries two costs. First, harms accumulate unseen, and the FBI's 2025 internet-crime report, the first to include an AI section, logged 22,364 complaints and nearly $893 million in reported losses, yet it shows only that AI was mentioned, not that it caused the losses. Quieter harms such as a screened-out job applicant or a denied loan have no comparable national record. Second, delay shifts power toward leading developers, which the authors describe as some of the world's most valuable companies, giving them more wealth, lobbying capacity, and control over the evidence regulators will later need.

They point to industrialization and the years before 2008 as precedents, noting that federal child-labor limits arrived in 1938 and modern workplace-safety rules in 1970, after costs were already entrenched. Europe has already written post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting for high-risk systems into law, and a declaration issued during UN General Assembly week shows a growing group of governments wants shared standards. The authors conclude that the first constraint on AI need not limit innovation but should limit opacity, so that the industry does not become powerful enough to define harm on its own terms. They present their case as a response to a debate they say has been framed too narrowly around speed. Their proposal, however, remains a recommendation, and the articles do not report any congressional action on it.

stories.Headline: What California’s new law means for legal teams using AI and whether other states could follow suit - News Channel 3-12
stories.Summary:
California has become the first state to regulate how attorneys use artificial intelligence by statute, through Senate Bill 574, which takes effect January 1, 2027. Senator Tom Umberg, chair of the state's Senate Judiciary Committee, introduced the bill in February 2025. After two rounds of amendments in the Senate and four in the Assembly, it passed both chambers on the last day of the session. Governor Gavin Newsom signed it on Sept. 30, 2026.

The law allows attorneys to use generative AI to assist in the practice of law but bars them from handing that practice over to the technology. Attorneys cannot enter confidential or personal identifying information into an AI system unless access is limited to them and the people they authorize. They must take reasonable steps to verify AI output and correct errors before using it, and they must personally verify every citation in a court filing. Attorneys who use AI must disclose it on documents submitted to a court, while for public-facing content they only need to consider disclosure. Arbitrators cannot delegate any part of their decision-making to AI and must tell the parties before relying on AI-generated information from outside the record.

Courts can sanction attorneys for citation errors, and firms are generally responsible for violations by their lawyers and staff. Attorneys usually get 21 days to withdraw or fix a challenged filing before sanctions apply. The bill does not spell out separate penalties for its other duties. The law does not define the line between assisting and delegating, nor does it say which AI tools trigger disclosure or what a disclosure should contain. An earlier version required attorneys to read every cited source personally, but lawmakers removed that requirement before passage.

The law applies to every attorney licensed in California, including in-house counsel, and its citation rule reaches anyone filing in a California court wherever they are licensed. Law firms will face the most impact in court filings, and because firms are generally liable for their staff, citation checks and disclosure must become firm-wide processes. For large filings with many contributors, the law does not identify which attorney is responsible for citations. In-house teams will feel the duties to protect information and check AI output in day-to-day work, including contract review, and the law does not say how these duties are enforced outside court.

Other states may follow, though the path may differ. In most states the state supreme court regulates the practice of law, so the next rules are more likely to come from courts than legislatures. New York's court system adopted a statewide rule on attorney AI use in June 2026, while similar disclosure bills have stalled in committee there. The Florida Supreme Court updated its rules so that signing a filing certifies its cited authorities exist and are accurate. The Illinois Supreme Court decided its existing rules were enough and does not require disclosure of AI use as long as lawyers review the output.

stories.Headline: The Archbishop of San Francisco on Staying Human in the AI Age
stories.Summary:
The Free Press published an opinion essay on November 10, 2026, by Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone of San Francisco, arguing that whether artificial intelligence serves humanity depends more on the virtue of its builders than on their brilliance. The archbishop writes from a city where some of the world's most powerful AI systems are being developed, and he says the people building them are making decisions that will shape how billions of people live. He reports that many of these developers, including some who are Catholic, some from other faith traditions, and some with no religion, have turned to the Church for moral guidance. He says they agree that questions about the proper use of such power cannot be answered by technical expertise alone.

The essay centers on Magnifica Humanitas, the first encyclical of Pope Leo XIV, released in the spring of 2026 as the first major teaching document of his papacy. The archbishop says the document is devoted to a single question, namely how to safeguard the human person in the age of AI, and he notes that many developers, even those without religious belief, have read it and appreciate its guidance. The article does not spell out specific policy changes or new obligations for companies or governments. Its request is moral rather than regulatory, asking that the people who build these systems take up the question of human dignity seriously.

Cordileone places the current moment within a longer history of technological upheaval. He recalls that in the late 19th century, factories and railroads transformed the world quickly, enriching some people while leaving workers in long hours, dangerous conditions and wages that barely sustained them. He quotes Pope Leo XIII's 1891 encyclical Rerum Novarum, which described workers as surrendered, isolated and helpless before the hardheartedness of employers and unchecked competition. The archbishop uses this precedent to suggest that the Church has confronted similar questions before and can again offer a framework for judging how new technology should be used.

The article is an opinion piece, so its claims reflect the archbishop's own view and are not reported findings. It does not describe any specific event beyond the publication of the essay and the encyclical, and it does not report on any government action or upcoming deadline. The Free Press is a subscription publication, and the essay appears under its Tech and Business section as part of a series on the economy and technology. The article does not indicate any further developments or next steps.

stories.Headline: Governor Hochul Declares NY Will Lead the Nation in AI Science and Safety; Launches New Research Institute
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research, based at State University of New York's Binghamton University, to advance AI science and safety. The announcement was made on November 10, 2026, and the Center is meant to bring together academic expertise to advance AI safety research, accelerate scientific discovery, and independently test advanced AI systems for safety and security. The Center will convene more than 80 leading scientists from colleges and research institutions across New York State who have expertise in AI safety, security and computer science. It is supported by Empire AI, Governor Hochul's $500 million public-private initiative to drive AI research for public good.

Greg Morrisett of Cornell Tech and Jeannette Wing of Columbia University will serve as interim co-directors of the Center. The Center's work will include independent testing of frontier AI systems, foundational scientific research, and the training of a new generation of AI safety experts. One of its first objectives is a national recruiting effort for experts in areas such as formal methods and verification, interpretability and alignment, and biosecurity. The Center will also give state officials objective evidence to inform policy decisions about AI safety and accountability. Separately, the state's Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) opened an online portal for large frontier AI developers to register by January 1, 2027.

Governor Hochul said that while the federal government fails to act, New York is leading the way on AI safety and holding big tech accountable. Tom Secunda, Empire AI Board Chair, said independent testing will help researchers understand what increasingly powerful systems can do and how to use them safely. SUNY Chancellor John B. King Jr. said SUNY would help ensure New York State is a national and global leader in advancing AI safety and security. Binghamton University President Anne D'Alleva thanked Governor Hochul and Secunda, a Binghamton alumnus and Bloomberg LP co-founder, for their support. The New York State Department of Financial Services Acting Superintendent, Kaitlin Asrow, said DFS is leading implementation of the RAISE Act through the DIGIT Office.

The RAISE Act requires large frontier AI developers to register with the state and meet strict safety, transparency and reporting standards. New York's requirement to report any critical safety incident within 72 hours is the strongest in the nation, according to the state. Beginning in January, large frontier developers must publish safety frameworks on their websites, and all frontier developers must report critical safety incidents and publish model transparency reports. The Center was first announced in January with a $30 million philanthropic gift from a group of donors led by Tom Secunda, along with a $25 million research investment from SUNY and operating capital from New York State. The announcement builds on Governor Hochul's broader AI safety agenda, which includes implementation of the RAISE Act.

At the state's request, the Center will be able to provide expertise, assessments and evidence to help inform state policymaking and oversight of frontier AI developers. The Center will coordinate with DIGIT to begin reviewing developers' published safety frameworks and recommending ways to strengthen requirements. Governor Hochul said that in the coming months she will continue exploring ways to build on the RAISE Act. SUNY describes itself as the largest comprehensive system of higher education in the United States, with 64 colleges and universities. The system's research expenditures were nearly $1.5 billion in fiscal year 2025.

stories.Headline: [Law Firms Now] Bae, Kim & Lee to Hold Seminar on 'Current Issues and Challenges in AI Regulation' on Nov. 16
stories.Summary:
Bae, Kim & Lee (BKL), the Korean law firm, is set to hold a seminar titled "Current Issues and Challenges in AI Regulation" on Nov. 16, according to a report by The Asia Business Daily published on Nov. 9, 2026. The event is billed as this year's second-half AI Law and Policy Forum. It is co-hosted by the offices of Assemblymen Lee Juhee and Choi Hyungdoo, along with KISDI and others. The report's excerpt says discussion will focus on the regulatory challenges surrounding agentic AI and physical AI.

The article's available text gives no further details on the program, such as the venue, speakers or registration. Choi Sukjin is credited as the author, and the item appeared under the paper's society section. The report is dated 14:14 Korea Standard Time on Nov. 9. Beyond the sponsors and the topics named above, the excerpt does not say who will present or how the sessions will be organized.

Two other articles from the same days show how AI is already reshaping legal work elsewhere. In a Bloomberg Law piece published Nov. 9, Patience Bin, Head of Enterprise AI and Data Governance, Law, and Compliance at Bristol Myers Squibb, wrote that clients expect their outside lawyers to use AI. She said she received an email from outside counsel marked "Privileged and Confidential" that simply reproduced a chatbot's seven-paragraph answer. Her reply was two sentences asking for the lawyer's own advice, and she argued that forwarding unverified AI output shifts the verification work and the risk to the client.

Bin set out several expectations for law firms. Lawyers should validate, understand and own their output, and should add things AI cannot, such as benchmarking insights, relationships with regulators and advice tailored to the company's risk appetite. She cited a 2026 Axiom survey in which 59% of legal leaders said their law firms had raised fees while promoting AI as a value-add, and she suggested well-scoped fixed fees for discrete questions. She also said clients will ask which AI tools firms use, whether client data can be used for model training, how it is protected and what human oversight exists, and will expect firms to sign those commitments in AI riders.

A separate ACG Insights article of Nov. 10 by Drew Sacher and Michael Lamm of Corporate Advisory Solutions argued that private equity's move into law firms through management services organizations (MSOs) is an AI bet. The authors said an MSO runs intake, case management, billing, marketing and referrals, work that AI reaches first, and that AI lets such companies carry more cases per employee. They said deals cluster in high-volume practices such as personal injury, mass tort, family law, immigration and insurance defense. One law firm advising on these transactions reported 35 closed legal MSO deals through September, and in October a 550-lawyer insurance defense firm took private equity money at a reported value near $700 million.

The same article described new state rules on the structure. Illinois signed a law in August, effective immediately, that bars MSOs owned or controlled by private equity or hedge funds from charging fees tied to a firm's revenue or profits. Colorado's law, which took effect in August and is set to expire in 2029, bars MSO fees tied to firm or case performance and reaches conduct outside its borders. California's AB 2305 bars MSOs and other investors from steering litigation decisions starting in 2027. The authors said they expect rules to keep getting more specific rather than shutting the model down, and that lenders should deepen the credit market as more deals close.

stories.Headline: The finance professionals scared of AI might just be using the wrong tools
stories.Summary:
Cornell University has launched an online certificate called AI in Finance, aimed at financial professionals who want to understand how artificial intelligence can be used in their work. The program, offered through eCornell, is a collaboration between the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering and the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business. It debuted in spring 2026 with 37 participants and is taught live online so students can interact directly with faculty and industry practitioners. The idea grew out of Victoria Averbukh's work directing the Cornell Financial Engineering Manhattan program, where practitioners kept raising AI questions. Averbukh said many experienced professionals feel overwhelmed by new terms and models and do not know where to start.

The certificate is intended less as training in a specific software tool than as a way to build enough understanding to make informed choices about AI. Participants do not need deep technical backgrounds, Averbukh said, since the focus is on understanding what AI models do, where they fall short, and why they were not built specifically for finance. The curriculum moves from AI foundations to financial use cases such as investment research, credit risk, fraud detection, compliance, client engagement and operational efficiency. It also covers hallucinations, data security, regulation and governance. The program ends with participants identifying AI opportunities in their organizations and developing strategies to pursue them.

The instructors include Cornell faculty such as Averbukh, Jamol Pender, David Goldberg and Jeffrey Varner, along with faculty from the SC Johnson College of Business. Industry contributors include Andrew Chin of AllianceBernstein, Dhagash Mehta of BlackRock, Kathryn Zhao of OKX, Mohamed Khalifa of J.P. Morgan Global Private Bank and Joseph Sommer of EY. Averbukh said Cornell faculty set the conceptual foundations, and practitioners then show how those ideas play out in financial institutions. Pender, who taught the data and AI portions, said accurate data can still lead to poor decisions if it is outdated or unavailable when needed.

Registration for the spring 2027 offering is now open. Classes will meet live online on Tuesday and Thursday evenings from 7 p.m. to 9 p.m. beginning May 18, 2027, with the final class on Thursday, June 24. Details and enrollment are available on the eCornell website.

stories.Headline: ‘AI-generated’ book purchase case: DMK’s Paranthamen moves Madras High Court seeking registration of FIR by DVAC
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, the Madras High Court's Madurai Bench, comprising Justices G.R. Swaminathan and M.D. Sumathi, directed the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption (DVAC) to immediately register a First Information Report over alleged fraudulent procurement of books for public libraries across Tamil Nadu. The Bench also flagged fake and AI-generated books in public libraries and ordered their removal. It further froze the bank accounts of Agal Vilakku Publication, its proprietor Mohan and others involved in the alleged scam. The order followed a writ petition filed by I. Paranthamen, joint secretary of the DMK Legal Wing, seeking a direction for the FIR.

The Bench ordered the State government to initiate disciplinary action, including suspension, against officials responsible for the fraudulent procurement. It directed authorities to identify the officials involved, remove suspect books and disclose procurement expenditure. The Court observed that compliance with its June 2024 transparency directions could have prevented the scam. The matter is to be heard next on November 11.

The Bench said that crores of rupees had gone out of the public exchequer and that such a crime could not have taken place without the active involvement of government servants. It said that both the BNS provisions and the Prevention of Corruption Act were attracted. The Court also held that AI-generated and plagiarised books could fall within the expression "doubtful taste" under the Tamil Nadu Public Libraries Rules, 1950. It noted that the State Public Prosecutor, R. John Sathyan, had asked for time for the DVAC to complete its detailed enquiry, and when asked, did not dispute that a crime had been committed.

Paranthamen's affidavit, filed through advocate A. Damodaran, said the Periyar Arivulagam library in Coimbatore cost ₹300 crore, including ₹50 crore for procurement of books. The Tamil Nadu government had constituted a 112-member book recommendation committee on November 5, 2025, and purchase orders were issued on February 2, 2026. The library was inaugurated on October 16, 2026, after which a controversy erupted over the quality of the books. Writer Perumal Murugan, a member of the committee, wrote an article on November 6, 2026, saying the library was filled with "AI generated" books carrying fictitious author names.

Paranthamen said he lodged a complaint with the DVAC on November 7, 2026, but the agency had neither registered an FIR nor informed him of a preliminary inquiry. In his complaint, he said Agalvilakku Publications and Phoenix Publications appeared to have supplied books generated using AI tools, with ISBNs obtained in bulk blocks rather than title-wise. The Court recorded that the State government had acknowledged serious irregularities, that IAS officer Jayanthi had been relieved as Director of Public Libraries, and that existing procurement orders had been cancelled. The DVAC had begun a detailed enquiry on November 7, 2026, on a complaint lodged by the School Education department on November 6, 2026.

stories.Headline: New Report: The Impact of AI on Student Safety and Learning Needs Strong Guardrails and Support for Educators
stories.Summary:
A new Texas 2036 report, "In Ctrl of AI in Schools," released on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, concludes that artificial intelligence's effects on Texas students depend on the decisions people make about it. The report finds that benefits appear when tools are built with safeguards, when clear guidance governs their use, and when educators keep control over how AI is used in instruction. It arrives as AI use in Texas schools outpaces the rules governing it. In a fall 2025 survey of school and district leaders by the University of Texas at Austin and the Texas Association of School Administrators, 86% said teachers were using AI and 61% reported student use. Only 29% of those leaders reported a district policy governing student AI use, and just 20% had one for teachers and staff.

The report was released as Texas lawmakers begin filing legislation for the 2027 session, and it is meant to inform the state's efforts to give schools and teachers the resources they need. The report identifies four priorities for K–12 education: establishing statewide guidance, putting student safety first, equipping teachers, and preparing students for an AI-driven future. Its author, Renzo Soto, deputy director of education and workforce policy at Texas 2036, said the early research does not show AI is simply good or bad for students. The research instead shows how much it matters that school leaders and teachers control how AI appears in classrooms.

The report analyzes mixed evidence, noting that some studies find real gains, others find real harms, and many find both. According to the report, the difference often depends on how tools are designed, how teachers guide their use, and whether students are equipped to think critically and independently. Texas passed three laws in 2025 establishing a foundation for responsible AI governance, including requirements affecting public school districts. Those broad standards, however, have not yet been translated into consistent, classroom-specific guidance.

The report finds that 42 states have issued some form of statewide AI guidance or model policies for schools, while Texas is among the eight that have not. The report also draws on Texas 2036's 10th Texas Voter Poll, in which nearly 85% of voters said protecting student data and privacy is extremely or very important if schools use AI. More than three-quarters prioritize safety and quality standards for AI tools, and 71% say teaching students to use AI responsibly and ethically is important. Mary Lynn Pruneda, director of education and workforce policy at Texas 2036, said parents should be able to trust that classroom technology is safe, protects privacy, and actually helps students learn.

The report does not call for putting AI in every classroom or banning it entirely. Soto said AI has not changed what works for students, namely a strong teacher who supports them and helps them build a solid academic foundation. The report is the first installment of Texas 2036's research on artificial intelligence in K–12 education. A second report will analyze policies, guidance, and resources from other states to help Texas build a statewide model policy that prioritizes student safety and learning.

stories.Headline: NetApp CEO advocates harmonised global AI regulations
stories.Summary:
NetApp chief executive George Kurian has called for AI regulations to be harmonised across the world, according to a report by PTI published in November 2026. He said that differing regulatory frameworks force businesses to comply with several sets of rules at once, which makes operations more complicated. Kurian pointed to requirements such as the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) and the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) as examples of rules companies must already meet. He made these remarks in an interview with PTI reported on November 9, 2026, and the coverage carried the same message on November 10. The articles do not say how any policymaker has responded to the call.

Kurian urged policymakers to agree on a shared approach to AI, much as the world did for cyber resilience standards, which he said let the industry deliver more capability. He suggested that data sovereignty should be part of that common approach so that businesses can build and deploy AI more effectively. He observed that Europe has the strictest sovereignty requirements, including mandates for local AI models. Other countries, limited by cost and resources, are increasingly turning to open-source and open-weight models to keep AI services affordable. These points are presented as his views rather than as formal proposals, and no specific legal changes are described.

Kurian, who has led NetApp as CEO since 2015, said India is the company's fastest-growing market in Asia. He named the BFSI, manufacturing, IT services and public sectors, including central and state government departments, as key drivers of that growth. He also described NetApp's Bengaluru centre as its largest, with about 4,000 engineers, and said it handles most of the company's global research and development. He further stated that NetApp is the number one player in India's all-flash storage market.

He said the company is giving its local teams more scope to expand through investments and partnerships. The articles frame these remarks as part of a wider industry debate about how AI should be governed across borders, but they do not report any pending international agreement or deadline. Kurian's comments were made in an interview and are not described as a formal submission to any government body. The coverage does not indicate what steps, if any, will follow from his call for harmonisation.

stories.Headline: U.S. Sen. Warren signals sweeping probes of Big Tech and Wall Street; China AI chips also face regulation
stories.Summary:
U.S. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the midterm elections held on the 3rd, and they are expected to open wide investigations into Big Tech companies, Wall Street financial firms and the Trump family's cryptocurrency businesses. Sen. Elizabeth Warren is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee when the new Congress convenes next January. According to CNBC on the 9th, local time, she plans to put easing the cost-of-living burden, tightening limits on advanced AI chip exports to China and stronger oversight of prediction markets among the committee's main priorities. The Democrats will take over key committees in both chambers from January, which lets them set each panel's agenda and use subpoena power to demand sworn testimony from senior officials and corporate executives. The Banking Committee covers monetary policy, banking and export controls, so Warren's role is expected to raise congressional pressure across both the financial and technology industries.

Warren intends to tighten limits on advanced AI chips sold to China and to build a new regulatory framework for the AI industry in the United States. That has raised the prospect that chipmakers such as NVIDIA, which want to grow in the Chinese market, could face more regulatory pressure. She has called the lack of oversight of prediction markets a "Wild West" situation and plans to push for tighter rules. Earlier, she joined Republican Sen. John Curtis in sending letters to Kalshi and Polymarket asking about safeguards and oversight for election-related prediction markets. The Trump family's crypto ventures are also expected to be examined, and there is speculation that subpoenas could be used to look into possible conflicts of interest between the family and private companies.

An aide to Warren told CNBC that she is preparing an aggressive oversight and investigation plan. She has asked Big Tech CEOs, Trump administration officials and Wall Street executives to preserve relevant documents. She has also urged people tied to the Trump family's crypto businesses to get ready for congressional investigations. The reporting presents all of this as Warren's plan, and it does not describe any investigation as having formally begun.

A Tech Policy Press essay by Alice Marwick, published on the 9th, offers context on why voters may support such action. It says the Democratic sweep was a referendum on many issues, including the cost of living, and that curbing the power of the tech industry was high on voters' minds. Several winning candidates ran against Big Tech, including Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and South Carolina Senator-elect Annie Andrews, who both backed a data center moratorium, and ballot initiatives to curb data centers passed widely. The essay argues that tech regulation should reach beyond AI, and it lists ideas such as a federal privacy law, easier subscription cancellation, disclosure of bot activity in advertising, a ban on crypto ATMs and liability for scam ads on social platforms. It also notes that President Donald Trump has promised to veto Democratic legislation, so many of these ideas may be more practical at the state level.

stories.Headline: Macron wants AI banned wherever it threatens children
stories.Summary:
On Monday, November 9, 2026, French President Emmanuel Macron said that artificial intelligence should be banned wherever it poses a risk to the mental health of children. He made the remarks in an interview with the French daily Les Echos, on the eve of the adoption of a charter on the subject at the Paris Peace Forum. Macron, who is also pushing for a ban on certain social networks for under-15s in France, said that if certain uses of AI put children at risk, those uses must be prohibited. He argued that AI should not be an unregulated space and said it should be barred when it threatens children's mental health or their brain.

The charter is meant to protect citizens from the threats posed by AI and to inform national and European legislative debates. Under it, research labs would commit to measures including independent evaluations of generative AI systems placed on the market and access to their models' data. Macron said companies would accept a pre-audit and pre-certification, with models reviewed before they are placed in children's hands. A committee of experts was due to give him recommendations on protection against AI on November 10, an area the articles describe as less explored than the impact of social networks. The charter is expected to bring together US firms OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Macron's office.

Macron framed the initiative as a call on Europe to lead, saying the EU would advance its own regulation and push Americans, Canadians and others to follow. He said the aim was a framework covering three categories of danger: children, democratic security, and major national security issues. On the same occasion, he held a videoconference with around 50 heads of state and government, international organisations, companies, researchers and laboratories to discuss AI risks to collective security. The British, Canadian, Norwegian, Dutch and Japanese prime ministers took part, as did the chief executives of OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral and Microsoft. Macron wrote on X that the diagnosis was shared and that action must be taken together.

The announcement comes as regional approaches to AI regulation diverge sharply among the United States, the European Union and China. The EU was due to hold its first summit of national AI ministers in Dublin on the Friday after, under the Irish rotating presidency, to help governments agree a new path for regulating AI and revive the bloc's sluggish economic growth. Leaders were also to review safeguards such as the AI Act. The articles do not say what outcome the Dublin meeting produced.

stories.Headline: New York's AI Safety Law Hits OpenAI, Anthropic Today
stories.Summary:
New York's RAISE Act, which the state calls its safety and transparency law for frontier AI, takes effect as regulators open a registration portal for large AI developers. The state opened the portal on Tuesday, and companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI must register by January 1, 2027. The law, which kicks in at the start of the year, targets large frontier developers with more than $500 million in annual revenue. Those companies must publish safety frameworks on their websites, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, and issue public model transparency reports.

The newly formed Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust, known as DIGIT, will implement the law and oversee the large frontier labs. Penalties can reach $1 million for a single violation and $3 million for later violations. The state can also bring enforcement actions against companies that fail to register, though a spokesperson declined to give specifics. Governor Kathy Hochul also launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at SUNY's Binghamton University on Tuesday.

Hochul, who backed the law, said during a press briefing that tech leaders argue AI is inevitable and that any collateral damage is worth winning the race. The new center will independently evaluate the safety, security, and operation of advanced AI systems and will work with DIGIT to review companies' safety frameworks. Hochul first announced the center in January with $55 million in donations and capital. She described the state's goal as building a national model for AI regulation that puts communities above corporations.

The RAISE Act is not New York's only AI safety law. Last year the state began enforcing a law requiring AI companion operators to tell users they are talking to a bot and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation and self-harm. In October, Hochul signed a separate chatbot safety law for minors, which takes effect June 1, 2027. Other states have passed similar measures, including California's SB 53, which took effect in January and requires safety frameworks, whistleblower protections, and incident reports within 15 days. Illinois' SB 315 takes effect at the start of 2027 and adds independent safety compliance audits.

stories.Headline: Trust Stamp launches biometric approval tool for AI-agent transactions
stories.Summary:
Trust Stamp, a company listed on the Nasdaq and the Irish Stock Exchange under the tickers IDAI and AIID, announced on November 10, 2026 a new product called Knowing Consent. The product confirms that bank customers knowingly approve each transaction that an AI agent starts on their behalf. The company said the tool uses proprietary processes protected by issued patents, along with a newer process that is being patented and is ready for immediate use. Both the AI agent and the financial institution can start the approval flow.

Customers complete biometric registration on first use to create a personal identity token. For later requests, they can be asked to take a secure selfie through SMS, email, push notification or the relevant software application. Proof-of-life and anti-spoofing checks, along with optional device verification and other authentication methods, confirm the account owner is present when approval is requested. In an integrated setup, the approval screen shows the specific action and its details before the customer completes live verification, so the approval is tied to that one request. The company said the step can be added in a matter of days, either through its Orchestration Layer or a single API call, and that it works within an institution's existing access and transaction policies without major changes to its authentication flow.

Chief executive Gareth N. Genner said the company has more than one hundred financial institutions integrated with its Orchestration Layer and that the approach gives banks a live, customer-centered approval step for agent-initiated activity. The company's announcement also cited a NIST article warning that credential sharing creates accountability gaps, reports that some major U.S. banks are blocking certain third-party agents from customer accounts, and comments from JPMorgan Chase and RBC about agent safeguards and stored passwords. Trust Stamp argued that its human-centered processes already exist and are effective, in contrast to proposals focused on agent identity. The announcement did not give pricing, customer names or an independent assessment of the product's performance.

stories.Headline: AI Debt Under Pressure: Credit Spreads Widen as Democrats Target AI Regulation - News and Statistics
stories.Summary:
Investors in the bond market have grown more cautious about debt tied to the artificial intelligence boom, Reuters reported, as worries mount that a Democrat-controlled Congress will try to slow AI investment and data center growth. During last Thursday's stock-market selloff, US high-yield credit spreads reached 348 basis points, according to ICE BofA US Corporate Index data, the widest level since May 2025. By Friday those spreads had tightened to 342 basis points. Larry Holzenthaler, a senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds in New York, said the market was clearly nervous and that further swings in high yield and loans would not be a surprise. Investment-grade spreads stood at 93 basis points last Thursday, compared with 91 the session before.

Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January and intend to introduce a large batch of legislation aimed at AI systems and data center development. Republican President Donald Trump has repeatedly rejected calls for mandatory AI rules. After his party suffered a historic midterm defeat over the weekend, however, he indicated a willingness to consider safeguards. Analysts said that a broader rethink of AI-related risk could widen credit spreads across both high-yield and investment-grade debt. Ali Hassan, a portfolio manager at Thornburg Investment Management, said investor appetite has grown more careful and selective.

Political and regulatory scrutiny is driving a reassessment of credits across the AI supply chain, from developers to contractors to suppliers, Hassan said. Data center bonds, heavily represented in the BB and single-B tiers of the junk bond market, have faced renewed strain in recent weeks, especially amid the technology selloff. Analysts said single-B spreads widened 35 basis points to 367 basis points, driving the high-yield deterioration and reaching their highest levels since March. Peter Yanulis, a multi-asset portfolio manager at Loomis Sayles, said any slowdown in the AI buildout would produce a second-order effect on power producers, electrical contractors, equipment makers and data center developers.

The pressure is visible in individual bonds. On November 5, Galaxy Helios Data Center bonds dropped to 89.25 cents on the dollar, pushing yields to 13% from the 9.875% offered when Galaxy Digital's wholly owned unit sold the B+ rated debt in late July. The bonds' price decline and the rise in yield show how quickly investors have repriced debt linked to data center construction. Analysts have pointed to the broader technology selloff as the backdrop for the strain. Solid corporate fundamentals remain supportive, according to analysts and portfolio managers, even as the risk outlook shifts.

stories.Headline: OpenAI's Q3 results and Nvidia's scandal impact on the AI ecosystem
stories.Summary:
OpenAI reported third-quarter revenue of $10 billion, up from about $6.7 billion in the prior quarter, according to a Yahoo Finance interview published November 10, 2026. The network's host, Deidre Bosa, said that growth was nearly 50 percent and almost triple the 18 percent growth OpenAI posted in the second quarter. Anthropic, which the host said is about to go public, reported $17 billion in third-quarter revenue, with 47 percent growth after 144 percent in the prior quarter. Bosa said the two companies' quarterly growth rates were now close to each other for the first time this year. She added that the exact size of Anthropic's lead was hard to pin down because the companies account for cloud sales differently.

Vinod Khosla, a founder of Khosla Ventures and one of OpenAI's earliest backers, was interviewed on the show about the comparison. He said his firm invested in OpenAI at a $1 billion valuation and chose not to invest in Anthropic. Khosla argued that quarter-over-quarter results matter less than the trajectory over the coming years. He said OpenAI invests heavily in research and compute, which he described as giving it a cost advantage. He also argued that token usage, rather than prices or revenue, is the better measure of real demand and of whether a bubble exists.

Bosa pressed Khosla on the rise of open-source models, which she said are taking a growing share of developer usage. Khosla responded that open-source models are not cheaper to run, because Nvidia's chips carry a premium of about five times the cost. He said OpenAI's own silicon would lower its per-token costs as it comes online over the next few years, and that Google's TPUs have begun competing with Nvidia. Bosa noted that companies such as Fireworks and Base 10 help serve open models efficiently, and asked whether chips developed for in-house use were lowering compute costs for others. Khosla said they were not, because Nvidia and Google both price their chips at a premium while a silicon shortage lasts for a couple of years.

The interview also included Bosa's separate conversation with OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar about the company's push into enterprise AI, its "dots" rollout, and the global AI model race. The episode was introduced as Deirdre Bosa Live, which airs daily at 4 p.m. The same broadcast flagged a hot consumer price index report that day that pushed markets lower, and said Nvidia and Microsoft were among the day's biggest stocks. The broadcast also said poor results from neo clouds were expected shortly. The articles do not say what follows OpenAI's results or Anthropic's public listing.

A U.S. election has raised questions about the company's data center plans. The robotics deal, which would have added a major industrial automation business, is now blocked by Beijing. Investors are watching closely to see whether the artificial intelligence strategy can still deliver the growth the company has promised.

The articles identify SoftBank Group as the company responsible for the strategy and the reported loss, with its reporting covered by Nikkei Asia's Tsubasa Suruga. The reporting describes the company's position as one of increasing uncertainty rather than quoting specific executive statements on the outlook. The articles also note that investors are focused on whether the AI growth strategy succeeds. Beyond the blocked robotics deal and the data center questions, the articles do not give further detail on the company's response.

The broader context is that SoftBank has tied much of its recent expansion to artificial intelligence, through stakes in OpenAI and related infrastructure projects. stories.Headline: Sh13bn initiative targets global healthcare gaps through AI
stories.Summary:
The Sh13 billion initiative, announced by Amazon Web Services (AWS) and reported by The Standard, will provide $100 million in AI and cloud computing resources over five years. The AWS Health Impact Initiative will support healthcare nonprofits, government agencies, research institutions and technology companies working on gaps in healthcare access and medical research. The programme will supply cloud infrastructure, artificial intelligence tools and agentic services for projects ranging from early-stage prototypes to systems ready for large-scale deployment. It comes as healthcare systems face staff shortages, rising demand and unequal access to treatment, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.

The World Health Organisation estimates that the global shortage of health workers could reach 11 million by 2030. Africa alone faces a projected shortfall of about 5.85 million health workers by the end of the decade. Artificial intelligence could help providers automate administrative tasks, support diagnostic processes and analyse medical data. Its effectiveness, however, will depend on reliable infrastructure, quality data and trained personnel. Dr Rowland Illing, AWS chief medical officer and director of healthcare and life sciences, said that these technologies too often do not reach the communities that need them most unless organisations know how to access and deploy them.

The initiative will focus on three areas: expanding access to healthcare services, advancing research in women's and children's health, and improving access to nutritious food. Under the healthcare access category, AWS will support projects involving community healthcare, outpatient services, hospitals, diagnostic testing and medical research, with attention to rural communities and low- and middle-income countries. AWS reported that 92 per cent of previous awardees focused on improving access to or the quality of health services, while 53 per cent incorporated artificial intelligence or machine learning. The women's and children's health category addresses research gaps, with AWS citing estimates that only five per cent of healthcare research funding goes to women's health. AWS also noted that malnutrition among pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers and adolescent girls rose 25 per cent since 2020 in the 12 countries hardest hit by the global food and nutrition crisis.

Eligible organisations can apply through their AWS account teams or a public application portal. Successful applicants will receive cloud credits based on estimated project requirements, with awards of up to $10,000 (Sh1.3 million) available for initial support. The credits will generally remain valid for 12 months, although extensions can stretch the period to a maximum of 24 months. Applicants must explain the healthcare problem they intend to address, outline their proposed solution and estimate the number of people expected to benefit. AWS said applications would be reviewed weekly.

In Kenya, several organisations are already using digital and cloud-based systems for medical services and research. AAR Healthcare is deploying a health management information system across rural hospitals, while Cogni-X Kenya is developing MOYO, an AI-powered wellbeing platform. Savannah Informatics operates an electronic medical records platform serving about 350 active users. TibERbu Healthnet is extending hospital and pharmacy systems across more than 200 facilities that the company says serve 30.4 million Kenyans. The growing use of artificial intelligence in healthcare also raises concerns about patient data privacy, clinical reliability, regulatory oversight and the cost of maintaining digital systems after initial funding ends.

stories.Headline: Nvidia spy scandal revives push to write China chip export limits into the defense bill
stories.Summary:
Reports that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman U.S. officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence have given Washington's chip hawks a fresh argument, and they are pressing it in this year's defense bill. Lawmakers and advocates told Reuters that Congress is now more likely to pass limits on China's access to AI chips, with three measures possibly headed into the National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal 2027. On Monday, Nov. 9, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he strongly supports chip restrictions in the final bill, after a classified briefing for congressional leaders. The woman is Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's big Southeast Asian customers, and she has not been charged. Huang has admitted being unfaithful to his wife, and Nvidia's board has opened an investigation into whether he was targeted by foreign intelligence.

The three measures already sit in the Senate's manager's package for the defense bill, after the House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced all of them earlier this year. The AI Overwatch Act would treat AI chip sales to adversary nations much like arms sales: Commerce would have to notify two congressional committees at least 30 days before licensing chips such as Nvidia's H200, and Congress could block a sale by joint resolution. Blackwell-class chips would face mandatory denial, and the House text would end existing licenses for covered exports. The Chip Security Act would require companies to track their chips to fight smuggling, and its House version passed committee unanimously.

The MATCH Act would push U.S. allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment sales to China. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks said in a joint statement that Huang's relationship with a suspected spy makes the national security concerns even more urgent, and they urged Congress to pass the AI Overwatch Act. Nvidia declined to comment and says it follows export laws, while its board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. China's foreign ministry calls the spying allegation unsubstantiated.

The White House did not comment on the bills, though The Information reported that its officials shared feedback with congressional staff in late October. President Donald Trump has backed Huang, calling him an amazing guy and saying Huang told him he had no idea the woman was a spy. Congress has been here before: a similar Senate provision, the GAIN AI Act, was dropped from last year's final defense bill after lobbying by the White House and Nvidia. A former congressional staffer told Reuters that Nvidia is the biggest opponent of the Chip Security and AI Overwatch Acts, and an industry group that counts Nvidia as a member also opposes them.

If the provisions are dropped again, they would return to a Congress run by Democrats from Jan. 3, with chip hawks such as Chris Coons and Warren in line for key chairmanships. Nvidia's licensed H200 sales to China were under 1% of data center revenue last quarter, so a congressional veto would mainly cap future sales. Huang was asked to give House Republican chairmen a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18, and Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Nov. 17. Nvidia shares fell about 5% on Monday, more than 20% below their peak a month earlier.

stories.Headline: Fed’s Bowman Warns of Stock Correction If AI Bets Don’t Pan Out
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Governor Michelle Bowman warned in written remarks delivered Tuesday local time at the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington that U.S. stock valuations could face a sharp correction if returns on artificial intelligence investments fail to meet expectations. She also singled out a sharp rise in private long-term interest rates as another potential trigger. The same day, the U.S. Department of Labor reported that October core consumer price index rose 0.3% month-over-month, above market expectations. Bowman said weakening stock prices could erode consumer spending, and rising borrowing costs would squeeze the housing market and small-business investment. She said that inflation persistence has exceeded her earlier assessment and that there is still work to do to bring inflation back to the 2% target.

Bowman said that persistent inflation pressure and tightening labor market conditions left her open to another rate hike at the December meeting. The Fed held rates steady at its October 27-28 meeting after a 25-basis-point hike in September, the first since 2023. Bowman said she supported holding rates steady last month to give policymakers time to assess the transmission of the September hike to the real economy. Governor Christopher Waller argued in a London speech that December should seriously consider a 50-basis-point hike if inflation data remain hot. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who holds a vote this year, said in Houston that the Federal Open Market Committee needs at least two more 25-basis-point hikes.

Bowman also expressed concern about AI-related debt, which she said is expected to exceed $800 billion this year in corporate bonds, private credit and project finance. She highlighted how large technology companies and hyperscalers use their strong credit ratings to enable smaller, higher-risk companies to pledge assets as collateral for data centers and accelerated computing equipment. She noted that cloud giants and chip designers have made equity investments in smaller companies that buy their products, creating what she called the appearance of revolving financing. She warned that once markets come under pressure, this web of capital linkages could amplify risk transmission.

The officials' hawkish remarks and hot inflation data pushed U.S. Treasury yields higher across the board. The 2-year yield surged 19 basis points to 4.75% on the day, its largest single-day increase since the reciprocal tariff measures in April 2025 triggered global market turmoil. Federal funds rate futures showed investors betting on a 25-basis-point hike in December and another in January, while Christopher Hodge of Natixis said the data are not strong enough to justify a 50-basis-point hike. Christopher Phelan, chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers, publicly opposed the aggressive approach, saying there is no reason to raise rates by 50 basis points in December. Before the December meeting, Fed officials will still receive one employment report and full inflation data.

stories.Headline: Immaculate Kassait Ends Six‑Year Term as Kenya's First Data Protection Commissioner
stories.Summary:
Kenya's Data Protection Commissioner Immaculate Kassait has finished her six-year term, which began in November 2020, and President William Ruto has nominated Lydia Sitienei Chelagat to succeed her. The nomination was announced on Monday 9 November 2026 after advice from the Public Service Commission, and it now awaits approval from the National Assembly before Chelagat can take office. Chelagat most recently served as Corporation Secretary and Director of Legal Services at the Communications Authority of Kenya. Her appointment matters for companies, including foreign tech firms, that handle the personal data of people in Kenya, since the commissioner oversees that work. Kassait led the office through its early growth, when it had fewer than ten staff housed in Communications Authority offices and now has its own headquarters and regional desks.

Registered data handlers rose from 7,223 in 2024 to more than 15,000 by early 2026, spanning finance, telecoms, health, education and digital commerce. The office handled 9,061 complaints by early 2026 and issued 195 determinations, 100 enforcement notices and 12 penalty notices during the 2025 to 2029 strategic period. Financial penalties are capped at KSh 5 million or 1 percent of an organisation's prior turnover, a limit Kassait said should be revisited along with stronger cross-border enforcement. The office's most prominent case involved the Worldcoin biometric identity project, where a court ordered the deletion of iris-scan data in May 2025 and an audit in January 2026 confirmed compliance. In September 2025 the office also received four awards at the Global Privacy Assembly in Seoul for leadership, public education, dispute resolution and innovation.

Kassait said data protection has become a public conversation in Kenya but warned that rapid digitalisation, AI-driven decision-making and biometric technologies will keep posing regulatory challenges. Chelagat, if approved, will inherit an institution with an established registration framework and a growing enforcement record. Her main task will be adapting privacy safeguards to emerging AI and digital-identity risks. The articles do not say when the National Assembly will vote on the nomination.

stories.Headline: Missoula AI company files lawsuit challenging city's data center restrictions
stories.Summary:
A Missoula artificial intelligence company, CubCloud AI, has sued the City of Missoula over zoning rules that restrict data centers. The lawsuit was filed in Missoula County District Court, according to the reporting, and the company's complaint says the city's ordinance is unconstitutionally vague. The Missoulian and Montana Free Press both reported the filing on November 9, 2026. The articles describe the lawsuit as the company's challenge to the city's new local zoning rules. The company says it has 16 employees and has put money into research and development that it says would be wasted under the restrictions.

Its leaders told reporters they want the city to allow the project to proceed while the case is decided. The company is also seeking to build a new 4,200-square-foot research facility in the area, a plan the Missoulian says is tied to the changes the city has proposed. The city has said it intends to tweak its data center regulations, but the articles say the city will not comment on pending litigation. The city's rules were adopted after a city council discussion, and the company argues that the restrictions amount to a de facto ban on data centers in parts of town. Its representatives say the city was working toward a new proposal that would give them a path to build.

Officials with the city defended the ordinance as a legitimate exercise of local land-use authority. The Goldwater Institute, a Phoenix-based free-market think tank, is representing the company, the articles report, and says the restrictions go beyond what the law allows. The case comes as Missoula weighs how to handle data centers and other high-energy uses, a question many Montana communities are also debating. The articles do not say when a hearing is scheduled or when the court might rule. The city has indicated it will revise its regulations, and the outcome of the lawsuit could determine whether CubCloud AI can move ahead with its planned facility.

stories.Headline: GeniosAI, which develops AI software for financial analysis and modeling, raised $19.1M across seed and Series A; FactSet led the Series A (Ryan Lawler/Axios)
stories.Summary:
GeniosAI, a financial intelligence startup that builds AI software for financial analysis and modeling, has raised $19.1 million across seed and Series A funding, according to CEO PD Singh, who spoke to Axios Pro exclusively. The announcement came on November 9, 2026, and it positions the company as a provider of AI that shows the reasoning behind its outputs. The funding comes from FactSet, Zoom and General Catalyst, with FactSet leading the Series A and acting as a strategic partner. The company says finance teams need to check the numbers and assumptions behind AI analysis before acting on it.

The company is building products for corporate finance teams, investment professionals and the office of the CFO. Its core pitch is that financial institutions need to keep the assumptions, calculations and review decisions behind each analysis, so staff can verify results, challenge conclusions and build on earlier work. Under its partnership with FactSet, geniosAI will bring FactSet's financial data into its platform. Zoom will support the settings where financial decisions get made, such as internal finance reviews and earnings calls.

The company said finance and investment teams at Fortune 500 banks and technology companies already use the technology to prepare for earnings and compare results with analyst expectations. FactSet's chief executive, Sanoke Viswanathan, said that the value of data depends on how well it can be acted upon, and that pairing FactSet's data with geniosAI's traceable analysis could help financial teams decide with more confidence and speed. The timing reflects a wider shift in enterprise finance, where companies are adding technology and must work out how to connect systems, keep controls in place and decide which capabilities to own. For CFOs, the expense of a modern finance stack often lies less in software licenses than in the effort needed to keep applications, data and processes linked.

AI adoption is also rising in financial services back offices, according to a PYMNTS Intelligence study. That study found that at least half of surveyed financial services firms used AI in 27 of 75 business tasks examined, with revenue recognition leading at 65 percent and credit risk assessment and sales forecasting at 60 percent each. Fragmented or poor-quality data, however, remained the largest obstacle to wider deployment for 30 percent of financial services leaders. Taken together, the reporting suggests that geniosAI is betting banks and investment firms will pay for AI that can explain its results, not just produce them.

stories.Headline: 'No permanent friends': Nvidia’s two-track play may reduce Korean chipmakers to subcontractors
stories.Summary:
Nvidia is keeping Korea's memory chipmakers close while reportedly pushing Taiwan's TSMC into the memory business, a two-track approach that experts warn could leave Samsung Electronics and SK hynix as mere subcontractors. The Taiwanese chipmaker has begun drawing up plans to produce 3-D DRAM at Nvidia's request, according to The Information, which reported on a Friday in November 2026. TSMC is weighing whether to build a new plant or convert an existing one. Unlike conventional DRAM, 3-D DRAM stacks memory cells vertically to pack more capacity into the same footprint. TSMC said it remains focused on contract chipmaking, its core business, and that its founding principle is that it "never competes with its customers."

Samsung and SK hynix supply the high bandwidth memory that powers Nvidia's AI chips, and SK hynix relies on TSMC to make the base dies for its HBM4 chips. A base die sits at the bottom of an HBM stack and links the memory layers above it to the processor. Nvidia unveiled its own custom HBM, NVHBM, in August, moving the memory controller into the base die. Nvidia reportedly asked Samsung, SK hynix and Micron last month to have their NVHBM base dies made on TSMC's 3-nanometer process. Industry sources worry that control over how memory is designed and made could tilt toward Nvidia and TSMC.

Nvidia's push is driven by a memory shortage, as HBM supply has failed to keep up with AI demand and prices keep climbing. Processors now compute faster than memory can feed them data, a problem the industry calls the memory wall. Designing memory structures and interfaces would let Nvidia boost performance and rely less on any single supplier. TSMC needs HBM to finish Nvidia's GPUs, so more say over memory production could cut GPU shipment delays and win it a bigger share of the AI chip supply chain. Kwon Seok-joon, a chemical engineering professor at Sungkyunkwan University, sees four ways TSMC could claim the most lucrative parts of the memory business without building a DRAM plant.

Kwon said Korean companies need to become co-designers of the base die and secure mass production capability in hybrid bonding before TSMC does, and should diversify their custom HBM customers to Google, AMD, Meta and others. Hybrid bonding, which joins chips directly without the tiny solder bumps used today, is expected to become essential once HBM stacks reach around 20 layers. If TSMC takes over that step, Nvidia and TSMC could control the design and manufacturing of the finished product even as SK hynix keeps supplying DRAM core dies. A former SK hynix executive warned that if the two Korean giants fail to lead in base dies, bonding and heat treatment, they could be reduced to subcontractors supplying only DRAM cells. Nvidia is also courting Korean partners beyond memory, having signed an MOU with SK Telecom and Rebellions at Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026 at Coex in Gangnam District on Monday.

The story sits within a broader pattern of AI companies drawing in capital ahead of public offerings, and the article's framing suggests that investors and suppliers are positioning for those listings. stories.Headline: Mashup Ventures Raises 25.9 Billion Won Fund for AI, Deep Tech Startups
stories.Summary:
Seoul-based early-stage investor Mashup Ventures said on November 11, 2026, that it has closed a 25.9 billion won ($17.6 million) fund, called Mashup First Believer Venture Investment Fund No. 5, without government policy money. The firm will use the fund to back promising startups in artificial intelligence and deep tech. Partners at Mashup Ventures are its largest contributors, and the fund also drew money from successful founders, startups, information technology and manufacturing companies, and financial institutions. The fund has a 10-year life and will focus on pre-seed companies, whose founders are still preparing to launch, and seed-stage companies, which are raising their first outside capital.

Its main investment areas are physical AI, vertical AI tailored to specific industries, energy and aerospace. The firm plans to expand its deep tech investments under Chief Investment Officer Park Eun-woo, who previously led global expansion as chief strategy officer at autonomous drone company Nearthlab. Mashup Ventures was led by Lee Taek-kyung, a co-founder of Daum, and has invested in about 220 companies since 2013, being the first institutional investor in 87% of them. Its portfolio includes Bucketplace, operator of the interior design platform Ohou, as well as MyRealTrip, Remember & Company, Wrtn Technologies and ScatterLab. More recently it has widened its scope to space, advanced materials and energy, with investments in O&B Space, NanoForge AI and Biologen.

The firm has also added specialists to strengthen its capacity to invest in technology startups. This year it recruited AI partner Yang Sung-min, a former engineer who has founded and sold companies, and venture partner Lee Sang-won, a co-founder of Silicon Valley deep tech company Quixo. The two will review the technology of early-stage portfolio companies and support product development and overseas expansion. Lee said the firm believed in founders who jumped into an uncertain market even as the paradigm shifted from the internet to mobile. He added that with AI now moving into robotics, energy and space, the firm intends to be the first investor to back founders before their technology is proven.

Separately, a Proximal Ventures fund was reported on November 10, 2026, by TechCrunch. Its founder, Sahir Raoof, a former SignalFire investor, raised $27.5 million for his first solo VC fund. The firm is betting that AI can automate the tools, infrastructure and services that support drug development, which pharmaceutical companies have historically outsourced. Proximal plans to write checks from $500,000 to $1.5 million to pre-seed and seed-stage startups, and has already backed seven startups.

stories.Headline: Bangkok Post - Global Medical AI Summit 2026 draws more than 400 executives from 263 organisations
stories.Summary:
The Global Medical AI Summit 2026 (GMAI 2026) was held on October 30 at the Grand Hall of True Digital Park in Bangkok, drawing more than 400 senior executives from 263 organisations. Attendees included medical professionals, investors, technology entrepreneurs and experts from countries such as the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines. The event also featured 25 exhibition booths showing innovations from startups and technology companies. The Artificial Intelligence Entrepreneur Association of Thailand organised the summit with the Technology and Innovation in Life Sciences National Agency (Public Organization). Its theme centred on making Thailand a gateway for medical AI innovation.

Prof Dr Yodchanan Wongsawat, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation, gave the opening keynote. He described a plan for Thailand to move beyond its role as a healthcare service hub and become a regional centre for medical AI research and innovation. He pointed to the country's strengths in tropical medicine, cancer, stroke and health data as a base for AI-enabled healthcare. He also called for technology transfer, shared research infrastructure, and incubation and accelerator programmes to strengthen the ecosystem. The summit also formally announced the Medical AI Network (MAIN), which is intended to link government agencies, universities, hospitals and private companies.

Organisations named in connection with the network included the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation, TILSNA, AIEAT, the Artificial Intelligence Association of Thailand, Thammasat University, Khon Kaen University and the Digital Council of Thailand. The network aims to support collaboration from research and technology development through clinical testing to commercial use in Thailand and overseas. International speakers included Dr Supachai Parchariyanon of SeaX Ventures and RISE, who discussed Thailand as a base for testing medical AI for global markets. Dr Ashraf Zarkan of BioTryp Therapeutics, based in the United Kingdom, spoke about AI in drug discovery. Five panel discussions and a Medical AI Showcase of seven companies, along with a pitching competition, rounded out the programme.
