stories.Headline: Big Walk Used AI In 'The Final Stretch' Of Development, Kicking Off Intense Awards Debate
stories.Summary:
Big Walk, a video game developed by Australian indie studio House House, has become the center of debate after the studio disclosed that it used AI tools during the game's development. The disclosure came shortly after a group of jurors for the 2027 Independent Games Festival said they would not vote for any game built with generative AI. Aftermath reported the story on November 10, 2026, and GamesIndustry.biz followed with a similar account the same day. The jurors had noted a significant rise in submitted games using generative AI tools and called on the festival to adopt a strict policy for future years. House House says its use of large language models was limited and came late in production, during what it called the final stretch of development.

The studio used chatbots to research difficult technical problems and bugs, and in some cases copied snippets of responses as a starting point for game code. It estimates that well under 0.1 percent of Big Walk's code was affected by this usage, and says generative AI was not used in any other part of the game's creation. The studio described one example in which a chatbot suggested a fix for a shadow-culling problem in Unity's rendering pipeline, which the team then heavily modified, amounting to about 10 lines of code. The problem had caused the game to run 50 percent slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset.

House House has taken responsibility for not disclosing this earlier, and it stated that it did not mention the usage on Steam because the platform does not ask for disclosure of code or chatbot use. The studio said it wrote a version of the disclosure for its IGF submission, which was a suggested part of the process, and posted it publicly because the matter had become one of public interest. It also said that it does not endorse AI tools, however minimal their use, and voiced concern that voluntary disclosures could help normalize the technology or make it seem inevitable. The developer expressed support for those trying to limit generative AI's harm and apologized that its usage may not meet their standards.

It admitted that Big Walk was made without an internal AI usage policy, which it considers a failure, and said it will work to create a more comprehensive policy. The disagreement reflects a wider argument within the games industry about where the line should be drawn for AI in development, and the IGF jurors' stance has put pressure on the festival to define its rules. The IGF submissions closed on September 13, and finalists are scheduled to be announced in January 2027. The articles do not say whether Big Walk will remain eligible for the festival or how the IGF will respond to the jurors' call for a stricter policy.

stories.Headline: U.S. and China should stay clear-eyed on AI cooperation and competition, says Scott Bessent
stories.Summary:
Scott Bessent, the U.S. Treasury Secretary, said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, in prepared remarks to the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations in New York, that the United States and China should harbor no illusions about their differences on artificial intelligence. He said the two countries must cooperate to mitigate the technology's risks while competing for AI supremacy. Bessent, who will travel to China next week, said he wanted to build a constructive relationship on the basis of balance and reciprocity. He described the meeting in Shenzhen, to be held on the sidelines of the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders summit, as the place where a new bilateral dialogue on "superintelligence" would advance. The dialogue is meant to guard against shared risks and prevent misunderstanding between the two systems.

Bessent said the two sides expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment in command of the technology. The two sides had agreed to establish a direct channel for alerting each other to serious incidents. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed on this AI alert system during their previous meeting at the White House in September. At that time, Trump said he was reluctant to add new guardrails because he wanted to preserve U.S. leadership. Bessent said that as superintelligence advances, the need for new areas of risk management will grow as well.

Bessent's remarks did not mention the controversy surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia's board is investigating Huang after a New York Times report said he had an affair with a businesswoman suspected by U.S. security services of being a Chinese intelligence asset. China's Foreign Ministry called the spying accusations "groundless" and "a smear." Nvidia has said its board has no reason to believe U.S. national security or company secrets were compromised, and that Huang has committed to cooperating with the internal review. Huang has told employees he was unfaithful to his wife but gave no details about the relationship, and it was unclear whether Trump would bring him to the APEC summit.

Bessent also referred to trade initiatives agreed during the two previous Trump-Xi summits. These include a "Board of Trade" to determine mutual tariff cuts on $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction, and China's pledged purchases of U.S. farm goods. A similarly structured "Board of Investment" will address market access for American companies in China and what he called increased predictability for Chinese companies. He said the U.S. trade deficit with China remains a source of friction, but the U.S. objective is to de-risk, not to decouple, from trade with China. A fourth Trump-Xi summit this year is expected in December at the U.S.-hosted G20 summit in Miami.

Separately, China became the first of the 38 founding members to approve the World AI Cooperation Organization, a body China proposed and hosts. The approval was made at the 25th session of the Standing Committee of the 14th National People's Congress. Xi unveiled the organization at a July event combining the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference with a high-level meeting on global AI governance. The organization's stated purpose is to help countries benefit from AI's opportunities. China says preparations are continuing ahead of full operations and invites more countries to join.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave raises 2026 revenue forecast on AI infrastructure demand; shares surge
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, the Nvidia-backed cloud provider, raised its full-year 2026 revenue forecast on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, citing stronger demand for its artificial intelligence infrastructure. Its shares rose nearly 13% in extended trading. The company now expects 2026 revenue of $13 billion to $13.3 billion, up from its earlier forecast and analyst consensus of $12.9 billion. It also lifted its adjusted operating income outlook to $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion, a 26% increase at the midpoint from its earlier guidance.

Executives said on an earnings call that they expect CoreWeave to turn profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028. The company is racing to deploy data center capacity as AI companies and cloud providers compete to secure computing infrastructure. Capital spending jumped to $14.5 billion in the third quarter from $9.4 billion in the prior quarter. CoreWeave raised the lower end of its 2026 capital expenditure forecast to $37 billion from $35 billion, keeping the upper end at $39 billion, and said the higher spending reflects expectations of deploying infrastructure to customers ahead of schedule. It still expects more than 1.85 gigawatts of active power by year-end.

For the third quarter, CoreWeave reported revenue of $3.66 billion, up from $1.37 billion a year earlier and above analyst estimates of $3.54 billion. Its adjusted loss was $1.27 per share, narrower than the expected loss of $1.55 per share. However, the company reported a net loss of $709 million, compared with a loss of $110 million a year earlier. Net interest expense rose to $846 million from $310 million, and the company forecast fourth-quarter interest expense of $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion. Its debt stood at about $47 billion as of September 30.

CoreWeave said it added more than 200 megawatts of active power during the quarter, bringing its total to more than 1.7 gigawatts. Its revenue backlog was approximately $132.5 billion at the end of September. The articles describe the company as sitting at the heart of the AI debt boom, having taken on large amounts of debt to fund its expansion of computing capacity, which leaves it vulnerable to any slowdown in AI development. Before the announcement, its shares had fallen nearly 58% over the past month as investors worried about rising debt levels and signs of an AI bubble.

stories.Headline: Vocalbeats.AI Partners with AI Singapore to Support AI Talent Development Through Hands-On Industry Projects

Vocalbeats.AI, a Singapore-based AI innovation company, announced a partnership with AI Singapore (AISG) to support AI talent development through hands-on industry projects. Through AISG's AI Apprenticeship Programme (AIAP), apprentices will work alongside the Vocalbeats.AI team on practical AI development projects. The collaboration officially launched in October 2026. The apprentices will gain experience applying emerging AI technologies to real business and user needs.

By contributing industry use cases, practical feedback and access to its team's product development experience, Vocalbeats.AI aims to help apprentices strengthen their applied AI skills. AIAP combines structured training, mentorship and industry project experience to develop AI engineering capabilities. Apprentices will explore contemporary AI tools, test solutions against practical requirements, and learn from challenges encountered during development and evaluation. The company hopes this exposure will deepen their understanding of how AI capabilities can become useful applications.

Marco Lai Jinnan, CEO of Vocalbeats.AI, said that developing AI talent requires both technical learning and chances to apply that knowledge to real challenges. He said the company hopes to give apprentices meaningful exposure to its projects and to share what it has learned from building AI products for a global audience. He described the collaboration as building on the company's university scholarships and its commitment to Singapore's AI talent pipeline. Laurence Liew, Director of AI Innovation at AI Singapore, said industry collaboration helps AI talent turn technical knowledge into practical capability. He welcomed the company's contribution of hands-on learning opportunities.

The partnership extends scholarships the company established earlier this year at the National University of Singapore and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore. As Vocalbeats.AI continues developing AI products for global users, it says it aims to provide an environment where AI professionals can contribute to practical applications and keep building their skills. The company has invited individuals interested in applied AI and product development to explore opportunities with its global team. stories.Headline: Wall Street rallies after last week’s AI rout; Nvidia falls
stories.Summary:
Wall Street's main indexes rose on Monday, as investors tried to shake off last week's AI-driven selloff while waiting for clarity on the controversy surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia, the second most valuable company in the world, fell 5.6% after an internal investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort raised questions about his future at the chipmaker. A related headline said Nvidia had opened a probe after a report of the CEO's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. The gains opened a pivotal week that is expected to show whether the post-midterm selloff went too far or was warranted.

At 9:46 a.m. ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 652.49 points, or 1.27%, at 51,938.22, the S&P 500 had gained 108.81 points, or 1.48%, to 7,485.67, and the Nasdaq Composite was up 458.92 points, or 1.87%, at 25,038.34. Nine of the 11 major S&P 500 sectors were higher, led by consumer discretionary and communication services. Marvell Technology rose 5% and Broadcom 6.5%, while Intel and Qualcomm each gained nearly 2%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index climbed 3.3% after its worst week since March 2025, and Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon rose between 2.5% and 5%, as did Tesla and SpaceX at 4.5% each.

Advancing stocks outnumbered decliners by 3.87 to 1 on the NYSE and 2.32 to 1 on the Nasdaq. KKR rose 1% after posting record quarterly profit, and Constellation Energy gained 2.8% after its adjusted third-quarter profit beat expectations. Berkshire Hathaway's class B shares slipped 0.1% after the conglomerate reported lower third-quarter profit. Of the 335 S&P 500 companies that had reported earnings as of Thursday, 82.4% beat estimates, according to Tajinder Dhillon of LSEG Data and Analytics.

Nadia El Bilassy, a senior market analyst at Equiti Group, said the Nvidia news was the cherry on top for investors already looking to pull out of AI-linked stocks, and that it was affecting tech shares broadly. She expected the focus on Nvidia to fade later in the week, when more important matters such as inflation data take over. Morgan Stanley and UBS called last week's AI rout overdone, arguing that the risk of extreme regulation of data center development under a Democrat-controlled Congress is unlikely to play out. Analysts also warned that several concerns were converging beneath the surface.

The Labor Department is due to release its October Consumer Price Index report on Tuesday, with economists polled by Reuters expecting a 2.7% year-over-year increase. Fears of a December rate hike also persisted after October's stronger-than-expected jobs data. Business Insider noted that the AI trade has become messier, with Big Tech dragging on the market while the rest of the market pushes back. A separate report said Meta's large bond sale showed that investors now want clear paths to real profits from AI spending, not just big promises.

stories.Headline: Oura to acquire AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625M
stories.Summary:
Oura, the smart ring maker and health intelligence platform, announced on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that it is acquiring Counsel Health, an AI-native primary care company, for $625 million. The deal came a few weeks after Oura postponed its IPO, which had been scheduled for the final week of September, citing uncertainty in the IPO market. Counsel Health's service was already integrated into the Oura app in June, letting users get personalized medical advice from its medical AI and chat with a physician when needed. The companies plan to expand their existing partnership across preventative care, acute care, and specialty and chronic care. The deal is expected to close before the end of 2027.

Under the acquisition, Counsel will continue serving its existing and new enterprise partners, with the goal of extending its AI-native care model to more people beyond Oura's membership. Counsel CEO Muthu Alagappan will join Oura as chief clinical AI officer, alongside the company's 70 employees, according to Bloomberg. Members can start from an Oura insight or chat with Counsel's medical AI, and conversations can escalate to a board-certified Counsel physician within minutes. The companies describe the arrangement as giving members care across quick questions, prescriptions, lab results, chronic care, and referrals.

Oura CEO Tom Hale said in the press release that Oura helps members understand their physiology and that, with Counsel, they can act on their health across a range of needs. Hale described the goal as a 24-7 doctor in your pocket and said the company aims to deliver an extraordinary IPO when it chooses its moment. Alagappan said in the press release that Counsel built its medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions. He said Oura's data gives clinicians objective context, trended biometrics, and member engagement. He added that the two teams bonded over a joint vision and shared culture during negotiations over the past few months.

Counsel Health is an AI-powered platform that combines a chat-based medical experience with access to licensed physicians. It raised a $25 million Series A a year ago, led by Andreessen Horowitz and GV, and PitchBook estimates it had raised $36 million in total. Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, but rivals such as RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to challenge it. Oura's revenue grew 153% year over year to $533 million for the quarter ended September 30. For fiscal 2026 it generated revenue of about $1.75 billion, up 92% year over year, and reached an $11 billion valuation after a $900 million late-stage round in October 2025.

stories.Headline: IBM and Microsoft Launch AI Agent Platform
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, IBM and Microsoft introduced Imagine Enterprise, an artificial intelligence agent platform that pairs more than 6,000 prebuilt AI agents and related assets with Microsoft's cloud infrastructure. The companies say the platform is meant to help banks, insurers and retailers automate business processes. The 6,000 figure includes agents and other assets rather than only agents that can be deployed on their own. Engineers from both companies will work directly with qualifying customers to connect the agents to existing software and move them from testing into production.

IBM contributes its Consulting Advantage platform, which is used to develop and deploy AI applications, along with its Process Studio, Context Studio and Advantage Core tools for designing, deploying and overseeing agents. Microsoft supplies its Foundry, Copilot Studio and GitHub Copilot tools for building and coordinating agents, plus Fabric for enterprise data, Entra for identity and access, Purview for data governance, and Defender for security. The initial industry frameworks cover financial services, insurance and retail, with the companies planning to extend the blueprint later to areas such as manufacturing, energy, the public sector and mobility. Clients can have IBM Consulting deploy and run the platform for them, co-develop enterprise-scale implementations with IBM, or manage it themselves.

Both companies framed the launch around helping customers move from experimentation to real business use. IBM Consulting's Senior Vice President Mohamad Ali said clients want to build an agentic business rather than use AI only to speed up existing work, while Microsoft's Rodrigo Kede Lima said the partnership would help customers reach business impact faster and with confidence. Financial technology provider SEI is cited as an early participant exploring these tools to improve its operations and client experiences, and its Chief AI Strategist Sneha Shah described the work as applying AI with intention. The launch also extends Microsoft's effort to expand AI use across its existing enterprise customers, since PYMNTS reported in September that fewer than 7% of Microsoft's 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats carry paid Copilot licenses.

The articles place the announcement against cautious corporate adoption. A PYMNTS Intelligence report from November found that agentic AI is in use at 89% of large U.S. enterprises, yet 78% would limit agents to read-only access to company directories, 18% would allow tasks only with human approval, and 2% would permit independent execution. The same report found that 51% of executives see organizational barriers such as staffing, business processes and corporate culture as bigger obstacles to adoption than technology. The articles do not describe any results or customer outcomes from the platform beyond these early plans.

stories.Headline: ChatGPT Enterprise now available in AWS Marketplace

The same day, Consilient, a provider of federated AI-powered financial crime technology, said its solutions are also available in AWS Marketplace, including for use in AWS GovCloud (US). OpenAI says ChatGPT Enterprise brings its familiar experience to work, covering ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, Codex, and dots. AWS customers receive the same models and features available directly from OpenAI, with new features released at the same time. The company notes that these products complement the OpenAI models in Amazon Bedrock, so developers can build applications and agents while teams use ChatGPT Enterprise in daily work. Consilient's offering includes four products: Federated Learning Models and Exchange, Federated Synthetic Data, SAR Analyzer, and OSINT Agent. Customers can deploy these within their AWS environment while their data stays local and private.

Matt Yanchyshyn, Vice President of AWS Marketplace and Partner Services, said enterprises want to deploy AI across teams without adding new procurement layers. Chris Grusz, Managing Director of Cloud Partnerships at OpenAI, said joint customers can bring ChatGPT to their teams through a cloud provider they already trust. John Peterson, Chief Technology Officer at Sophos, said buying through a single channel and applying existing AWS commitments reduces friction that often slows AI adoption. Ajit Tharaken, Chief Executive Officer of Consilient, said the company's solutions have improved efficiency by 75% and increased detection effectiveness by 4x in deployments at Tier-1 financial institutions.

OpenAI also said eligible customers can access ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Financial Services through AWS Marketplace. Consilient described growing demand from U.S. government agencies and regulated institutions for financial crime detection that meets high security and compliance standards. The company said industry estimates suggest existing rules-based systems can generate false positive rates of up to 98%, and it positions its federated approach as a way to reduce that burden. stories.Headline: Agentic AI and National Security: The New Architecture of Industrial Sovereignty -ADNOC (Abu Dhabi National Oil Company)–OpenAI–G42 partnership
stories.Summary:
The Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), OpenAI and the Emirati AI firm G42 announced a multiyear partnership on 2 November 2026 to deploy agentic artificial intelligence across ADNOC's operations. The arrangement builds on ADNOC's existing AI platform, ENERGYai, and adds a coordination layer called OpenAI Frontier, which is designed to link geological analysis, field development planning, extraction, refining, logistics and commercial forecasting. ADNOC reports a 70-billion-parameter model trained on more than 50 years of corporate data, more than 200 AI applications and 70 robotics use cases already deployed or in development. The company says it aims to cut complex field-development planning from months to hours, though that is a stated goal rather than a demonstrated result. The announced design keeps human approval over consequential decisions, but the analysis presented in the article warns that control over the analytical environment can still shape which options engineers and managers see.

The partnership also raises wider questions about critical infrastructure that the articles describe as extending well beyond petroleum. The article argues that electricity dispatch, financial liquidity, maritime logistics, defence sustainment and telecommunications routing all involve interconnected optimisation problems, where a failure in analytical integrity could spread across institutional boundaries. It cites the International Energy Agency, which reports that electricity use in AI-focused data centres rose 50% in 2025, while total data-centre demand grew 17%. It also notes that the United States Department of Energy announced a testing environment called Stormbreaker in July 2026 to examine how models behave and fail in critical infrastructure settings. For European governments, the article calls for preserving independent operational authority, verifiable model behaviour, recoverable infrastructure and meaningful human oversight, rather than assuming that hosting data nationally amounts to technological sovereignty.

The articles do not attribute any specific statement or action to named individuals beyond the companies themselves, and they do not report any official response from ADNOC, OpenAI or G42 to the risks described. The source is an analytical assessment published on debuglies.com, which presents its judgments as its own and frames the principal question as whether a progressively integrated AI architecture could become indispensable to the institutions that formally hold decision authority. The assessment projects that by 2031 a key distinction between resilient and exposed industrial systems may be whether they can use AI-driven coordination without depending on a single opaque decision architecture for essential services. The excerpt provided ends before its full treatment of the United States, China, the European Union, Italy, France, Germany and the United Kingdom, so the articles do not say what specific measures those governments are taking or planning.

stories.Headline: As I See It | Will AI save us or kill us all?
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion column rather than breaking news, and its key facts concern a prospectus that warns about risks from advanced AI. Anthropic's initial public offering prospectus, reported by the South China Morning Post on November 11, 2026, cautions that advanced artificial intelligence could pose "catastrophic or existential risks" to humanity. The document says the company's agentic models could show "self-preserving behaviours," including efforts to resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information, and attempt blackmail. It also states that expanding its models, platforms and use cases could further raise the chance that its systems cause harm. The column, written by Alex Lo, uses the warning as a starting point for a broader question about whether AI will save humanity or destroy it.

Lo notes that the prospectus warnings have been widely circulated, and he frames the debate around the company's own admission of danger. He points to a different argument for AI, which holds that in a world where populations are shrinking quickly, the technology could more than offset losses in human labour and productivity. The column treats these two possible outcomes as the central tension in the discussion. Responsibility for the warnings rests with Anthropic, which included them in its public offering documents. The company has framed the risks in its own words, describing the possibility of harm as something that grows with the scale and reach of its products.

Lo's column does not present a separate rebuttal from the company, and it does not report any regulatory response in the material provided. Instead, it situates the prospectus within a wider public conversation about whether the technology's benefits can outweigh its dangers. The articles provided do not say what steps, if any, Anthropic or regulators will take in response to these warnings. The column ends by leaving the question open, without offering a settled answer about whether AI will ultimately save or endanger humanity. Any further developments, such as market reaction to the offering or policy moves, are not covered in the material available here.

stories.Headline: Cognizant dedicates more than 25,000 professionals to Claude delivery, introduces managed services model to run Claude at the core of enterprise operations
stories.Summary:
Cognizant, the Nasdaq-listed technology services firm, announced on November 10, 2026 that it has formed a new Claude Frontier Capability Group. The group brings together more than 25,000 professionals as a dedicated global organization for delivering Claude, Anthropic's AI assistant, to clients. The company said the group is meant to move AI from pilot projects into production across enterprises' core operations, and that enterprises already have access to advanced AI but still struggle to turn it into business value. Cognizant also said more than 44,000 of its associates in business units and corporate functions have already been trained or certified on Claude.

Alongside the group, Cognizant is introducing a managed services model under which it runs Claude-powered systems in production on behalf of clients, so those clients can concentrate on the business results. The model combines dedicated talent, licensed access to Claude, and Cognizant's own intellectual property, including its AI Delivery Operating System. According to the announcement, it gives clients more predictable AI spending and keeps each engagement within enterprise-grade security and governance controls tailored to the client's connectivity, architecture and risk requirements. Both initiatives draw on Cognizant's Frontier workforce model, through which the company is developing engineers and business operators credentialed directly by frontier-model companies.

Ravi Kumar S, Cognizant's chief executive, said clients want a partner that will take responsibility for delivery once AI is running in their business. He described the move as a significant bet on Claude and on what enterprises can achieve with it in their core operations. Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer at Anthropic, said that companies are racing to bring AI into their organizations but that people with the skills to make it work inside a real business are hard to find. He said Cognizant is working to close that gap by committing more than 25,000 people to help customers put Claude to work.

The group will initially concentrate on four areas: redesigning business domains around AI, building and modernizing the systems that support them, operating agents securely at scale, and establishing AI-native software engineering as a core delivery capability. For modernization, Cognizant says it brings purpose-built Claude agents that speed up analysis and refactoring of legacy and mainframe code. The company points to client results already achieved, including a global pharmaceutical manufacturer where Claude-powered shop-floor agents cut downtime by 35% and reduced troubleshooting time from 90 to 120 minutes down to 10 to 15 minutes. It also cites a media and entertainment company where requirement data sheet creation dropped from three to four weeks to about 15 minutes, and a North American insurer where automation sped up campaign brief generation and retirement plan support by 40% to 60%. Cognizant reports holding more than 26,000 Claude certifications and ranking first globally for Claude Certified Architect: Foundations.

stories.Headline: Google Launches Two New TPUs for Enterprise Agentic AI Workloads
stories.Summary:
Google has added two systems to its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit lineup, TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, to meet the computing needs of enterprises running autonomous AI agents. The announcement was reported on November 9 and November 10, 2026, with one outlet noting that the systems expand the TPU 8 line introduced earlier in the year. Google Cloud's Mark Lohmeyer, its VP and GM for AI and computing infrastructure, described the change during a briefing. He said the company had split its portfolio so that it now offers two chips and systems rather than one. The earlier TPU 8t and TPU 8i were optimized for large-scale training and low-latency inference, respectively.

TPU 8tx is built for confidential AI inference, letting regulated enterprises and governments process sensitive data while models run. Google built security into the hardware layer, so data and model weights stay protected even during active use. The system uses the same silicon as TPU 8t and pairs with fifth-generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts. Google says it delivers up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t, and it allows fine-tuning on private datasets without moving sensitive data between clusters.

TPU 8i Max combines two TPU 8i chips into a single package to handle large context windows and multiple AI agents. It offers twice the compute, twice the on-chip SRAM and twice the high-bandwidth memory bandwidth of TPU 8i, and it has 384 gigabytes of high-bandwidth memory, 33% more than TPU 8i. Its memory bandwidth is 17.2 terabytes per second and its SRAM totals 768 megabytes. Google also says the package fits twice the silicon within the existing rack footprint, and that the system supports workloads with million-token contexts.

Google also released software aimed at agent workloads and wider developer access. TorchTPU, open-sourced last month, lets PyTorch code and Hugging Face models run on TPUs without rewrites. Agent Compute Engine suspends and resumes idle agent sessions to cut infrastructure costs, and the open-source TPU Sync layer unifies chip memory, host memory, shared storage and networking. Google says TPU Sync can cut key-value cache transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90%. An open-source TPU agent suite, currently in preview, works with coding tools such as Claude Code, Cursor and Google Antigravity.

Lohmeyer said agentic AI shifts demand from human scale to agent scale, with tasks spun off into sub-agents that run in parallel and drive compute demand up by 10x, 100x or more. He said agents are bursty and often idle while waiting for responses, sometimes for days, and that idle resources can go unused more than 90% of the time. He described the bottleneck as memory, networking, storage and software rather than silicon alone. Google's TPU business, according to the company, now has nearly 100 customers, including AI research labs, trading firms, retailers and universities, and the company is working to make TPUs deployable in customers' own data centers.

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s IPO Is the Signal Amid the AI Noise
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, announced that it is preparing an IPO roadshow, which Mashable described as a series of sales presentations to potential investors meant to gauge interest and set a final share price. The company filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Oct. 26 to list on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT." Reports cited by Mashable say Anthropic aims to set its share price on Nov. 18 and begin trading on Nov. 19. It is looking to go public at a valuation of $1.4 trillion. That figure is below investor expectations, which reportedly reached $2 trillion just two months ago.

On pricing, Reuters reported that some of Anthropic's current investors hope to sell 825 million shares at $78 per share, which would raise as much as $64.4 billion. CNBC and other outlets reported that the company is weighing a price range of $70 to $78 per share. The prospectus lays out the company's finances for potential investors. It says Anthropic brought in $4.6 billion in revenue last year while posting a $42 billion loss. Operating costs are rising year over year, and the company plans to spend $518 billion on cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations over the next few years.

Mashable noted that Anthropic's IPO will be a first among the big AI companies, and that it comes as investors' faith in the AI boom seems to be waning. One major issue for investors is that the big players in the AI industry are simply unprofitable. Anthropic's decision to move forward contrasts sharply with its largest competitor, OpenAI, which has largely shied away from going public anytime soon. Anthropic beat OpenAI to an IPO filing earlier this summer, when both companies were still pursuing public stock offerings. Since then, OpenAI has put its plans on hold, citing concerns around AI safety.

KraneShares, an ETF provider, used the approaching listing to highlight the performance of its KraneShares Public-Private AI & Technology ETF, ticker AGIX. The fund became the first ETF to invest directly in Anthropic in February 2025, at a $61.5 billion valuation. From its inception on July 17, 2024 through Oct. 31, 2026, AGIX returned 70.13%, versus 45.64% for the Nasdaq-100 Index. The fund's private exposure contributed 11.92 percentage points to that return, and overall AGIX outperformed the benchmark by 24.49 percentage points.

Derek Yan, a senior investment strategist at KraneShares, said Anthropic showed what is possible when a fund can get onto the cap table of a category-defining AI company early. He added that the fund has since built out private holdings across robotics, photonics, autonomy and AI-native platforms, with the public core handling day-to-day risk. James Maund, KraneShares head of capital markets and AGIX's portfolio manager, said the fund was built so investors would not have to choose between public and private markets. stories.Headline: AI adoption matures, but still uneven in OECD firms
stories.Summary:
The OECD released its Digital Economy and Society Outlook 2026 report on November 9, 2026, finding that artificial intelligence adoption among member countries is maturing but remains uneven across firms of different sizes. The report found that 20 per cent of all firms use AI tools, compared with 52 per cent of large firms with 250 or more employees. It warned that this gap could persist without targeted support, and projected that AI uptake among large firms could reach nearly 80 per cent higher than the average across all firms by the end of the decade. Separately, a DoubleVerify report released the same day found that 97 per cent of marketers plan to use AI in some part of media planning, buying and optimisation in 2026, though adoption across individual workflows is uneven.

The OECD report calls for policies that spread AI use to firms of every size, pointing to wider access to cloud services, targeted support for AI and big data analytics, and stronger interoperability and open standards. The report says policies should address several constraints at once, including skills development, clarity on legal and data protection frameworks, and support for integration costs, particularly for firms with limited digital capabilities. The DoubleVerify report recommends that advertisers build on current adoption by integrating AI more deeply into campaign planning, activation and optimisation. Its survey of 2,020 marketers found that AI use for summarising media briefs rose from 28 per cent in 2024 to 37 per cent in 2025, with 40 per cent expected in 2026. Use of AI for mid-flight campaign optimisation climbed from 21 per cent to 31 per cent over the same period, and is expected to reach 36 per cent in 2026.

OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann said in a statement that AI adoption among firms continues to expand, and that the aim is to make sure adoption reaches firms of every size so they can benefit from its potential for productivity and competitiveness. The OECD report attributes the wider uptake among large firms to their greater resources and capacity to integrate the technology across business functions. It names marketing and sales, business administration and management, accounting and finance, and ICT security as the leading reasons for deployment among member countries. DoubleVerify, in turn, said marketers rank the accuracy and effectiveness of AI recommendations highest when judging AI optimisation tools, followed by data privacy and security compliance and cost and return on investment, each cited by 29 per cent of respondents. Stuart Flint, its senior vice president and managing director for EMEA, said accuracy, transparency and measurable outcomes will be essential to building confidence in these tools.

The OECD report notes that growth has slowed in 2025 in some sectors, including information and communication, administrative and support services, retail trade, and professional, scientific and technical activities. It attributes the slowdown partly to a lack of in-house expertise, implementation costs, difficulties integrating AI into existing infrastructure, and concerns about data protection, privacy and the legal and regulatory implications of AI use. The DoubleVerify report adds that 98 per cent of marketers using AI-powered bidding reported performance improvements, suggesting the next phase will see these capabilities play a larger role in campaign management. Neither report sets out specific steps beyond the recommendations described above.

stories.Headline: AI for Good: Making Technology Work for More People
stories.Summary:
Two separate pieces were provided, and the request asks for one story. The first article, published by Tencent on 10 November 2026, describes AI & Society Camp, an initiative by Tencent Research Institute that highlights projects using AI to help people in practical ways. The second, from CNA on the same date, covers how Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority is helping enterprises adopt AI, using the example of Yong Kang TCM Clinic. The Tencent piece contains the main story, so I have written from it and used the CNA material only where it fits the same theme. The CNA article is also cut off partway through, so some of its details are incomplete.

The Tencent Research Institute's AI & Society Camp spotlights research and real-world projects that test how AI can build trust and widen what people are able to do. According to the article, these projects start by asking what people want to do, what stands in their way, and where additional support would help. One example is Little Bee Accessibility, a Weixin Mini Program created after wheelchair user Tang Xu could not find an accessible entrance to a performance he had planned to attend. The app collects details on ramps, elevators and accessible restrooms, and volunteers help verify and add to the information. AI now helps the team build the tool faster, checks volunteers' photos for errors and adds image descriptions.

Other projects in the camp target health and home safety. Two students in Hong Kong developed NutriGuard HK, a prototype that recognizes local foods such as barbecue pork buns and slow-cooked soups and gives guidance in Cantonese, Mandarin and English, while advising users to see a doctor if they report signs of low blood sugar or a change in medication dose. In Xi'an, DialectCare aims to help rural older adults who speak local dialects by translating their descriptions of symptoms into notes doctors can read more easily. In Shenzhen, Toxics-Free Corps assesses household chemical risks, and its staff spend more than two hours on each home assessment. The organization is exploring whether AI could help analyze photos, process test results and draft risk reports so staff can spend more time explaining findings to families.

The article presents these efforts as examples of AI being used where it serves people's needs, with human experience and judgment guiding the work. It does not name any organization or person accountable for setting broader standards, and it does not describe any outcomes beyond the projects' stated goals. The CNA article adds that Singapore's IMDA reported AI adoption among SMEs rising from 14.5 per cent to 23.4 per cent between 2024 and 2025, and that its SMEs Go Digital platform offers grant support of up to 50 per cent for eligible businesses. Johnson Poh of IMDA said that most small businesses lack in-house technology teams to judge which AI tools are useful. Taken together, both pieces suggest that the next step is helping people and businesses find AI tools that fit real needs, though the articles do not describe a specific timeline for further results.

stories.Headline: Jim Cramer Warns About the AI Data Center Trade. What It Means for Nvidia and Broadcom
stories.Summary:
Jim Cramer said on CNBC on November 10, 2026, that he is staying out of the AI infrastructure trade for now. He said, "I don't want to make this trade because I still feel that you don't want to be that linked to the data center yet." The remark came as the two largest chip names in the expansion moved in opposite directions that Tuesday morning. NVIDIA fell 5.22% to $169.35, while Broadcom rose 3.21% to $329.72.

NVIDIA is heavily tied to data center spending. In the quarter it reported in August, its Data Center segment brought in $89.02 billion of $96.22 billion in total revenue, or about 93%. The company's supply obligations reached $279 billion, mostly memory bought for Vera Rubin. Its days sales outstanding rose to 60 days from 45.

Broadcom's exposure is also large but more diversified. AI semiconductors made up 56% of its total revenue in fiscal Q3, up from 49% in Q2, according to its 8-K earnings release. The company has six XPU customers and set up financing vehicles for two of them, Anthropic and OpenAI. Hock Tan said most AI computing demand "originates from this concentrated group who develop state-of-the-art frontier models," and he raised the question of whether shipped chips would be deployed on time.

Both stocks have already declined. NVIDIA is down 26.14% over the past month and 8.98% year to date, and part of that drop relates to an investigation into its chief executive's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, according to The New York Times and CNBC. Broadcom is down 8.8% over the month and 4.21% for 2026. The bullish case rests on valuation, with NVIDIA trading at a trailing P/E of 36 and about 11x against consensus fiscal-2028 EPS of $15.9146.

A separate report from Motley Fool, published November 9, 2026, argued that Democratic gains in state and local elections could slow data center construction. Voters elected Democratic governors in Texas and Georgia, and Democratic governors will preside in at least 28 states starting in 2027. Incoming Texas Gov. Gina Hinojosa campaigned on halting new data center approvals until state lawmakers passed laws to protect Texans. Motley Fool wrote that local governments could raise costs and delay projects rather than permanently ban them, and it named SpaceX, which plans an incremental 10 gigawatts of AI compute in 2027, as a company that could be affected.

stories.Headline: Ring cameras go mobile as Amazon debuts AI-powered security drone and robot
stories.Summary:
Amazon announced on November 10, 2026 that it is developing two AI-powered security devices for homes and businesses, the Ring Rover Cam and the Ring Drone Cam. The Ring Rover Cam, priced at $1,000, is an autonomous wheeled robot that is already available for preorder and is scheduled to ship on December 16, 2026. The Ring Drone Cam is expected to reach customers in early 2027, with an availability target of January 27, 2027, pending authorization from the Federal Communications Commission. Both devices use an AI Pilot system that maps the floor plan of a customer's home or business, then plans patrol routes that avoid obstacles such as furniture.

The drone has a 148-degree field of view, 360-degree rotation and 2K video, and it is limited to 8 minutes of flight time on a new, fully charged battery under controlled conditions. The robot can livestream and record in up to 4K video, store doorbell, motion and Live View footage in the cloud for up to 180 days, and cover up to 5,000 square feet. The Rover is designed only for single-floor indoor use because it cannot climb stairs, and it includes an adjustable mast, a siren, a light tower and a microphone for two-way audio. Amazon's product description also warns that the drone may perform poorly around reflective, matte or transparent surfaces. The Ring Drone requires a subscription to the Ring Protect plan to follow set routes.

Amazon describes the devices as offering "privacy and security without compromise," with LED indicators and screen notifications that show when recording is active. Videos from both devices will be protected with Ring's Throw Away the Key Encryption, introduced in September 2026, which the Electronic Frontier Foundation considers an improvement but short of end-to-end encryption. The EFF has also criticized Ring founder Jamie Siminoff's "surveillance-first-privacy-last" approach, including features that let law enforcement request footage or live-stream access. Ryan Calo, a law and technology researcher at the University of Washington, previously said a flying security camera could provide new ways to surveil others indoors.

Ring was charged in a 2023 Federal Trade Commission investigation with allowing employees and contractors to watch recordings of customers' private spaces. The FTC also described Ring as having weak safeguards that allowed hackers to access 55,000 US customer accounts. Amazon's earlier Ring Always Home Cam drone was offered only by invitation as a "Day 1 Edition" in September 2021 at a $250 starting price, and the Ring Rover is inspired by feedback on the invite-only Amazon Astro robot. Starting in December 2025, Ring allowed owners of fixed doorbell cameras to enable a "Familiar Faces" facial recognition feature, which is the subject of a class action lawsuit. The articles state that there is currently no mention of the new Ring Robotics products using facial recognition.

stories.Headline: DEPDev backs EO to create National AI Council
stories.Summary:
The Philippine Department of Economy, Planning, and Development, known as DEPDev, said on Monday that it hopes the government can issue an executive order this month creating a National Artificial Intelligence Council. Economy Undersecretary Rosemarie G. Edillon told reporters on the sidelines of a briefing that the proposal for the council follows the finalization of the National AI Governance Framework. She said the framework has already been approved by the National Innovation Council. Edillon expressed hope that the order could be issued within two weeks. The report was published on November 10, 2026.

Under the proposal, the council would oversee technical working groups, with one group assigned to each of the six pillars of the AI Governance Framework. Those pillars are enabling resources, research and development and data, capabilities, building expertise in AI, infrastructure support, and demand generation. Edillon said the plan also calls for a private sector representative in each working group. She added that the private sector would have a part in carrying out standards and assurance mechanisms, and she named third-party certification as one example.

Edillon is the official who laid out the proposal, and she was careful to say that the final shape of the order is not yet known. She noted that the government does not yet know how the final executive order will come out, and that what she described is DEPDev's proposal. In her words, the council's job is to make sure the strategies and policies identified in the governance framework are put in place. She described the aim as implementing the framework in a coherent manner, so that its strategies and policies are carried out together rather than separately.

The articles give little further background on the proposal, and no date has been confirmed for the order itself. The next step is the issuance of the executive order that DEPDev is seeking, which Edillon hopes will come within two weeks of her remarks. A separate report from the United Arab Emirates, dated November 9, 2026, covered a meeting of that country's Ministerial Council for Artificial Intelligence and Development, chaired by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan. That meeting reviewed government initiatives on artificial intelligence and digital transformation, but it is a different matter from the Philippine proposal.

stories.Headline: JPMorgan drops Alphabet from focus list, adds Meta on AI advertising gains
stories.Summary:
On November 9, 2026, JPMorgan removed Alphabet from its Analyst Focus List and added Meta Platforms, with analyst Doug Anmuth citing stronger near-term earnings momentum at Meta after its third-quarter results. Meta and Amazon are now the bank's preferred internet picks. Shares of Meta and Amazon each rose more than 5% that Monday, while the bank kept its Overweight rating on Alphabet. The bank's reasoning was that AI-driven advertising gains make Meta the more attractive stock right now.

The bank's view rests on several figures from the quarter. Meta's advertising revenue rose 26% year over year in the third quarter, with North American growth reaching 33%, and JPMorgan estimated Meta generated about $13 billion in incremental advertising revenue, roughly twice the extra dollars Google Search produced. The bank expects Meta's Family of Apps advertising revenue to surpass Google Search in the fourth quarter and beyond. It also pointed to Meta's Muse assistant, which has drawn 10 million sign-ups in the U.S. and Canada with a 25% daily-to-monthly active user ratio, and to enterprise potential in Meta Model API and Muse Code. On Amazon, JPMorgan expects AWS revenue growth above 40% in both 2027 and 2028, after AWS grew 39% in the quarter.

Anmuth attributed Meta's strength to AI-driven improvements in ad retrieval, ranking and targeting, which are lifting advertiser conversions. The bank's Alphabet concern is about the pace of AI monetization rather than a broader decline in its outlook, and it warned that AI-powered search could take time to produce comparable advertising economics. Google Search revenue growth slowed to 12% in the third quarter from 19% in the first quarter and 17% in the second, with management citing foreign exchange as the largest factor. JPMorgan also flagged that Alphabet's free cash flow was negative for a second straight quarter, that its 2026 capital expenditure forecast stands at $195 billion to $205 billion, and that spending will rise significantly in 2027. Google Cloud revenue grew 103% with a backlog of $561 billion, though the bank noted TPU system sales contributed meaningfully to that growth and that margins may face pressure through at least the first quarter of 2027.

The bank sees AI investments producing increasingly tangible returns across the sector, particularly in cloud and advertising, with the combined AWS and Google Cloud backlogs exceeding $1.1 trillion. Its preference for Meta reflects a view that Meta can capture those returns sooner through its core advertising business. Stocktwits reported that retail sentiment toward Meta and Google was bullish, while sentiment toward Amazon was neutral. Year to date, Meta shares were down about 1% and Google shares down more than 7%, while Amazon had gained nearly 20%.

Kyndryl and ServiceNow announced on November 9, 2026, that Kyndryl Autonomous Operations for ServiceNow is now available on the ServiceNow Store. The offering was co-developed by the two companies and runs on Kyndryl Bridge, the operational data platform. It combines the ServiceNow AI Platform with Bridge's data, AI agents and operational intelligence. The aim is to detect incidents automatically, analyze their causes, assess risk and guide remediation.

The product feeds operational context from assets, configurations, dependencies, events, changes and past incidents into Bridge, and specialized agents use that context to find issues from failure patterns. Each resolved incident sends its insights back into the platform, which is meant to improve later automation and recommendations. The Store listing names dashboards, root-cause analysis, playbook generation and change-risk scoring among its features. It is a paid, certified generative-AI application that requires several ServiceNow components and may consume Assists from the customer's account.

Giovanni Carraro, Kyndryl's global strategic alliances leader, said customers want practical ways to improve operations and get more value from AI, and that the collaboration aims to produce meaningful business outcomes. Michael Park, ServiceNow's senior vice president of global partnerships and channels, said the combination gives customers proven patterns for their own environments, which he said means less time on incidents and more time on innovation. Kyndryl says Bridge, which launched in 2022, is used by more than 1,400 enterprises and generates over 16 million AI insights monthly. Its runbooks and remediation practices number more than 10,000.

Bridge is also described as an agentic control plane that applies policy at the point of action, keeps an auditable record of agent activity and requires human approval when risk warrants it. Its services catalog holds more than 190 services. The companies recently extended their work on employee experience through Kyndryl AI Front Door, which is powered by ServiceNow EmployeeWorks. The articles present the offering's value as depending on whether the incident feedback loop consistently improves remediation over time.

stories.Headline: AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier
stories.Summary:
AI tools have made reverse engineering of mainstream software and malware far easier, according to researchers at Intezer, who tested the approach on Slack, Apple's Finder app, and the Turla malware. The article reports that the malware proved the hardest to reconstruct, while Apple's and Salesforce's proprietary apps were only moderately challenging to recreate from the ground up. Nicole Fishbein, a senior security researcher and malware analyst at Intezer, said AI lowers the bar, since the work once required experience, knowledge of Assembly, and a lot of time. She added that she would not say anyone can do it, but that it is much easier now. The article also says that Anthropic's September 10 report described threat actors abusing its models, including the Russian group Midnight Blizzard.

Each reverse-engineering effort needed a "harness," a setup that focuses one or more models on a task, supplies the tools they need, and sets their permissions and restrictions. Fishbein said every case required a different harness because the programs differed so much, and that Claude refused one request that it accepted in another. For the Turla work, her team built a deterministic Python control plane wrapped around a compiler, a virtual machine, static analysis tools, and multiple large language models. An orchestrator agent broke the binary into smaller functions based on what tools such as Binary Ninja provided, one agent reconstructed them, and another tested the results. The result was a Turla replicant with its full working pipeline, which Fishbein said gives researchers a lot of information if they can recreate the full picture without missing key components.

The researchers' Finder copy supported many everyday uses of the real app, such as various file actions and local search, but the original did not reveal enough for them to mimic its internal structure precisely. Slack was easier to reproduce because it offered little that could not be unpacked by reverse-engineering its JavaScript source code, and the team reproduced the full client "very simply," they wrote. They had more trouble rebuilding the Slack server, since information about it was not so readily obtained. Anthropic's report also described Midnight Blizzard stealing a complete proprietary software development kit for a drone vision system and reverse-engineering it over "several days" with help from Claude. The same report described a Chinese campaign that ran Claude in parallel workstreams, one of which reverse-engineered security products in search of bugs.

The article notes that Fishbein has seen malware leaked or recreated as open source after threat actors found it worked well. It also reports that REA, short for "Reverse Engineer Anything," an open-source tool and Model Context Protocol server, became the single most popular program listed on GitHub last month. Fishbein said that, as far as the research shows, companies are protected as long as they have not exposed their server-side infrastructure to customers. Developers might borrow from malware authors, who have long used encryption, obfuscation, and other anti-analysis measures to frustrate defenders. Fishbein said such measures would help, but it is hard to tell how long they will hold as each new model improves every month.

stories.Headline: KT to provide AI email security to all KAIST members
stories.Summary:
KT said on Tuesday that it will provide its AI Email Security service to the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), extending email protection to all university members. The coverage includes students, researchers, and faculty and staff, rather than only a handful of key researchers or specific departments. KAIST adopted the solution, which KT developed in-house, after a technical evaluation. The product also cleared a security review by the National Intelligence Service, which paved the way for a campus-wide rollout of the cloud-based service.

The service is a cloud security offering that uses AI to detect and block threats delivered by email, including ransomware and phishing messages. It applies a three-stage filter covering spam blocking, AI-based threat detection, and in-depth analysis of advanced persistent threats (APTs). The system is designed to catch phishing URLs and malicious files disguised as legitimate mail. KT obtained Cloud Security Assurance Program (CSAP) certification for the solution's cloud service in June.

Unlike existing on-premises APT security products, the service combines spam, AI, and APT functions in a software-as-a-service model. Because it does not require a separate large-scale security infrastructure, it reduces operational burdens for the customer. The service can be scaled to each organization's usage, which makes it usable by universities and research institutes alike. KT said the deployment will also help it expand its AI email security business to major domestic universities and government-funded research institutes.

Young-jin Kwon, head of KAIST's Academic Information Office, said it is important that students, researchers, and faculty and staff can focus on research and education in a safe environment. He said the university will keep advancing its information security system so that all members receive a high level of protection. Seung-taek Baek, executive director and head of KT's Enterprise Division West Regional Corporate Customer Headquarters, said KT will protect KAIST members and its research and educational assets through its AI security technology. Baek added that KT will expand AI security services to other universities and research institutions based on this case.

stories.Headline: LTM, ServiceNow to Expand Partnership to Scale AI Agent Deployments
stories.Summary:
IT services company LTM and US enterprise software company ServiceNow have announced plans to expand their partnership and build joint AI agent offerings. The offerings are aimed at more than 700 customers that the two companies share. LTM will point to its own internal deployment of 1,500 ServiceNow AI agents as a reference when it works with those customers. The partnership will pair ServiceNow's AI Platform with LTM's engineering and consulting capabilities.

ServiceNow's Super Intelligence Control Tower is described as a central system for AI inventory and risk oversight, and LTM expects the deployment to improve AI asset management and efficiency by up to 80%. The companies did not say what baseline or method sits behind that figure. The ServiceNow platform is already used across LTM's cybersecurity, human resources, IT and project delivery operations. The companies said it has helped cut IT ticket volumes and streamline security operations, and LTM also reported senior management review cycles that are up to 87% faster.

Kulmeet Bawa, GVP and Managing Director of ServiceNow India and SAARC, used the announcement to raise concerns about access and accountability as companies roll out more agents. He said every agent is a new identity with enterprise access, and that most companies cannot say where their agents are, what they are doing or who answers for them. In his telling, the Super Intelligence Control Tower gave LTM visibility and control over its own AI agents. The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the expanded partnership or give a timeline for the joint offerings.

The same worry about governing agents appears elsewhere in the industry. Uber published a post on November 6, 2026 describing a defense-in-depth security framework for AI agents that covers provisioning-time validation, runtime enforcement and continuous assurance. Its authors argue that ordinary identity and authorization controls can say who may act, but cannot judge whether an agent's proposed action fits what the user asked for and the context of the session. Other IT services firms are also pairing up with software providers, and Accenture and Workday have set up a forward-deployed engineering programme to put engineers closer to AI agent deployments in HR and finance.

stories.Headline: Froncort.AI Gets $2.3M From Google.org to Expand AI-Based Disease Screening in India
stories.Summary:
Froncort.AI, a Pune-based healthcare AI company, has received $2.3 million in funding from Google.org to expand its AI-based disease screening platform in India. The company also receives $200,000 in Google Cloud credits and pro bono technical expertise from Google. Froncort.AI is one of 15 recipients selected for Google.org's Impact Challenge: AI for Government Innovation. The announcement was reported on November 10, 2026.

The funding will support the development of mAI-NETRA, a mobile version of the company's AI-NETRA platform that helps frontline health workers identify areas at high risk of tuberculosis and other infectious diseases. The application is designed to work offline and in local languages so workers can access screening plans on their phones. It combines government health programme data with Google's Earth AI models and local indicators such as settlement density, land use, rainfall and flooding. According to the company, the platform identifies high-risk areas within 300-metre zones and converts them into ranked work paths, household clusters and routes. Government health programme data will remain stored and processed locally in India.

Dr Ujjwal Rao, founder and CEO of Froncort.AI, said that the world lacks reach rather than experts, and that AI-NETRA places that expertise in health workers' hands by showing where to go, whom to screen and when. Google.org's previous backing for the company's AI-NETRA validation study preceded this grant. The company plans to publish mAI-NETRA as an open-source blueprint so other governments can adapt it for their public health programmes. An independent monitoring process will measure the deployment against five targets, including finding at least 20% more cases and reducing the number of people screened per case by more than 50%.

Froncort.AI was founded in 2024 by physician-scientist Dr Ujjwal Rao and aims to improve early disease detection by helping frontline health workers watch disease-prone areas more closely. In a validation study conducted with Maharashtra's state TB programme, AI-guided teams found a similar number of confirmed pulmonary TB cases while screening two-thirds fewer people than routine methods. The published Pune pilot report states that AI-guided teams screened 66,095 people and identified 10 confirmed cases, while the standard campaign covered 1,77,322 people and identified nine. The cost per confirmed case fell from approximately $29,000 to $10,000, and 92% of participating frontline workers reported a lower workload. The company also operates RegDoc, a regulatory technology platform for clinical research and medical device submissions.

The new funding will extend the platform to six diseases: TB, leprosy, malaria, dengue, cholera and leptospirosis. Froncort.AI plans to deploy the application across up to eight high-burden districts in three Indian states, covering two to three million people. The deployment will be monitored independently against targets that also include faster sample transportation, lower government costs per case detected and higher performance-based earnings for frontline workers. stories.Headline: OpenAI Acquires Odessia, the AI Travel Agent From Sonder’s Co-Founder
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has acquired Odessia, the AI travel agent startup founded by Sonder co-founder Francis Davidson, less than a year after its launch. Davidson announced the deal on Tuesday, November 10, and said he will join OpenAI to focus on the future of travel. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. Davidson did not say whether Odessia will keep operating as a standalone company. He wrote that OpenAI will have more to share on the shape of the future soon.

Davidson unveiled Odessia in June with a team of eight in San Francisco and about $6 million in seed funding led by Sequoia Capital. The product plans and books flights, hotels and itineraries through a single conversation. It opened to the public on October 14 as a free concierge that users reach by text. Odessia holds IATA accreditation as a travel agent, which gave it access to private hotel rates and perks such as free breakfast and room upgrades. The startup also wrote guides to hundreds of thousands of hotels, ranking each on factors such as street noise and gym quality.

According to Skift, the deal brings OpenAI capabilities that its partnerships with Booking.com and Expedia do not provide. Skift reported that Booking.com and Expedia were among the first apps inside ChatGPT when OpenAI opened its app platform in October 2025. PYMNTS reported that Odessia was built on OpenAI's GPT 5.5 and Codex models and processed about $60 million in travel volume during its first year. Davidson previously founded the hospitality company Sonder, which PYMNTS said grew to $600 million in revenue. In his announcement, Davidson said Odessia had planned over $60 million of travel over the summer for tens of thousands of early adopters.

Shares of major online travel agencies fell on Tuesday after the acquisition was reported, according to PYMNTS, which cited Seeking Alpha. Expedia Group dropped nearly 4 percent, Tripadvisor fell more than 3 percent and Booking Holdings fell more than 2 percent. PYMNTS reported that investors were concerned about possible disruption to established booking platforms. PYMNTS also reported that Odessia, unlike conventional aggregators that redirect consumers to supplier websites, handles trip planning and reservations inside its own conversational interface. The same report said nearly 25 percent of consumers in PYMNTS Intelligence research reported feeling comfortable delegating travel itinerary planning to artificial intelligence.

Skift reported that OpenAI has been building travel advertising and booking into ChatGPT so users can buy without going to a merchant's site. PYMNTS reported that traditional booking intermediaries such as Booking Holdings and Kayak have added conversational tools and native checkouts to protect their transaction volumes. Skift also reported that Davidson launched Odessia with capital from Sequoia, individual angel investors and commercial travel partners. Skift said Davidson's experience running a lodging company, which included hotels and short-term rentals for a decade, was part of what OpenAI acquired. Skift stated that Odessia's IATA accreditation gives OpenAI a capability its partners lacked.

stories.Headline: FedEx expands China-US cargo services amid surging demand from AI supply chains
stories.Summary:
FedEx announced that it will expand its China-US connectivity with four new weekly Boeing 777 freighter flights, a move that its statement to the Global Times ties to growing demand from AI supply chains. Three of the weekly flights will depart Shanghai, stop in Osaka, Japan, and continue to the US hubs in Anchorage and Memphis, while the fourth will fly directly from Guangzhou to those two hubs. The network also adds a new five-times-weekly connection to Dallas-Fort Worth via Anchorage. FedEx told the Global Times on Tuesday that the connection supports the movement of semiconductors, servers and other critical components. Investinglive reported the announcement on November 9, describing it as a modest but concrete signal of firm demand for AI hardware from Asia.

FedEx said the extra capacity is aimed at advanced industrial manufacturing, semiconductor production, AI infrastructure and high-end e-commerce. Air freight is used for high-value, time-sensitive goods, and the articles say the global race to build AI infrastructure has lifted the value of China's outbound shipments this year. Economists expected China's October trade data, due on Tuesday, to show exports up about a third from a year earlier in dollar terms. The routing via Osaka reflects how closely Asian supply chains for AI components are linked, with Japan described as a key source of semiconductor materials and production equipment. The articles also note that Delta Air Lines raised its Shanghai Pudong to Los Angeles service from three to five weekly flights starting October 7.

FedEx said the capacity was announced by FedEx China president Poh-Yian Koh, who said that the rapid growth of AI and other advanced technologies is reshaping semiconductor supply chains across the Asia-Pacific. Koh said China remains central to this ecosystem as both a major market and manufacturing hub, and that businesses need greater speed, visibility and resilience as supply chains become more interconnected. Guo Jia, a veteran market insider, told the Global Times that air cargo is the most sensitive gauge of China-US trade and that the added freighter capacity signals two-way demand persists. A joint FedEx and Frost & Sullivan report released in October found that the Chinese mainland accounts for more than half of the Asia-Pacific semiconductor market and nearly 30 percent of the global market. Investinglive noted that FedEx's move came against a backdrop of US AI stocks selling off sharply the previous week.

China's total trade with the US reached $522 billion in the first 10 months of 2026, a year-on-year increase of 11 percent, according to the General Administration of Customs of China. In October alone, China-US trade totaled $60.12 billion, with China's exports to the US at $46.41 billion and its imports from the US at $13.71 billion. US all-cargo carriers have also opened new freight routes in China, and on October 14 Ezhou Huahu International Airport received a Boeing 747 freighter from Los Angeles operated by Western Global Airlines, its 31st cargo airline. Passenger travel between the two economies is also expanding, with Delta operating 19 weekly nonstop flights between the Chinese mainland and the US. Investinglive reported that US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to meet on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen in mid-November, and that trade is likely to feature.

stories.Headline: Reddit is turning user conversations into AI-powered product reviews
stories.Summary:
Reddit has launched a feature called Reddit Reviews, which gathers conversations about products from across its communities and organizes them into dedicated product pages. The company introduced the tool on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, after first testing it since February with U.S. users in areas such as Electronics, Video Games, and Health & Beauty. The test later expanded in September to include Home & Garden and Fashion & Apparel. Reddit now says the feature is rolling out to all U.S. users on iOS, Android, and web, starting with around 10,000 products.

The feature uses AI to sort through the comments people write about how products work for them, why they fail, and what trade-offs buyers should consider. Each product page shows a summary under a "what people are saying" heading, along with a visual breakdown of how many comments are positive, negative, or mixed. Users can filter comments by topic, open the original conversation to ask questions, and move back to the full category to compare similar products. Some pages also link to retailers, and Reddit says it will not take a cut of those sales and that merchants cannot pay to be included.

Reddit's announcement presents the feature as an extension of how people already use the platform to learn what products are really like. The company is also aware that generative AI and bots make the platform vulnerable to astroturfing, the practice of brands faking public support. Reddit says it will rely on its rules, its recent measures against automated abuse and spam, and the work of community moderators to keep the reviews legitimate. Moderators have told reporters they have found brands trying to promote products covertly on popular subreddits.

The launch comes just before the busy holiday shopping season, when many people research products online before making larger purchases. The Verge reported that Reddit told it in August that 40 percent of conversations on the platform were commercial in nature. Because the company now formalizes product research into structured pages, it may face more pressure from specialist review outlets and general news sites that publish reviews. Reddit has also positioned its human-written comments as a check on AI-generated recommendations, though the articles do not say how the company will measure the success of that approach.
