stories.Headline: PAM: Securing Digital Identities In The Age Of AI
stories.Summary:
The National Institute of Standards and Technology, known as NIST, has proposed ten principles for managing the identities and permissions of autonomous artificial intelligence agents. The recommendations were published on October 27, and they address how organizations can securely authorize AI systems to act on behalf of individuals and businesses. Unlike traditional software, these agents can make decisions, interact with several applications, and carry out complex tasks with limited human supervision. The proposal is part of a broader federal effort to define how such systems are identified and controlled.

The framework asks that each agent receive a distinct digital identity, so that an organization can verify which system is acting, who authorized it, and what it is allowed to do. The ten areas cover assigning unique identities, limiting permissions, establishing accountability, managing access credentials, and monitoring activity. It also calls for the ability to revoke authorization when needed and for continued human oversight of sensitive operations. NIST describes these as technical guidelines rather than binding laws. The emphasis reflects growing use of AI in financial transactions, business operations, and online services, where secure digital identification could become essential.

The principles were issued by NIST, the federal agency responsible for developing measurement and cybersecurity standards. The agency framed them as design tenets for agent identity management systems and placed them on its cybersecurity insights blog. Coverage of the proposal appeared in Biometric Update on November 3. The article under review also draws a comparison to Isaac Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics, while noting that NIST's guidance is not a legal code for robot behavior. Its author links the question of machine accountability to broader concerns about autonomous systems.

The article then connects the NIST work to Revelation 13:16–17, which describes a future system in which people must receive a mark to buy or sell. It argues that digital credentials and automated authorization illustrate the infrastructure through which such restrictions could become technically possible. The article itself states that NIST's recommendations are not the mark of the beast. The articles do not describe any scheduled next steps for the NIST framework beyond its publication as a proposal.

stories.Headline: Update: China's foreign trade growth picks up pace on stellar imports, booming AI demand - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
China's foreign trade in goods kept strong momentum in the first 10 months of 2026, with imports rising sharply and demand for artificial intelligence lifting exports of electronic components, official data showed on Tuesday. Total imports and exports grew 20 percent year on year to 44.81 trillion yuan, about 6.67 trillion U.S. dollars, accelerating from 18.8 percent in the first nine months. Imports surged 23.6 percent while exports rose 17.6 percent over the January-October period, according to the General Administration of Customs. Both imports and exports have posted double-digit growth for six straight months through October, and goods trade expanded 31.2 percent in October alone.

Imports from more than 150 countries and regions grew, and imports from ASEAN, Latin America and Africa all reached record highs for the period. Mechanical and electrical products rose 25.2 percent in exports and made up 64.7 percent of total exports, up 3.9 percentage points from a year earlier. Exports of integrated circuits and memory components jumped 101.9 percent and 132.5 percent, respectively. Exports of electric vehicles, photovoltaic products and lithium batteries grew 46.5 percent, and wind turbines and their components gained 19.7 percent.

Lyu Daliang, director of the customs administration's Department of Statistics and Analysis, said the trade had shown greater resilience and vitality this year. Wang Qing, chief macro analyst at Golden Credit Rating, said the global AI investment boom kept pushing up prices of chips and other electronic components and computer parts, while domestic manufacturing upgrades improved the competitiveness of new energy vehicles and high-tech products. Zhang Di, a macro analyst at China Galaxy Securities, said China would keep benefiting as a global hub of electronics supply chains while the AI cycle stays in an upswing. Zhang added that the green transition and rising competitiveness in mechanical equipment would sustain growth in new energy vehicles and ships.

Trade with ASEAN grew 24.2 percent in the first 10 months, trade with the European Union rose 8.5 percent, and trade with the United States expanded 6.3 percent. Trade with Belt and Road participating countries grew 18.5 percent over the same period. Experts expect strong exports to extend through the end of the year. Separately, an AMRO blog post by Allen Ng and Haobin Wang said Thailand's real GDP grew 2.4 percent in the first half of 2026 despite an energy shock from the Middle East conflict. Private investment expanded 11.6 percent, and Board of Investment digital-sector applications reached THB 1.12 trillion, already above the THB 746 billion recorded for all of 2025.

The authors said Thailand's growth rests on a narrow set of drivers, while traditional industries remain under pressure, household incomes are subdued and lending to smaller firms keeps shrinking. Public debt sits near its statutory ceiling of 70 percent of GDP, limiting fiscal room to cushion shocks. AMRO estimates Thailand's potential growth has fallen from around 7 percent before the Asian Financial Crisis to below 3 percent today. Global producers in Thailand already supply several data-center components, and exports of AI-enabling goods rose about 50 percent in 2025. The authors recommended supplier development, wider access to cloud and AI services, and broader investment beyond AI, and said the 14th National Economic and Social Development Plan offers a timely framework to coordinate these efforts.

The products are Lunit INSIGHT CXR for chest X-rays and Lunit INSIGHT MMG for mammography. The deal will be carried out through stc Group's ICT subsidiary, Solutions by stc, which will act as systems integrator while Lunit provides the AI licenses. Lunit's tools will connect to MNGHA's existing picture archiving and communication system, so local staff can see AI results without leaving their current reading environment.

MNGHA is the medical organization under the Ministry of National Guard, which oversees the Saudi Arabian National Guard, and it has served National Guard personnel, their families and the public since 1982. It runs hospitals and medical centers in major regions, centered on Riyadh and Jeddah. The company says MNGHA is recognized for its global competitiveness in digital healthcare, and King Abdulaziz Medical City Riyadh became the first in the world to reach Stage 7, the highest grade, in four categories of the HIMSS digital maturity assessment in 2022. Lunit has built a presence in Saudi Arabia before this deal. In 2023 it took part in the SEHA Virtual Hospital project and a healthcare sandbox program under Vision 2030, and it supplied Lunit INSIGHT MMG to Dr. Sulaiman Al Habib Medical Group.

Suh Beom-seok, Lunit's chief executive, said MNGHA is one of the world's most advanced digital medical systems and that the agreement was reached because of Lunit's technology and its ability to integrate with large-scale medical systems. He said the company would expand its presence in the Saudi healthcare market through its partnership with a leading local ICT company and broaden the reach of AI cancer screening across the Middle East. Lunit plans to accelerate its push into Saudi Arabia and the wider region as the Saudi government pursues digital transformation of healthcare as a core task of Vision 2030. AuntMinnie reported the same agreement on November 9, 2026, noting that the products will be integrated into MNGHA's PACS so clinicians can view AI results within current workflows.

stories.Headline: AI Voiceover: Faster, Cheaper… But Better?
stories.Summary:
AI voiceover is being weighed by game developers against three familiar priorities: time, cost and quality. Writing in a thought leadership piece published on 10 November 2026 by Bo Crutcher, Studio Head at Blindlight, a Keywords Studios company, the author argues that AI does not simply make voice production faster or cheaper. Crutcher notes that some writers prefer realistic AI placeholders to inform their writing, while others choose robotic voices so that an imperfect imitation does not shape creative decisions. The core question posed is whether AI changes the traditional time-cost-quality balance or merely introduces new trade-offs. The author draws on experience across film, television and video game casting, voiceover and performance capture.

On time, the article says AI can speed up stages such as generating temporary dialogue, prototyping characters without booking sessions, and testing dialogue timing. It also adds work, including prompting and refining synthetic performances, reviewing output and integrating it into existing pipelines. On cost, AI can lower the expense of temporary dialogue and early recording, but developers must also account for licensing, subscription and computing charges, engineering, quality assurance and legal compliance. The article distinguishes scripted AI voiceover, which can be reviewed before release, from dynamic dialogue generated during play, which may carry ongoing expenses for years. Crutcher points to Character AI as an example of the financial pressure on generative platforms, where infrastructure costs can run into millions of dollars a month.

The article separates quality into intelligibility, naturalism and dramatic performance, arguing that natural-sounding speech is not the same as compelling acting. It says the right standard depends on use, with accessibility narration, background NPC lines and major cinematic performances each needing different things. Dynamic dialogue adds concerns about narrative consistency, character memory and the risk of a character inventing information. The author also stresses rights and consent: permission to record a performer does not automatically authorise a digital replica, and SAG-AFTRA signatory productions must follow contractual terms while nonunion productions must address consent, licensing and applicable law. Crutcher concludes that the central question for developers is whether AI helps them deliver the experience they intend, and that it does not remove the decisions about time, investment and quality.

stories.Headline: AI giant Anthropic sets prices for initial public offering

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company, still plans to go public later this month, according to a Wall Street Journal report cited by Gizmodo published on November 9, 2026. The company's shares, which would trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, could become available as soon as October 19 or 20, though the report's dates appear inconsistent with its November timing. Expectations for the offering have fallen sharply, with the valuation once speculated at roughly $2 trillion now seen by investors as nearer $1.5 trillion, and CNBC reporting on a range of $1 trillion to $1.25 trillion as more likely. The shift followed a rough stretch for AI-linked stocks, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq posting its worst month in quite a while in October.

Those market losses have hit chipmakers particularly hard, and Nvidia's share price fell from an all-time high of $243.37 on October 6 to $204 at the end of that month and closed at $178.67 on Monday, November 9. Nvidia also faced separate turmoil that day after reports that CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, and investors worry he may have harmed U.S. national security by selling AI technology to an intermediary for the Chinese government. Huang has publicly apologized to his wife and children. President Donald Trump said at a press conference that the FBI was investigating the matter, and he expressed hope that no problem existed while describing Huang as suffering greatly.

Anthropic's regulatory filings show $33 billion in revenue from January to September 2026, and those same filings state that AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. The article notes that investors are nervous about the AI trade overall, since the fortunes of major stock market indexes depend heavily on these companies succeeding. Rival OpenAI confidentially filed to go public in June, but the article says it will not list before the end of the year. The author suggests the more probable danger is an AI arms race that places powerful hacking tools in the hands of bad actors, which could disrupt the U.S. financial system.

stories.Headline: Israel Plans National AI Model to Reduce Foreign Dependence, Protect Control of Critical Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Israel plans to build its own national artificial intelligence model to reduce reliance on foreign technology and keep control of critical infrastructure. Brig. Gen. (res.) Erez Askal, head of the National AI Directorate in the Prime Minister's Office, presented the plan on November 9, 2026, at AI Week at Tel Aviv University.

He said the country's AI systems would need to stay under national control, warning that the government would otherwise lose control over essential services. The announcement came as officials worry that AI is becoming central to electricity, water and health care. Askal's concern is that commercial providers may have interests that differ from those of the governments they serve. The proposed infrastructure is large and costly. Askal said Israel would need about 2 gigawatts of electricity capacity to support AI computing facilities, data centers and semiconductor manufacturing.

The plan also calls for roughly 300,000 graphics processing units, with about 100,000 serving domestic needs such as universities, government agencies, the military and startups. A nationally controlled foundation model, the underlying technology behind applications such as chatbots, is also part of the strategy. Askal did not give a budget or timetable for these targets during his presentation. He added that the government has issued a tender for an Israeli-built national quantum computer. Askal framed the effort as a matter of sovereignty, arguing that governments cannot be sure foreign AI services will remain available or aligned with their needs.

He said Israel does not intend to produce every component itself or cut off international markets, only to control the critical elements. He also suggested the country might build its advanced model with allied nations facing similar challenges. Askal said AI could help solve practical problems, and a new body, the National Institute for Impact-Driven Artificial Intelligence, will coordinate ministries, businesses and universities on projects in health care, education and transportation. He also called for workforce retraining and clear rules on cybersecurity and accountability. The strategy comes as countries worldwide grapple with the influence of major technology companies over AI infrastructure and computing resources.

The institute plans 10 to 14 initiatives a year, aiming to move five of its first 10 projects into implementation within one year. Askal's broader five-year framework targets 10 challenges annually, with examples such as improving fourth-grade mathematics and reducing congestion on Highway 6. Whether Israel can secure the electricity, hardware, investment and partnerships needed remains unresolved. Askal summed up his position by saying that countries that act will keep control, and that Israel has decided to act.

stories.Headline: Sierra Leone's President Julius Maada Bio Calls For Stronger Global Cooperation On Frontier AI Security, Demands Greater African Voice In Global Governance – Office of the President of Sierra Leone
stories.Summary:
Sierra Leone's President Julius Maada Bio has urged stronger international cooperation on the safe and responsible development of frontier artificial intelligence, while insisting that African and other developing countries must help write the global standards. He made the call on 9 November 2026 while addressing a high-level virtual meeting convened by French President Emmanuel Macron. Bio reaffirmed that the development and use of AI must stay under human direction, oversight and control. He recalled that Sierra Leone had endorsed the Call for Control of Frontier AI Models at a United Nations General Assembly roundtable in September, which Kenya and Finland co-hosted.

The President outlined what international cooperation should involve, including common and credible standards for evaluating advanced AI models, clear accountability among developers and deployers, and mechanisms for reporting serious incidents and sharing information on emerging threats. He argued that independent evaluation, transparency and coordinated responses matter because the benefits and risks of capable AI systems cross national borders. He also said that developing countries need investment in scientific expertise, institutional capacity and evaluation tools so they can assess AI systems used within their own jurisdictions. Bio welcomed the proposed Paris Declaration and called for its commitments to be turned into practical measures backed by credible evaluation and timely information sharing.

Bio described Sierra Leone's domestic progress, saying the country has completed a National AI Readiness Assessment that will inform its first National AI Strategy. He explained that the government is studying how AI could improve agriculture, healthcare, education and public service delivery, and noted work through ECOWAS on a proposed Regional Data Embassy Framework that would protect national control over data. He stated that the country must build safety, security and accountability into its approach from the outset. He also stressed that sovereignty means choosing the terms on which countries work together, not doing everything alone.

The meeting included several heads of government and ministers, among them the prime ministers of the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, Norway and the Netherlands, the Finnish President, the United States Treasury Secretary and the Crown Prince and Prime Minister of Bahrain. Senior representatives of technology firms, including Microsoft, OpenAI and Mistral AI, also took part. The discussions build on earlier efforts by Norway and Finland to strengthen safety protocols and independent testing for powerful AI systems. For Africa, the debate ties into economic opportunity, digital sovereignty and the need to avoid simply adopting standards set elsewhere.

stories.Headline: Anthropic wants Claude to join your meetings
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced several new workplace features on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, according to TechCrunch reporter Aisha Malik. The most prominent is Claude Meetings, which brings Claude into video calls so it can begin working on tasks while participants are still talking. The company also unveiled Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets. The launch comes just weeks after OpenAI rolled out its own workplace tools, and it places Anthropic among several firms competing to turn their products into office suites that rival Microsoft and Google.

With Claude Meetings, a team can add Claude to a call as a visible participant, and it follows the conversation and works in real time. It can draft the plan under discussion, map out a timeline on a whiteboard, answer questions in the meeting chat, and pull information from connected work apps. Afterward, the meeting notes, action items, and other materials are available in claude.ai. Claude identifies itself in the meeting chat, will not join calls with external guests unless an admin authorizes it, and leaves automatically if an external guest joins.

The feature is in beta on Team and Enterprise plans and works with Google Meet for now. Claude Whiteboards is a shared board where teams can talk through a plan and have Claude turn it into an organized visual workspace with timelines and deadlines, and the board can be converted into a document or slide deck when finished. Claude Sheets lets teams create and edit spreadsheets collaboratively, such as a campaign tracker or hiring budget, with each change outlined so users can see what Claude did. Both are in beta on paid plans across web, desktop, and mobile.

Anthropic also made Claude Data, formerly called Claude Dashboards, generally available, along with interactive connectors that open full versions of apps like Adobe, Atlassian, and HubSpot inside Claude. The articles report the announcements as Anthropic's own, and they describe the company's stated goal of turning discussions into actions during the meeting rather than afterward. The articles also note that Meta has entered the same race with its Muse AI agent, which can build mini-apps on the fly. They do not say when support for additional calling platforms or plans will arrive beyond the note that it is expected to follow.

stories.Summary:
Samsung SDI has won a CES 2027 Innovation Award for its SDI U8A3-UPS, a prismatic battery solution that supplies emergency power to artificial intelligence data centers. The Consumer Technology Association announced the award on November 9 local time, and Samsung SDI reported it on November 10. The product was selected in the Enterprise Tech category. The award marks the third year in a row that the company has been recognized at the event, having first entered in 2025.

A UPS, or uninterruptible power supply, is a battery system that provides emergency power to key facilities such as data centers when a blackout suddenly cuts off the main supply. The product uses prismatic battery cells with a lithium manganese oxide chemistry. Samsung SDI says it delivers ultra-high output and high energy density, improving space efficiency by 33 percent over existing products. This allows a data center to supply power stably with fewer batteries. When power demand surges during AI computation, the system supplies auxiliary power to prevent server failures and data damage.

The product also passed a large-scale fire test for indoor facilities run by UL Solutions, a global safety certification body. Samsung SDI says it was the first product in the world to meet all of the test's evaluation criteria. The company said the award recognizes the innovativeness of a core power solution for the AI era. A company representative said Samsung SDI will continue to lead the market with products that combine the performance and safety customers require. The Korea Herald reported that the award reflects the technology's potential as a power solution for the AI era, according to a Samsung SDI official.

At CES 2026, Samsung SDI received a Best of Innovation award for its ultra-high-output cylindrical battery, the SDI 25U-Power. It also received an Innovation Award for its thermal propagation blocking technology, called No TP, which is designed to keep fires from spreading between battery cells. The Korea Herald reported the same technology under the name No Thermal Propagation. CES 2027 will be held in Las Vegas, United States, in January next year.

stories.Headline: David Ellison Is Very Bullish On AI’s Creative Potential
stories.Summary:
Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison said on his company's first earnings call as head of both Paramount and Warner Bros. that artificial intelligence could become the biggest creative breakthrough in modern Hollywood history. The remarks came on November 9, 2026, and drew on his view that AI would help studios make content faster and more cheaply. He also drew a line against what he called low-quality "AI slop," saying premium, hand-crafted storytelling would remain valuable. The comments were made while he was pitching the merged company as a tech-forward enterprise.

Ellison compared AI to the arrival of CGI and digital composites in the early 1990s, which he credited with enabling films such as Jurassic Park and Terminator 2. He argued that the tools could make budgets more manageable, using James Cameron's original Terminator, made for about $4 million in 1983, as an example. By his estimate, a shot-for-shot remake today would cost $60 million to $70 million. He said these tools could help the company take bigger creative risks on original stories. Skydance plans to spend $30 billion a year across its content portfolio.

Ellison framed AI as a tool for artists rather than a replacement for them, and he said the company has been building its own AI tools. He also said that franchise intellectual property, which he described as the company having 40 franchises worth $1 billion each, would act as a protective barrier against the flood of AI-generated content. Skydance is also seeking about $6 billion in cost savings from combining Paramount and Warner Bros., with AI workflows scaled across the company. He said that merging Paramount+ and HBO Max within a year was an "ambitious target" made possible by the latest AI tools. He has also been backed publicly by Cameron, whose own studio recently bought an AI-driven 3D post-production firm.

Industry reaction is divided, as the technology is widely seen as a threat to traditional Hollywood production methods while also being adopted by studios. Netflix has used AI on more than 300 titles through a VFX firm associated with Ben Affleck, according to the reporting. The articles do not say how the combined company will balance these competing pressures in practice. The companies have also said that a bundle of HBO Max and Paramount+ would launch in early 2027.

stories.Headline: The Odds of an AI Bubble-Bursting Event Appear to Be Sharply Rising
stories.Summary:
A Motley Fool piece published Nov. 10, 2026, by analyst Sean Williams argues that the odds of an AI bubble-bursting event are rising, pointing to three developments. The first came on Election Night, when Democrats retook both houses of Congress in the midterms and Democratic candidates flipped at least five governorships previously held by Republicans, with two races still uncalled by the Associated Press as of Nov. 6. The flipped seats include Texas, Georgia and Ohio, all central to data center planning and construction. Williams also points to tightening lending conditions for so-called neoclouds and some large cloud companies, along with a stock market that is historically expensive.

On the numbers, Cleanview data cited in the article says 41% of America's planned data center capacity, or 158.6 GW across nine states, sits in states where the governor backs a pause on development. Texas leads with 88.4 GW, followed by Ohio at 21.9 GW, Georgia at 20.2 GW, New Mexico at 11.0 GW and New York at 9.9 GW. Williams notes that President Donald Trump has pledged to minimize AI regulation and threatened to use his veto to keep the status quo in Congress, but that a veto cannot touch state-level changes made by Democratic governors. He adds that the market entered 2026 at its second-highest valuation in 156 years by the Shiller price-to-earnings ratio. That measure has topped 30 during a continuous bull market six times in the past century, including now, and the previous five were followed by declines of 20% or more in at least one major index.

Several people and groups are named as responsible for the shifts. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has vowed to impose a moratorium on new data center approvals until the legislature passes laws covering electricity and water rights, among other issues. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, speaking after the Federal Open Market Committee's Oct. 28 meeting, said interest rates have had an effect and that market participants are discriminating between the kinds of investments they want to make. He said credit spreads for certain assets have widened sharply, which Williams reads as a sign that borrowing is becoming less favorable for neoclouds, a view he says is backed by falling corporate bond prices for those firms and some hyperscalers.

A second article, from the Idaho Dispatch on Nov. 6, looks at the same risk locally, citing an October 2026 report from the Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund that warns heavy, debt-financed AI spending could cause problems well beyond the technology industry. In Idaho, data center projects qualifying with at least $250 million in investment and 30 jobs can receive sales tax exemptions, and bills to cap that break failed in 2025 and 2026. Lawmakers did pass House Bill 911 in 2026 to keep the costs of serving large electricity customers from falling on existing ratepayers, and House Bill 895 to limit certain water use for cooling new data centers. A federal lawsuit filed in September over Idaho's authority to administer federal water rights at Idaho National Laboratory, and a Bannock County moratorium on data center permit applications in unincorporated areas, show the debate there is still unfolding.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Latest Fable 5.2 is a Crippled Model 3 Early and They Have Model 4 Internally
stories.Summary:
Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on November 9, 2026, two versions of the same underlying model. The company says the models are designed for difficult technical work and show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision. In one test, Fable 5.2 formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean in 30 hours, using about 1,000 AI agents with minimal human intervention. The previous system needed 11 days for a comparable task, used roughly three times more action tokens, and produced a proof seven times longer.

Anthropic reports that over 90% of changes merged into its core codebase are now written by Claude, with human guidance. Beyond that, the articles describe several demonstrations. Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics about black holes using holographic duality, one completing a 2003 calculation and the other finding the exact limit of a technique used for over 15 years to rule out candidate quantum gravity theories. Mythos 5.2 accurately modeled 28 of 34 adeno-associated virus capsid structures it attempted, which biologists could use to design gene therapy delivery shells faster and more cheaply. One engineer used Fable 5.2 to coordinate more than 1,000 subagents for eight days to build a bootable prototype operating system from an empty folder.

The articles also describe Anthropic's decision to limit certain capabilities during training. Anthropic says it deliberately restricted the capabilities that most directly speed up AI development, namely accelerator kernel optimization and LLM architecture improvement, holding them at about Opus 5.5 level. The articles report that Fable 5.2 scored 74.2% on Humanity's Last Exam with tools. Anthropic is the company responsible for these releases, and the articles quote its statements about the models and their training.

The articles attribute the acceleration claims to METR, an independent assessor, which found that Anthropic's models are improving at about twice the previous rate, with roughly 80% of that acceleration attributed to AI itself. METR reported that staff self-reported speedups reached about 12 times for an internal model called Model 4, and it found "signs of life" for fully autonomous AI contributions to the training pipeline. METR also found no convincing bottlenecks for the next 12 months. One Anthropic researcher is quoted as saying the company is now "only bottlenecked on ideas & compute, no longer bottlenecked on code."

According to the articles, Model 4 is an internal, unreleased Anthropic model identified in METR's October 2026 assessment, which finished training between September and October 2026. It was the first model in METR's test set to score above 50% on all 15 benchmarks evaluated. Model 4, along with internal predecessors METR calls Model 2 and Model 3, comes from METR's report, and Anthropic has not confirmed Model 4 publicly. Anthropic gave METR access to internal data but redacted significant portions of the underlying evidence before publication. The articles state that Fable 5.2 is Model 3 Early.

METR uses "AI R&D acceleration" to mean AI systems helping speed up research and the building of better AI, as opposed to speedups from buying more computing power. Its estimate that about 80% of recent capability gains come from this effect carries real uncertainty, according to the articles. The articles describe this as an early form of recursive self-improvement under the definition used by Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis: AI making researchers several times more productive while humans review and direct the work. A "closed loop" version, where AI does research without human review, has not been confirmed in METR's findings, though the report notes early signs of more autonomous contributions.

stories.Headline: Gix Internet: Quantum X Labs Expands AI-Powered Quantum Error Correction Program to Three IBM Quantum Processors
stories.Summary:
Quantum X Labs, a Nasdaq-listed quantum technology company, announced on November 9, 2026 that it had expanded its AI-powered quantum error correction program to datasets from three IBM quantum processors: IBM Fez, IBM Kingston and IBM Pittsburgh. In preliminary benchmarks using experimental data from these processors, the company reported up to 20% fewer logical decoding failures. The company said the results came from its noise-model calibration method, which is meant to help decoders find and fix errors that occur during quantum computations. A later release dated November 10, 2026 repeated these findings from Gix Internet Ltd., which holds about 13% of the company, or 2,818,585 shares. The expanded work builds on earlier research that used experimental surface-code datasets linked to Google's quantum hardware.

The expansion matters because the company is testing its approach across more than one hardware vendor and code family. Its stated goal is hardware-agnostic error correction that can adapt to different architectures and noise characteristics. The benchmarking workflow now connects experimental quantum measurements, noise-model calibration, GPU-accelerated AI training and decoder performance evaluation. The company described the work as one step toward more reliable and scalable quantum computing systems. Quantum processors are sensitive to environmental interference, hardware imperfections and operational noise, which can introduce errors and limit their practical reliability.

Prof. Nir Sharon, the company's Chief Quantum Scientist, said that improving logical decoding performance on different processors is an important step toward fault-tolerant quantum computing across the industry. He said that as processors grow in size and complexity, efficient error correction is expected to become essential to practical systems. The releases attribute the announcements to the company itself and to Gix, with Gix describing the results as preliminary and warning that any benefit to QXL may not translate into value for Gix's investment. Both releases include forward-looking statements and caution that actual results may differ materially.

The articles do not say whether the results have been independently verified or when the company expects them to be published in peer-reviewed form. Gix Internet, a separately listed technology company focused on hospital logistics automation through its deliverz.ai subsidiary, presented the milestone as part of its minority stake in Quantum X Labs. The articles frame the work as part of a broader strategy to develop quantum infrastructure and software for more commercially viable platforms. They do not describe specific product launches, commercial timelines or further benchmark dates beyond the current preliminary results.

stories.Headline: Lawyers need AI education, not AI legislation
stories.Summary:
Nicole Black, a Rochester, New York attorney and Legal Tech correspondent, argues in a November 9, 2026 column that lawyers do not need new ethics rules, opinions or laws governing generative AI. She says AI is simply a new technology and no different, for the purposes of practicing law, than the tools that preceded it. In her view, existing ethics rules and opinions already give lawyers enough guidance on confidentiality and competence. She says she is in the minority on this point.

Black notes that bar associations have issued at least twenty ethics opinions and guides on AI since ChatGPT's public release in November 2022. She says that pace and volume far exceed what came with earlier technologies. California, she writes, has taken the unusual step of passing a law regulating AI use by its practitioners. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed bill SB 574 on September 30, and it will likely take effect January 1, 2027.

Black says the California law reiterates existing ethical obligations. It forbids lawyers from delegating the practice of law to AI and bars entering confidential or nonpublic information into systems not restricted to authorized persons. The law also requires lawyers to verify the accuracy of AI outputs, correct hallucinated output, and personally verify every citation in filings, including citations supplied by AI. Black calls these duties of competence, supervision and responsibility for court filings that already exist.

Black also objects to a provision requiring lawyers to disclose AI use to the court for all documents submitted, and to consider disclosure when AI creates content provided to the public. She says AI is already built into most technologies lawyers use, so courts should simply assume lawyers have used it. She adds that many recent ethics opinions already contain this requirement, which makes it duplicative. She concludes the law is unnecessary and discourages technology adoption.

Black writes that knee-jerk reactions to technology are not uncommon in the legal profession but rarely survive the test of time. She cites email, the internet, social media and cloud computing as examples, where initial requirements such as client consent often gave way as the technologies became routine. She expects the same to happen with AI, and faster than before, since it is already embedded in nearly every technology used in law firms. She argues that the wiser course is to double down on education so lawyers can use technology to serve clients better. She says she hopes other states will not follow California's lead, though she is not optimistic.

stories.Headline: Forbes' First Top Lawyers For AI List Has A Gender Story And A Map
stories.Summary:
Forbes published its first America's Top Lawyers For AI list this week, and it shows that women hold 18 of the 50 spots. The list names attorneys who litigate against and defend the largest companies in artificial intelligence, as well as lawyers who advise firms on how AI products must comply with the rules. Forbes made the ranking as a companion to its 2026 AI 50, a list of the most promising private AI startups, where women lead just four companies. The article notes that the lawyers on this list are the ones deciding what AI development will cost to carry out.

Among the copyright disputes highlighted, Jennifer Maisel of Rothwell Figg represents The New York Times and other newspapers in their suits against OpenAI and Microsoft. Davida Brook of Susman Godfrey also represents the Times. On the defense side, Angela Dunning of Cleary Gottlieb helped Meta win a ruling in Kadrey v. Meta, in which a federal judge found that training on books was fair use. Annette Hurst of Orrick led the team that won Microsoft and GitHub the first federal appeals court decision on generative AI, in September 2026.

Women are also prominent in advisory work, where nine of the 22 lawyers in that category are women. Anna Gressel of Freshfields focuses on agentic AI, systems that take action, and Maneesha Mithal of Wilson Sonsini co-chairs a privacy practice that handles government investigations into AI. Katherine Forrest of Paul, Weiss is a former federal judge, and Kathi Vidal of Winston Taylor previously led the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. Geographically, Palo Alto is the only place where women make up the majority of honorees, with five of its six. Across the Bay Area women hold 8 of 15 spots, but outside that region they hold 10 of 35, and cities such as Chicago, Seattle and Houston have only male honorees.

The article points out gaps as well: none of the five honorees in technology transactions, project finance or appellate work is a woman, and those are the practices tied most directly to financing AI's expansion. The author notes that 18 of 50, or 36%, is not parity, though it exceeds the 26.5% share of equity partner seats women held at U.S. law firms in 2025, according to NALP. Forbes describes the list as a sign that women are prominent among the lawyers managing AI's legal risks even as they are absent from the deal work. The article suggests that as AI moves from writing to acting, the risk side of that work will keep growing.

stories.Headline: Elizabeth Warren Slams Trump for 'Wining and Dining' AI Billionaires Instead of Protecting Americans: 'It Needs to Stop'
stories.Summary:
Senator Elizabeth Warren criticized President Donald Trump on a Sunday post on X, saying his administration is favoring wealthy tech executives over public safety and national security. In that post, dated November 8, 2026, she called for stronger government oversight of advanced artificial intelligence and warned that weak rules could leave Americans exposed. She said the president was taking a hands-off approach to the technology while cultivating relationships with industry leaders. Her message framed the issue as one of governing versus courting billionaires, and she ended by calling for the practice to stop.

Warren said that instead of setting rules, Trump was hosting AI billionaires and letting them do as they wish. She argued that this approach put the American people and national security at risk. Her call was for strong rules to limit advanced AI and protect people. The articles do not describe any specific bill, deadline, or dollar figure tied to her demand, so her criticism rests on the call for tighter oversight.

Warren's criticism follows several other moves the articles describe. Last month, Trump said he planned to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in government documents and signed an executive order directing federal agencies to use that terminology. The administration also planned to move three senior officials from the Commerce Department's Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence to the White House after coordination problems. Other Democrats have raised related concerns, including Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna, who questioned the role of tech executives in shaping AI rules.

Sanders accused Google of pressuring schools to adopt AI by threatening to cut off Google Search access if they restricted student use, which he called extortion. Khanna criticized a voluntary AI agreement he said Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg helped draft, warning that tech billionaires should not write their own industry rules. The articles present these disputes as part of an ongoing debate over whether AI should be governed by federal rules or left largely to industry. They do not report any final resolution of these disputes or any scheduled vote.

stories.Headline: Chimes AI Achieves 2.9x Faster AI Inference with FPT AI Factory
stories.Summary:
Chimes AI, a Taiwan-recognized startup, announced on November 10, 2026 that it is using the GPU computing power of FPT AI Factory to speed up generative AI applications on its Tukey platform. The collaboration came in a release issued from Hanoi, Vietnam, and was described as strengthening Chimes AI's technology and supporting its push into industrial and manufacturing markets in Vietnam and across the region. Tukey was built to handle factory tasks such as predictive health management, failure risk prediction, parameter optimization, and virtual quality prediction. The platform is meant to help manufacturers shift from reactive maintenance to proactive, data-driven operations.

The article explains that equipment inspection and maintenance in sectors such as food processing, electronics, and semiconductors still depend heavily on manual work and the experience of engineering teams. Machine learning can flag anomalies or predict failures, but engineers must still find root causes, review standard operating procedures, search maintenance records, and decide on fixes. Chimes AI added generative AI to Tukey so that it interprets alerts, performs root cause analysis, retrieves relevant procedures and records, and produces prioritized maintenance recommendations. In the company's validation, its industrial AI solution reached over 90% anomaly detection accuracy, cut unplanned downtime by up to 30%, and reduced maintenance labor time by up to 50%. The approach is also said to lessen reliance on a few senior experts by making embedded knowledge available across operations teams.

Running these workloads demanded more computing power, since large language model inference, long-context processing, and retrieval-augmented generation need high-performance GPU infrastructure. Chimes AI moved to NVIDIA H100 GPUs on FPT AI Factory, where it deploys the Qwen3.6-27B model with vLLM. In a 2K-input benchmark, end-to-end latency fell from 9.54 seconds to 3.28 seconds, roughly 2.9 times faster. Dora Hsieh, Executive Assistant to the CEO at Chimes AI, said FPT AI Factory delivered a smooth, low-latency inference experience that met the company's expectations and gave it a solid base for next-generation industrial generative AI services. The article adds that FPT AI Factory, with infrastructure in Vietnam and Japan, is positioned as a high-performance option for AI companies and startups expanding across Asia-Pacific.

stories.Headline: Bill Gates Microsoft Copilot AI Predicts a SOL Crypto Explosion
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates' Microsoft Copilot AI has projected that Solana could reach between $1,000 and $2,000 by January 1, 2027, with a stretch target above $2,500, according to a November 9, 2026 report. The forecast rests on a hypothetical scenario in which a return of a strong crypto bull market is driven by a groundbreaking event. At the time of the report, SOL was trading near $87, so reaching the stretch target would require a gain of roughly 25 times. The report itself describes the prediction as intentionally extreme and well beyond typical forecasts.

The AI expects a major global consortium to adopt Solana as its main high-throughput blockchain for consumer apps and real-time payments. In that scenario, demand for the token would rise both as a tool for transactions and as a speculative asset. The technical picture is less dramatic, with Solana consolidating between $70 and $75 after recovering key levels. A sustained break above $100 to $120 would open a path toward its prior all-time high near $296, and the report says a move into the $1,000 range would need a dramatic expansion of real-world and consumer activity. Nearer-term support sits between $100 and $115.

Several recent developments are cited as possible near-term catalysts. Formation Securities has told the SEC it plans to run the first tokenized securities venue on Solana, targeting early 2027, and intends to list tokenized shares of companies including Galaxy Digital, Exodus, and Forward Industries. Asset manager Schroders has also placed an emerging-markets debt fund on-chain through Centrifuge on Solana. On the payments side, Samsung Wallet has launched USDC accounts on Solana for eligible U.S. Galaxy users, letting them buy, hold, send, and receive the stablecoin. The report also points to technical upgrades, including target slot times cut to 200 milliseconds and the Alpenglow consensus upgrade, which aims for about 150-millisecond finality.

Breakpoint 2026 in London, scheduled for November 15 to 17, is expected to draw builders, institutions, and policymakers, and could bring new announcements. The report concludes that these real-world asset, payments, technical, and event-driven developments could together support renewed upward pressure on SOL. It also notes that the multi-thousand-percent gains implied by the Copilot targets would require an extraordinary surge in real-world adoption. The article carries a standard disclaimer that crypto is high-risk and that investors could lose all their capital.

stories.Headline: Wall St brokerages say AI selloff overdone, downplay Democratic regulation risks - CNA
stories.Summary:
Wall Street brokerages have argued that last week's sharp selloff in artificial intelligence stocks went too far, and they have played down the chance that a Democratic-controlled Congress will impose heavy rules on data center development. The sell-off, which Jefferies' Jane Gibbons described as occurring on November 5, hit the AI trade hard across the market. Analysts at several firms, including Morgan Stanley and UBS, said the risks they were pricing in were unlikely to materialise. Instead, they pointed to other events they expect to move the sector more, namely Anthropic's upcoming initial public offering and Nvidia's quarterly earnings report.

Nvidia is scheduled to report results after the market closes on November 17, and analysts expect data center revenue to rise by more than 12 per cent on a quarterly basis. Morgan Stanley said the selloff looked overdone and that its main effect would be to push some projects from 2028 into 2029 rather than derail the spending boom. The bank said that delay could lengthen the AI capital expenditure cycle, which it sees as bringing a smoother balance between supply and demand across the data center supply chain. It also cited a better credit outlook and higher lease rates for computing capacity. Morgan Stanley said it recommended buying the dip.

Morgan Stanley said it remained positive on AI hyperscalers including Amazon.com, Meta Platforms and Alphabet, and it highlighted opportunities in chipmakers Nvidia and Broadcom, data storage firms Seagate and Western Digital, and optical networking firms Coherent and Lumentum. HSBC said it was using the correction to add back equity exposure, with a tilt toward technology stocks in the United States and Asia, and it sees Anthropic's IPO as the main catalyst in the coming weeks. UBS analysts said markets had become too pessimistic about AI political risk, AI credit risk and AI spending. Gibbons said the November 5 decline looked reactionary rather than a fundamental reset, and she noted that past daily drops in the S&P 500 of more than 4 per cent were typically followed by strong returns, with the index up 11.9 per cent over six months and more than 20 per cent over 12 months.

stories.Headline: Federal Appeals Court Urged To Block Minnesota AI Law Over Free Speech Fallout
stories.Summary:
Minnesota's House File 1606 was passed to combat nonconsensual, sexually explicit deepfakes, but the law is now before a federal appeals court after a challenge from the Liberty Justice Center. The group asked the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to block the statute, which it says reaches far beyond its intended target. The filing challenges a federal judge's refusal to grant a preliminary injunction against the law. The article, published November 9, 2026, describes the dispute as a clash between legislative aims and constitutional limits.

The law allows the state to impose civil penalties of up to $500,000 per violation for creating or sharing nonconsensual, sexually explicit AI-generated media. According to the group's amicus brief, the statute does not require proof of malicious intent or actual knowledge. The group argues that a person could face liability even if the depicted subject consented, or if the generated file was never uploaded and stayed on a private device. Minnesota officials defend the law as a privacy protection for victims of digital exploitation. The group warns that fines of this size could push AI platforms to geoblock image-generation tools throughout Minnesota.

Timothy R. Snowball, senior counsel at the Liberty Justice Center, said the case concerns more than one company's product and touches Americans' freedom to create, criticize, and take part in public debate. He said that when a law pressures platforms to shut off lawful expression tools, the harm reaches both users and the audiences who would otherwise see their work. The group's brief is its third legal filing against the statute, following an August 2026 district court filing and an earlier request for emergency relief. The brief argues the lower court gave near-total deference to state regulatory power while overlooking the First Amendment rights of creators and viewers.

The article notes that independent artists, political satirists, grassroots campaigns, and small businesses that depend on generative tools could lose access if platforms withdraw service from Minnesota. Snowball said the public interest includes the speech rights of Minnesotans and the interest of others in hearing them, and that courts should weigh those interests. The 8th Circuit has not yet set a date for its decision. Until it rules, digital rights advocates and state regulators are waiting to see where the court will draw the line between personal privacy protection and limits on creative technology.

stories.Headline: In a report, Railway says it believes the October hack targeted AI provider keys for resale, and unauthorized spend on the stolen keys was estimated at ~$740K (Lawrence Abrams/BleepingComputer)
stories.Summary:
Railway, a cloud hosting provider, disclosed on October 22 that hackers had exploited vulnerabilities in its infrastructure to steal customer authentication secrets and generate approximately $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage. The company had warned customers to rotate their secrets after detecting unauthorized access to systems storing environment variables. In a new incident report published on November 10, Railway said attackers gained access to its internal source code and decrypted customer environment variables for at most 1.85% of its workspaces, or about 100,000. The company described that figure as the maximum number of potentially affected workspaces rather than the confirmed number whose secrets were stolen. Railway said it was working with affected providers to reimburse customers and would cover any charges providers declined to refund.

The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway's build infrastructure to escape filesystem isolation and obtain an internal credential. The attackers used that credential to access stored build histories and retrieve a copy of Railway's internal source code, which they analyzed to find further ways into the platform. They then exploited a second vulnerability involving an improperly configured trust relationship to reach additional infrastructure and obtain credentials used to decrypt customer environment variables. Railway described the episode as a roughly 26-hour contest between its engineers and threat actors using AI-powered agents to find and exploit weaknesses. Railway said the attackers were fully removed from its systems on October 21 and that all exploited vulnerabilities have since been remediated.

Railway said its investigation found that the attackers specifically searched for AI provider credentials, although some queries also targeted cloud, database, and payment service credentials. The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to 1,852 users, including GitHub OAuth tokens and AI agent keys, and Railway said it reset those tokens and notified affected users. The company quoted its own statement that the attacker probed many potential routes in parallel while Railway hardened those routes in parallel. Railway also cited security firm Wiz in describing the contest as one of agent speed. The company said it found no evidence that the hackers downloaded customer Git repositories or accessed customer databases.

Railway believes the attackers were focused on stealing AI credentials for resale or for use in AI model distillation. The company linked the incident to a recent wave of attacks against AI developer platforms that Wiz has dubbed "Black October." That campaign has targeted numerous AI development platforms during the past month, including Northflank, OpenCode, Warp, and Lightning AI. The article reports the disclosure as the company's own findings and does not identify the attackers beyond these descriptions. Railway's earlier warning to customers came on October 22, two days after the company said the attackers were removed from its systems.

stories.Headline: Chapman Advances Healthcare AI Research and Training
stories.Summary:
Chapman University's School of Pharmacy is expanding how it teaches and studies artificial intelligence in healthcare, according to a Chapman Newsroom article published November 10, 2026. The work is led by Sherry Yun Wang, Ph.D., an assistant professor of pharmacy who joined the school in 2021 and has become a leading voice on the subject. In 2025, she was named Women in AI's AI Researcher of the Year for North America and received a $250,000 grant from the National Institutes of Health to study bias in AI prescription tools. Her research focuses on NarxCare, an AI platform that analyzes Prescription Drug Monitoring Program data.

The article says the concern is that NarxCare flags patients who use multiple pharmacies or physicians, or who have overlapping prescriptions, patterns that do not always indicate misuse. Such patterns can also describe patients who move often, lack transportation, or live in medically underserved areas. Wang said the tool is used in other states' monitoring programs, where some patients have been denied opioid refills, and noted that the California Department of Justice never allowed it in California. To address these issues, Wang founded the Healthcare AI Initiative at Chapman, which examines ethical questions such as data privacy and develops equitable machine learning approaches. She also created an AI elective within the School of Pharmacy focused on practical applications for future clinicians.

Wang is the primary figure in the article, and Jennifer Totonchy, Ph.D., associate dean of research and graduate programs, is quoted saying that students need to be comfortable with AI to be prepared for their careers. Totonchy argued that generative AI gained a negative reputation as a tool for cheating, and she said these tools can handle routine tasks so people can focus on analysis and decision-making. In Wang's classroom, pharmacy students without coding experience use AI tools to run geospatial analyses and answer clinical research questions. Two PharmD students, Elena Wu '27 and Harvey Duong '27, worked with Wang on a study that analyzed more than 64,000 prescriptions, and in March 2026 their research on the safety of certain diabetes and weight-loss medications was selected as one of ten Featured Research Posters at the American Pharmacists Association Annual Meeting. The article does not describe any further steps or planned outcomes beyond these programs.

Articles.Title: Chapman Advances Healthcare AI Research and Training

stories.Headline: Recent Advances in AI Are Creating a ‘Paradigm Shift’ for Robotics
stories.Summary:
Researchers at UC Berkeley, working with NVIDIA, have described a new approach to robot programming called "agentic robotics," reported on November 9, 2026. The work was led by Ken Goldberg, a Berkeley roboticist and professor of engineering, together with Spencer Huang, director of robotics engineering at NVIDIA, and a team of researchers. Goldberg presented the approach and months of testing at the Conference on Robot Learning that week. The team said it could address two long-standing obstacles in the field, the large amounts of data needed to train robots and the heavy engineering effort needed to program them.

Under the new method, teams of AI agents generate robot-control programs, test them in simulated environments and revise the code when something fails. Tasks are broken into individual skills, such as finding an object, planning a grasp and moving the gripper without collisions, which the team calls Graph-as-Policy. Engineers can still review how the programs work for fine-tuning and verification. The team is also releasing open-source code built on NVIDIA's Isaac simulation framework, along with an industry-standard benchmark for evaluating robots across industrial tasks. Goldberg has said the approach requires no additional data, which he described as a way around what he once called a "100,000-year data gap."

Goldberg and Huang say the aim is to make robot programming faster and more adaptable while keeping the structure needed for reliable industrial systems. In a demonstration, researchers gave an AI tool a short video of a robot wiping ink off a metal bar with a sponge, and within an hour the tool built a simulation that closely reproduced the video. The resulting program worked on a real robot after repeated testing in simulation. In one failed trial, the robot pushed over the bar, and the AI used video of that attempt to improve its model and revise the control program. Goldberg said he was excited by the results, and he said home assistants folding laundry should not be expected yet.

Berkeley-based Ambi Robotics, which works on logistics and warehouse order fulfillment, applied the methods to parcel sorting data earlier this year. According to the article, tests showed an increased capacity of more than 15,000 packages sorted annually per robot, and the change is now deployed across 30% of the company's U.S. fleet. Jeff Mahler, the company's co-founder and chief technology officer, said the methods converted production data into robot behavior updates while keeping engineers in control. Goldberg said the implications are already promising in repetitive, large-scale industrial settings. He compared the moment to the release of the World Wide Web in 1993 and ChatGPT in 2022, and called agentic robotics "a true paradigm shift."

Articles.Title: Recent Advances in AI Are Creating a ‘Paradigm Shift’ for Robotics

stories.Headline: Librarian Katelyn Golsby Publishes Article on Controlling Student AI Use in Legal Research Assessments
stories.Summary:
Librarian Katelyn Golsby, the School of Law librarian at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, recently published a short article in the Legal Writing Institute's online journal, The Second Draft. The article is titled "Assessing Research Skills in the Age of Generative AI: Asking Questions that Machines Cannot Answer." It was posted on November 9, 2026, according to the university's website. The piece addresses how legal research assessments are affected by artificial intelligence tools used in student work.

The article describes the kinds of questions an instructor can ask to limit the use of AI tools from Lexis and Westlaw when students complete assessments. It also gives examples of how AI can be built into legal research instruction in a useful way. Those examples are meant to do so without letting students skip important steps in the legal research process. The article therefore aims to keep the core skills of legal research intact while acknowledging that these tools exist. Instructors may use it as a guide when designing their own assignments.

Golsby is the author of the article, and the university's news office announced its publication. The university's post, written by Jessica Rittenhouse, describes the piece as short and summarizes its purpose. The announcement presents the work as a contribution from a member of the law school's library staff. The articles provide no additional statements from Golsby beyond the description of her work.

The publication comes at a time when law schools are weighing how generative AI should fit into legal writing and research courses. The articles do not say whether the School of Law plans any policy changes or further publications on this topic. Readers seeking more detail would need to read the full article in The Second Draft. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Can AI replace therapy? A UAB expert explains the risks and benefits
stories.Summary:
A UAB psychiatry expert, Merida Grant, Ph.D., professor of psychiatry and behavioral neurobiology at the University of Alabama at Birmingham Marnix E. Heersink School of Medicine, discussed the benefits, risks and limits of using artificial intelligence for mental health support in an article published on November 9, 2026. The piece explains that more people are turning to chatbots for emotional help as digital tools become part of everyday life. Grant warns that the rising use of AI for emotional support is potentially concerning to psychiatry professionals. The article examines who may be most vulnerable and when people should seek care from a licensed professional instead.

AI chat systems build their answers from live web searches, large datasets, patterns in a user's inputs and next-word prediction. The article notes that AI responses are largely limited to general resources found on the web, along with replies shaped by the specific prompt, data and platform. Because of pattern recognition, AI may unintentionally reinforce a user's existing feelings, beliefs or behaviors rather than prompting the deeper reflection a conversation with a clinician can offer. Grant says AI can tailor information to individual needs when used inside a clinical setting, but alone, with insufficient history, it can produce erroneous diagnoses and treatment recommendations. The article also says patients should disclose any AI use to their clinician so that inaccurate information can be addressed.

Grant points to cost, insurance coverage, provider shortages, location and societal pressures as factors that may be driving more people toward AI assistance. For mild to moderate concerns, she sees AI as a possibly reasonable short-term strategy until a provider or other resources become available, while cautioning that its responses may contain errors that a qualified professional should verify. The article adds that younger adults under 30 are more likely than adults over 50 to seek AI mental health support, according to KFF. Grant says teens may rely on AI without telling trusted adults about critical situations, while older adults may face social isolation and missed signs of cognitive impairment. Before using any platform, she advises users to confirm its privacy terms regarding protected health information and HIPAA, and she stresses that AI is not designed to respond to someone in crisis, mania or psychosis.

The article directs anyone with suicidal thoughts, or anyone who needs immediate crisis support, to call or text 988 for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline or call 911. It also lists the Birmingham Crisis Center at 205-323-7777 and the National Crisis Text Line, reachable by texting "UAB" to 741-741, as 24-hour options through UAB's partnerships. For ongoing care, UAB's Community Counseling Clinic serves the greater Birmingham area at a fee of $10 per session. Grant says licensed care should be sought immediately for addiction treatment or for severe mental illness involving psychosis or suicidal or homicidal thoughts.

Articles.Title: Can AI replace therapy? A UAB expert explains the risks and benefits

stories.Headline: The U.S.–China AI Competition: Two Paths to Artificial General Intelligence - CSET | Center for Security and Emerging Technology
stories.Summary:
The Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) published a commentary on November 9, 2026, by William Hannas, Huey-Meei Chang, and Owen Daniels, previewing a forthcoming study on how the United States and China are competing to build artificial general intelligence. The authors argue that the two countries hold different ideas of what AGI means and different strengths in reaching it. The United States leads in computing resources and frontier AI models, while China is pursuing broader routes that include robotics, embodied AI, and brain-inspired systems. The piece notes that the study is not yet released in full, so its complete findings and scoring of each country's position are not yet public.

The authors describe how U.S. developers generally define AGI as a system that can reason, learn, and perform a wide range of cognitive tasks at roughly human levels, with artificial superintelligence referring to capabilities that exceed humans across those tasks. Chinese researchers, by contrast, describe general intelligence as something that must be grounded in interaction with the physical world, which the authors say explains China's interest in embodied AI, neuroscience-inspired computing, and hybrid human-machine cognition. The commentary says these differences do not mean China avoids large models or that American companies ignore robotics, since both countries pursue several approaches at once. The authors contend that the route proving most productive could change which national advantages matter most.

According to the article, the American edge lies in semiconductors, hyperscale computing, frontier reasoning models, private investment, and influential research institutions. China's strengths include engineering capacity, a large technical workforce, expanding power infrastructure, and the ability to deploy AI in physical settings at scale. The authors also say the United States must keep its appeal to global researchers, since policies that discourage them would weaken its position, while China has been increasingly able to keep domestic talent. They advise U.S. policymakers not to treat current model rankings as a permanent verdict, to avoid relying on a single technical track, to protect high-risk capabilities while cooperating narrowly on shared risks, and to track what China actually builds rather than headline benchmark scores. The article is a preview, so the specific tables and detailed recommendations in the full report are not reproduced here.

Articles.Title: The U.S.–China AI Competition: Two Paths to Artificial General Intelligence - CSET | Center for Security and Emerging Technology

stories.Headline: Generative AI Becomes Lesson in Intergenerational Learning at VSU
stories.Summary:
Two Valdosta State University students, Jacob Bachrach and Tyler Horne, recently taught a generative artificial intelligence class to members of the university's VSU Learning in Retirement program, a group of older adults. Both are students in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering Technology, and neither had much experience teaching technology to others before the class. The students said the older learners had grown up without computers, smartphones, or the internet being part of everyday life. The story was published by the university on November 9, 2026.

Bachrach and Horne designed a 90-minute session to give participants a technical foundation in artificial intelligence and generative AI. The lesson covered how the technology works, how it can be used, and the ethical questions that come with it. Bachrach described generative AI as a broad subject with many areas outside his personal expertise, but said expanding his knowledge through teaching was worthwhile. Horne said he wanted the older learners to leave feeling confident enough to use AI in their daily lives.

The article notes that one member, an author, had already used AI to turn his published book into a video. The students were invited by Dr. Anne Price, executive director of the Mary Virginia Terry Center for Experiential Learning, after she met them during the Blazer Summer Research Institute in 2026. Bachrach and Horne were among six student-faculty research teams selected for that competitive program, which pairs undergraduates with faculty mentors on research projects. Their faculty adviser, Dr. Ahana Roy Choudhury, an associate professor of computer science, took part in that program as well.

The article describes the teaching idea as a way for the students to challenge their teaching skills while using their knowledge of artificial intelligence. The students said the older participants asked questions that often led directly into the next part of the presentation, and several shared resources with them after the class ended. Bachrach expects to earn a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science and a minor in Art in May 2028, and Horne expects to earn a Bachelor of Science in Computer Information Systems and a minor in Music in the same month and year. The article does not describe any plans for future classes of this kind.

Articles.Title: Generative AI Becomes Lesson in Intergenerational Learning at VSU

stories.Headline: From fossils to artificial intelligence: Adam Stewart’s winding path through science - Cornell David A. Duffield College of Engineering
stories.Summary:
Adam Stewart, a Cornell graduate of 2014, has built a career that moved from paleontology to artificial intelligence, according to a Cornell Duffield Engineering profile published on November 9, 2026. He grew up collecting fossils along a creek in Tioga Center, New York, and first arrived at Cornell intending to study paleontology. Over time his interests widened, and he now works as a postdoctoral researcher at the Technical University of Munich in Germany. There he develops artificial intelligence tools that help scientists study the Earth using satellite imagery.

Stewart's path included several stops that the article describes as anything but straightforward. He worked as a software engineer at Lockheed Martin and then as a high-performance computing system administrator at Argonne National Laboratory, where he helped researchers install and manage scientific software. That work exposed him to open-source development, including Spack, a software management tool for scientific computing. He then earned a doctorate in computer science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, where his research combined machine learning with Earth observation. During an internship with Microsoft's AI for Good lab, he began developing TorchGeo, a software library that helps researchers apply artificial intelligence to geographic and satellite data.

TorchGeo has grown into an international collaborative project with approximately 150 contributors and millions of downloads, and Stewart now chairs its independent organization. The organization brings together researchers and developers from academia and industry. The article reports that Stewart says his work has followed a steady thread of curiosity about the natural world, which he describes as the drive to find out why. He has also taught since his days with the Boy Scouts and is pursuing opportunities to become a professor. Looking back, he attributes his career to a willingness to explore unexpected opportunities rather than to a carefully constructed plan.

The story has its roots in Stewart's early research and his student experiences at Cornell. A research poster he saw in Snee Hall, showing how satellite imagery could track glacier movement, drew him toward remote sensing. He joined research led by professor Matthew Pritchard on glacier movement in the Russian High Arctic, and worked alongside Andrew Melkonian, Ph.D. '15, whose programming experience sparked his own interest in computer science. Cornell's flexible curriculum allowed him to create his own concentration in computational geophysics, combining earth science with mathematics, physics and programming. The article does not give further details about his future plans beyond continuing his Munich work and pursuing a professorship.

stories.Headline: Nigeria: Manufacturers Charged to Deploy Ai, Energy-Efficient Technologies to Cut Costs
stories.Summary:
The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) has urged manufacturers to adopt artificial intelligence, advanced technologies and energy-efficient solutions to counter rising production costs and weak energy supply. The call was made on November 9, 2026, at the 2026 Manufacturers Energy Security and Energy Efficiency Summit in Lagos, which was jointly organised by Manufacturers Power Development Company Ltd. (MPDCL), GIZ and the Nigerian Energy Support Programme (NESP). Industry leaders and government representatives discussed how technology, reliable energy supply and structured financing could help manufacturers meet their energy challenges. The summit drew attention to the difficulties that continue to hurt Nigerian industry. Reporting for Vanguard, Yinka Kolawole described the event as a platform for practical solutions.

MAN's President, Ifeanyi Okoye, said an industrial energy cost reduction and adoption programme would promote factory rooftop solar installations, battery energy storage systems, captive natural gas solutions and smart energy management networks. He said the programme targets the rising cost of energy, which has significantly weakened manufacturing operations and competitiveness. According to him, manufacturers spend about 40 per cent of their profits dealing with energy problems, while high electricity tariffs, unreliable grid supply and dependence on fossil fuels continue to undermine production. He added that the summit aims to help manufacturers gain access to long-term financing, climate funds, green investments and asset-financing mechanisms for moving to more efficient energy systems. Okoye framed these measures as a route to a steadier industrial base.

MAN's Director-General, Segun Ajayi-Kadir, said emerging technologies have become essential for raising production efficiency, cutting energy use and making manufacturing operations more resilient. He noted that AI and smart manufacturing systems could help factories optimise energy use, reduce production losses, lower operating costs and improve product quality, especially given persistent electricity shortages. John Aluya, Chairman of the Board of Directors of MPDCL, said the high cost of self-generation has reduced manufacturers' profit margins and weakened their competitiveness. He stressed that reliable and affordable power is critical to the survival of Nigerian industries, and that the summit was meant to explore solar photovoltaic systems, battery storage, captive gas power, energy efficiency and carbon credit monetisation.

Ulf Brackmann, Chief Executive Officer of IKAPITAL Family Office & Friends, delivered the keynote and argued that AI could significantly raise industrial productivity and create new jobs rather than displace workers. He cautioned, however, that AI can cut costs and improve efficiency only where factories have dependable electricity and sound digital foundations. Brackmann also warned manufacturers against treating AI as a quick fix for their production problems, rejecting the idea that it will solve every difficulty. The article presents his remarks as a note of realism in an otherwise optimistic discussion. The summit therefore left manufacturers with a mix of encouragement to invest in technology and a reminder that reliable power must come first.
