stories.Headline: Parents and teachers decry Google pledge to yank Search if schools block AI: ‘This threat is nothing but extortion’
stories.Summary:
Google has told schools that any school choosing to block its AI tools will also lose access to Google Search. The announcement came last week, alongside a range of new AI tools for schools and classrooms and options allowing teachers and administrators to restrict their use. Chris Phillips, vice-president for education at Google, said schools should have control over AI in their classrooms. Access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.

Parents and teachers across the United States have criticized the pledge. They raised concerns with the Guardian about AI's potential to weaken students' critical-thinking skills and about the growing influence of big tech in education. A father of two boys in Amissville, Virginia, said AI will weaken people's ability to think critically and that even the best models are often flat-out wrong. He called the threat "nothing but extortion" and said he hopes a Democratic Congress will pass legislation to protect schools from corporate malfeasance.

Jen Atay, a 51-year-old teacher in Hawaii, said that when software is free, the user is the product, and that Google should not test or develop AI with minors. Eyla Whitemoon, a mother and educator in Kernville, California, said Google and Meta created a false dependency in public schools and that these companies got society hooked on their products. A 64-year-old educator in Ann Arbor, Michigan, said there are alternative search engines and that those will now be what teachers turn to. An 84-year-old retiree and mother in Maryland urged schools to tell Google to go pound sand and use DuckDuckGo instead.

Rachel Dominguez, a 42-year-old parent in Minneapolis, Minnesota, suggested schools use academic databases such as Academic Search Premier, JSTOR and arXiv, which most school districts already subscribe to. Not everyone backs blocking AI. A 67-year-old emerging technology teacher in Texas said AI is not going away and that schools need to teach how to use it properly. A California resident said Google Search has existed since the 90s and that it is crazy to remove it instead of just removing Gemini. That resident said schools could use Gemini to show students that AI sources are not always valid.

stories.Headline: Health researchers warn proposed federal privacy law could expose sensitive medical data
stories.Summary:
Health researchers have warned that Canada's proposed federal privacy legislation contains gaps that could leave sensitive medical information open to commercial exploitation as artificial intelligence spreads through the health-care system. Their concerns centre on Bill C-36, the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, which the Carney government introduced in June as part of an effort to modernize private-sector privacy rules. The critics published their commentary in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, arguing that some provisions would let companies collect, use or disclose personal information without direct consent in certain circumstances. One provision in particular allows organizations to rely on a legitimate business interest when they judge that the expected benefits outweigh reasonably foreseeable harm to individuals.

Dr. Sheryl Spithoff, a clinician scientist at Women's College Hospital in Toronto and a co-author of the commentary, says this gives companies too much discretion over how personal data is used. She argues that firms should have to inform regulators from the start and that the clause should apply only in rare cases, with higher standards for sensitive information such as health records. The researchers also point to the European Union's data protection regulation, which sets a higher bar of proof and says legitimate interest does not override the fundamental rights of data owners. Teresa Scassa, a research chair in information law at the University of Ottawa and another co-author, warns that advances in AI may make it impossible to fully anonymize data, since records can be linked with other information and used to profile people as high-risk for costly conditions. Under the bill, deliberately re-identifying personal information would be an offence, though Scassa noted that this could be hard to prove.

The bill requires that personal information be de-identified by modifying details such as names and health card numbers, but it does not protect anonymized data, which is stripped of personal information so that no reasonably foreseeable risk of identification remains. The researchers say anonymized data often carries societal biases that can be built into AI systems and lead to discrimination, and they cite a widely used American hospital algorithm that allocated fewer resources to Black patients. Ottawa's position is that the legislation would strengthen privacy protection, improve corporate accountability and introduce safeguards on automated decision-making. AI Minister Evan Solomon's office repeated the bill's definition of legitimate interest and said organizations relying on it would have to assess and mitigate privacy risks, without detailing those safeguards. Some physicians, including Dr. Amol Verma of St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto, argue that de-identified health data is valuable for research and hospital efficiency when handled safely, and that privacy protection and innovation can go hand in hand.

Bill C-36 remains before Parliament, and the debate reflects a broader tension between technological innovation, commercial use of data and Canadians' privacy rights. Other jurisdictions are facing similar problems, including a class-action lawsuit filed earlier this year against Chicago-based Tempus AI, which the plaintiffs allege obtained patients' genetic and clinical data and sold it without consent. Last year, a study that Spithoff worked on found that millions of Canadians' de-identified health records, including medical histories and prescriptions, were being sold to pharmaceutical companies. The study's authors warned that such sharing could improve care but could also let drug companies put their economic interests ahead of patients' and push up prices. Critics say stronger restrictions and independent oversight are needed to prevent commercial misuse of sensitive information, and the bill's path through Parliament will determine whether those changes are made.

stories.Headline: Legal AI Adoption Highlights Need for Better Lawyer Training
stories.Summary:
Legal AI use is growing fast, and a new report argues that lawyers need better training to use it safely. Wolters Kluwer's 2026 Future Ready Lawyer survey, published in November 2026, looked at how attorneys use AI and what gets in their way. The survey gathered responses from 810 lawyers working in law firms and corporate legal departments in the United States, China, and eight European countries. It ran online from August 8 to August 25, 2025. Ninety-two percent of respondents said they use at least one AI tool in their daily work.

Even with that wide adoption, lawyers still face obstacles. The survey found that ethical and data privacy concerns and a lack of training each drew 39% of responses, making them the most common barriers. The findings suggest that using AI well requires more than learning how a tool works. Lawyers must check the results they get, protect client information, and follow professional rules. The report's authors, Wolters Kluwer, present the results as evidence that training should keep pace with the technology.

The article itself, published by a legal career site, draws practical lessons from the survey. It says lawyers should verify every case and source an AI tool produces, check quotes and facts, know which tools their firm permits, and protect confidential client data. Those habits matter across litigation, business law, research, and legal operations. The piece also suggests that job candidates explain in interviews how they check AI output and handle privacy, and that they ask prospective employers how they train staff and supervise AI-assisted work.

It notes, however, that not every firm uses the same tools, so candidates should rely on current postings and firm materials. The broader message is that AI can speed up legal work but does not replace professional judgment. The article argues that as more firms adopt the technology, proper training will matter even more. The sources provided do not describe any specific regulatory changes, deadlines, or enforcement actions tied to this survey, so the outlook beyond these recommendations remains unclear.

stories.Headline: Australia is drafting legislation for an AI safety regulator empowered to impose "significant penalties" after an OpenAI model hacked a government site in Sept. (James Mayger/Bloomberg)
stories.Summary:
I can't write this one the way the rules require, because the articles supplied do not contain enough material for three paragraphs of four to five sentences each. What they contain is a single long feature about Hamburg's data protection regulator using an OpenAI-based chatbot called LLMoin. They do not contain the Australian story named in the headline, which is the only item the headline names, so I have nothing to report on that. The Hamburg material is substantial, but the piece is clearly cut off partway through a list of safeguards, so the full account of what was assessed and concluded is not available to me.

Given that, the honest course is to write the Hamburg story from what the articles actually state, and to flag that the headline's subject is missing. Hamburg's data protection commissioner, the HmbBfDI, published a nine-page case study dated November 5, 2026, reviewing LLMoin, a chatbot the Hamburg administration built on an OpenAI model, and found its safeguards sufficient. The regulator now uses the same system to draft letters responding to privacy complaints, which rose 62 percent to 4,220 in 2025. The authority does not claim the model is free of personal data, and instead assumes it is probably not anonymous, then concludes it can still be used if the system around it prevents such data from being extracted. Humans make every decision and supply the legal reasoning, and the most sensitive complaints are kept away from the tool.

The case study rests on EDPB Opinion 28/2024 of December 18, 2024, which the authority says makes its earlier Hamburg Theses no longer authoritative, and it openly concedes that the opinion leaves data erasure questions unanswered. The HmbBfDI says machine unlearning has not reached technical maturity, and that filters do not amount to erasure under Article 17 of the GDPR, a position it attributes to the German data protection conference. The Senate Chancellery is planning to move the model onto on-premises hosting at Dataport in 2027, and the authority ties the choice of hosting to data protection requirements and the geopolitical situation. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Innocean turns Seoul billboards into outdoor AI art galleries
stories.Summary:
Innocean, the Seoul advertising agency, said on Wednesday that it has launched a public art project that shows works by AI artists on large digital billboards across the city. The Innocean Open Museum project is led by the agency's AI creative research team, i-Lab, and it departs from ordinary outdoor advertising by showing artists' work instead of promoting brands or products. The first installations appeared in mid-October at The Monte Gangnam and Shinsegae Gangnam Gate DS at Central City. Works were also shown at Central City Underworld DS throughout October, and the K Finance screen in Myeong-dong joined in November.

Under the inaugural theme "Open," three artists and creative teams explore different approaches to AI-driven art. Designer Kim Ji-young's "Alien Beauty" challenges conventional beauty standards through unusual skin textures. Kim Ji-hyun of the creative studio Anreal presents "Aperture," which draws on the growth and dispersal of dandelions. The creative duo Neither.I offers "Behind," which combines video, photography and electronic music to reveal scenes beyond a large curtain. Innocean has adapted each work to the dimensions of its billboard, and it will document the artists' creative processes through interviews and an online archive.

The project follows a concept called "Open Inquiry," which lets artists experiment freely with AI as a creative tool, a collaborator or a subject. Innocean's CEO, Kim Jung-ah, said that AI is changing creative methods and possibilities and that the company wanted to open its capabilities and urban screens to artists. She added that the initiative would grow through partnerships with artists and brands. The article does not give further detail on how those partnerships will be structured.

The installations will run through the end of the year, and new works are scheduled to follow during that period. Innocean also plans to recruit more AI artists and to explore collaborations that connect artists' creative visions with brands. The article does not say how many new works or artists are planned, or what the project will cost. Its launch comes as AI tools move further into commercial creative work, and the company presents the project as a way to give those tools a public audience in the city.

Articles.Title: Innocean turns Seoul billboards into outdoor AI art galleries

stories.Headline: SEC Wins 5.8 Billion Won HBM Inspection Order From Micron
stories.Summary:
SEC, a company known for its electron beam technology, said on November 10, 2026 that it had signed a contract worth 5.8 billion won with Micron's Singapore subsidiary. Under the deal, SEC will supply X-ray inspection equipment for Micron's high-bandwidth memory production. The order covers SEC's NF120 series of manual X-ray inspection systems, which will be installed on a mass-production line. The deal is expected to help SEC move further into the semiconductor market, beyond its existing businesses in electronic components, batteries and defense. SEC first began working with Micron in 2023, and the new contract strengthens that relationship.

Micron is investing $7 billion in HBM and advanced packaging facilities in Singapore, with operations scheduled to begin in 2027. The articles say that as Micron keeps spending on HBM and DRAM, SEC could win further orders for inspection equipment. SEC is also moving from manual systems toward automated inline inspection equipment. In October it won an order for its Semi-scan Wafer system, to be used on a wafer-level packaging mass-production line run by a global outsourced semiconductor assembly and test company.

The company is also seeking to enter the market for inline HBM inspection equipment. An SEC official said the Micron order shows how important X-ray inspection has become in HBM manufacturing. The official expects demand for inspection equipment to keep rising as global chipmakers expand HBM production capacity and capital investment. The articles identify the official only by role and do not name them.

Articles.Title: SEC Wins 5.8 Billion Won HBM Inspection Order From Micron - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

stories.Headline: AI training startup Mercor valued at $20 billion in latest funding round - CNA
stories.Summary:
AI training startup Mercor said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that it had raised $750 million in a funding round that valued the company at $20 billion. The round, labeled Series D, drew participation from Benchmark, Felicis, Fundomo, Nvidia and funds managed by affiliates of Apollo, among others. The San Francisco-based company began as an AI-powered hiring platform. It now connects technology companies with subject-matter experts whose knowledge is used to train, test and improve AI models and agents.

Mercor said it will use the new funding to help train and test AI agents on professional tasks. Co-CEO Brendan Foody argued that every job in the economy will need its own AI agents, and that every company will need a way to train and evaluate those agents on its own work. The article describes this as part of a wider surge in investor interest in AI, which has pushed private funding sharply higher this year. It also notes that a growing group of heavily capitalized startups now carry multibillion-dollar valuations.

The article places the round within a broader funding boom. According to Crunchbase, AI-driven startups raised $102 billion in the third quarter of 2026, or 64 per cent of global venture capital. Mercor is backed by Jack Dorsey and venture capitalist Peter Thiel. Its valuation was about $10 billion after it raised $350 million in October of the previous year, so the latest round roughly doubled that figure.

Articles.Title: AI training startup Mercor valued at $20 billion in latest funding round - CNA

stories.Headline: TSMC, Microsoft executives debate AI's impact on Day 2 of Nikkei Dialogue
stories.Summary:
TSMC and Microsoft executives were scheduled to speak on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, on the second day of Nikkei's 2026 Global Management Dialogue in Tokyo. The event, which opened its second day in the Japanese capital, was set to keep artificial intelligence at the top of its agenda. Among the participants was a senior executive from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the world's largest contract chipmaker. Other speakers were also scheduled to take part in the program. The articles describe the session mainly as a forum for discussing AI's broader effects.

The event is the second day of a multi-day gathering organized by Nikkei, and the articles present it as a platform rather than a source of new rules or policy changes. The conference also features speakers from fitness and martial arts, according to the subheading of the coverage. Nikkei's reporting connects the discussion to wider industry concerns, including memory chip prices and AI-driven demand that other coverage in the same publication has covered. The articles do not state any formal requirement, deadline, or change arising from the debate. No specific figures, commitments, or outcomes from the sessions were reported in the material available.

Responsibility for the program rests with Nikkei, which organized the dialogue and commissioned the related content through its Global Business Bureau. The articles do not include direct statements from the TSMC or Microsoft executives in the form of quotations, so their positions on AI are not reported here. The coverage notes that other executives at the event have expressed views on AI, such as the Siemens CEO saying that AI will not take jobs but those who can use it will, and a Foxconn chief downplaying bubble concerns. Those remarks come from separate reports and are not drawn from the TSMC or Microsoft sessions. The articles carry no further information about what will follow the event beyond the conclusion of the dialogue.

Articles.Title: TSMC, Microsoft executives debate AI's impact on Day 2 of Nikkei Dialogue

stories.Headline: 14-year-old creates tool for AI agents to band together like a team
stories.Summary:
A 14-year-old Austrian developer, Stanislaus Hees, has built an open-source tool called Autark that lets AI agents work together like a team without waiting for constant prompts. The tool was reported by The Register on November 10, 2026. Users place tasks in an inbox, where a manager agent hands them off to other agents, which carry out the work and report back. Agents can also ask clarifying questions when a task is too vague. Hees said he built it because he wanted a system that could take ongoing responsibility for work rather than only answering his next message.

Autark can be connected to OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Kimi Code through those services' command-line tools, and local models are also supported. The tool's website says agents wake on a schedule, a timer, a new task, a message, or an event, then decide what to do next. However, the project does not put walls around its agents, so there is no sandboxing, approval prompts, or permission gates. Agents run with the privileges of the machine's user, and the limits users set are described as guidelines rather than rules. The access page says that in live test runs, agents given a vague request reached real repositories, backups, SSH keys, and .env files within minutes, and one changed the permissions of a file it had found.

Hees has said he would not claim the app is suitable for unattended access to sensitive systems. The articles say Autark encrypts stored passwords and keys and refers to them by IDs so their values stay out of prompts, and that its servers do not store user data, using a meeting server only to relay encrypted traffic between devices. Users can self-host the entire project, including the meeting server code, which is available on GitHub under an Apache open source license. The Register's view is that the tool has real potential but that using it safely depends on users building their own guardrails, and it advises running it only on machines holding nothing that would be painful to lose.

Articles.Title: 14-year-old creates tool for AI agents to band together like a team

stories.Headline: Andhra Pradesh Cabinet clears policy frameworks to attract investments in AI, electronics, renewable energy
stories.Summary:
The Andhra Pradesh Cabinet, chaired by Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu at the Secretariat on Tuesday, approved a series of proposals aimed at drawing investment in artificial intelligence, electronics, renewable energy, pharmaceuticals and manufacturing. The approvals covered the Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming, Comics and Extended Reality policy for 2026 to 2031 and the Robotics and Physical AI policy for 2026 to 2036. The Cabinet also cleared amendments to the Semiconductor and Display Fab Policy for 2024 to 2029. Decisions on infrastructure, education and administration were taken alongside these investment measures.

Among the largest approvals is a ₹31,387 crore investment by AM Intelligence for a 512 MW green integrated AI data centre at Amanam in Bheemunipatnam mandal of Visakhapatnam district. The Cabinet also cleared a ₹4,000.20 crore advanced materials project by Carbon Cosmo at Naidupeta and allotted land in Tirupati to Dixon Technologies for a ₹700 crore investment. About 25 acres were allocated to Reliance Industries for a gigascale AI data centre at Bhogapuram in Vizianagaram district. An ₹570.20 crore Epack unit at Rambilli in Anakapalli district is expected to employ 2,565 people, and Hetero Group received 173.82 acres in the Nakkapalli Bulk Drug Park.

The Cabinet approved the creation of a Directorate of Traffic Management and Road Safety under the Director-General of Police, with its headquarters at Mangalagiri. It also sanctioned a ₹236.92 crore expansion of Ravali Spinners in West Godavari district, expected to employ 1,569 people, and a 30-acre industrial park for women entrepreneurs at Jaggayyapet in NTR district. Compressed biogas plants were approved for NTR, Prakasam and Vizianagaram districts, and the government agreed to study small modular nuclear reactors as an alternative to thermal power. The Cabinet also transferred 5.50 acres of APGENCO land to the Vijayawada Municipal Corporation for a 15 MW waste-to-energy plant.

The articles do not name anyone outside the Cabinet as responsible for the decisions beyond the Chief Minister, who chaired the meeting. The Hindu's report, published on November 11, 2026, attributes the investment figures to sources in the government. Other measures included a 30-year lease of 192.68 acres of Wakf land in Anantapur district for a solar project, a Kendriya Vidyalaya site in the capital region, and the withdrawal of earlier land allotments made to Websol Renewables and Metro Decorative at the Naidupeta Special Economic Zone. The articles do not describe any next steps or timelines for these approvals.

Articles.Title: Andhra Pradesh Cabinet clears policy frameworks to attract investments in AI, electronics, renewable energy

stories.Headline: AI infrastructure provider Fireworks says hackers accessed some customers' datasets, incomplete model weights, and billing information over the past month (Anna Tong/Forbes)
stories.Summary:
Fireworks, an AI infrastructure provider, says hackers accessed some customers' datasets, incomplete model weights, and billing information over the past month, according to a report from Forbes reporter Anna Tong that was republished by Techmeme on November 9, 2026. The company's statement, as described in the aggregated coverage, concerns a breach of its systems rather than a single incident on one day. The articles provided describe the affected categories of data but do not give the number of customers involved, the exact dates of intrusion, or whether the data was copied or altered. Because the source material is a short listing that relays the Forbes headline without the full text, specifics beyond that are not available here. The articles do not spell out what, if anything, customers must now do, nor do they state any regulatory filing or required notice.

They also do not say how the intrusion was detected or whether it has been contained. Datasets and billing records can contain sensitive information about the companies that use Fireworks, but the coverage supplied does not say what those customers were told. Anything beyond the headline's description of the breach would be speculation based on this material. Fireworks is identified as the company that disclosed the breach, and the Forbes report is the source cited for its account. The provided material does not include a direct quote from a Fireworks executive or an official spokesperson, so the company's position is known only through the headline's summary.

No attribution of blame to any particular hacking group or individual appears in the articles. The surrounding material in the same Techmeme snapshot concerns unrelated reporting about Nvidia and a Commerce Department chip investigation, and it does not address the Fireworks incident. The articles give no indication of what comes next for the company or its customers. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI infrastructure provider Fireworks says hackers accessed some customers' datasets, incomplete model weights, and billing information over the past month (Anna Tong/Forbes)

stories.Headline: Grab, SoftBank to invest $1.85bn in Malaysia AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Grab and SoftBank Group announced on Monday, November 10, 2026, that they will invest $1.85 billion in artificial intelligence infrastructure projects in Malaysia, including data centers. The announcement came from the companies themselves, and the articles describe the investment as two projects. The companies say the goal is to capture the growing demand for digital services across Southeast Asia. The article is datelined Singapore and was written by Kentaro Takeda for Nikkei Asia.

The projects involve building data centers in Malaysia to support AI services. The article describes the investment as aimed at serving regional demand rather than only Malaysian demand. The related coverage in the same feed indicates that SoftBank's work includes an AI infrastructure development in Malaysia's Sarawak state. Other linked stories describe Grab expanding its AI functions across its services. The articles give no figures beyond the $1.85 billion total and the reference to a separate plan of $50 billion attributed to a Malaysian prime minister.

Grab and SoftBank are the companies responsible for the investment, and their announcement is the source of the figures. The coverage reports that the companies are seeking to capture demand as Southeast Asia's digital economy expands. The articles do not supply direct quotations from company executives in the portion provided. Context in the feed includes Grab's pending acquisition of Atome Financial for $1.49 billion and a Taiwan deal that the articles say was blocked, which the article links to Grab's wider AI ambitions. The articles do not say when the data centers will be completed or what the next steps will be.

Articles.Title: Grab, SoftBank to invest $1.85bn in Malaysia AI infrastructure

stories.Headline: With AI, Korea faces balancing act between driving growth and disgruntling public
stories.Summary:
Korea's exports hit a record in September, with total shipments topping $120 billion for the first time, driven almost entirely by demand for AI-related memory chips. Semiconductor exports more than tripled from a year earlier to a record $60.3 billion, and chips made up 49.9 percent of total exports. Memory shipments rose from $11.79 billion to $54.07 billion in one year as data centers bought more and prices climbed. Exports from January to September reached $814.5 billion, already surpassing last year's full-year record of $709.3 billion.

The gains, however, are concentrated in a few companies. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix together control more than 80 percent of the global high bandwidth memory market, while less than 1 percent of Korea's workers are in the chip sector. Employment among people aged 15 to 29 fell by 285,000 between June 2022 and June this year, according to a Bank of Korea report released in August. About 94 percent of those drops came from industries where AI usage is prioritized. The Yongin chip cluster, where Samsung and SK hynix are building new labs, will need around 15 to 16 gigawatts at full operation, reportedly about 25 percent of Seoul's electricity demand.

Samsung's loss-making foundry division and system large-scale integration divisions skipped entry-level hiring in both rounds of recruitment last year. SK hynix paid employees a performance bonus worth 2,964 percent of their monthly base salary for 2025. Samsung Electronics Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun said at the company's March shareholders' meeting that the chip division's bonus payout rate falls short of competitors. The Bank of Korea's employment research team head, Oh Sam-il, said AI is accelerating the trend of a diminishing career ladder for young people.

The Semiconductor Special Act, which gives chipmakers bigger tax credits and priority access to electricity and water, passed in January without an exemption from the 52-hour weekly work cap that chipmakers had sought for R&D engineers. In a union survey last year, 90 percent of Samsung's unionized R&D staff opposed the exemption. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said at an August 6 forum that the current 52-hour system must be revised. The Korea Electric Power Corporation is pursuing a 37 trillion won project to move coastal power plants to inland Yongin, scheduled to finish in 2036, and residents in the affected area are resisting the relocation.

Articles.Title: With AI, Korea faces balancing act between driving growth and disgruntling public

stories.Headline: Amelio AI Wins CPA Practice Advisor 2026 Technology Innovation Award
stories.Summary:
Amelio AI, a platform built by certified public accountants, was named a winner of the 2026 Tax & Accounting Technology Innovation Awards from CPA Practice Advisor, according to a November 10, 2026 announcement from HKMP Technologies, LLC. The awards, now in their 23rd year, recognize new technologies that help tax and accounting professionals work more efficiently. An independent committee of technologists, thought leaders, and industry influencers chose the winners from a large field of nominees. Most nominees this year had artificial intelligence at their core, and Amelio AI was one of six winning products.

Amelio is a workflow and methodology platform for accounting firms that replaces standalone workflow tools and works alongside the engagement, document, and practice management systems a firm already uses. Firms define their own forms, workflows, and methodology inside the platform, which then enforces them on every engagement. Amelio AI serves as the intelligence layer within that system, following the firm's rules and standards while a professional reviews and approves everything it prepares before it becomes final. The announcement describes three capabilities: WorkPaperAi, which prepares current-year workpapers from client schedules and source documents using skills the firm has taught it; Risk Assessment AI, which suggests and rates risks from client documents for an auditor to accept or adjust; and Alli, a Microsoft Teams assistant that answers questions about deadlines, open work, and engagement status.

Steve Barrett, President and co-founder of Amelio, said the company built the platform so firms could define their own processes, and it built Amelio AI the same way. He said a firm's process works because it fits its staff, clients, and tools, and that the firm sets the rules, Amelio AI does the work within them, and a professional signs off before anything is final. Amelio's own description of itself says the firm, not the software, defines the rules, standards, and workpapers. The announcement was issued by HKMP Technologies, LLC, which owns Amelio, and the full list of winners is available at CPA Practice Advisor.

Articles.Title: Amelio AI Wins CPA Practice Advisor 2026 Technology Innovation Award

stories.Headline: Exclusive: Former Meta and OpenAI Contractor Sama Liquidates, Citing Lawsuits
stories.Summary:
Sama, a data annotation firm that had worked for Meta and OpenAI, is winding down its operations and liquidating its assets, according to a letter to creditors dated November 6, 2026 that TIME reviewed. The letter blames declining revenue, driven by competition and by class-action litigation that would have taken years and significant resources to defend. It does not name the lawsuit it means, though Sama has faced separate class actions in Kenya and the United States. An unaudited balance sheet attached to the letter lists about $1 million in assets against $17 million in liabilities as of October. On October 23, the U.S. entity operating as Sama, Samasource Impact Sourcing, Inc., transferred its assets to a newly formed company, Sama ABC, to oversee their sale and distribute proceeds to creditors.

The letter says Sama ABC is run by professionals who specialize in liquidating financially distressed companies, and that it is not corporately affiliated with Sama despite the similar name. A bank holds a priority claim to substantially all of the company's assets, according to the letter. Earlier reporting by TIME found that Sama performed content moderation for Meta and data labeling for OpenAI, work that employees said exposed them to traumatic content without adequate safeguards. Sama and Meta also face Kenyan lawsuits from former content moderators who allege they were exploited, illegally fired after raising concerns, and blocked from unionizing. The letter does not say what the liquidation means for that case.

Those Kenyan cases include a 2022 suit by Daniel Motaung, a former moderator fired in 2019 after trying to organize a strike, which alleges violations of constitutional rights, forced labor and human trafficking. It has since been consolidated with a separate petition from former moderators who say they were unlawfully made redundant and blacklisted. Sama has said it complied with Kenyan labor law, and Meta has denied responsibility for the working conditions. Separately, Sama drew criticism earlier this year over its handling of footage from Meta's AI-powered smart glasses, after workers told Swedish newspapers they had to review private content, including people using the toilet and having sex. Plaintiffs dropped their claims against Sama in August, and Meta says it will fight the privacy claims against it.

The letter praises Sama's model of deliberately hiring people from marginalized communities in East Africa, saying it reached more than seventy thousand people with training and well-paid digital work. Sama's CEO, Wendy Gonzalez, did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and an email to the company's press inbox bounced. Sama ABC representatives did not respond to emails or calls. Whether the liquidation ends the Kenyan litigation, or how the claims against Sama will be handled through the winding-down process, is not addressed in the articles.

Articles.Title: Exclusive: Former Meta and OpenAI Contractor Sama Liquidates, Citing Lawsuits

stories.Headline: Why Jensen-Gate May Actually Help the AI Boom
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair, and the company's board is investigating whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. According to The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal, US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, was recruited to spy for China. Business Insider has not independently verified that assessment, and the claim is not established fact. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. The episode has shaken Silicon Valley, and Wall Street's reaction on Monday suggested it would have little effect on the AI boom.

The article argues that demand for AI is unlikely to fade because of the scandal. It cites Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello, who wrote that he still expects Nvidia's forecast of $3 trillion to $4 trillion of annual AI infrastructure spending by 2030 to come to fruition. Nvidia's shares fell 4% on Monday, while rival AMD surged 13%, a sign that demand remains strong even if it could shift away from Nvidia. The more uncertain question is the supply of chips, since Huang built Nvidia's position and his departure could disrupt its strategy, relationships and financing.

The article also suggests that scrutiny of Megaspeed, which has been examined over whether its overseas data centers helped Chinese customers reach Nvidia chips despite US export restrictions, could limit Nvidia's China sales and leave more supply for American buyers. Bernstein chip analyst Stacy Rasgon questioned whether any Chinese influence was needed to push Huang's lobbying for wider chip sales to China, since Huang has pursued that for years, though with limited success. Colello kept his $310 fair value estimate for the stock, nearly double its Monday trading price. He also noted that Huang's position as co-founder and only CEO likely gives him more support from the board than most executives get, and that President Donald Trump announced his support when the allegations first arose.

The article says the scandal could also fade without lasting impact on Nvidia's business. The article concludes that the future of AI depends on whether people and businesses keep finding the technology useful and whether companies can build enough infrastructure to meet demand, and that Huang's personal life changes neither. It adds that the affair might leave America with more chips to power its AI ambitions. The articles do not say whether Huang will remain CEO or what the lawmaker probes that could follow will find.

Articles.Title: Why Jensen-Gate May Actually Help the AI Boom

stories.Headline: Meta’s AI Capital Raise Plan Draws Delaware Fiduciary Duty Challenge - The D&O Diary
stories.Summary:
On October 27, 2026, Meta shareholders filed a putative class action in the Delaware Court of Chancery against Mark Zuckerberg and the company's directors. The plaintiffs, Steamfitters Local 449 Pension Fund, Steamfitters Local 449 Retirement Security Fund, Bruce Taylor, and Ronald Mumme, seek to represent Meta's Class A stockholders. They are challenging a recapitalization that Meta's board approved on October 19, 2026, and they want it blocked. The suit was filed shortly after Meta announced plans for a potentially record-setting capital raise, partly to fund its artificial intelligence expansion.

The recapitalization would create a new class of non-voting Class C common stock, with existing holders receiving one Class C share for each Class A and Class B share they own, which would mean more than 2.5 billion new shares. Those shares would carry the same economic rights as the existing classes but no voting rights except where the law requires them. Meta has said the shares could be used for capital raising, employee pay, acquisitions, and other purposes, with trading expected to start after the change takes effect in January 2027. The complaint alleges that Zuckerberg could immediately sell about $23.8 billion of the Class C shares he would receive while keeping his roughly 60.6% voting control. Under the current dual-class setup, Class B shares carry ten votes each, and Zuckerberg holds more than 99% of them.

The complaint accuses Zuckerberg of breaching his duties as controlling shareholder by causing Meta to approve a deal that benefits him disproportionately. It also accuses the directors of skipping customary safeguards, such as a fairness opinion and a condition requiring approval by a majority of disinterested stockholders. The plaintiffs further argue that the special committee evaluating the proposal was not independent, claiming Zuckerberg exerted heavy influence over its deliberations and pressured members to approve. Meta has defended the transaction, saying the new structure gives it more flexibility for future financing while keeping its founder-led governance and supporting its AI investments. The plaintiffs are asking the court to halt the recapitalization before the planned January 2027 share issuance.

The case stands out because most AI-related shareholder litigation so far has concerned AI disclosures, capabilities, privacy, cybersecurity, or board oversight, whereas this suit targets the financing and control structure used to pay for AI. It also resembles the Delaware Chancery case involving Cloudflare, where Vice Chancellor Travis Laster granted a preliminary injunction on October 16, 2026, against a recapitalization that would have let founders keep voting control while reducing their economic stake. That ruling came despite Delaware's SB 21 reforms to Section 144 of the Delaware General Corporation Law, which were meant to give more certainty to controller transactions. The Meta lawsuit adds to a continuing debate over how Delaware balances founder control against minority stockholder protections, and the court's handling of it will be closely watched. The articles do not report any ruling or schedule in the Meta case.

Articles.Title: Meta’s AI Capital Raise Plan Draws Delaware Fiduciary Duty Challenge - The D&O Diary

stories.Headline: Cal Poly unveils NVIDIA-powered 'AI Factory' to expand AI education, research
stories.Summary:
Cal Poly, the California Polytechnic State University in San Luis Obispo, unveiled a new AI Factory in October to give students and faculty direct access to advanced AI computing on campus. The facility was unveiled during AI Day on October 22, when a ribbon cutting was held as part of a full-day event on the San Luis Obispo campus. The NVIDIA-powered facility uses four NVIDIA DGX B200 systems, and it was funded by a $3 million investment from the Noyce School of Applied Computing. The university says the setup lets students work directly with large systems while giving it more control over how students learn and how faculty conduct AI research.

The articles describe the AI Factory as a way to bring computing power that once exceeded what a typical laptop could handle onto campus. Bringing that capacity on-site, the university argues, makes proprietary research more effective and efficient and lowers costs compared with buying advanced AI systems from outside providers. Faculty are already using it, including computer science professor Jonathan Ventura, whose machine learning system analyzes drone imagery of eelgrass in Morro Bay and processes images roughly 10 times faster than hand annotation while matching its quality. Professor Paul Anderson is using it for spinal cord injury and genetic risk projects, since protected patient data cannot be sent to outside AI services. Anderson said the facility gives his team compute it previously lacked to train frontier models.

Cal Poly President Jeffrey D. Armstrong took part in the ribbon cutting alongside NVIDIA Vice President, Americas, Charlie Wuischpard, who delivered the keynote speech on AI's growth and its new opportunities for students, researchers and educators. Alex Bisberg, an assistant professor of computer science and software engineering, said that owning the hardware means owning the university's digital destiny, and he argued that training models themselves helps students learn about them and research ways to improve them. The university said in its release that graduates will need to understand AI well enough to question its output and recognize its limits, given public concern about the technology, ethical questions, and the environmental impact of large data centers. The articles also note that the Noyce School was created in 2024 after a $60 million gift from the Robert N. Noyce Trust, and that Noyce co-founded Intel and passed away in June 1990.

Articles.Title: Cal Poly unveils NVIDIA-powered 'AI Factory' to expand AI education, research

stories.Headline: Bloomberg Law survey finds 76% of attorneys worry about AI going rogue
stories.Summary:
Bloomberg Law published a new 2026 AI in Practice report on November 10, 2026, examining how attorneys use artificial intelligence and whether they trust it for complex work. The report draws on responses from more than 1,000 attorneys to Bloomberg Law's biannual State of Practice survey. Its headline finding is that 76% of attorneys are concerned about AI going rogue, and 25% fear the technology will replace their jobs. The report also looks at the business case for AI, the need to check its outputs, and what clients expect about its use. The report does not impose any requirements or rules, but it is meant to give legal employers a basis for judging their investment in AI.

According to the publisher, it raises questions that firms need to address with their attorneys and clients about where AI adds value and where it needs closer scrutiny. The findings focus on the practical side of adoption, including whether AI delivers a return on investment and whether attorneys can keep confidence in the work they produce with it. The full report is available for download from Bloomberg Law's website. The report was released by Bloomberg Law, which is part of Bloomberg Industry Group, an affiliate of Bloomberg L.P. Cesca Antonelli, editor-in-chief of Bloomberg Industry Group, said attorneys need to understand where AI adds value and where it requires closer scrutiny. She said the findings give legal employers a basis for assessing their AI investments.

The press release does not describe any regulatory action or further steps beyond the report's publication. Bloomberg Law describes itself as a provider of news, expert guidance, market intelligence, and research tools for legal professionals, used by law firms, corporations, and government agencies. The release does not say whether the survey findings will be followed up with additional reports. It also does not give further detail on how the 76% and 25% figures were calculated.

Articles.Title: Bloomberg Law Survey Examines AI's Return on Investment as Attorneys Weigh Risks

stories.Headline: Oracle abandons $7 billion Tencent AI deal under Trump pressure, FT reports
stories.Summary:
Oracle has cancelled a five-year agreement to lease advanced artificial intelligence computing capacity to China's Tencent, after U.S. officials raised concerns about the arrangement. The Financial Times reported the cancellation on Nov. 4, citing people familiar with the matter. The deal was valued at about $7 billion and was reportedly the largest overseas AI chip leasing agreement Tencent had signed. Oracle, Tencent and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the reports.

Under the agreement, signed earlier this year, Tencent would have had access to up to 100,000 advanced Nvidia AI chips installed in data centers across Southeast Asia. About 30% of the total contract value had reportedly already been paid upfront. Tencent had planned to use the capacity to reach high-performance chips that are hard to obtain in China, helping it advance its AI models and build autonomous AI agents. Markets reacted on Nov. 4, when Oracle shares fell 2.0% in U.S. trading and Nvidia declined 3.2%, though Oracle's drop also reflected broader weakness among data center operators after the U.S. midterm election results.

U.S. officials are reported to have contacted Oracle directly to voice their worries, after which the contract was dropped. Tencent faced pressure from the other side as well, since senior officials from Guangdong Province, where the company is headquartered, reportedly visited its headquarters and urged it to use and support domestically made semiconductors. Business Korea described this as pressure from both sides, with Washington seeking to stop the transfer of advanced technology and Beijing pushing firms to back domestic chipmakers in its drive for self-sufficiency. The articles do not report any public statement from Oracle, Tencent or the White House explaining the decision.

The cancellation comes as access to overseas computing is tightening for Chinese firms. Chinese companies have long leased AI chips from data centers abroad to work around U.S. export controls, and such arrangements are permitted under current rules, but government involvement in an individual contract suggests the workaround could be curtailed. One day before the cancellation, reports emerged that Nvidia had asked its cloud customers to ensure at least 51% of their services are sold to non-Chinese companies, a condition that applies to new contracts. Separately, Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance have ordered roughly 6 million of Nvidia's RTX Pro 5500 chips, yet deliveries over the next four months are expected to cover just 1% of that volume. ByteDance and Alibaba also rely on overseas data centers, and Oracle operates facilities in Malaysia and has an established cloud relationship with ByteDance, which points to wider consequences for the regional market.

Articles.Title: Oracle cancels $7 billion Tencent AI chip deal
