stories.Headline: The industrialization of AI: 8 critical considerations for building an AI gigafactory
stories.Summary:
The European Commission is working to establish multiple AI gigafactories, centralized facilities built to train next-generation AI models with trillions of parameters. A standard corporate AI setup might use a few hundred or thousand GPUs, while a gigafactory scales to tens or hundreds of thousands of nodes. Its power needs are measured in megawatts or gigawatts rather than as an ordinary budget line item. The article, a sponsored piece based on a white paper from HPE and AMD and published on November 9, 2026 by CIO, frames this as a generational infrastructure shift. It is written for CIOs and technology leaders who must plan these investments to run for about a decade.

The article lists eight considerations for planning such a facility. Power and land come first, since many organizations find late that the existing grid cannot support their compute plans, and the sites must sit near strong grids and independent backup generation. Liquid cooling is needed because dense AI chips make air cooling obsolete, and liquid systems can carry up to 3,000 times more heat than air while using less energy. Networking must be overbuilt, because bandwidth has to grow far faster than compute to keep costly GPUs from sitting idle. The remaining points cover designing for hardware and software failure with self-healing fault domains, deploying orchestration and governance before the hardware goes live, choosing suppliers with high-performance computing experience and open ecosystems to avoid vendor lock-in, keeping utilization high to justify the capital cost, and running a proactive communications plan with transparent reporting for public stakeholders.

The article attributes this guidance to HPE and AMD, the sponsors, who argue that their large-scale system design expertise and their processors and accelerators can support these facilities. The piece itself is promotional, and the article does not provide independent verification of the figures or claims it makes. It frames the gigafactory as a launchpad for economic progress, scientific discovery, and national competitiveness, and it states that addressing these constraints early lets technology leaders deliver lasting value and operational sovereignty. The article does not describe a specific timeline for the European facilities or outline next steps beyond pointing readers to a companion white paper.

Articles.Title: The industrialization of AI: 8 critical considerations for building an AI gigafactory

stories.Headline: ‘Highly selective’: Singapore banks see strong AI financing demand but stay alert to debt risks
stories.Summary:
Singapore's three largest banks, OCBC, UOB and DBS, say they remain eager to finance the booming data centre sector in South-east Asia, but they are picking their borrowers carefully. The banks made these points during their third-quarter results briefings, where all three stressed prudent lending standards and a focus on financially strong customers. Industry watchers said established operators with solid financial backing and long-term customer contracts continue to attract funding, while smaller developers are facing tighter liquidity conditions. The cautious stance follows a sharp sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday, November 5, led by stocks tied to artificial intelligence. Fears that the data centre boom could stall followed the midterm election results, and those worries have added to growing unease about debt-funded spending on AI infrastructure.

The banks' approach therefore reflects both the strong demand for financing and the wariness about how much debt the sector can carry. The article does not give figures for lending volumes or loan sizes. The banks themselves framed the message as one of discipline rather than retreat, with each emphasising that it is prioritising sponsors with strong balance sheets and reliable cash flows. The article attributes these positions to the lenders' briefings and does not offer further detail on individual loan decisions.

Its coverage of the bankers' remarks is paraphrased rather than quoted at length. The article does not say how long the selective approach will last or whether lending standards are likely to tighten further. It also does not indicate what outcome the banks expect if the Wall Street sell-off deepens or if AI spending slows. Readers should watch for further guidance from the banks and for signs of whether smaller developers begin to lose access to funding.

Articles.Title: ‘Highly selective’: Singapore banks see strong AI financing demand but stay alert to debt risks - The Business Times

stories.Headline: Europe should lead on a global AI incident reporting compact
stories.Summary:
A Bruegel commentary by Mario Mariniello argues that Europe should lead on a global mechanism for sharing information about artificial intelligence failures across borders. The piece notes a growing sense that AI needs more oversight, pointing to an AI selloff after United States midterm election results amid fears of stricter regulation, China's plan to impose mandatory domestic AI safety standards, and EU leaders discussing how Europe can contribute to international AI governance. It also says the interests of major countries overlap little, and that a Global Dialogue on AI governance launched by the United Nations has produced no negotiated outcome. The article was published on 9 November 2026.

The author proposes a well-defined structure for sharing information about AI incidents, which would be activated when a failure crosses borders. Using the example of banks in Berlin, Rio de Janeiro, Singapore and Washington relying on the same Chinese-developed model to score mortgage applicants, the piece argues that an early warning shared by the first affected bank would stop others from being harmed and give the model developer a chance to fix the bias. The mechanism would need to be sustainable, so that joining does not force countries to slow AI development or lose ground in capability rankings, and it should avoid creating security risks or imposing foreign values. The article cites the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), which requires providers of powerful models and high-risk applications, the latter from December 2027, to report serious incidents.

The author suggests the European Commission should not act alone, since a unilateral move could be seen as "regulatory colonialism," and should instead build a coalition. Mariniello names India, Canada, the United Kingdom and Brazil, a co-founder of China's World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, as possible partners that could pilot the mechanism from early 2027 before taking it to the UN and G20. The goal would be a common floor for reporting AI failures using shared protocols and formats, with countries that do not report receiving less from the shared pool. The article compares this to the Montreal Protocol, which grew out of the 1985 Vienna Convention and was accepted by every state by 2009. It concludes that the common floor would not stop the race at the AI frontier, but would let governments report future failures in a common language.

Articles.Title: Europe should lead on a global AI incident reporting compact

stories.Headline: LCPS launches AI pilot program at 7 schools
stories.Summary:
Seven Loudoun County public schools are taking part in a generative artificial intelligence pilot program with Google, according to an article published by the Loudoun Times on November 10, 2026. The program is being launched by Loudoun County Public Schools, known as LCPS. The schools named in the article are Clarke Lightfoot, Brambleton Middle, Lansdowne High, Loudoun Valley High, and Sterling Elementary. The article says the program is intended to allow students and staff to use generative AI tools in a responsible and ethical way.

It describes the program's aims as expanding the district's understanding of artificial intelligence, examining its benefits and risks, and developing guidelines for its use. Participants will reportedly be asked to test AI-powered tools in classroom settings and provide feedback. The article notes that LCPS did not say how long the program will last. The Loudoun County School Board's Curriculum and Instruction Committee has reportedly been drafting policies governing district use of generative AI and data privacy.

The article identifies the pilot as one of several steps the district is taking alongside its broader technology plans. The program is overseen by the LCPS Office of Instructional Technology, and a district spokesperson was quoted describing the initiative as a careful, measured approach. Some parents and community members reportedly expressed concern at a recent board meeting about student data privacy and whether AI tools could affect academic integrity. The article says the district responded that data protections are a central part of the pilot's design.

It also notes that Loudoun County has been a leader in technology integration in its schools for several years. The article indicates that the district expects to share findings from the pilot with the school board and the public once initial results are available. It does not give a date for that report. Additional schools may be added to the program depending on the outcome of the initial phase, according to the article.

Articles.Title: LCPS launches AI pilot program at 7 schools

stories.Headline: Chicago Public Schools blocks generative AI on student account as Google threatens to block search access
stories.Summary:
Chicago Public Schools has decided to block generative AI tools such as Google Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude on student accounts, a move the district announced in a statement released on Monday, November 10, 2026. The district said the decision was made for student privacy and safety, and that the apps will be blocked on CPS-issued devices and on the CPS network for all students. CPS said it has blocked unapproved third-party AI products to protect confidential student information and to comply with federal and state privacy laws, naming FERPA, COPPA and SOPPA. The district also stated that it has no plan to add generative AI tools to student devices.

The timing comes as Google announced the previous week that schools which turn off AI in its education apps will lose access to Google search. Google said it is turning off all AI features in its K-12 education tools unless administrators choose to enable them, with each tool, including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search, off by default. Because Google's search engine now shows an AI overview at the top of results, schools that opt out of AI would also lose search access, according to Google vice president Chris Phillips, who described the message students would see in such cases. CPS has not yet decided how it will respond to that restriction. The change affects a wide range of districts, since Google says 150 million students and teachers worldwide use its Google Classroom platform.

Google's policy drew sharp criticism from several officials. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused the company on social media of using its monopoly power to force AI into public schools, while Democratic Senator Ed Markey wrote to Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai asking the company to reverse the policy. Markey argued that the policy puts schools in an impossible position by forcing them to choose between a potentially dangerous technology and a critical research tool. An Alphabet spokesperson said Google's AI features are now so tightly built into search that the company cannot offer search without AI enabled. Former Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan also criticized the move on social media, saying Google was using its search dominance to push schools toward AI.

The dispute comes amid broader concern about AI in classrooms. New York City and Los Angeles have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools while they assess safety and develop policies. Google had earlier turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students in August, after previously allowing it only for students 18 or older. Advocates such as Josh Golin of the children's group Fairplay said Google's approach aims to build brand loyalty rather than support learning, and he urged schools to turn off Google's AI tools as soon as that option is available. He also suggested that schools consider privacy-focused search alternatives if they lose access to Google search.

Articles.Title: Chicago Public Schools blocks generative AI on student account as Google threatens to block search access - CBS News

stories.Headline: How will LAUSD respond to Google’s AI mandate? What families should know
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District said it is reviewing how to respond after Google announced last week that schools will lose access to its search engine unless they opt in to artificial intelligence. Google said that in the coming months, products like Gemini and Google Search will be turned off by default for schools until they turn them on. The company said it believes schools should have control over AI in their classrooms. Because Google Search by default includes an AI chatbot and uses AI to summarize results, schools that restrict AI would lose access to Google Search. The district had already placed a moratorium on students using generative AI on district-issued devices earlier this school year.

LAUSD's Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee is scheduled to meet on Friday, Nov. 13, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., with the agenda posted publicly. The board meets in person at 333 S. Beaudry Ave. in downtown Los Angeles, streams its meetings online, and offers American Sign Language and Spanish interpretation. Community members can request interpretation in other languages by contacting the Board Secretariat at secretariat@lausd.net or (213) 241-7002.

For now, students can still use Google to search for information, but the AI mode, where they can converse with the chatbot Gemini, is turned off. Some searches may still show AI-generated summaries, and the district has asked Google to allow those summaries to be turned off. Google's vice president for education, Chris Phillips, told The New York Times that search and AI are deeply integrated. He said that if a school bans AI, students will not have access to search and will see a message from the school saying it is unavailable. Google also said that if a school opts in, it will offer a "guided learning" tool in its chatbot for student accounts to help them work through problems.

Lila Byock, founder of Schools Beyond Screens, which pushed for the AI moratorium, said Google is refusing to accept no for an answer. Her group is calling on district leaders to reclaim their authority from corporate interests and divest from Google. The dispute comes as the district weighs its options under a broader policy debate over AI in classrooms, with the ad hoc committee's next meeting on Nov. 13 expected to add to that discussion. LAUSD's own statement said emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, can enhance teaching and learning when introduced thoughtfully, responsibly and with clear safeguards. The articles do not say what the district will decide or when any change to Google's default settings will take effect.

Articles.Title: How will LAUSD respond to Google’s AI mandate? What families should know

stories.Headline: Congress faces year-end deadline for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence legislation
stories.Summary:
Congress returned to Washington in November 2026 with a tight calendar and a deadline of December 11 for the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015, the law that gives companies legal protection when they share threat data with the government. Lawmakers are also weighing the renewal of the Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act and the Technology Modernization Fund. Those provisions are being debated as part of the National Defense Authorization Act, which has run into procedural hurdles in the Senate. The reporting comes from SC Media, which cites Nextgov for the original account.

Beyond infrastructure, Congress is examining artificial intelligence proposals, including the FRONTIER Act and the AI Kill Switch Act. According to the article, these bills would require safety disclosures and emergency shutdown capabilities for advanced AI models. The discussions follow high-profile security incidents involving AI labs. The session may also address Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, an intelligence-gathering authority that lapsed earlier this year.

The article presents the session as a last opportunity before a transition in congressional leadership in January. It frames the current window as the chance to secure existing protections and set regulatory frameworks for emerging technologies. The article does not name individual lawmakers or report specific positions taken by them. It also does not say how or when the pending votes will be resolved.

Articles.Title: Congress faces year-end deadline for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence legislation

stories.Headline: The use of artificial intelligence in regulatory activities – key areas and considerations
stories.Summary:
On 9 November 2026, the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations (IFPMA) published a position paper on the use of artificial intelligence in regulatory activities for medicinal products. The paper presents reflections from the innovative pharmaceutical industry on how regulatory authorities might apply AI in their work. It draws on publicly available initiatives and emerging experience to set out key considerations about opportunities, challenges, and implementation. The aim is to inform dialogue among regulators, industry, and other stakeholders. The paper describes AI as a way to strengthen regulatory capacity, make better use of complex data and evidence, and support more efficient regulatory processes.

Regulatory authorities are considering its use in internal operations, regulatory documentation, medicinal product review, scientific assessment, inspections, and other procedures. According to the paper, such tools could support regulatory activities and inform regulatory decisions. The document does not set binding requirements or new rules, and it presents its points as observations and considerations rather than mandates. IFPMA, which represents the innovative pharmaceutical industry, is the body behind the paper. The federation states that frameworks governing the responsible and ethical use of these technologies must keep pace with innovation while preserving the rigour, trust, and confidence that underpin regulatory decisions.

It also argues that greater alignment on principles, terminology, and strategies among national regulatory authorities could help avoid fragmentation. In its view, such alignment would support shared learning, capacity building, and more efficient global development and regulatory pathways. The paper sits within a wider discussion that IFPMA has been pursuing in 2026. In statements delivered in May and August of that year, the federation addressed harmonizing regulatory approaches and governance for data, digital health, and artificial intelligence at the World Health Assembly, and the regional regulatory strategy for medical products in Africa. The articles provided do not say what follow-up steps regulators or the federation will take after this paper.

Articles.Title: The use of artificial intelligence in regulatory activities – key areas and considerations

stories.Headline: K Altman Law Highlights School Artificial Intelligence Controls and Questions for Families
stories.Summary:
Google said on November 3 that it plans to turn off access to the Gemini application, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search for kindergarten through twelfth-grade student accounts until school administrators explicitly enable them. The company described these changes in an announcement about administrator controls and new learning features in products used by schools. It said it would provide schools with further details in the coming months, before the changes roll out. The announcement also described learning features in Search and Classroom, along with the timing of the proposed updates.

K Altman Law, a firm led by Keith Altman, has highlighted questions for families and schools as artificial intelligence tools become more common in educational technology. The firm says that artificial intelligence features may appear in standalone applications, classroom products, or search experiences, and that disabling one product does not automatically disable every such feature in another. Availability and controls can depend on the product, the school's configuration, the account, and the timing of any changes. The firm suggests that a clear school technology policy can explain which tools are available and how students are expected to use them.

Altman said that families should have understandable information about the technology students can access through school accounts. He said schools and parents can support informed use by discussing available controls, privacy expectations, and the appropriate ways for students to seek help from trusted adults. The release does not name any official responsible for enforcing these changes beyond Google's own announcement. Google's plans were described as proposed, and the release does not say how those plans will apply to any particular school district.

The firm recommends that families ask schools which artificial intelligence tools and search features are available through a student's account and device. It also suggests requesting the school's current technology-use, privacy, monitoring, and parent-notification policies, including any anticipated changes. Families are advised to ask whether separate controls apply to standalone applications, classroom tools, and search, and when changes are expected locally. The release notes that students who use accessibility tools or receive disability-related services should ask how any technology changes will affect their access. The release is general information, not legal advice, and laws and procedures vary by jurisdiction.

Articles.Title: K Altman Law Highlights School Artificial Intelligence Controls and Questions for Families

stories.Headline: East Lyme zoning commission withdraws proposed Black Point rezoning after resident pushback
stories.Summary:
The East Lyme Zoning Commission voted unanimously on November 5, 2026, to withdraw its own proposal to rezone a northerly section of Black Point Road. The proposal would have changed the area from CA commercial to R-10 residential. The vote followed a public hearing at which several neighbors spoke. The articles describe the withdrawal as coming after resident pushback. Neighbors who testified raised concerns about property values and traffic safety.

The articles say the commission will revisit alternative approaches, but they do not describe what those alternatives would be. The withdrawal means the rezoning will not proceed in its current form. The article provided does not say whether any timetable has been set for the next steps. The zoning commission, which initiated the proposal itself, took the action on its own motion following the hearing. The articles do not include direct statements from individual commissioners explaining their reasons.

They also do not name the individual residents who spoke at the hearing. The Black Point area has been the subject of zoning discussion, but the articles provided do not offer further background on earlier proposals. More details are expected as the commission considers its alternatives. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Q&A: Exploring generative AI's impact on student thinking during programming and debugging
stories.Summary:
Yazid Albadarin, a doctoral researcher, had his dissertation on generative AI and student thinking announced for examination at the Faculty of Science, Forestry and Technology, Joensuu campus. The article, a question-and-answer piece published by phys.org on November 10, 2026, describes the work as a study of how AI affects higher-order thinking, creativity and cognitive processes during programming and debugging. The research asks whether AI helps students develop deeper understanding and long-term learning, not just faster task completion. Albadarin frames the topic as urgent because generative AI is already becoming part of everyday education.

The articles report that students who used generative AI performed better and faster in some debugging tasks. However, students who worked without AI showed stronger knowledge retention when tested seven weeks later. The study also found that AI users showed stronger links between comprehension, application and creativity, while non-AI users showed stronger links between analysis and evaluation. Albadarin suggests AI may support certain forms of creativity without improving overall creativity. He recommends using AI as a learning assistant rather than a source of direct answers, with methods such as Socratic questioning, scaffolding and gradually reducing AI support.

The research is described as three connected studies using mixed methods. A systematic review covered 14 empirical studies on ChatGPT in education. A quasi-experimental study involved 152 university students comparing those who used LLAMA 3.1 during programming and debugging with those who did not, drawing on assessments, surveys, interviews and a retention test. A third study involved 132 students and applied cognitive network analysis to five critical thinking skills: comprehension, application, analysis, evaluation and creativity. Albadarin says his work is not opposed to generative AI in education but aims to clarify how it shapes the way students think and learn.

The article gives no further details on the examination date or outcome, and it does not describe next steps beyond the dissertation process. The findings are presented as relevant to educators, institutions and policymakers who are integrating AI into teaching. The article notes that the full dissertation is available as a PDF from the university repository. The piece is a Q&A based on the researcher's own account, so its conclusions reflect his interpretation of the results.

Articles.Title: Q&A: Exploring generative AI's impact on student thinking during programming and debugging

stories.Headline: Planning commission deadlocks on rezoning 150-acre Burgetts Cove site; item goes to council with no recommendation
stories.Summary:
The Johnson County planning commission deadlocked on a request to rezone roughly 150 acres at the southeast corner of 175th Street and Lone Elm Road, sending the item to the city council without a recommendation. The application, designated Z26-5, asks to change the site from RR (Rural Residential) to M1 (Light Industrial). The article is dated November 5, 2026, and reports that the commission vote ended in a 3-3 tie. Planning staff presented the request and recommended approval.

Under the M1 designation, the articles say warehousing, limited manufacturing and a range of commercial uses would be allowed, but the district's performance standards require operations to be indoors and restrict outdoor storage. Staff told the commission that data centers were removed from the M1 zoning designation and are not permitted there. The developer's representative, from Opus Development, said the firm plans to market the property for build-to-suit industrial users and is not seeking data centers. Public commenters urged caution and raised concerns about traffic, drainage and property values.

Because the commission split evenly, no recommendation will be forwarded to the city council, which will take up the rezoning request on its own. The articles do not say when the council will consider the item or what vote it may take. The reporting is limited to the commission meeting itself, so the outcome of the council's review remains open. Residents and the applicant will presumably have further opportunities to weigh in before a final decision, though the articles do not specify the schedule.

Articles.Title: Planning commission deadlocks on rezoning 150-acre Burgetts Cove site; item goes to council with no recommendation - citizenportal.ai

stories.Headline: Texas lawmakers file bills to end data center tax breaks and require state permits as filing opens for a divided Legislature
stories.Summary:
Texas lawmakers filed bills on Monday, the first day of bill filing for the 2027 legislative session, to strip data centers of a major state tax break and to put new permit requirements on their construction. The most supported measure is SB 293 by Sen. Joan Huffman, R-Houston, which would repeal the sales and use tax exemption for data centers in Tax Code sections 151.359 and 151.3595. The bill would end existing exemptions on its effective date and deny applications still pending with the comptroller. Community Impact counted 23 of the 31 senators and senators-elect as joint authors, and lawmakers from both parties filed similar repeal bills.

Sen. Judith Zaffirini, D-Laredo, filed a separate package of data center bills. SB 32 would require developers to obtain a permit from the Public Utility Commission before construction, and SB 33 would require that data centers not raise electricity costs for Texas residents. SB 34 would change counties' authority to regulate data center development, while SB 35 would require large facilities to report their water use to the Texas Water Development Board. SB 36 would bar new local tax incentives and stop cities and counties from renewing existing ones.

Huffman has argued that Texas should welcome investment but should not write a blank check. The comptroller estimates the exemption will cost about $3.3 billion in sales tax revenue in the next two-year budget, up from $14.6 million in its first biennium after 2013. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on blocking data center approvals until the Legislature passes laws to protect Texans, and outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott halted new data center grid connections on Aug. 3 and ordered an audit due at the end of the year. Companies are already seeking terms, with CoreWeave asking Hinojosa to let permitted projects finish.

The Legislature is divided, with Democrats controlling the Texas House while Republicans keep the Senate, and Democrats won the governor's office and every other statewide race. More than 1,260 bills had been filed by 5 p.m. on Monday. The session convenes Jan. 12, and bill filing closes March 12.

Articles.Title: Texas lawmakers file bills to end data center tax breaks and require state permits as filing opens for a divided Legislature - MLQ.ai

stories.Headline: Opinion | Google to AI-averse schools: We’ll our take our ball and go home
stories.Summary:
Google has reportedly said it will restrict its traditional search tool for K-12 students at schools that ban artificial intelligence, according to a November 3 report that a letter writer cites. The reporting, which the writer points to in a letter published on November 10, 2026, describes the move as a response to school districts that reject AI tools. The plan would effectively force those schools to choose between AI features and conventional search. The writer's letter does not give a date for when any restriction would take effect. Google's vice president for education reportedly argued that the AI feature and traditional search are too deeply integrated to be separated.

The writer doubts this claim, arguing that the two systems draw on different sources and therefore produce different results. As an example, the writer says a search for patient safety at a hospital returned results drawn mainly from mainstream outlets and ratings from Leapfrog, a hospital quality organization, in AI mode. In the same case, publicly available records that a standard Google search found were left out of the AI results. The writer also says the AI does not remember a nonmainstream source once it has been fed to it and will not recall it in later searches. The letter is written by Anne Hartwell Boxford, who argues that Google must address these omissions before imposing an all or nothing rule on schools that ban AI.

She says that when she questioned the AI about leaving out relevant references, it apologized and explained its limitations. Her central point is that the results of AI mode and traditional search are not the same. The letter is an opinion piece, and the article does not include a response from Google beyond what the reporting attributes to its education vice president. The context here is a dispute over whether schools can use one Google product while rejecting another. The articles do not say whether Google has finalized the restriction, which schools or districts would be affected, or how the company plans to handle the concerns raised about search omissions.

Articles.Title: Opinion | Google to AI-averse schools: We’ll our take our ball and go home - The Boston Globe

stories.Headline: Congress’s Permitting Bill Is a ‘Massive Giveaway’ to the AI Data Center Industry, Critics Warn
stories.Summary:
The Senate voted on Monday to advance a bipartisan bill called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which is meant to ease the construction of new energy infrastructure. The bill has support from labor leaders, who say it will produce thousands of jobs, and from clean energy advocates, who think it could unlock wind and solar projects. Its sponsors want it passed before the current Congress ends in January. Critics, however, say it would speed up an AI data center buildout that voters rejected in the midterm elections.

BAAJA would force data centers to pay the full cost of the grid upgrades they trigger and includes transmission reforms meant to modernize the grid. It would also weaken some environmental protections and could lead to more gas-powered data centers and more construction on public lands. Its permitting provisions could fast-track projects that are now waiting for approval and limit judges' ability to halt construction over environmental review. One study estimates data centers would pay about $55 billion in transmission charges over ten years, roughly $35 billion more than under current policy. Hundreds of local and national groups, including the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council, have urged Congress not to pass the bill as written.

Supporters, including Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic sponsor, argue the bill ends data center cost-shifting onto households and businesses. Sierra Club's Holly Bender and Earthjustice's Meg Slattery have warned that gas and fossil fuel investment could rise instead. Oil Change International's Allie Rosenbluth called the bill a massive giveaway to the data center industry. President Donald Trump urged the Senate to pass it, saying China would take any data center the United States does not want. Tribal leaders have written that the bill would weaken their ability to protect historic and cultural sites threatened by federally connected projects.

The vote is a test for Democrats after the midterms, since the bill must still pass a Senate vote to take it up, face amendments, and then pass the House in identical form before reaching Trump. Gas-powered data center projects have grown sharply, from roughly 4 gigawatts in early 2024 to 189 gigawatts in development by mid-2026, according to Global Energy Monitor data reported by Wired. Critics on the left, including Michele Jawando of Omidyar Network, want Democrats to wait for the next Congress, which will include many new House members. Supporters hope to pass it this year as a rare bipartisan win on affordability.

Articles.Title: Congress’s Permitting Bill Is a ‘Massive Giveaway’ to the AI Data Center Industry, Critics Warn - Time Magazine

stories.Headline: CrowdWorks Joins Government Manufacturing AI Project
stories.Summary:
CrowdWorks, an artificial intelligence technology company, has partnered with agentic AI company Enhans to take part as an official partner in the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources' 2026 AI Model Development Project Based on Manufacturing Tacit Knowledge. The announcement was published by The Elec on November 10, 2026. The project's goal is to turn large volumes of unstructured field data, which hold the experience and intuition of highly skilled manufacturing experts, into high-quality training datasets. It also aims to build an ontology-based AI guidance model to help frontline workers.

Within the project, Enhans will lead the development of an ontology and guidance AI model drawn from the tacit knowledge of experts in the refining and petrochemical industries. CrowdWorks will handle preprocessing of the unstructured field data and will use its Alpy Knowledge Compiler, which relies on automated document parsing to convert tables, images, performance curves, graphs and mathematical formulas into text that AI can be trained on. The company plans to build infrastructure able to process up to 7.5 million pages over the project period. CrowdWorks described the work as its full-scale entry into the emerging market for manufacturing tacit knowledge.

The article attributes the announcement to CrowdWorks, which said the project marks its entry into this market and that it expects to play a leading role in the manufacturing industry's AI transformation data market. The article does not include a direct statement from the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources or from Enhans. It does report that the ministry plans to raise its budget for AI solutions using manufacturing tacit knowledge from 48 billion won this year to 290 billion won next year. The article does not say what outcomes the project will be judged against or when the guidance model is expected to reach frontline use.

Articles.Title: CrowdWorks Joins Government Manufacturing AI Project - www.thelec.net

stories.Headline: Democratic Congress, Trump and AI investment for SP:SPX by Swissquote
stories.Summary:
The Democratic Party's victory in the US midterm elections triggered selling pressure across the technology sector, particularly among semiconductor stocks. Market participants fear that large planned investments in AI infrastructure could be questioned or delayed by Democratic legislative efforts at the federal and local levels. The new Democratic majority in Congress can influence AI-related regulation, and Democratic officials in individual states and localities may also try to block or slow the physical deployment of AI infrastructure. The article argues that these fears may be exaggerated, since there is no unified Democratic push to undermine AI momentum in the United States. It adds that the Republican minority and the White House still hold significant tools to resist such moves.

The article explains the new balance of power between the White House and the Democratic-led Congress over AI investment. President Donald Trump can veto legislation, and Democrats would need a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override that veto, a threshold the article describes as particularly difficult to reach given their simple majority. Local authorities, by contrast, control urban planning, zoning and building permits, so they can reject projects, impose extra requirements or suspend developments, and a presidential veto cannot overturn such municipal decisions. Environmental limits, water use and heavy electricity demand are also possible sources of opposition. Congress can additionally apply pressure through hearings, investigations into large technology companies and budget debates, which can add regulatory uncertainty without new legislation.

The article identifies the companies most exposed as Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta, which are the hyperscalers building large data centers. It says these firms could keep their massive investment budgets while facing greater difficulty obtaining permits, securing electricity connections and accessing the computing capacity needed for new facilities. The analysis distinguishes between a broad federal blockade, which presidential powers constrain, and operational delays to individual infrastructure projects, which are the more realistic risk. The author, Vincent Ganne writing for Swissquote, concludes that the political shift adds a risk to the timeline for deploying AI infrastructure but does not necessarily undermine the structural investment momentum in the sector.

The article does not describe specific next steps beyond this assessment. The main issue for equity markets, according to the article, is the gap between the capital spending announced by hyperscalers and the actual commissioning of new computing capacity. Investors are therefore advised to watch that gap rather than focus solely on the election result. The article is framed as market commentary for informational purposes and is not investment advice.

Articles.Title: Democratic Congress, Trump and AI investment for SP:SPX by Swissquote - TradingView

stories.Headline: Estevan council considers AI research lab, billboard sites and demolition orders
stories.Summary:
Estevan City Council is set to consider several community and development matters at its regular meeting on Monday, November 9, 2026. The main item is a request for a city letter of support for an application by Southeast College to the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada for up to $200,000 in equipment funding. The college wants to set up an on-premises AI test bed at its Centre of Sustainable Innovation, and the city would not be asked for funding or staff time. The application deadline is November 18.

The proposed facility would let local businesses and organizations test how artificial intelligence could be used without relying on cloud-based services that send their data elsewhere. Equipment would range from entry-level computers to higher-end AI workstations, helping businesses judge what suits their needs and budgets. The project would also give students hands-on experience and support local technology capacity and economic diversification. Council is also weighing three billboard proposals on city-owned land, at Kensington Avenue near Walmart's south entrance, at Souris Avenue and King Street, and near Canadian Tire's north entrance. Administration recommends approval of all three, with conditions requiring sign owners to mow grass within one metre of their billboards where applicable.

Council will also consider demolition orders for two properties, 905 Fourth Street and 1132 Fifth Street, based on a report from Bylaw Enforcement Officer Justin Herod. The city has received numerous complaints about 905 Fourth Street since July 2025, and the building has remained uninhabitable, raising public safety concerns, previous break-ins and squatting. That demolition order is set to take effect after December 4, 2026. For 1132 Fifth Street, administration recommends an exemption if its sale to new owners goes through, while the existing order to remedy would stay registered against the property.

Council will receive the October building permit report, which shows four permits worth $2,565,500 compared with three valued at $871,900 in October 2025. Year to date the city has issued 44 permits worth $13,844,489, against 35 permits worth $8,768,810 at the same point last year. The October water quality report notes no water main breaks and no failures to meet testing regulations, and upgrades to the Smith Street Reservoir are on schedule for completion by the end of December 2026. Council will also consider letters of support for the Estevan Curling Club's bid to host the 2028 Saskatchewan High Schools Athletic Association High School Provincial Doubles Curling Championships, which involves no financial request, and appoint Western Municipal Consulting Ltd. to manage the 2027 Board of Revision process.

stories.Headline: 6 Members of Congress Set for 'Broadband and AI' as Reps. Pramila Jayapal and Jennifer McClellan Join Keynote Lineup
stories.Summary:
Broadband Breakfast announced that two House Democrats who are writing artificial intelligence legislation, Reps. Pramila Jayapal of Washington and Jennifer McClellan of Virginia, will deliver keynotes at its Broadband and AI in the Next Congress conference. Their additions raise the number of members of Congress on the program to six. Rep. Greg Landsman of Ohio will take part in a fireside chat with the outlet's editor and publisher, Drew Clark. Sen. Ed Markey, Rep. Buddy Carter and Rep. Nanette Barragán were announced earlier as keynote speakers.

The announcement was published on November 10, 2026. The conference is set for Tuesday, December 1, at the National Press Club in Washington. Registration for in-person attendance costs $245, and Breakfast Club members receive an additional $100 off. The program begins at 9 a.m., with doors opening no later than 8:30 a.m., in the Grand Ballroom.

Comcast and Broadband Nation Expo are gold sponsors, and INCOMPAS is a silver sponsor. Full program details and registration are available on the event page. Jayapal has represented Washington's Seventh District, which includes most of Seattle, since 2017, and she co-leads the House version of the AI Civil Rights Act. That bill would bar companies from using biased algorithms in high-stakes decisions and require testing before and after deployment.

In October 2026 she released a framework for a national AI charter that would require AI companies to meet public-benefit conditions. McClellan has represented Virginia's Fourth District, which includes Richmond, since 2023, and in March 2026 she introduced the bipartisan AI-Ready Networks Act with Rep. Jay Obernolte. That bill, H.R. 7783, would direct the National Telecommunications and Information Administration to report on how AI is being adopted in U.S. commercial telecommunications networks. Landsman has written legislation requiring data centers to cover the full cost of their energy and infrastructure needs, while Barragán introduced the Artificial Intelligence Environmental Impacts Act with Rep. Don Beyer.

Markey, who authored the Telecommunications Act of 1996 in the House, released an AI Accountability Agenda in July 2026. Carter is the lead sponsor of the American Broadband Deployment Act, H.R. 2289. The conference is organized around four panels covering catastrophic AI risk, permitting reform, data center power and ratepayer protection, and federal preemption versus state AI rules. Additional speakers are still to be announced.

stories.Headline: Infineon, SoluM to Develop HVDC Power Solutions for AI Data Centers
stories.Summary:
Infineon Technologies Korea said on Nov. 5 that it signed a memorandum of understanding with SoluM to jointly develop high-voltage direct current power solutions for AI data centers. The agreement was signed by Adam White, president of Infineon's Power Systems division, and SoluM CEO Jeon Seong-ho. The two companies will cooperate on three product areas: server power supply units, battery backup units and intermediate bus converters. HVDC distributes electricity inside data centers as direct current instead of alternating current, which reduces the number of power conversion stages and so cuts energy losses.

Under the deal, Infineon will take part from the early stages of projects, proposing products, developing reference designs and providing technical support. It will supply silicon, silicon carbide and gallium nitride power semiconductors, along with microcontrollers and sensors. SoluM will design and manufacture the server power solutions and power modules. The companies also agreed to hold regular technical exchanges to develop next-generation technologies. SoluM was set up in 2015 as a spin-off of Samsung Electro-Mechanics' Digital Module division and makes power modules for televisions and servers, as well as electronic shelf labels.

White said AI data centers increasingly need power infrastructure with higher efficiency, reliability and power density, and that SoluM's server power expertise and Infineon's semiconductor knowledge complement each other. Jeon said the collaboration will strengthen SoluM's high-voltage, high-efficiency power design capabilities and open new business in the next-generation AI data center power market. At a press conference the same day at Infineon Korea's Seoul headquarters, White set out the company's "From Grid to Core" strategy and said its chips are used across the whole power supply chain of AI data centers. A report on the event also listed Hyosung and LS Electric among Infineon's expanding partnerships in Korea.

White projected that data centers' share of global electricity generation will rise from 3% today to 7% to 8% by 2030. He said power use per server rack will grow from 100 to 150 kilowatts now to more than 1 megawatt after 2028, as the power draw of each GPU climbs from 1,000 watts to above 2,000 watts. The 800-volt direct current architecture, which Nvidia is promoting, converts incoming power straight to 800V DC and steps it down only once or twice near the GPU, cutting losses, heat and the space taken by cabling and power supplies. Nvidia plans to widen its use alongside shipments of its Kyber racks in 2027. A Simply Wall St article on Nov. 7 noted that the SoluM tie-up gives context to growth assumptions for Infineon, whose shares were at €45.76 and had gained 60.5% over three years, and it judged the stock modestly undervalued on a discounted cash flow basis.

Articles.Title: Vertiv partners with Infineon to scale power semiconductors for AI data centers

stories.Headline: US law professors urge court to reject blanket fair-use exemption for AI training
stories.Summary:
Seven US law professors have asked a federal court in New York to reject a broad fair-use exemption for using copyrighted books to train AI models in the OpenAI copyright litigation. They filed an amicus curiae brief on November 6 before the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, supporting the plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment. The brief argues that copyright law does not allow a blanket exemption for AI training and that each use must be judged on its own facts. The professors warn that accepting OpenAI's position would let developers use copyrighted works without permission or payment and then build commercial systems that could compete with those works.

The professors say the fair-use doctrine under Section 107 of the US Copyright Act requires courts to examine the specific purpose and effect of each use. In their view, acquiring books, keeping or distributing copies, using them to develop a model, and deploying that model are separate activities that each need their own legal assessment. The brief also separates AI tools built for purposes such as translation and accessibility from commercial systems designed to produce expressive works that compete with the originals. Relying on the US Supreme Court's 2023 decision in Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts v Goldsmith, the professors argue that a new purpose does not by itself establish fair use.

The brief further contends that unauthorised use could damage an emerging market for licensing books and other creative material for AI training. It points out that publishers and AI developers, including OpenAI, have already signed licensing arrangements for training material. The professors argue that widespread unauthorised copying could cut licensing revenue and discourage authors from creating original works. They also raise concerns about market dilution, noting that AI systems trained on copyrighted books could flood the market with competing content and reduce the visibility of original works.

To support these points, the professors cite the Third Circuit's September 29, 2026 decision in Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH v ROSS Intelligence Inc., which concerned copyrighted legal research headnotes used to build a competing AI-powered research platform. They urge courts to ask whether AI-generated products compete in the same market as the works used for training, rather than treating model development as automatically transformative. The professors have asked the court to reject any categorical fair-use ruling covering copying books for AI training, research or development. They also ask the court to grant the plaintiffs' motion on distinct unauthorised downloading, copying and distribution activities to the extent the undisputed record supports it. The court has not yet ruled on the arguments in the brief.

Articles.Title: US law professors urge court to reject blanket fair-use exemption for AI training - ETLegalWorld.com

stories.Headline: Lawyer builds private AI server with eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs — up to 215 tokens per second to keep legal files offline, costing about $2,400 per four-GPU board
stories.Summary:
A lawyer who posted on Reddit has built a private AI server from eight used 2018-era Nvidia Tesla V100 data center GPUs so that case files never have to leave the office. The system uses two four-card SXM2 NVLink boards, four PEX switches and SlimSAS cables, and the builder has already suffered one burnt power connector along the way. It now runs the open DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model with every expert held in GPU memory, reaching up to 215 tokens per second. The builder bought the four-GPU boards for about $2,400 apiece.

The hardware uses eight V100-SXM2-32GB cards, each with 32GB of HBM2 memory, which plug into Nvidia's SXM2 socket rather than standard PCIe slots. The cards sit on two baseboards, with all four cards on each board linked by NVLink for 128GB per board, while the two boards communicate with each other only over PCIe. Each board connects to the host through two PEX switch cards, and the host includes a Threadripper Pro motherboard, a 12-core 3945WX processor, 256GB of DDR4 memory and two power supplies totaling 2,800 W on separate office circuits. The article notes that used V100 SXM2 32GB cards now sell for about $900 on eBay, more than double the roughly $400 apiece cited in the original post, and that prices appear to be still rising.

The builder, who is a lawyer, says the server is used daily for first-pass work on case files, including pulling out facts, dates and numbers, summarizing records and making a first attempt at routine drafting. The builder stresses that nothing leaves the office without a full human review, and that the setup protects client files that cannot be sent to a cloud or frontier model. The model is compressed to mostly 2 bits, with weights totaling 248.8GB, and about 110GB of lookup tables stay in ordinary system RAM. Code generation is fastest, at up to 215 tokens per second, while legal writing runs at up to 118 tokens per second. The builder estimates that 50% to 60% of their AI work can now skip frontier models, and the server currently handles only one request at a time.

Articles.Title: Lawyer builds private AI server with eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs — up to 215 tokens per second to keep legal files offline, costing about $2,400 per four-GPU board - Tom's Hardware

stories.Headline: Practical workshops on Artificial Intelligence Applied to Legal Research begin today - Universitat de València
stories.Summary:
The Regulation Research Group at the University of Valencia began a series of practical workshops on artificial intelligence applied to legal research today, 9 November 2026. The sessions are taught by Andrés Marzal Varó of the Universitat Jaume I and will run on 9, 16 and 23 November 2026, with a final session on 14 December 2026. Each session runs from 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m.

In-person classes take place in Room 3P12 of Administrative Law at the Faculty of Law, and online attendance is also available. The course is built around four highly practical sessions in which participants work directly on their own laptops. Its theoretical part is limited to a conceptual framework covering how generative AI learns, why it is not deterministic, what hallucinations are and how to reduce them, what an AI agent is, and how these systems connect to external sources such as the internet, databases and personal documents. The main goal is to learn how to carry out common research tasks efficiently and to verify what AI systems produce.

Each session ends with a usable output, such as a configured research assistant, a case-law summary workflow, an AI-assisted thematic wiki, or tools for tracking developments in a research area. Participants must hold an active Claude Pro subscription during November, which the article puts at about €20 for one month. The course itself is free, and the subscription can be cancelled once the training ends. The workshops are organised by the Regulation Research Group, which belongs to the University of Valencia, and the article identifies Andrés Marzal Varó of the Universitat Jaume I as the instructor.

The article presents the programme as a response to the growing role of artificial intelligence in legal research, and it states that this role is likely to become more important in the short and medium term. It does not describe any dispute, incident or regulatory change behind the course. The article is a university announcement, so it gives no information on outcomes or enrolment numbers. It also does not say whether further editions are planned after the series ends.

stories.Headline: AI Makes Contracting Faster Yet Businesses Are Struggling to Show the ROI
stories.Summary:
A new report from World Commerce & Contracting, produced with support from Deloitte and the contract lifecycle management provider Ironclad, finds that artificial intelligence is speeding up the work of legal and contracting professionals but has not yet produced clear business results for many organizations. The research, published in November 2026, found that 62% of the organizations surveyed saw greater individual productivity from AI without being able to show a matching impact on the wider business. Individuals are finishing tasks faster, yet those gains are not adding up to better outcomes at the organization level. The findings were reported by Tony Thompson on law.com on November 9, 2026.

The report also shows that AI use in contracting remains concentrated on individual tasks rather than shared processes. Only 4% of the organizations surveyed use AI as a cross-functional platform that spans teams. The authors suggest that fragmented systems and processes may be limiting returns, since AI layered on top of disconnected workflows can speed up pieces of the job without changing the whole. The implication is that organizations need to rethink how contracting work is structured before AI can deliver measurable value.

Simply making existing work faster is not enough to show a return. Tim Cummins of World Commerce & Contracting and Craig Conte of Deloitte Legal are the named voices in the coverage, and both argue that businesses should point AI at commercial outcomes rather than treating it as a tool to accelerate current contracting routines. In their view, the question for organizations is what the contracting function is meant to achieve for the business, and AI should be measured against that goal. Their comments, as reported, reflect a call for a shift in focus from activity to results.

The article attributes these positions to them without adding further detail on specific recommendations. The findings arrive as many companies are investing heavily in AI tools and face growing pressure from executives to justify those costs. The gap between personal productivity and organizational return is a central tension in the report, and the coverage does not go beyond what the survey and the commentary describe. The article does not specify any follow-up steps, timelines or planned changes by the organizations involved, so the practical next moves for businesses remain open to them.

Articles.Title: AI Makes Contracting Faster Yet Businesses Are Struggling to Show the ROI - Law.com

stories.Headline: AI SOC ROI for 2027: The Number Your CFO Will Actually Sign
stories.Summary:
The only article supplied is a LinkedIn sponsored post, published on 10 November 2026, that promotes a paid "AI SOC Pricing & ROI Kit 2027" from UnderDefense. The post argues that AI SOC vendor pitches often count freed analyst hours as cash savings, which a chief financial officer will question. It says that hours become money only when a planned hire is not made, and that until then they are capacity, which should be shown on a separate line. It values an analyst hour at $100.30 fully loaded, built from a $129,180 BLS median salary and 1,840 productive hours. In its worked example, handling 3,000 alerts a month with two hires not made returns an 11.1% cash ROI in year one, with payback in 10.8 months. The post is part of a feed on the Cyber Security Hub newsletter page, which carries many unrelated security stories from the same period. stories.Headline: Pennsylvania Enacts Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania enacted the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act after Governor Josh Shapiro signed Senate Bill 806 on October 22, 2026. The bill became Act 99 of 2026 and sets a disclosure requirement for advertisers who use synthetic content in ways that create a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of advertised goods or services. The law defines synthetic content as images, video, audio clips, or text that AI has significantly modified or generated, and its definition of AI includes generative AI. It does not require disclosure every time an advertiser uses AI, because the duty is tied to content that creates a false impression.

The law takes effect 60 days after enactment, which is December 21, 2026. A disclosure must be clear and conspicuous, appearing in a size, color, contrast, location, duration, and volume that make it noticeable, readable, understandable, and audible. It must be in the language the consumer uses, must not contradict nearby information, and must appear the first time the synthetic content is shown, in the same medium, and, where technically feasible, in a form that is permanent or very hard to remove. The law excludes content that is evidently fictional, parody, satire, commentary, or criticism, and content limited to text.

The Pennsylvania Attorney General or the appropriate district attorney can seek an injunction when a prohibited practice is occurring or about to occur and proceedings would serve the public interest. They can also bring a civil action, and a court may award a civil fine of up to $3,000 plus actual attorney fees and court costs. The statute does not expressly create a private right of action, and it says disclosure of AI use does not limit any other recourse available under law. The articles say businesses should review consumer-facing ads that use AI-generated or significantly AI-modified images, videos, and audio, and should check the controls used by advertising agencies and third-party marketing vendors.

The articles describe the law as narrower than a general AI transparency mandate and as another state-level requirement in the evolving legal framework for generative AI in commercial communications. They say the most immediate concern is not the use of AI itself but the potential for synthetic content to create a misleading impression about a product, service, customer experience, or endorsement. Businesses should not assume that a disclosure buried in fine print or added after the content has already been presented will suffice. The articles say reviewing advertising practices and putting disclosure controls in place before the December 21 effective date would be a prudent compliance measure.

Articles.Title: Pennsylvania Enacts Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act - Inside Global Tech

stories.Headline: Huang Scandal Spurs U.S. Congress to Block AI Chip Exports
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers from both parties in the U.S. Congress have called for bills banning exports of H200-class and more advanced semiconductors to China to be folded into the National Defense Authorization Act. The call followed a scandal involving NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. A floor vote is seen as possible in the second week of December. Export restrictions stemming from NVIDIA are expected to ripple through supply strategies at South Korean chipmakers.

Republican Rep. Jim Banks and Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren issued a bipartisan statement urging immediate action on export controls for AI semiconductors bound for China. Among the bills cited are an AI monitoring act barring exports of H200-class and more advanced chips to China for a set period, a chip security act and the MATCH Act. A presidential signature after mid-December is described as a realistic scenario. The articles do not give the vote count or the full text of the amendment.

SK hynix supplies more than 50% of NVIDIA's HBM, raising the possibility that tighter export rules could disrupt its plan to expand its plant in Dalian, China. A former senior U.S. official said some restrictions could appear in economic and technology exchanges between the United States and China. Huang's own role in the scandal is not described beyond the reporting already noted. The articles give no statement from NVIDIA or from the Chinese government on the proposed bills.

Market reaction in Seoul has been sharp in both directions. The KOSPI closed at 5,239.13 on the session reported, up 220.28 points, or 4.39%, after foreign investors who had sold 12.5835 trillion won over the previous seven sessions swung to net purchases of 358.6 billion won. Samsung Electronics rose 4.74% and SK hynix 6.69%. Morgan Stanley cut its target price for Samsung Electronics to 309,000 won from 381,000 won and for SK hynix to 1.6 million won from 2.6 million won, citing expanding semiconductor supply and slowing investment in AI data centers.

Google unveiled two new chips, the TPU 8tx and 8i Max, while AMD began selling its Helios server rack, and AMD shares jumped 13% after Oppenheimer set a $600 target price. Anthropic plans to list on the Nasdaq on the 19th or 20th under the ticker ANT, with a target valuation cut to $1 trillion from $2 trillion. The articles say that if its large offering draws funds out of existing AI technology stocks, it could pressure flows into South Korean semiconductor shares. Whether the rebound in Korean chip stocks can hold is left open by the reporting.

stories.Headline: Anwar says AI Governance Bill to complement cybersecurity, data laws
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the Malaysian government is finalising an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance Bill that will work alongside existing laws such as the Cybersecurity Act and data protection regulations. He made the remarks at the launch of Ant International's Global Development Centre in Kuala Lumpur. At the event, he said the government would ask technology companies, including Ant International, for input as the Bill is drafted. He said officials and the relevant ministry would hold discussions with the company because of its expertise and familiarity with regulations in many countries.

Anwar said the Bill would form part of the final phase of the Malaysian Digital Economy Blueprint and that digital trust is the foundation for building a digital nation. He said artificial intelligence and large language models would change how businesses operate, how credit is assessed, how risks are managed and how markets connect across borders. He said that when applied responsibly, such models could remove barriers, aid communication and open new opportunities for trade and innovation. He also warned that these technologies could concentrate large amounts of power among those who control data platforms and digital infrastructure. He stressed that human judgment must remain at the centre of decision-making as machines become more capable.

The Prime Minister said trust and security must remain central to the digital finance industry, arguing that customers need assurance that their money and information are protected and that decisions about them are fair. The AI Governance Bill was first flagged in mid-2025 by Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo, who said he hoped to table the legislation in the second half of 2026. The articles do not give further details on the Bill's contents or a firm date for its tabling in Parliament. The article was published by the New Straits Times on November 8, 2026.

Articles.Title: Anwar says AI Governance Bill to complement cybersecurity, data laws - NST Online

stories.Headline: AI gives websites, virtual worlds second act in South Korea
stories.Summary:
Park Jin-won, a Korean creator, built a Buddhist temple online in about 30 minutes using AI coding tools, and it drew a crowd in less than a week. The story, published by KED Global on November 10, 2026, describes the temple as one of many amateur-built online sanctuaries in South Korea. The site, sansatemple.com, is one example of a wider trend in which individuals and businesses are building websites and virtual spaces again. The article covers this revival in the context of AI tools making such projects quick and cheap to produce.

Businesses are also building sites of their own, with the aim of appearing in results from AI search tools. The article lists related topics such as e-commerce, domain names, metaverse platforms and digital sanctuaries as part of the same shift. Separate items in the same feed describe Anthropic's Claude gaining ground in South Korea's paid generative AI market, driven by corporate demand. Another item reports that monthly subscription payments for generative AI services have reached a record, with a reported figure of $58.3 million. The articles say these subscriptions are spreading among professionals, especially those in their 20s and 30s, who are folding AI into everyday tasks.

The articles name Park Jin-won as the builder of the temple, and they attribute the speed of the project to AI coding tools. Kakao Healthcare, a digital healthcare unit of South Korea's Kakao, is described as selected to operate a metaverse healthcare project in the medical sector. The feed also quotes a co-founder of the metaverse startup Spatial, who said the company wants to grow into a platform where users share interactive content, a goal he linked to demand for shared experiences during COVID-19. The articles do not give further detail on what these actors have committed to beyond those statements.

The wider context is that virtual worlds, which many companies had written off, are finding new users as AI lowers the cost of building and searching for content. The articles say that remote work has also changed daily life, citing a Zigbang manager who has worked away from the Gangnam office for about four months. The available reporting does not set out next steps, timelines or regulatory responses. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Digital Health and AI: Key Regulatory, Reimbursement and Policy Developments
stories.Summary:
Last week, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services finalized its 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System rule and its Medicare Physician Fee Schedule rule, both of which address digital health and artificial intelligence. In the outpatient rule, CMS coined the term "Software as a Medical Service" for software that supports clinical decisions through algorithmic analysis. CMS also created an interim payment pathway, assigning qualifying services to New Technology Ambulatory Payment Classifications and establishing a new status indicator, O1. The policy does not guarantee separate payment for every AI-enabled tool, since payment still depends on service and coding requirements. CMS also finalized separate payment for certain stand-alone algorithmic analyses of previously completed laboratory data, including secondary analyses of genomic sequencing results.

The physician fee schedule rule did not create an AI-specific payment pathway, but it signals growing attention to how technology affects physician work and quality measurement. CMS issued a Request for Information seeking industry input on technology-enabled primary care and on how Medicare payment might account for clinical AI. The rule cites an estimated 25 percent penetration of AI documentation tools, such as ambient scribes, among U.S. physicians. CMS also said more than 40 percent of U.S. physicians had self-reported using OpenEvidence, an AI application that answers clinical questions from peer-reviewed sources. Many commenters expressed skepticism and urged CMS to ensure that any Medicare-paid AI demonstrates proven clinical value.

CMS said it would consider that feedback in future rulemaking. CMS addressed AI in the Medicare Annual Wellness Visit, stressing that a physician or other health professional must still perform the visit and that clinicians must retain responsibility for clinical decisions. The agency said AI may support components such as administering the Health Risk Assessment, reconciling medications for clinician verification, and drafting a personalized prevention plan for clinician review. CMS said it was not aware of how AI could conduct a cognitive assessment under the current standard.

Beneficiary-facing software used to implement a prevention plan must not constitute the practice of medicine or replace the beneficiary-clinician relationship, and it must comply with fraud and abuse laws, including the Anti-Kickback Statute. CMS may issue further guidance in future rulemaking. CMS also tightened oversight of remote patient monitoring and remote therapeutic monitoring after findings by the Office of the Inspector General about potential fraud, waste and abuse. The rule extends the established-patient requirement to remote therapeutic monitoring, so practitioners must furnish a separately reportable initiating face-to-face visit, in person or via telehealth, before monitoring begins.

CMS also finalized a requirement that clinical staff performing these services be directly employed by the billing practitioner or practice, subject to incident-to requirements. That requirement may materially affect digital health companies that provide outsourced monitoring services. CMS delayed its implementation until Jan. 1, 2029, giving providers and vendors more time to adjust their operating models. Separately, the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology streamlined portions of the federal health IT certification framework, and the American Medical Association released a clinical AI liability framework.

The AMA framework would allocate responsibility among clinicians, AI developers and deploying healthcare organizations based on each party's authority, access to information and ability to control or mitigate risk. It rejects the assumption that keeping a physician "in the loop" automatically shifts responsibility away from developers or health systems. Congress has also extended several Medicare telehealth flexibilities through Dec. 31, 2027, including audio-only telehealth and access from beneficiaries' homes. Pending legislation, including the PATIENT AI Act and Doctors Not AI Act, reflects continued congressional attention to AI reimbursement, oversight and privacy.

Articles.Title: Digital Health and AI: Key Regulatory, Reimbursement and Policy Developments - JD Supra

stories.Headline: Governor's 2027 preview touches Alexandria's asks on housing, solar, and AI, but not transit or school funding
stories.Summary:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger released the first preview of her 2027 legislative agenda on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at the State Capitol in Richmond. The preview, called "Moving Virginia Forward," was outlined alongside House and Senate Democratic leaders and touches several of Alexandria's requests for the General Assembly, including housing near transit, solar energy, and artificial intelligence. It does not mention transit funding, the state's school funding formula, or immigration enforcement, all of which appear in the city's draft legislative package. The preview landed hours before City Council was scheduled to receive that draft at its Tuesday night meeting.

The release and a two-page summary describe the agenda as a set of select proposals rather than the full program. Spanberger and legislators are expected to travel the state in the coming weeks to announce more. Council plans to hold a public hearing and adopt Alexandria's package on Saturday, November 14. The General Assembly session begins January 13, 2027.

Together, these dates set the timeline for how the city's requests will be weighed against the governor's priorities. The governor's office issued the release, and Spanberger and the Democratic leaders of the House and Senate presented the agenda in person. The Alexandria Brief, a local outlet, reported on the preview and on the city's pending package, which is the document Council will consider. The articles do not describe any response from city officials to the omissions on transit and school funding.

Alexandria's requests on housing, solar, and AI have been met in part by the governor's preview, while transit and school funding remain unaddressed in it. The articles do not say whether those omitted issues will appear in the later announcements. Council's vote on Saturday will determine what the city formally asks the General Assembly to consider. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Governor's 2027 preview touches Alexandria's asks on housing, solar, and AI, but not transit or school funding - The Alexandria Brief

stories.Headline: Legaltech Hub CEO Joins Davis Polk As AI Chief
stories.Summary:
The chief executive of Legaltech Hub is leaving the legal technology insights and analysis company to take a new post at Davis Polk & Wardwell LLP. Steven Lerner reported the move for Law360 on November 9, 2026. The new role is chief artificial intelligence and knowledge officer at the firm. It also does not describe what the new position will require beyond the title.
