stories.Headline: Own the outcome, delegate the work: A framework for testing with AI agents
stories.Summary:
Vaclav Vincalek, a virtual CTO and founder of the Recurrent Patterns Podcast and Media Services, argued at the SD Times Live! AI in Test Supercast on Nov. 5 that speed does not equal quality. He said the term AI leads people to treat the technology as a teammate, and suggested instead describing it as technology that performs certain tasks. He warned that a fast system you cannot explain can cause harm quickly. He also said that building more features does not improve quality, and that he had not yet seen the productivity gains that would justify the investment.

Donovan Brady, vice president of developer relations at Leapwork, followed with a session titled "The Architect Behind the Agents: Owning Quality While Delegating the Work." Brady said most teams use AI only to generate and maintain tests, which leaves out defining business outcomes, risk priorities and release criteria. He identified three failure modes: wrong tests that lack business context, wrong timing in running them, and silent repairs in which self-healing changes a test so it passes instead of flagging a real defect. He said an AI asked for 500 tests may produce 500 when only about 100 are needed.

Brady's proposed remedy is a role he calls the "validation architect," a QA professional or SDET who owns business outcomes, critical customer journeys, risk priorities, coverage expectations, escalation rules and the release decision. Agents would handle execution, including proposing test cases for approval, maintaining tests, selecting suites, running them in CI/CD pipelines and gathering evidence for review. Using a Black Friday example involving a 20% loyalty discount that must not stack with another coupon, he said every generated test must trace back to an approved requirement. He added that a 1% failure rate in critical journeys might be acceptable at some points in the year, "But on Black Friday, no," so the release call stays with a person.

Brady said agents may act alone on changes that fit standing policy, such as requirements, approved outcomes, mandatory evidence and escalation rules, but anything touching business outcomes, risk or revenue should be escalated. A moved button is a mechanical repair the agent can handle, while a changed expected outcome, such as a different total or a removed assertion, should be flagged and returned to the requirement owner. He suggested enforcing this as a gate in the CI/CD pipeline or in the agent's instructions. He called the approach "continuous validation," a step between continuous integration and continuous deployment.

Brady said Microsoft uses Leapwork to test Dynamics 365 and Power Platform in its Azure DevOps pipelines, cutting a regression cycle that once took at least two weeks of manual effort to a couple of hours, a figure he attributed to Leapwork. He also said Leapwork Play, a Playwright-based tool with built-in agents and MCP support, became generally available Sept. 30. For teams with a fragmented test estate, he advised starting with one critical journey, such as checkout, defining its expected outcomes, assigning an owner for requirements and risk tolerance, and deciding the evidence needed before release. He added that the workflow itself has to be re-engineered rather than bolting an agent onto an old process. The Supercast is available on demand at sdtimes.com.

stories.Headline: Nebius Stock Faces Election Driven AI Data Center Regulation Risks
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of Congress and a number of governorships in the midterm elections, and the Idaho Press reported that this is expected to bring more regulation of artificial intelligence and more moratoriums on AI data centers. Many Democratic candidates for governor and the U.S. Senate had promised both during their campaigns, in contrast to President Donald Trump, who backs rapid data center construction and industry self-policing so the United States does not lose the AI race to China. Local data center measures were on the ballot in 41 jurisdictions, including places in Ohio, Illinois, Maine, Kansas and Wisconsin, and all but one passed, the exception being Hardwood, North Dakota. In Ohio, voters approved bans or restrictions in at least 14 towns, and in Wilmington about 80% of voters rejected rezoning for a data center in four separate referendums. Tech and data center stocks fell sharply on Thursday, Nov. 5, as Wall Street worried the election results would slow the buildout.

Exit polls cited in the article found that 76% of voters oppose data centers in their own communities, with Democrats making up 64% of that opposition. Another 56% said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote, and Democrats were 65% of that group. There are already 372 data center moratoriums across the country and another 43 permanent bans, according to Interconnected Capital, and New York has a statewide moratorium in place. Metro Colo Advisory tracking shows 105 utility filings tied to data centers across 45 states, and nine state utility commission seats were on the ballot. Democrats won governor's races in Texas, Iowa, Wisconsin, Ohio, Minnesota, Arizona, Nevada and Georgia, while Republicans held Florida, Tennessee and South Carolina.

Several people weighed in on what comes next. Wannie Park, founder and CEO of PADO AI, said local worries about energy costs, grid demand and community impact drove voters, and he expects stricter local rules and more moratoriums, with other Democratic-led states possibly following New York. Nic Puckrin of Coin Bureau noted that Texas elected its first Democratic governor since 1990 and its first Democratic senator since 1988, and that Gov. Gina Hinojosa wants an immediate statewide moratorium on new data center approvals. James Mercer of Metro Colo Advisory expects pressure mainly through power bills, such as long minimum contracts, collateral requirements and developers paying for their own grid upgrades, which he said would change which projects get built rather than stop them. In Congress, Arizona Rep. Yassamin Ansari called for a pause on advanced AI development, and Sen. Bernie Sanders wants a national moratorium on new data centers.

The political shift lands on companies that are borrowing heavily to expand. A separate Yahoo Finance report said Nebius Group secured a US$3.5 billion senior secured facility from Citi to fund global AI capacity, and that its shares face risk from leverage layered onto heavy spending just as scrutiny of data centers and power costs grows. Nebius reports earnings on Nov. 12, which will show how its long-term contracts are turning into cash. Trump has promised vetoes in response to the Democratic agenda, and Texas, already second to Virginia in data center count, may become the next major battleground.

stories.Headline: ‘Everyone now uses AI’: chemistry students share how and why they’re using AI tools
stories.Summary:
Chemistry students across the UK and US are increasingly using AI tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot in their studies, according to a report by Chemistry World published on 10 November 2026. The tools are freely available to undergraduates and PhD students, and they can find papers, explain reactions, summarise concepts and draft reports or emails. Students say these tools save time and improve productivity. The article is based on interviews with several students and researchers about how and why they use them.

Concern about the trend is growing. A recent study found that nearly 30% of science, technology, engineering and maths dissertations submitted in the US this year contained AI-generated text, up from just under 2% in 2023. The researchers behind that work warned that AI is displacing part of the work through which scientific expertise is developed. A survey of more than 1,000 full-time UK undergraduates by the Higher Education Policy Institute found that over 95% used AI in at least one way, and 94% said they used it to help with assessments. Only 48% felt they were being taught to use it effectively, although more than 68% considered such skills essential.

The student voices in the article vary. Dion Josh, a second-year chemistry student at the University of Oxford, uses AI agents to break down concepts, though he finds them less reliable for organic reaction mechanisms, so he asks several agents the same question. Ellie Yates, a PhD student at the University of Sheffield, says AI often produces hallucinated answers when searching literature and worries that students may miss the chance to build writing skills through lab reports. Jasper Butcher, who recently finished a PhD at the University of Washington, uses AI for code and experiments, and he worries that students are now working alone with AI rather than with peers.

Fraser Scott, who researches chemistry education at the University of Strathclyde, says AI use is widespread from undergraduate to PhD level and that institutions have responded too slowly. He argues that educators should teach students how to use generative AI appropriately, much as they teach the use of textbooks and calculators, and he notes that many educators use AI themselves. Josh observed that undergraduates now rely heavily on AI, and he questioned how anyone could get through university without it. The article does not describe any formal policy changes or next steps by universities.

project44 announced on November 10, 2026, an integration with Snowflake that powers Mo, its AI supply chain analyst. Mo lets teams ask questions in plain language and receive answers and recommended next steps. The integration combines project44's logistics ontology, semantics, and network data, drawing on about 1 trillion shipment records gathered over the last decade, with Snowflake Cortex AI. The companies say this setup helps supply chain teams turn natural-language questions into answers grounded in their own operational data and business definitions.

The articles say Mo is designed so that answers are consistent and traceable, since logistics terms such as on-time performance can mean different things to different customers. Mo applies project44's logistics semantics and each customer's contract terms, transportation modes, and exceptions to interpret questions, then uses Cortex Analyst to translate them into SQL and retrieve results from the data in Snowflake. Customers reportedly have seen a $6 million reduction in detention and demurrage exposure, $200,000 freed up in working capital from a single question, and nearly $750,000 in savings from one disruption-related initiative. In internal testing, Mo answered 10 of 10 verified questions correctly against 2 of 10 for a general-purpose large language model, gave the same answer all 10 times against 2 of 10, and responded 2.5 times faster. The company says 210 customers now use Mo, which has answered more than 50,000 questions.

project44 CEO Jett McCandless said that reliable data, a reliable signal, and reliable action together make a capable model something operations teams can trust with real decisions. Snowflake's Will Allen said Mo helps teams ask questions in business terms and use the answers to respond to disruptions and find cost savings. Ford Motor Company's Doug Cantriel said Mo gives people accurate, data-grounded answers without waiting on reports or analysis. Mo is available now to project44 customers as part of its Decision Intelligence Platform.

In a separate announcement reported on November 8, 2026, Sphera launched new AI capabilities that connect external supply chain risk signals directly to the suppliers, products, and operations they threaten. Sphera's research across five markets found that 58% of COOs say their most significant disruptions began at least as much outside their organizations as within, rising to 71% in the UAE. The same research found COOs struggle most with identifying exposed suppliers (33%), choosing mitigation (30%), and quantifying business impact (29%). Sphera's CEO, Paul Marushka, said the company's AI helps close the gap between external signals and business effects while keeping people in control of key decisions.

stories.Headline: Department of Justice forms AI task force
stories.Summary:
The Justice Department announced on Thursday that it has formed a new unit called the Super Intelligence Task Force, or DOJ-SITF, to deal with the misuse of artificial intelligence. Attorney General Todd Blanche set it up in an Oct. 13 memo, and the department made the formation public this week. The name follows a late September executive order from President Donald Trump telling federal agencies to call AI "super intelligence." The group is meant to protect American leadership in the technology from being compromised by bad actors. Those include foreign state and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individuals or companies engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct.

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss will co-chair the task force. It will coordinate the department's criminal and civil enforcement work involving AI, recommend enforcement priorities, and develop guidance on prosecuting unlawful AI-related conduct. It will also absorb the AI Litigation Task Force, which the department created in January under then Attorney General Pam Bondi to challenge state AI laws. The new group will serve as the department's main point of contact with the Super Intelligence Force, a White House body Trump announced last month and put under National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton. That body coordinates the government's engagement with various organizations and AI companies.

Blanche said the Justice Department will keep identifying and prosecuting people whose use of the technology breaks the law, including by targeting American taxpayers, critical U.S. infrastructure, or other national security interests. He added that the task force will take affirmative steps, as appropriate, to promote American dominance in the field, and that it will help the department work with Clayton to make sure critical technologies serve the American people. Weiss said the department has a responsibility to use its law enforcement tools to deter improper use. The department also said it will push companies deploying AI to keep strong internal controls so the technology behaves as intended.

The announcement did not say how many staff the task force will have, what it will cost, or when it will report. The name change adds a wrinkle, since super intelligence already has an established meaning, a term philosopher Nick Bostrom defined as any intellect that greatly exceeds human cognitive performance in virtually all areas of interest, separate from AI generally. Some coverage gave the announcement date as Nov. 5, while one report dated it to Thursday of this week. The Super Intelligence Force that the new unit will work alongside was created in early October, according to one report.

stories.Headline: Judge urges expert witnesses to declare AI use right away
stories.Summary:
Joanna Smith, interim deputy president of the UK High Court's business and property division, has told expert witnesses to disclose their use of artificial intelligence now rather than wait for a formal rule. She made the point at the Bond Solon Expert Witness Conference at Church House in Westminster, as reported by the Law Society Gazette on 7 November 2026. Her warning was that experts whose evidence is shaped by AI they have not declared could face searching questions under cross-examination. She told the audience that there is currently no rule requiring such disclosure, but that experts who stay silent may find themselves open to criticism.

The instruction follows a report from the Civil Justice Council published in late October 2026, on AI and the preparation of court documents. Smith co-chaired the working group behind it. The council recommended that experts make a declaration where AI tools have generated or influenced the substantive content of a report, and that this requirement be added to the 2014 guidance on instructing experts in civil claims. Smith said the declaration should give enough information to allow effective scrutiny, which could include the method used, confirmation that AI was appropriate for that purpose, and, in exceptional cases, the tool itself. She also advised experts to check at the point of instruction whether AI use is permitted, citing intellectual property, data protection and regulatory compliance.

Smith placed the responsibility on experts themselves, reminding them that their credibility depends on their fundamental duties to the court. She said AI has not changed those duties, and that the obligations of independence, objectivity, transparency and professional competence remain exactly as they were. In her keynote she identified the main danger as the erosion of independent judgment, where experts hand their opinions over to an AI agent and lose their integrity. She listed practical risks including inadequate oversight, poor training, and a weak understanding of what AI can do. She also advised experts to disclose intended AI use to their instructing solicitors even when the instructions say nothing about it.

The context includes a recent case, Cornwall Council v M & Ors [2026] EWFC 306, in which an independent social worker used Microsoft Copilot to prepare a parenting assessment, assessments of potential kinship carers and an addendum report. The judge found that AI use had influenced a significant part of the report and therefore gave the evidence limited weight. The articles do not say whether a formal rule will follow or when. Smith concluded that experts who understand both the capabilities and limits of AI, and use it transparently where necessary, will be best placed to meet their overriding duty to the court.

iL has gathered operational data on tasks, movement and responses to obstacles by running humanoid robots at actual industrial sites. In September, the company recorded its first revenue in the business from a contract to supply humanoid robots and physical AI data. The company plans to use the membership to widen cooperation with domestic industry, academia and research institutes. It also intends to work with ADRA's European network on international joint research, data standardization and global industrial field testing. The company frames these moves as a way to test the potential of a business model built on operational data.

Jung Moon-sik, chief AI officer at iL, said the core competitiveness of physical AI lies in securing operational data generated at industrial sites and linking it to AI training and performance gains. He said the company will keep building global competitiveness on technology verified at domestic sites and on its experience commercializing data. He also said the memberships in Europe's ADRA and the Korea Physical AI Association will expand its cooperation networks at home and abroad. His stated goal is for iL to become a physical AI operational data platform company that represents South Korea.

stories.Headline: IBM's Confluent Refreshes Streamhouse While Apptio Turns to AI Cost Tracking - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
IBM's Confluent unveiled a set of enhancements to its Streamhouse architecture on November 4, aimed at keeping business context current for AI agents, applications and analytics. The update centers on Lightning Tables, a read-only serving layer in Confluent Cloud that stores and materialises Apache Kafka data into tables and keeps them updated as data changes. Customers can query that data through SQL or a direct API. Confluent positioned the platform as a layer alongside data warehouses, data lakes and lakehouses, bringing streaming, connection, processing, governance and query functions into one place. IBM's Apptio, another subsidiary, announced new integrations with AI systems and expanded tools for tracking AI spending and usage.

The changes are meant to reduce the need to move streaming data into separate databases to serve applications. Lightning Tables applies governance controls, including schemas, lineage and access policies, from data capture through to serving. The platform now groups its functions into five areas: Stream, Connect, Process, Govern and Query. Stream is based on Apache Kafka and Confluent's Kora engine, while Process uses Apache Flink to combine and enrich data close to its source. Connect includes more than 150 managed and custom connectors, and the new Query layer adds Tableflow and a Real-Time Context Engine that serves business context to AI agents through the Model Context Protocol.

Confluent, which sits within IBM, argued that older architectures were built mainly for reporting and batch processing, while AI systems increasingly need current operational data from several systems at the moment decisions are made. Its example involved an airline disruption, where separate systems for flight operations, scheduling and reservations each hold different versions of events, so an automated rebooking proposal could look valid alone yet fail once aircraft location, departure time and seat availability are considered together. Shaun Clowes, General Manager of Confluent and Data at IBM, said that a Streamhouse lets each agent and application work from a live, governed view of the business. Accenture said it adopted a Streamhouse architecture based on Confluent across its global business.

Confluent's internal testing showed Lightning Tables can serve newly created data in about 100 milliseconds, with query latency of 10 to 100 milliseconds and throughput above 1,000 queries per second, though the company said actual performance depends on configuration and workload. The company also said the service can support machine learning by storing features computed in Flink for tasks such as real-time personalisation. Separately, IBM's Apptio focuses on helping enterprises forecast AI outlays and weigh them against the business results they produce. The articles present these moves as part of a broader push by IBM to strengthen the data foundation that AI tools rely on.

stories.Headline: North Carolina Department of Information Technology looking for AI vendors
stories.Summary:
North Carolina's Department of Information Technology, known as NCDIT, has opened a search for artificial intelligence vendors to help put generative AI to work inside state agencies. The request was reported on November 9, 2026, by Spectrum News reporter Kennedy Chase, who described the effort as a way for AI to play a bigger role in state services and in the technology government workers use. The article frames the plan as a deliberate, cautious rollout rather than a mandate. Proposals from potential vendors are due November 30.

The stated goal is to give agencies a simpler path to secure, trusted AI tools while providing employee training and security safeguards. The articles say the work includes protecting people's personal information, making sure the public can understand how the state reached its decisions, and keeping humans accountable when something goes wrong. Laura Rodgers, the state's director of cybersecurity, described AI as one tool among many rather than a complete solution for improving state services. She said the agency has put guardrails in place first and has not required employees to use AI under threat of firing, as some industry employers have done.

NCDIT Secretary and State Chief Information Officer Nate Denny said in a statement that the department is always looking for ways to deliver government services better and faster, and that the new approach should let employees spend more time serving North Carolinians. Rodgers argued that public trust will depend on the state continuing to take the careful path and keep safeguards in place ahead of deployment. The Daily Tar Heel's earlier reporting adds context on the wider policy picture: Attorney General Jeff Jackson joined a bipartisan group of attorneys general in a September 23 letter urging Congress to set federal AI rules, and the state has previously passed a law covering AI-generated sexual images. Its 2025 executive order created an AI Leadership Council, AI Oversight Teams and an AI Accelerator within NCDIT. The articles do not say when vendors will be selected or what products the state will ultimately adopt.

stories.Headline: Trump Signals Openness to AI Safeguards, Says US Must Not Fall Behind China
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump said in an interview with CBS's 60 Minutes, broadcast on November 8, 2026, that he is open to artificial intelligence safeguards. He used the word "guardrails" and said he did not mind them. Trump also said AI risks could be managed and expressed willingness to work with Democrats on AI safety measures. He did not announce a specific regulation, legislative proposal or government policy.

The remarks leave the details of any safeguards undecided. Trump did not say which safeguards he would support, whether they would be voluntary or legally binding, or how they would be carried out. He stressed that he did not want rules that would leave the United States in what he called "a deep second position" behind China. He also said China did not have comparable restrictions on AI development, though this was his own characterization rather than an established finding.

He added that the risks of AI were not as serious as some people suggested. The comments come amid a broader debate in Washington over how to balance AI innovation, public safety and national security. Policymakers face questions about accountability, data protection, employment disruption and the growing influence of large technology companies. Potential safeguards could affect developers, researchers and businesses working with advanced AI systems.

Trump has previously favoured letting technology companies take greater responsibility for oversight instead of imposing sweeping government restrictions. Attention now turns to whether the administration develops concrete AI safety proposals and whether talks with Democratic lawmakers lead to legislative cooperation. Any future framework will depend on later policy announcements and legislative action. For now, the articles indicate only that Trump is open to safeguards, not that a new regulatory framework exists.

stories.Headline: Norway's grid operator and Australia's NextDC pause data center growth as limits spread from Texas
stories.Summary:
Norway's state grid operator Statnett said on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, that it would temporarily stop reserving grid capacity for data centers to protect the power system. The halt lasts until Aug. 1, 2027 at the latest, and data centers already connected are unaffected while approved facilities can still connect. Data centers in Norway hold 4,200 MW of reserved capacity, with 9,100 MW in the queue and a further 18,000 MW requested, all against a record national peak of just over 25,000 MW. Statnett's Peer Olav Østli said the pause is needed to put measures and a framework in place. Denmark's grid operator Energinet had already paused new grid connection agreements in March, after about 60 GW of projects queued against peak demand of roughly 7 GW.

On the same day, Australia's NextDC said it had paused work on projects without customer contracts, while it concentrates on its delayed M3 site in Melbourne. The delay began when network company Jemena suspended parts of a 66kV line upgrade that would raise grid supply to M3, citing community opposition and a lack of council consent. NextDC cut its FY27 underlying EBITDA guidance to A$245-265 million from A$385-410 million on Oct. 21 and put all new development projects and land acquisitions on hold. Jemena does not expect to restart the works before February 2027, and NextDC does not expect a permit decision on stages 6 and 7 until 2027. Chief executive Craig Scroggie said the work can't restart until the company has clearly communicated that the problem is solved.

Texas froze new data center grid connections on Aug. 3, when outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott also ordered an audit of power demand, environmental effects and tax breaks, due in December. ERCOT is tracking more than 400 GW of data center projects seeking connection. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who takes office Jan. 19, has pledged a moratorium on all data center approvals until the legislature passes protections. In Michigan, Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has proposed new conditions on data centers, including that projects avoid raising electricity prices and use union labor, and that communities be able to reject them. Meta's president said last week that hyperscalers are now asking whether they need to build outside the United States.

The pauses show that data center growth has run into the time it takes to add grid capacity, and grid operators and governments are now deciding who waits. Norway is preparing a licensing scheme for data centers, and its energy regulator NVE has warned that continued growth could cause power deficits and higher prices. Abbott wants Texas data centers to pay for their own electrical infrastructure, and a Senate permitting bill would require them to cover the full cost of grid upgrades. Norway's pause ends by Aug. 1, 2027 at the latest, while Texas's audit is due in December. NextDC's board is expected to report on its capital expenditure review by its Nov. 20 annual meeting, and Victoria votes on Nov. 28.

stories.Headline: AI 'Wild West' Causes a Gaming 'Civil War' as an Expert Warns Some Developers Should Be 'Very Worried'
stories.Summary:
An expert in artificial intelligence and gaming has said that the industry is divided over generative AI, a split he described as something like a civil war. Julian Togelius, a professor at New York University and director of its Game Innovation Lab, made the remarks in an interview with the Daily Star published on 8 November 2026. He said enthusiasts and critics are clashing over how the technology is trained and used, with critics arguing it is theft and a threat to their livelihoods. The articles do not give a number or a specific event that triggered the dispute, so the story is best understood as an ongoing debate rather than a single incident.

Togelius argued that developers making low-effort derivative games should be very worried about competition from AI-generated titles, which he called AI slop games. He said original, polished and ambitious games were less likely to be affected. Noah Wardrip-Fruin, a professor of computational media at the University of California, Santa Cruz, warned that the market was already crowded and that AI-made releases would make it harder for independent developers to get their games noticed. Togelius also described the legal position around generative AI as a Wild West, saying there are not yet enough court cases to settle the legality of many practices and that clarity could take years. Daniela Romano, a professor of artificial intelligence and games at De Montfort University, added that because models can be trained on material from many countries and sold worldwide, questions of copyright, ownership, licensing and liability are becoming more complicated, and the legal framework is still evolving.

Togelius said he sympathised with both sides but thought the more productive approach was to focus on the new kinds of games that could be invented with AI. Romano argued that the technology could cut development time and let teams spend more effort on creativity, and that it could produce more immersive and personalised experiences for players. Both experts were quoted in the interview as voicing these views, with Togelius acknowledging the concerns of critics and Romano stressing the potential benefits. Neither expert's comments were presented as settled fact, and the articles do not describe any regulatory or legal decision that has been made so far.

stories.Headline: Futures Rise, CoreWeave Jumps In Good News For AI
stories.Summary:
Futures on the Dow Jones, S&P 500 and Nasdaq rose overnight after CoreWeave jumped following its late Tuesday report, a move that lifted neocloud and AI stocks. Investor's Business Daily reported the rise as Wall Street looked ahead, and the earlier session had been hit by a hot CPI inflation report and hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Gov. Christopher Waller that sent Treasury yields soaring. Nvidia kept sliding in the same period over CEO Jensen Huang's espionage affair. Those are the only details the articles give about the overnight move, so the account stops there.

Separately, Cloudflare rose 20% to $293.43 in morning trading after reporting Q3 2026 results on November 5, with revenue up 39% year over year to $782.5 million against a $738.3 million consensus. Its adjusted earnings per share of $0.38 beat the $0.34 consensus, and CEO Matthew Prince called it the company's best quarter ever. Cloudflare raised its full-year revenue outlook to $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion and projected fourth-quarter sales of $845 million to $846 million. Its GAAP net loss, however, widened to $34.1 million from $1.3 million a year earlier, weighed down by $174.1 million in stock-based compensation.

IREN, a GPU cloud provider, rose 15% to $20.81 after reporting Q1 FY2027 results on November 5, when its revenue climbed to $228 million from $137 million in the prior quarter. Sales in its AI Cloud segment jumped to $200 million from $71 million, and its adjusted EBITDA of $66 million exceeded forecasts. Its net loss narrowed to $263 million from $684 million in the previous quarter. Since quarter-end, IREN signed a five-year contract at $22 million per megawatt, with the customer prepaying 90% of the related GPU capital costs, and a separate short-duration contract at $40 million per megawatt.

CoreWeave gained 10% to $48.07 even though its latest earnings report dates to August 11, a gain the article reads as sector-wide rather than company-specific. Over the month through the prior session's close, CoreWeave had fallen 48% as concerns about its debt load pressured its bonds, and IREN had fallen 50%. Cloudflare had been down 17% over the same period. The October jobs report added to risk appetite, with the U.S. adding 165,000 jobs against Bloomberg's expectations and unemployment ticking down to 4.1%. September's job gain was revised up to 60,000 from 29,000.

The articles describe the business models that separate these companies. Cloudflare sells security, networking and developer tools from its global edge network and markets itself as the first "agentic cloud," a subscription model far less capital-intensive than building GPU clusters. IREN owns the land, power and data centers under its business, much of it converted from crypto mining, which management says lets it pace spending to funding conditions. CoreWeave runs a debt-financed GPU cloud for AI labs, hyperscalers and enterprises. For IREN, the key question is whether more than $4 billion in annualized revenue run rate comes online by January 31, 2027, a target that may slip to the end of February.

Bulls point to rising contract prices, customer prepayments and Cloudflare's fastest revenue growth in nearly four years. Bears point to IREN's $6 billion in planned capital spending still to be funded, CoreWeave's heavy debt and Cloudflare's lower free cash flow margin. Market participants can watch for signs that the bounce reaches beyond the reporting companies, and the article notes that keeping share exposure smaller could be a wise policy until the AI cloud funding question resolves. Nebius Group and Akamai Technologies are also named as companies investors are watching in the sector.

stories.Headline: The realities of scaling AI agents: ‘You don't have an AI problem, you have a content problem’
stories.Summary:
Sifted published an article on 9 November 2026 about the challenges of scaling autonomous AI agents, drawing on a Sifted Talks panel held in partnership with the content management platform Box. The piece describes a shift from AI copilots, which wait for human instructions, to agents that can access databases, draft and send emails, process invoices, organise files and make decisions in real time. Because these agents work at high speed, the article notes, a single mistake can affect business operations within seconds. The panel discussion focused on how businesses can integrate such agents safely through a plan for data, security and governance.

The article says the main difference between copilots and autonomous agents is that the latter make decisions without human prompting, so trust and autonomy must be earned over time. One panellist compared deployment to onboarding a new salesperson, starting with a defined scope, limited system access and ongoing supervision, and said agents should never receive full autonomy across business management systems on day one. Another panellist warned that an agent's speed and capacity make the potential for damage much larger than a human employee's mistake, and said that when agents can reach databases, the potential blasts of an error escalate significantly. The panel also stressed that humans must remain accountable, since people provide agents with their capabilities and the right to act.

The article states that the panellists want organisations to organise their business data and context before an agent carries out any task, because agents can hallucinate and fail when fed disorganised data, duplicates or outdated files. Chief AI officer Hanah-Marie Darley of Geordie AI argued that "human-in-the-loop" has become an overused term because it does not specify who the reviewer is or what information that person needs. Panellists also described a zero-trust approach in which the model is assumed to be compromised and the business defines and enforces what the agent can and cannot do. The article adds that access should be task-specific, time-bounded and context-aware, and that controls must be applied at the content level to stop agents from exposing restricted information. Darley, according to the article, identified a "silent failure" in which agents operate without alarm bells and without any real-time understanding of their behaviour.

The article credits Hébrard, from Box, with the central point that "you don't have an AI problem, you have a content problem," and attributes to panellist McNeil the view that governance, compliance and risk teams should be involved before pilots begin, since they will either enable or hinder successful scaling. The article also reports that McNeil said companies often focus too heavily on technology rather than on the underlying business process. Hébrard, it says, recommended that organisations log every prompt and reasoning step so they can explain what happened during audits. The article frames these recommendations as the practical response to the risk that unsanctioned tools spread when employees lack sanctioned options that work.

stories.Headline: SF confidence, reality checks and AI bubble anxiety come to the Rise venture salon in the Alps
stories.Summary:
Sifted's managing editor Tom Nugent reports from the second Rise venture salon, held last week on the Lansersee estate just outside Innsbruck, Austria. The four-day event brought together robotics founders and investors to talk about the state of physical AI in Europe and what the continent needs to win in a field some in tech see as its last chance to stay relevant. Guests spent the days networking and chatting about European robotics and the wider tech scene. The article is a dispatch from the gathering rather than a news report on a single announcement. The readable parts of the article give few hard figures.

One company is described as raising a large round, with a sum of €0.5 billion mentioned against a valuation of 188%, though the surrounding text is too garbled to say which company or what the numbers measure. The piece also refers to a €2.35 billion figure and to a span from 2018 to 2026, but the articles do not make clear how these relate to each other. Beyond these, the text carries few reliable names, dates or amounts. The article suggests the mood at the salon mixed confidence borrowed from San Francisco with sober reality checks and unease about an AI bubble. Attendees appear to have discussed whether European physical AI companies can compete with American rivals, and whether investors in Europe are willing to back the sector at the scale needed.

Nugent writes as Sifted's managing editor, a role in which he covers robotics, chips and university spinouts. Most of the quotes and attributions in the piece cannot be recovered from the text supplied. The surrounding material points to physical AI, deeptech and robotics as the themes Sifted is tracking, but it names no next steps, follow-up events or decisions arising from the salon. Because so much of the article is unreadable, the specific claims, speakers and figures cannot be confirmed, and nothing more can be said without adding to what the articles carry. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Five9 Buys Level AI for $325MN to Take CX AI to the Next Level
stories.Summary:
Five9 agreed on November 5, 2026, to buy Level AI for about $325 million in cash, a deal announced alongside its third-quarter results. Level AI builds AI software for analyzing customer conversations, supporting contact center agents and automating interactions across voice and digital channels. The two companies have worked together since 2022, and Level AI's products already connect with Five9's cloud platform. Five9 expects the deal to close in the fourth quarter of this year and plans to fund it from its balance sheet.

The acquisition lets Five9 sell Level AI's tools as standalone products to enterprises that still run on-premises systems or rival cloud platforms, without requiring them to switch to Five9's contact center software first. CEO Amit Mathradas described this as selling "AI first and then CCaaS second." Five9 estimates that 40% to 50% of the market remains on-premises. Level AI's products will also be sold inside Five9's Genius CX Platform, and the company says it will sustain roughly 50% annual recurring revenue growth over the next 12 months. Level AI reported about $20 million in annual recurring revenue as of October 31.

Mathradas framed the strategy as automating the right tasks rather than automating as much as possible. Michael Fauscette of Arion Research said the standalone option gives Five9 a way into accounts that are not ready to replace their platforms, though he flagged execution as the open question. Five9's CFO, Bryan Lee, said the deal should dilute adjusted EBITDA margin by about one percentage point in 2027, with Level AI reaching breakeven within roughly six months. Mathradas also acknowledged some overlap with Five9's existing AI products, and said the sales structure and handling of that overlap were still being worked out before closing.

The deal sits within a wave of consolidation in contact center AI. NiCE acquired Cognigy in 2025 for about $955 million, and Salesforce announced an agreement to acquire Cresta on November 2. Analysts say buyers want tools that analyze conversations, assist agents and automate routine work across channels. Whether Five9 can keep Level AI credible on other vendors' platforms while folding it into its own offerings will determine how much value the deal delivers.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang's Eldest Daughter Madison Huang Cancels South Korea Trip One Day Before Arrival; Nvidia AI Day to Proceed as Planned
stories.Summary:
Madison Huang, a senior director of product marketing for Omniverse and Robotics at Nvidia and the eldest daughter of CEO Jensen Huang, called off her South Korea visit one day before she was due to arrive. She had planned to enter the country on Nov. 8, attend Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026 at COEX in Seoul on Nov. 9 and 10, and hold talks with relevant government ministries. According to the South Korean government and the IT industry on Nov. 7, she cited family reasons and no further details were given. Her absence does not affect the conference, which is expected to go ahead as scheduled.

The cancellation also scrapped a Nov. 8 meeting with Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT Bae Kyung-hoon, where the government and Nvidia had meant to discuss high-level cooperation. It would have been her fourth trip to South Korea this year. In April she visited Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, LG Electronics, Hyundai Motor and Doosan Robotics, in June she accompanied her father and met SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, and in August she toured LG Electronics' robot data factory construction site. The event itself is expected to draw about 2,000 attendees and 20 partner companies, with day-one keynotes from Deepu Talla, vice president of Robotics and Edge AI, and Jonathan Cohen, vice president of Applied Research, followed by 15 afternoon sessions across three tracks. Day two includes a hands-on workshop in Korean, an AI for Science Forum and a Physical AI Startup Connect program.

No official explanation beyond family reasons has been offered, though some in the industry speculate that recent foreign media reports about a Chinese spy connection involving someone close to Jensen Huang may have played a part. The New York Times reported on Oct. 29 that U.S. intelligence authorities concluded Alice Huang, a Chinese national and businesswoman and a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer and cloud partner, passed information to Beijing and had grown close to the CEO. The report said no evidence showed Jensen Huang knew of any espionage and that President Trump took no action after being briefed about a year ago. Nvidia said the CEO's dealings with her were not unusual, since meetings with customer executives are part of the job, and Huang himself called their interactions entirely normal. The Financial Times reported on Nov. 7 that the U.S. government viewed the relationship as romantic and drafted an internal memo; Nvidia declined to comment, and no link between that allegation and the canceled trip has been confirmed.

On the political side, the chairs of three U.S. House committees, covering the Select Committee on China, Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, wrote to Jensen Huang on Nov. 4 asking him to attend a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 over concerns about Chinese technology infiltration and espionage risks. In Seoul, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, which supply the high-bandwidth memory used in Nvidia's AI accelerators, are due to present cases using Nvidia software in chip design and manufacturing. LG Electronics, Naver Cloud, Doosan Robotics and Coupang are also taking part as partners. Intel will hold its own AI Summit Seoul 2026 at the same venue on Nov. 12, with an SK hynix vice president giving a keynote.

stories.Headline: Protecting Tribal College Data in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Tribal colleges and universities are adopting artificial intelligence while trying to keep sensitive data under their own control. According to a Tribal College Journal article by Chad J. Davis, director of cybersecurity at the American Indian Higher Education Consortium, the colleges are doing so through training, policy, cybersecurity upgrades, vendor review and on-premises systems. The article was published on November 10, 2026, in Volume 38, No. 2 of the winter 2026 issue. It describes these steps as ways to protect institutional and tribal data as AI tools spread across campus operations, teaching and technology work.

Colleges are building AI skills among faculty, staff and students, with the AIHEC partnering with the National Institutes of Health through its AIM-AHEAD initiative. Eric Johnson, AIHEC's health initiatives communication coordinator, said participants learn to use AI responsibly, with attention to data sovereignty, privacy, ethics and community trust. Programs often start with publicly available or practice datasets before any sensitive tribal data is used. Some colleges have also formed AI committees, and Sarah Barott, an English instructor at Red Lake Nation College, said those committees built frameworks guided by seven grandfather values.

On the security side, the article says colleges are classifying institutional data, including student information, financial records and intellectual property, to make sure AI use complies with policies, tribal laws, state and federal rules such as FERPA. They apply identity and access management and encryption so that only people with relevant job duties can reach sensitive data. Colleges also monitor and audit how data is accessed and shared within AI systems, and they conduct risk assessments and write incident response plans. The National Science Foundation's Tribal Colleges and Universities Program supported Lac Courte Oreilles Ojibwe University in improving its cybersecurity infrastructure, including its server, wireless network and firewall.

Jeremy Bennet, interim chief information officer at Leech Lake Tribal College, said every technology solution goes through a risk assessment and that contracts, privacy statements, security practices and data ownership terms are reviewed against institutional standards. He said data governance and Indigenous data sovereignty are institutional issues, not only technology issues, and that leadership must prioritize them. The article says colleges are also negotiating with vendors collectively and writing privacy agreements to define Indigenous data sovereignty in practice. Several colleges are building on-premises AI capabilities so that tribal information, Native languages and student data are not used to train public open-source models.

The College of the Muscogee Nation's Onvkuce Voice Database illustrates this approach. Dr. Colton Wood, general studies coordinator at the college, said the project creates a multimedia language database to revitalize Mvskoke as a living, spoken language. The project uses audiovisual equipment and speech-to-text technology to collect, transcribe and label new and archival material on a central platform. Access to that platform is governed by culturally informed controls and protocols. The article also says colleges are building long-term relationships with other tribal colleges, tribal organizations and higher education institutions to share expertise and infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Samsung, Hyundai Motor Deepen Physical AI Alliance
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics and Hyundai Motor Group, two long-standing rivals that have cooperated across three generations of their founding families, have announced a deeper strategic alliance aimed at future industries. The partnership, which began in semiconductors, batteries and automotive electronics, now extends to robots and artificial intelligence. On November 9, Samsung hosted an event called "HMG Appreciation Day" at its Seocheon Training Institute, inviting key Hyundai executives in what was the first large-scale invitation of its kind from Samsung to a major domestic conglomerate. The gathering was held under the theme "One Harmony Toward the Future" and drew 177 people, including Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun and Hyundai Vice Chair Chang Jae-hoon.

The cooperation is already producing business results. Samsung Electronics agreed to supply its Exynos Auto V920 in-vehicle infotainment chip to Hyundai Motor Company, and Samsung SDI signed its first long-term electric vehicle battery supply contract with Hyundai in 2023. Its high-nickel prismatic batteries are slated for Kia's compact electric SUV, Hyundai's Ioniq 3, and the Genesis GV90 flagship. The two sides have also begun jointly developing batteries for robots, widening their work into the robotics sector. Analysts quoted in the report suggest that combining Samsung's semiconductor, sensor and battery technology with Hyundai's robotics and autonomous driving know-how could strengthen their future mobility competitiveness.

Jun Young-hyun said in his welcoming speech that the two groups are reliable partners that have written Korean industrial history together, and he hoped their combined strengths would open up new possibilities. Chang Jae-hoon said that cooperation now reaches beyond vehicle components into robots and energy, and that the strengths built over three generations would create greater synergy. The article also recounts the history between the groups, including a 1985 birthday visit by Samsung founder Lee Byung-chull to Hyundai founder Chung Ju-yung, and a 2020 meeting between Lee Jae-yong and Euisun Chung to discuss next-generation electric vehicle batteries. Observers quoted in the report describe the groups as moving from eternal rivals to pragmatic strategic partners.

A separate report from the same period describes Nvidia's AI Day Seoul 2026 at COEX, where the company outlined its physical AI cooperation with South Korean firms, including Hyundai Motor Group, Doosan, SK Hynix and LG Electronics. Nvidia is working with Hyundai on robot simulation for automotive production lines using its Omniverse and Isaac platforms, and with Doosan on robotic precision polishing of car body surfaces. Dipu Talla, Nvidia's vice president of robotics and edge AI, said South Korea would play a very important role in physical AI over the next decade. Nvidia positions itself as a platform company supplying core technology rather than building robots itself, with South Korea serving as a proving ground.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang’s Troubles Leave the AI Industry Reeling
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, long one of the most influential figures in the artificial intelligence boom, now faces a serious threat to his position. Reports published on November 9, 2026, say Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company whom US intelligence services concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia's board said it would investigate the matter, and Huang said he fully supports the review and will cooperate with it. The incident has also drawn the attention of a US congressional investigation, according to Asian business reporting on the matter.

The stakes for the industry are large. Nvidia controls about 90 percent of the market for chips used to train frontier AI models, and it has invested billions in companies that buy those chips, including OpenAI and Anthropic. Corporate filings show Huang earned $36 million last year and owned about 3.5 percent of the company as of March, and he is an at-will employee who can be dismissed at any time without severance. Analysts note that Nvidia has no other executive of comparable prominence and no apparent successor. Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday while broader market indices rose.

Experts say the board's inquiry will likely focus on whether Huang broke company policy, though the FBI could examine whether any laws were broken. Congress may also look into whether the affair influenced US policy on chip sales to China, and some analysts say it raises questions about whether sensitive information about AI companies or US strategy reached China. Huang has been outspoken against tougher export controls on China, which could leave his credibility on that issue in doubt. The Trump administration loosened some restrictions in its second term, giving China access to older Nvidia chips.

Researchers at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology expect the scandal to speed efforts to tighten chip exports, with more scrutiny from the Commerce Department over shipments routed through third countries such as Singapore and the Middle East. In South Korea, semiconductor and manufacturing firms that have built plans around Nvidia's AI technology are watching closely, and analysts say the impact on memory chipmakers may be limited given ongoing shortages. Some observers also warn that possible changes in Congress after the US midterm elections could bring stricter rules on AI data centers, which could affect investment across the supply chain. Nvidia's board has not yet said how long its investigation will take.

stories.Headline: Subtle Energy Corrections Reshape Condensed-Phase Property Predictions from a Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential
stories.Summary:
The arXiv preprint "Subtle Energy Corrections Reshape Condensed-Phase Property Predictions from a Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential," posted on November 10, 2026 by Haihui Wang and seven co-authors, reports that small energy adjustments can noticeably change how a machine-learning model predicts the behavior of liquids. The team started with a baseline potential called MACELES-OFF and fine-tuned it at the ωB97M-V/def2-TZVPD level of theory. They tested two corrections: a counterpoise term that addresses basis-set superposition error, and an explicit three-body dispersion term called Axilrod-Teller-Muto, which is parameterized with D4 and added during molecular-dynamics inference. Across the analyzed SPICE2 configurations from OMol25, the mean atom-normalized contributions were 0.222 meV/atom for the counterpoise correction and 0.205 meV/atom for the dispersion term.

The authors compared four versions of the model across 39 organic liquids: the baseline, counterpoise-only, dispersion-only, and both corrections together. Relative to the baseline, the mean system-wise density changed by -1.17% for counterpoise-only, -10.38% for dispersion-only, and -11.93% for the combined version. Enthalpy of vaporization changed by -2.79%, -14.74%, and -18.32% for the same three variants. For the 11 liquids that have experimental self-diffusion data, mean self-diffusion rose by 17.66%, 203.02%, and 230.36%. The paper states that both corrections lower density and enthalpy of vaporization while increasing molecular mobility on average, with the dispersion term producing most of the change and the counterpoise term a smaller share.

The article is attributed to the authors listed on the arXiv record, who report these findings and do not make claims beyond the configurations and liquids they analyzed. Their central point is that a model can reproduce electronic-structure reference labels accurately and still give unreliable condensed-phase predictions. The abstract says corrections with sub-meV/atom mean values on the analyzed configurations can substantially reshape predicted structural, thermodynamic, and transport properties. The article itself does not describe follow-up steps beyond presenting these comparisons.

stories.Headline: Germany's Deutsche Telekom to expand Munich AI data center by 20MW
stories.Summary:
Deutsche Telekom announced on November 9, 2026 that it will expand its Industrial AI Cloud, often called an AI factory, at Munich's Tucherpark by 20 megawatts. The expansion adds NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra (B300) GPUs alongside the existing B200 and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition systems, and the company says the new chips roughly double the number of chips of that class it operates. The original facility went live in February 2026, and the company says its first expansion phase increased Germany's available AI computing capacity by 50 percent and was fully booked within seven months. Telekom is investing nearly a quarter of a billion euros in the project, which it presents as a way to give companies, startups, research groups and the public sector high-performance AI infrastructure that meets European standards for data protection and control.

CEO Tim Höttges announced the expansion at a company press conference in Munich, arguing that Germany must not only use AI but also create value from it. He said Telekom wants to turn AI into a scalable business model that delivers efficiency gains, new products and added value in Germany and Europe. Federal Digital Minister Karsten Wildberger praised the company's speed, saying it went from idea to operation in months and that the federal government would help support further progress. Industrial customers named by the company include Siemens, Daimler Truck, Currenta and EDAG, which use the infrastructure for simulations, robotics, digital twins and language model training. Telekom also says it is in intensive talks with partners about expanding its commitment in Bavaria, but it has not made a final investment decision and says any such move depends on financing and economic viability.

The company reports that the Munich facility has a power usage effectiveness figure of 1.2, meaning it needs less than 1.2 kilowatt-hours of electricity for each kilowatt-hour used by IT equipment, and that its waste heat will later supply the surrounding Tucherpark district. Trade coverage places the expansion within a broader German market in which Munich ranks as the third-largest data center market by capacity, behind Frankfurt and Berlin, according to a 2024 DC Byte report. The same coverage notes that Munich and other sites were among those pitched for the European Union's AI gigafactory initiative, which SAP and Deutsche Telekom also sought to join. The articles do not give a completion date for the added 20 megawatts.

stories.Headline: Nvidia, SK Telecom, Rebellions forge AI chip alliance
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, SK Telecom and Korean chipmaker Rebellions signed a memorandum of understanding on Monday, November 9, 2026, at Nvidia's AI Day Seoul event at Coex in Seoul. The Ministry of Science and ICT said the agreement will bring locally developed AI processors into Nvidia data center systems. Under the deal, the firms will use Nvidia's NVLink Fusion technology to link Rebellions' neural processing units with Nvidia GPUs as SK Telecom builds AI data center infrastructure. Rebellions will connect its Rebel R200 neural processing units to Nvidia's open infrastructure platform for rack-scale inference. The companies say the systems are expected to be ready for deployment in 2028.

NVLink Fusion lets third-party chipmakers integrate their processors into Nvidia's rack-scale computing architecture, allowing different types of accelerators to run within a shared infrastructure. For Rebellions, the arrangement creates a chance to test its chips within Nvidia's data center architecture and seek customers overseas. The ministry said access to Nvidia's platform could help Korean chipmakers move beyond standalone product development. The agreement follows rising demand for AI inference, which uses trained models to generate responses, and the ministry said combining NPUs and GPUs could help data centers balance performance and power use. The companies plan to use Nvidia GPUs for one stage of AI response generation and Rebellions NPUs for another to improve throughput and power efficiency.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Korea has the talent, technology and industrial ambition to become a world leader in AI, and that the collaboration builds a computing foundation for Korea to produce its own intelligence. Rebellions CEO Sunghyun Park said the announcement marks a turning point for sovereign AI in Korea. SK Telecom CEO Jung Jai-hun said the work will strengthen the company's full-stack sovereign AI competitiveness. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT Bae Kyung-hoon said the government will actively support the collaboration. The ministry said it wants to extend the partnership model to other domestic NPU makers and has pursued similar links with AMD.

The Ministry of Science and ICT also held an AI startup partnership forum with Nvidia on Monday, bringing together 22 Korean companies working in semiconductors, AI models, robotics, video analysis and computing infrastructure. Participants included Upstage, Twelve Labs, FuriosaAI, DeepX and Rebellions, and Nvidia executives Deepu Talla and Jonathan Cohen attended. Lee Do-kyu, deputy minister for ICT policy, said the forum would help Korean companies find opportunities for cooperation with Nvidia and expand into global markets. The ministry pledged support for follow-up work, including joint research, commercialization and eventual overseas sales. Rebellions is backed by Aramco, Arm, Kindred Ventures, KT, Mirae Asset Group, Samsung, SK Hynix and SK Telecom.

stories.Headline: What to Buy After the AI Stock Plunge? Oppenheimer: Focus on the 'Realization of Returns' Theme, with Microsoft, Oracle, and SAP as Top Picks
stories.Summary:
Microsoft is winding down an arrangement to rent AI computing capacity from Oracle, according to a Bloomberg News report published on a Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. The decision is part of a broader reassessment of Microsoft's cloud partnerships, which involve billions of dollars. Microsoft had been gradually cutting back its rented capacity from Oracle in recent months and declined to renew the contract. The report also said the Oracle hardware relied on an older generation of Nvidia chips that became less valuable to Microsoft as its needs evolved.

An Oracle spokesperson told Reuters that demand for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure's AI infrastructure remains strong, even for earlier-generation GPUs. Microsoft is rethinking how it secures computing capacity so it can get the most from its large AI investments. Separately, AI cloud company IREN said on a Thursday that it had delayed some infrastructure deliveries because Microsoft asked for changes to its network design. That shift moved IREN's target for bringing more than $4 billion in annualized revenue capacity online from year-end to January, with a possible further delay until late February. Bloomberg also reported that day that Microsoft is tightening oversight of data center projects run by neocloud providers, including IREN, Nebius, and Nscale, because of delays and rising costs.

Oracle and Microsoft had announced a multi-year deal in 2023 under which Microsoft would use Oracle's AI infrastructure to power the AI-assisted version of its Bing search engine. The financial terms of that agreement were not disclosed. The articles do not say how much capacity Microsoft is shedding or when the wind-down will be complete. They also do not indicate whether the Bing arrangement is affected by the reassessment.

stories.Headline: Nvidia, SKT, Rebellions to jointly establish heterogeneous computing system for AI
stories.Summary:
On November 9, 2026, Nvidia Corp., SK Telecom and the domestic AI chip startup Rebellions agreed to combine their strengths to build a heterogeneous computing system for artificial intelligence. The three companies signed a trilateral memorandum of understanding on the sidelines of AI Day Seoul, a two-day tech event hosted by Nvidia in southern Seoul. The signing was announced at the event's opening on Monday. The deal was reported by Yonhap News Agency under the byline of Kang Jae-eun, with the datelined report published that day.

Under the memorandum, the companies will connect Nvidia's graphics processing units with neural processing units designed by Rebellions, and the combined system will be used to build SK Telecom's AI data centers. The arrangement will rest on Nvidia's NVLink Fusion program, which lets hyperscalers and custom chip designers plug their own AI processors into Nvidia's rack-scale infrastructure. The South Korean science ministry added that the tie-up is based on that program. The ministry also expects the partnership to widen where advanced domestic semiconductors can be applied and to open opportunities for local firms in global markets.

Jesse Clayton, principal manager for AI infrastructure at Nvidia, said at a media round table after the signing that South Korea is a technology leader and that the collaboration could help accelerate innovation there. Nvidia also held a startup forum with more than 20 Korean startups, in cooperation with the science ministry, and announced plans to invest in Point2 Technology and make additional investments in Motif Technologies, RLWRLD and Upstage. The same day, an Nvidia official declined to comment on the abrupt cancellation of a visit by Madison Huang, a senior director at the company and daughter of CEO Jensen Huang, along with reports about his alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. The official said the matter was unrelated to the event.

The questions about Huang came as pressure grew from the U.S. Congress. On Thursday, U.S. time, three Republican committee leaders asked Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing about his alleged relationship with a businesswoman reportedly identified as an intelligence asset for Beijing. Nvidia then said it had opened an internal probe after Huang sent an email to employees acknowledging he had been unfaithful to his wife and took full responsibility. Reporters asked whether that pressure could affect Nvidia's partnerships with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix and its scheduled GPU deliveries to South Korea, and the company did not address the question directly.

stories.Headline: Agoda's AI Assistant Brings Travel Planning and Booking into One Conversation
stories.Summary:
Agoda, the digital travel platform, has introduced a new AI Assistant that lets travelers plan and book trips in one conversation. The tool was first tested in September and has now expanded to users across 21 markets through Agoda's mobile app. Announced in a PR Newswire release dated November 10, 2026, it is the first new booking experience the company has launched in its more than 20-year history. Travelers can use it to discover, plan, and book travel without moving between separate apps.

Trip planning often requires switching between AI chats, search engines, review sites, maps, and booking apps. Even after finding a place they like, travelers still need to know whether the price is accurate, whether rooms are open on their dates, and how to complete the booking. The assistant draws on Agoda's live inventory of more than 6 million accommodations, flights, tours, attractions, and other travel products. Users can explore ideas, compare options, check prices and availability, and continue booking without restarting at each step.

The release gives one example in which a traveler asks the assistant to plan a five-day family trip to Osaka, compare neighborhoods, look at restaurants and attractions, and find accommodations and flights for chosen dates. The assistant keeps track of preferences and trip details as the plan grows. Those details appear on a trip planner canvas where users can arrange upcoming bookings, places to visit, and unfinished plans, and they can reply in conversation or tap suggested options. Agoda says early beta data shows customers using the assistant are more likely to book a "connected trip" combining hotels, flights, attraction tickets, and tours. Agoda has also added web search so the assistant can offer current information alongside its own inventory.

Agoda's Chief Executive Officer, Omri Morgenshtern, is quoted in the release describing travel planning as fragmented and saying the company wants to remove repetitive work so travelers can decide with more confidence. The release names OpenAI models as the source of the assistant's core conversational intelligence. For restaurants and points of interest, it says Agoda uses Gemini with Google Maps Grounding to show ratings, photos, opening hours, and locations. The announcement does not describe any further rollout plans beyond the current 21 markets.

stories.Headline: AI Opportunity Fund Expands AI Skills Training Across Asia Pacific with 28 Phase Three Local Implementing Partners
stories.Summary:
AVPN, Asia's largest platform for social impact, announced on November 11, 2026 the 28 organisations selected as local implementing partners for phase three of the AI Opportunity Fund: Asia-Pacific, supported by Google.org and the Asian Development Bank. The new cohort extends the Fund's AI skills training into schools, universities and workplaces across 19 markets, including through organisations taking part in AI Ready ASEAN, led by ASEAN Foundation. Most of the new partners will work directly with K-12 teachers, university students and faculty, reaching the educators who shape the next generation of workers. Other partners will reach healthcare workers, agricultural and service-sector workers, and employees of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. The same day, AVPN also launched the AI Opportunity Learning Platform.

The platform gives learners access to localised AI training and recommended learning pathways in 16 languages, with a pathway suggested after a short assessment. Certification is available on completion of training. A Gemini-powered assistant helps users navigate the platform and provides guided learning. For phase three, AVPN brought on two new strategic partners: the Raspberry Pi Foundation, which will help local partners localise its Experience AI content, and the Ayala Foundation, which will give educators and students in the Philippines access to Google AI learning resources and support local partners there. Among the funded organisations, Pratham Education Foundation in India will train teachers to use AI critically, JA Korea will pair Google's AI training with formal certification for public school educators, and AI Edu Corp in Vietnam will support embedding AI literacy into national teacher standards.

AVPN chief executive Naina Subberwal Batra said that AI tools are already entering classrooms and workplaces across the region, and that the challenge is helping people use them well and know when not to rely on them too heavily. She said local organisations understand the languages and communities they serve and can adapt training in ways a regional programme alone cannot. Marija Ralic, head of Google.org APAC, said access to AI skills depends on whether people can find relevant training in a language and setting that works for them, and that the platform brings training and local partners together in one place. The Fund was launched in 2024 with a USD 15 million commitment, received a further USD 10 million in phase two in May 2025 and another USD 10 million in phase three in May 2026, bringing Google.org's total commitment to USD 35 million. To date, the Fund has trained more than 850,000 workers and 63,000 small businesses through almost 60 local implementing partner organisations, delivering programmes in more than 30 local languages.

stories.Headline: CNCF Welcomes Vultr as a Platinum Member to Advance Open and Sovereign Cloud Infrastructure for AI
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation announced that Vultr had upgraded its CNCF membership to Platinum, at a time when cloud native and AI infrastructure are converging on shared, open interoperability. The announcement was made at KubeCon and CloudNativeCon North America, held in Salt Lake City. The upgrade builds on Vultr's deepening partnerships with CNCF projects and on the recently launched Vultr Open Source Alliance. The alliance brings together work across open infrastructure, cloud native technologies, AI, and developer ecosystems.

The move centers on the idea that developers should be able to choose the infrastructure, frameworks, models, tools, and protocols that suit their workloads without being tied to a single technology stack. Vultr contributed both CPU and GPU infrastructure capacity to support CNCF project testing. Its Vultr Kubernetes Engine is a CNCF Certified Kubernetes product. Vultr also serves as a member of the Agentic AI Foundation, a separate Linux Foundation initiative that stewards open standards for the agentic AI stack.

Chris Aniszczyk, CTO of CNCF, said AI factory infrastructure should be open and fungible rather than another walled garden, and he described Platinum membership as a real commitment to building that open future. Kevin Cochrane, Chief Marketing Officer of Vultr, said open source is the foundation of modern AI infrastructure and that developers should be free to choose their frameworks, models, and infrastructure. Cochrane said the Platinum upgrade builds on five years of work alongside the CNCF community. Vultr's engineering team has worked directly with maintainers on CNCF projects including Kubernetes and Kubeflow.

Vultr first joined CNCF as a Silver Member in 2021. Its infrastructure runs heterogeneous GPU and CPU capacity that supports open source frameworks, including PyTorch for model training and Kubernetes for inference. The engineering work includes contributing feedback and improvements upstream rather than only consuming the technology downstream. The CNCF describes itself as hosting critical components of the global technology infrastructure, including Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Envoy. It is supported by nearly 800 members and over 200 startups, and it is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation.
