stories.Headline: Rackspace and Together AI Announce Strategic Agreement to Support Enterprise AI Inference
stories.Summary:
Rackspace and Together AI announced an initial multiyear strategic AI infrastructure agreement on November 10, 2026, in San Antonio. Under the deal, Rackspace expects to provide and operate dedicated NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 infrastructure, connected with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking, to support Together AI inference workloads. Deployment is planned for 2027, subject to certain conditions. The companies also signed a separate, non-binding letter of intent to explore a joint go-to-market approach for enterprise-focused AI solutions. Rackspace is described as the operator of the full enterprise AI stack.

Rackspace expects to supply the dedicated NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra infrastructure, including power, liquid cooling, networking and storage. Together AI expects to provide the managed cloud platform running on that infrastructure, including access to open source models, inference optimizations and developer tools. The parties expect to evaluate additional security, governance and compliance controls for future offerings, depending on customer requirements. Rackspace intends to build a repeatable model to support AI platform companies, systems integrators and enterprises. Its approach is to seek contractual commitments for dedicated capacity and manage related financing with the goal of aligning to expected customer demand and the useful life of the hardware.

Gajen Kandiah, Chief Executive Officer of Rackspace, said that enterprise AI requires more than compute, and that success depends on bringing compute into production and operating it reliably. He said Rackspace brings more than 25 years of experience operating complex enterprise environments. Vipul Ved Prakash, founder and CEO of Together AI, said that scaling in the enterprise requires infrastructure that can grow with the company's ambitions. Raj Mirpuri, Vice President of Global AI Clouds and Infrastructure Ecosystem at NVIDIA, said that Rackspace and Together AI can run inference workloads efficiently with NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra. Rackspace, an NVIDIA Cloud Partner, plans to operate the deployment in a purpose-built, liquid-cooled facility.

Effective November 6, 2026, Rackspace entered into a share purchase agreement with an investor group led by Voss Capital, LP, providing for an aggregate $66 million private placement of common stock. Rackspace expects to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, working capital, capital expenditures and growth capital, including GPU-related initiatives. Rackspace expects to seek separate financing for the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems and is in active discussions with potential lenders. However, no definitive GPU financing commitment had been obtained as of the release date. The release states that Rackspace's obligations to proceed with the deployment are subject to the financing condition and other conditions in the definitive agreement.

Together AI, described as the AI Native Cloud, was founded in 2022 and says it powers over two million developers. The release says the non-binding letter of intent contemplates evaluating how Together AI's inference, post-training and reinforcement learning capabilities could be combined with Rackspace's infrastructure and engineering services. Any joint offerings would depend on further agreement between the parties and applicable customer requirements. The release also says that the availability of any deployment configurations, including data residency and compliance features, would be determined by the specific offering. The release does not say what happens next beyond the planned 2027 deployment and the exploration of joint offerings.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave Delivers Another Blowout Quarter. Is It Enough To Save the AI Trade?
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, the largest of the neoclouds, tumbled over the last month and dragged the AI sector down with it after a social media post showed its bond yields had reached as high as 15%. That observation set off another round of concerns that the AI build-out is unsustainable. The worries were magnified after Democrats swept the midterm elections, in part by campaigning on increased regulation for data centers. Against that backdrop, CoreWeave reported third-quarter results on Tuesday afternoon, and the company made clear that demand for its services, which essentially consist of renting AI compute, continues to skyrocket.

Revenue in the quarter jumped 168% to $3.66 billion, ahead of the analyst consensus of $3.54 billion. The revenue backlog improved from $104 billion at the end of the second quarter to $132.5 billion at the end of the third. Its GAAP operating margin rose from 4% to 6%, as GAAP operating income climbed from $52 million to $207 million. Those figures point to strong demand and improving profitability at the operating level.

The bottom line still carries heavy costs. CoreWeave has taken on tens of billions in debt to fund its rapid data center expansion and chip purchases. Interest expense rose from $310 million a year earlier to $846 million, and the company finished the quarter with a GAAP net loss of $709 million, or $1.27 per share, against expectations of a $1.21 loss per share. On a free cash flow basis, it lost $7.7 billion in the quarter, and its debt jumped to $47 billion.

Investors mostly shrugged off the report, with the stock up 2% in after-hours trading before the 5 p.m. ET earnings call. Management said it would not use the unsecured debt market at current interest rates, which offers some encouragement to investors worried about rising bond yields. CoreWeave expects interest expense to reach $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion in the fourth quarter, on $4.7 billion to $5 billion in revenue, and it raised its full-year revenue forecast to $13 billion to $13.3 billion. On the earnings call, CEO Michael Intrator argued that prices for older GPUs had been resilient and were in fact rising, even for Nvidia chips that are three generations old.

The company plans to collect $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits in the fourth quarter, which should offer some reassurance to investors. The Fed is expected to raise interest rates at its next meeting in December after a hot Consumer Price Index report. CoreWeave has a current ratio below 0.5, and its interest expense is more than 20% of its revenue. From CoreWeave's perspective, demand looks set to outstrip supply for years to come, and the company believes it has several levers to pull to fund the build-out.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave Says Demand Is Outstripping Capacity – CFO Defends AI Expansion: ‘Today’s Environment Very Profitable’ For Differentiated Technology
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reported third-quarter results on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, beating expectations and raising its annual forecasts, which lifted its shares more than 7% in overnight trading. Revenue rose 168% to $3.66 billion, and backlog climbed to $132.5 billion from $104 billion in June. Peers Iren Ltd and Nebius rallied 4.5% and nearly 9% respectively. The rebound followed a difficult stretch for the neocloud sector, and CoreWeave shares had dropped over 47% in the previous three months.

CoreWeave raised full-year revenue guidance to $13 billion to $13.3 billion and adjusted operating income forecast to $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion. Full-year capital expenditure guidance now stands at $37 billion to $39 billion, up from $35 billion to $39 billion. The company closed the quarter with about $4.12 billion in cash against nearly $47 billion of debt. Its net loss grew more than six-fold to $709 million, with net interest expense rising to $846 million from $310 million.

CEO Michael Intrator said on the earnings call that CoreWeave has 10 times as much qualified demand as available capacity through the end of 2027. He said the company expects to finance most of the remaining capital spending through delayed draw term loans matched to specific customer contracts. Intrator also said more than 75% of committed capital expenditure through 2027 is tied to investment grade and enterprise customers. He added that he sees no impact from the Democrats' win in Congress, which many believe will slow data center buildout.

CFO Nitin Agarwal acknowledged that the company operates in "a dynamic macro environment" but argued that today's environment is very profitable for companies with demand for differentiated technology that can execute. Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman wrote in an X post that the quarter reminded the market that CoreWeave's demand and growth prospects remain positive. Analysts and retail investors praised the call's outline of robust demand and a coordinated plan to fund spending through debt and customer prepayments. Fears about the durability of data center spending by Big Tech companies and debt-fueled business models had weighed on neocloud stocks in recent months.

Retail sentiment for CRWV flipped to "extremely bullish" from "bearish," and it was the top trending stock on Stocktwits at the time of writing. One trader said he expected UBS, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan to upgrade or reiterate their ratings the following day. Another user noted that concerns about roughly $1 billion in quarterly interest expense sat alongside $133 billion of backlogged revenue. The articles do not say how the analysts ultimately rated the stock.

stories.Headline: 'I don't like them' | AI data center backlash fueled election votes as Bottoms plans project pause
stories.Summary:
Voters in several places pushed back against AI data center construction in the recent midterm elections, and the backlash has now reached local government and company policy. The articles describe the backlash as a factor in election votes, with ballot measures meant to limit the construction boom passing widely. On Thursday, November 5, OpenAI said it would change how it deals with communities where it builds its large data centers, which it now calls "compute campuses." Its announcement came two days after those ballot measures drew broad support. Separately, a politician named Bottoms was reported to be planning a pause on projects.

OpenAI described a National Community Compact under which each future campus it owns and operates will have its own local agreement and an annual public report. The company pledged to pay the full cost of the electricity it uses along with the grid upgrades needed to serve it. It also said it would post financial guarantees so local households and businesses would not be stuck paying for grid upgrades if a project were canceled. The company added that it would publish water and power use for each site. It also said it would stop requiring public officials to sign nondisclosure agreements, except in narrow security and trade-secret cases.

OpenAI's Stargate project in Abilene, Texas, is one of the largest data centers under construction in the country, and the company's pledges are a direct response to the local resistance. The company's own statement framed the changes as a commitment to the towns that host its facilities. The articles attribute the policy shift to OpenAI itself, which made the pledges public. Other stories in the same news cycle covered unrelated matters, so the articles do not link those to the data center debate.

The articles do not say whether the pause Bottoms is planning will take effect, what form it would take, or how OpenAI and other developers would respond. They also do not describe how the new compact will be enforced or whether other companies will adopt similar terms. The coverage leaves open how much the local backlash will shape the next round of AI construction. Further details on the pause and on how the compact is implemented would be needed to judge its effects.

stories.Headline: Testing the new generation of AI-enabled fire-extinguishing drones
stories.Summary:
Fire crews in Aspen, Colorado are training to pilot a new generation of drones made by the California-based company Seneca, and the Aspen Fire Protection District will be the first fire department in the country to operate them independently once training is complete. The drones are about 10 by 12 feet wide, have four large arms with propellers, and are designed to work in a swarm. Five of them can carry 500 to 1,000 gallons of finished fire foam, and firefighters reported they were easy to operate. Andy Fisher, deputy chief of Aspen Fire, said the department's program could launch as early as next year. So far the drones have only been used on prescribed burns in California with support from Seneca's staff.

Fisher wants to send the drones to hard-to-reach fires, such as remote lightning strikes, before firefighters arrive. The city of Aspen is surrounded by dense forests and has few evacuation routes for residents and visitors. Seneca's founder, Stuart Landesberg, said the drones have a range of 5 to 10 miles, double that when empty, and can cross steep or treacherous terrain quickly. Hovering over a fire, an AI-supported sensor suite calculates distance and wind speed, then releases water or retardant at a specific angle and velocity. Landesberg said the drones will not replace air tankers on big fires but can carry tools, monitor fires and help extinguish hot spots.

Landesberg said the drones could make aerial firefighting far cheaper than helicopters, saying they could be "the next best thing at two orders of magnitude less cost." Aspen Fire says it will pay about $2.5 million over the next five years, with private donors covering the bill. Joe Stutler, a firefighter with nearly 60 years of experience who is not affiliated with Aspen Fire or Seneca, said he is a "big proponent of technology" and hopes the drones can fight fires overnight, when manned aircraft are often grounded. He also hopes they will reduce risk to pilots flying helicopters and air tankers. Stutler remains skeptical, saying he has not seen results from real wildfires and that claims need to be backed by data.

The FAA granted Aspen Fire a waiver in late October, allowing the department to fly the drones up to 200 feet in Pitkin County once training is complete. The drones cannot fly over populated areas, and someone must keep eyes on them at all times, including a spotter on a ridgeline who can communicate with the pilots. If the drones prove useful, Aspen Fire hopes to expand the waiver and help fight fires elsewhere in the state. Before other fire departments invest in the technology, many are watching Aspen to see how effective the drones can be.

stories.Summary:
Jason Wang, a 28-year-old media operator in Zhengzhou, Henan province, swapped his long-held habit of buying gold for tech-themed funds at the end of last year. He had no grounding in how tech companies work, but he joined a bull run that lasted until the middle of this year. The gains on his semiconductor funds climbed to a peak of 170 per cent before dropping to just over 10 per cent recently. He described the stretch as an emotional roller coaster, and the reversal caught him and other Chinese investors off guard. The swings have raised concern that they could widen the gap in funding between China's national champions and smaller players.

Retail money has poured into sectors such as semiconductors and robotics, and the sharp reversal has tested how those investors respond when prices fall. The article frames the episode as a test of the country's tech funding divide, with fears of an AI bubble rattling markets. Those fears have made investors question whether the earlier rally was built on solid foundations. Ben Jiang, the reporter who wrote the piece from Beijing, presents the market reversal as the central development. The article does not attribute the downturn to a single official decision or company, and it leaves open who will bear the largest losses.

Instead, it relies on the experience of individual investors like Wang to show how the mood has shifted. Its account is limited to the investor view and the broader worry about an AI bubble. The article does not describe any official response or policy change tied to the downturn. It also does not say how long the uncertainty will last or what regulators or companies plan to do next. The piece ends by framing the shift as an open question for the tech sector, leaving the outcome for later reporting to settle.

stories.Headline: AI, Smart Robotics and Direct Sourcing Shape Trends at October China Gift Fair
stories.Summary:
The 34th China (Shenzhen) International Gifts and Home Products Fair, organized by RX Huabo, closed on October 23 at the Shenzhen World Exhibition & Convention Center. The event brought together 4,500 exhibitors and more than one million products across nearly 300,000 square meters. It recorded over 260,000 buyer visits from Europe, the United States, and the Middle East. The show's press release, distributed through PR Newswire, was published on November 10, 2026.

Smart robotics and artificial intelligence drew strong interest at the consumer electronics halls, where Middle Eastern buyers looked for distribution and wholesale deals. UBTECH showed AI educational robots, while Robosen displayed officially licensed Transformers with voice control, automatic transformation, and programmable features. Mini robots powered by large language models also attracted attention for conversational interaction and gifting aimed at technology enthusiasts. Small-appliance makers showed coffee makers, humidifiers, and seasonal products, and one leading manufacturer said it ships dozens of containers each month, mainly to Europe and the United States. Another exhibitor that supplies Costco and Walmart pointed to continued growth through direct-to-consumer websites and global agency networks.

For buyers looking beyond established suppliers, the 2026 edition offered a wider range of sourcing options. More than 1,000 first-time exhibitors brought new brands and products to the floor. Ten specialized zones covered consumer electronics, home lifestyle, brand services, and emerging categories, giving visitors more ways to find products and build supplier connections. The organizer said these additions were designed to deepen the range of what buyers could discover at the event.

RX Huabo, which describes itself as having more than 30 years of industry experience, is part of RX, a global events and exhibitions group. The company says it runs 16 professional B2B exhibitions a year at home and abroad, bringing together over 10,000 exhibitors and one million products for three million buyers. It also operates the online platform Limaotong, which it describes as an omni-channel B2B trading platform for year-round procurement. The next edition, the 35th China (Shenzhen) International Gifts, Handicrafts, Watches & Houseware Fair, is scheduled for April 25 to 28, 2027.

stories.Headline: Symatics unveils new processor architecture designed for faster AI responses
stories.Summary:
Singapore-headquartered semiconductor startup Symatics unveiled its Morphic Processing Unit (MPU) architecture on November 10, 2026, at the Business & Philanthropy Forum 2026 in Singapore. The company presented the design as a new way to organise and carry out AI computations, aimed at interactive AI, complex reasoning and AI agents whose usefulness depends on how quickly a single request is completed. The announcement was distributed through PR Newswire. Symatics said it will develop the architecture with research and industry partners in Singapore, which it described as supporting its global ambitions and the region's AI computing capabilities.

The MPU reorganises AI computing around row-column parallelism, mapping the parallel steps of a computation and their dependencies onto a row-column array so that data supply is matched to where each calculation happens. Intermediate results stay on the chip and are used nearby, which the company says reduces repeated reads and writes to external memory and redistribution of data. A compiler decides in advance where computations take place, how information moves between them and the order of operations, with the aim of cutting the time spent coordinating tasks during execution. The architecture also targets the speed of individual requests rather than only total throughput, spreading one request across more MPUs when bandwidth or compute limits a single stream. The company says this lets operators raise per-request token rates as they add hardware.

Mo Zining, Founder and CEO of Symatics, said that simply adding computing power is not always the answer as AI becomes more sophisticated. He argued that the next stage of AI computing requires rethinking how information is processed and moved, and said the MPU is meant to address those underlying inefficiencies. Symatics also said that under its open architecture it will support partners in customising chips and systems, share reference designs and implementation experience, and later offer a configurable B2B infrastructure platform. With research and industry partners, the company plans to build a Singapore implementation standard and demonstration projects, connect Asia-Pacific manufacturing, and offer customised chip and system engineering to enterprises and national customers.

Symatics describes itself as a semiconductor startup developing the MPU to improve the performance and efficiency of AI workloads, with engineering teams in Singapore, Taiwan and Toronto. The company says it is advancing the architecture through research and engineering development and intends to serve the global AI infrastructure market. The articles do not give a timeline for commercial availability, pricing, or performance figures, and they do not say when the planned demonstration projects or platform will arrive. More details on the company's plans are available on its website, symaticslab.com.

stories.Headline: Tester joins AI, data and surveillance company with MAGA ties
stories.Summary:
Former Montana U.S. Senator Jon Tester has taken a job as a senior advisor at Palantir Technologies, an artificial intelligence, surveillance and data analytics company with ties to the GOP and the Trump administration. The company's software is used by U.S. immigration enforcement and the Israeli military, drawing scrutiny from the American Civil Liberties Union. Palantir was co-founded by billionaire conservative Trump ally Peter Thiel. The Palantir opportunity reached Tester's desk in July.

Tester said working for Palantir is not the same as working for data centers, though the two are connected. He said data centers are "screwed up big time" because they can overload energy grids, and he argued that communities need to be driving the decisions about them. He called for complete transparency from data center operators. He also said there will be congressional hearings, accountability and oversight on AI.

Tester said he hopes to use his experience as a third-generation organic grain and crop farmer to streamline the paperwork-heavy parts of food production with AI. He said AI could let the U.S. Department of Agriculture and crop insurers interact without overlapping paperwork. He pointed to medical record sharing between Veterans Affairs facilities and the private sector, where Palantir is already active. He said his official role is limited to advising on real-world uses of AI and improving efficiency and ease of use.

The Chronicle asked Tester about earlier statements by Palantir CEO Alex Karp that AI could disrupt white-collar jobs such as coding, writing and legal work. Tester said he did not reach his decision overnight and had talked with Karp before accepting the position. He said people at the company he spoke with one-on-one respected civil liberties and privacy. Karp has contended that only vocational or technical workers and neurodivergent individuals with out-of-the-box problem-solving skills can thrive in an AI-driven world.

Tester said Congress needs to put "sideboards" on AI and that it "bears watching." On July 23, Democratic California representative Ted Lieu and Texas Republican Nathaniel Moran introduced an AI Kill Switch Act, which remains in limbo. Polling from The AI Policy Institute found that 86% of voters support legislating a guaranteed shutdown capability. Tester-endorsed Democratic Representative-elect Sam Forstag proposed a kill switch during an Oct. 26 visit to Montana State University, and Tester said he had not compared notes with Forstag but likes him a lot.

stories.Headline: An analysis of the tech job market in late 2026: product managers seem to be benefiting most in the AI era, demand for engineers is plateauing, and more (Lenny Rachitsky/Lenny's Newsletter)
stories.Summary:
Lenny Rachitsky's newsletter published a report on November 10, 2026, titled "State of the tech job market: late 2026," analyzing hiring trends at tech companies. The report is based on two datasets: TrueUp, which tracks global job openings at more than 9,000 tech companies, and Live Data Technologies, which tracks job changes for 124 million professionals, with hiring figures specific to the United States. Rachitsky said the report is his second of 2026 and the most surprising of the five he has produced over the past few years. Product managers appear to be benefiting most in the AI era, according to the report. Open PM roles are at their highest level in nearly four years, up 75% from the March 2023 low, and PM openings grew 56% since the start of 2023, compared with 43% for engineering.

PM's share of hiring rose from 16% in 2021 to 21% today, even though hiring for every core product role has been flat or declining. Rachitsky wrote that this suggests growing demand for PMs but that landing strong candidates is getting harder. Engineering demand has plateaued, the report says. Open engineering roles grew 29% through 2024, 15% through 2025, and just 2.5% in the past year, and there are fewer open engineering roles today than in March. U.S. companies hired about 113,000 software engineers between May 2025 and April 2026, less than half the 2022 peak of 239,000, and the number has dropped every year since 2022.

Rachitsky pointed to recruiter openings, which are up nearly 300% since mid-2023, as a possible sign that engineering hiring could reaccelerate. He also noted the rise of forward deployed engineer roles, with about 1,500 open globally after a 4.6x increase over the past year. Design and user research roles are declining sharply, according to the report. There are about 1,900 open product design roles at tech companies globally, the lowest since tracking began and down 28% from a year ago, and U.S. companies hired about 12,600 product designers in the past 12 months, less than half the 27,600 hired in 2022. User researcher hiring fell 66% from 5,300 in 2022 to about 1,800 over the past year, and only 108 UXR jobs are open globally.

Rachitsky attributed the decline to faster product development, with teams releasing products earlier and relying more on post-launch iteration, along with better tools that let non-researchers conduct user research. The report also tracks skills and location trends. "LLM" is now the most mentioned skill in PM job descriptions, while "Claude" is the second most mentioned skill in designer job descriptions this spring. Fifteen percent of open tech roles are now based in the Bay Area, up 43% from a year ago, and only 14% offer a remote option, the lowest on record and down from 21% in late 2022. Rachitsky said the report's final takeaway, that the tech job market is growing outside of software roles, was reserved for paid subscribers, so the article's text available here does not describe it.

stories.Headline: Coframe, which uses AI to make websites that test and personalize themselves for each visitor, raised a $25M Series A, bringing its total funding to $35M (Ben Bergman/Business Insider)
stories.Summary:
Coframe, a startup that uses AI to build websites that test and personalize themselves for each visitor, raised a $25 million Series A, according to Business Insider's Ben Bergman. The round was co-led by Khosla Ventures and Hanabi Capital, and it brings the company's total funding to $35 million. The valuation was not disclosed. Khosla Ventures had also backed Coframe at the seed stage.

Vinod Khosla, the billionaire venture capitalist and founder of Khosla Ventures, told Business Insider that AI has enabled extreme customization of the web. He said the company wants to turn websites into what it calls the "living internet." Khosla argued that online shopping has grown worse over the past 15 years, using Amazon as an example, because the company pushes what it wants to sell instead of showing each user what is most relevant. He said writing code for every page would be too expensive and too slow, which is why he sees AI as the enabler.

Coframe was founded in 2023 by Josh Payne, an AI researcher and entrepreneur who studied mathematics and computer science at Stanford and previously co-founded Autograph, a sports and entertainment startup backed by Tom Brady. Payne said the company grew out of the manual, labor-intensive work he encountered while trying to grow a consumer-facing business. He said that when ChatGPT came out, he saw generative AI as a possible solution. He told Business Insider that websites are static, built once as one-size-fits-all and then costly to improve over time.

Payne said Coframe's advantage will come from learning what drives a particular customer to click and buy, rather than simply generating a more attractive landing page. He described the experience as bespoke, saying it is meant to better represent what a business does and the goods and services it provides. Coframe says it has generated more than $300 million in incremental revenue for customers including Dropbox, BCG, Block, Backcountry, and Sur La Table. The company says conversion rates rose 158% at Dropbox, 410% at Replit, and 60% at Cash App.

According to the article, marketing technology has rarely attracted strong interest from venture capitalists. Payne said the market has settled into a handful of entrenched giants, including Adobe and Salesforce, along with many vendors selling incremental tools for testing, targeting, and measuring campaigns. The article notes that Optimizely, once a Silicon Valley favorite, was acquired for an undisclosed sum in 2021. Payne said he believes AI gives the category a second act, and he said the internet is going to have its own sense of life.

stories.Headline: Graphon, which wants to resolve AI agent memory limitations by mapping connections across docs, videos, and images, raised a $35M Series A led by RRE Ventures (Shubhangi Goel/Business Insider)
stories.Summary:
Graphon, a San Francisco startup, raised $35 million in a Series A round led by RRE Ventures, according to a Business Insider exclusive published November 10, 2026. The company is building software that lets AI agents store and retrieve information over time, which it says addresses the "amnesia" that makes agents lose track of past conversations. Graphon has now raised $35 million to further build and sell that technology. The round also drew participation from Energy Impact Partners, Hitachi Ventures, Gaia VC, and HP.

Graphon takes its name from "graphons," a mathematical framework that founder and CEO Arbaaz Khan used during his Ph.D. research into coordinating swarms of robots. Rather than treating a company's documents, videos, and images as isolated snippets, the software maps the connections among them, including where information came from and when it changed. Khan compared common AI search systems to tearing pages out of a book, crumpling them, and tossing them in a bin, where each piece is left living on its own. Graphon instead creates what Khan called a connected fabric of information.

Graphon says it has two groups of customers in mind: individual developers and companies with large stores of technical and operational data, such as industrial businesses, financial services, and healthcare companies. Khan said the product is compatible with off-the-shelf agents, so a user can point an agent such as Claude or GPT to Graphon. He said any amount of data can be pushed into the system. The company says the San Francisco 49ers and HP already use its software.

Graphon, which has 20 employees, closed a roughly $8 million seed round earlier this year. It plans to use the new funding primarily to hire engineers and researchers, along with some sales and go-to-market staff. Khan said the company expects to stay focused on enterprise customers before moving further into personal devices and consumer products. The article reports that Graphon has shared the pitch deck it used to secure the funding.

Anthropic released two new AI models on Monday, November 9, 2026, called Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2. The company describes them as upgrades to its most capable line, built for the hardest technical work, with gains in coding, reasoning and vision. Anthropic says the two are the same underlying model, but Fable carries strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards, which is what lets the company offer it to all users. Mythos is available through the company's expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs, to which organizations pursuing beneficial work in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply.

On price and speed, the new models cost $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, which is 20% below the 5.1 versions according to the headline figure. They generate output up to 30% faster than Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1. An optional fast mode speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times and costs $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. In Anthropic's benchmarks, Fable 5.2 scored 49.1% on the FrontierCode 2.0 agentic coding test at Xhigh effort, against 32.4% for Fable 5.1, while Mythos 5.2 rose from 61.7% to 76.3% on the CyScenarioBench cybersecurity test. CNET reported that eligible Claude subscribers will receive between one and three Fable resets this week, depending on how long they have subscribed.

The announcement came from Anthropic itself, which said that during prerelease testing the models helped its engineers complete software migrations that would otherwise have been infeasible and formalize a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours. The company said Claude now writes more than 90% of the changes merged into its core codebase, with human guidance, and that in one experiment Fable 5.2 coordinated over 1,000 subagents across eight days to build a working operating system from an empty folder. On safety, Anthropic said it believes high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low and that the model did as well as or better than its recent models on most alignment measures. It added that Fable 5.2's cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as Fable 5.1's but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, alongside what it called its strongest protections yet against distillation attacks.

CNET's Blake Stimac noted that average users may not see much benefit from the new models, which Anthropic itself positions for the most ambitious, open-ended work. Anthropic recommends that most users start with Claude Opus 5.5 for everyday coding and knowledge tasks, moving up to Fable or Mythos or down to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Haiku 5.5 as the scope of the work requires. It also says Fable 5.2 can act as an Advisor that smaller models consult on harder problems, or as an Orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to them. Mythos 5.2's cybersecurity features remain restricted to participants in Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program, and the company points to its system card for full details on testing and methodology.

stories.Headline: Broadcom contributes VM API to CNCF for Kubernetes, AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Broadcom has contributed an application programming interface for virtual machines to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, the body that steers Kubernetes. The move was announced at KubeCon North America 2026 and was reported on November 10, 2026. Its stated purpose is to let virtual machines run as first-class Kubernetes workloads and to simplify the management of AI infrastructure. Alongside it, Broadcom is supporting a newly formed Workload Conformance Working Group, which aims to set objective standards for making Kubernetes workloads portable across environments.

The contribution centers on standardizing APIs so that virtual machines can be provisioned declaratively, whether they are proprietary or open-source projects. Broadcom's diagnostic tool Sonobuoy is central to the certification effort tied to the new standards. The company is also pushing customers to consolidate monolithic, cloud-native and AI workloads on its VMware Cloud Foundation platform, with the aim of lowering IT costs by running diverse workloads on one platform. Broadcom says over 2,600 organizations have licensed VCF 9, spanning more than 24 million processor cores. It has also validated 30 partner offerings to run on the VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, an optimized Kubernetes distribution for VCF.

Prashanth Shenoy, chief marketing officer for Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation division, said the VM API contribution is meant to ensure virtual machines are treated as first-class citizens within cloud-native computing environments. The articles attribute the broader rationale to the Linux Foundation, which reported that virtual machines make up 53 per cent of production applications. It also found that 34 per cent of respondents expect to expand their VM footprint for AI and agentic workloads. Together, these figures are presented as the backdrop for why Broadcom is pressing for tighter integration between VMs and Kubernetes.

The articles frame this as a bid to bring virtual machines into the same orchestration model that governs containers, at a time when AI workloads are driving infrastructure demand. They do not describe timelines for when the working group will publish its standards or how the CNCF will adopt the API. Nor do they report any reaction from competing vendors or open-source maintainers. The coverage stays focused on Broadcom's announcement and the figures it cites.

stories.Headline: Traefik Hub extends AI gateway to SUSE, Spectro Cloud, VMware, Nutanix
stories.Summary:
Traefik Labs announced at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 that its Traefik Hub now runs on four enterprise platforms. The platforms are SUSE AI Factory with NVIDIA, Spectro Cloud PaletteAI, VMware Cloud Foundation from Broadcom, and Service Provider Central on Nutanix Cloud Platform. The announcement was reported by TechGig on November 10, 2026. The expansion brings the company's AI gateway to these environments so that model, agent, API, and application traffic can be governed from one place.

On each platform, Traefik Hub's AI Gateway and MCP Gateway send model calls and agent tool calls through a single control point. The gateway identifies callers and enforces policies on which models and tools may be used. It also masks personal data and secrets, blocks unsafe requests, and meters token budgets. Sudeep Goswami, CEO of Traefik Labs, said the gateway goes wherever the workload goes, so the same controls apply consistently. The articles describe these functions as the core of the offering across all four platforms.

Traefik Hub is certified for SUSE AI Factory with NVIDIA and is available as a SUSE AI Factory partner blueprint. For Spectro Cloud's PaletteAI Model as a Service, Traefik is the default gateway, adding identity-aware policy, data masking, prompt injection blocking, and a signed audit log. Broadcom has published a validated reference architecture for deploying Traefik Hub on VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service within VCF, which positions it as a unified entry point for virtual machines, KubeVMs, and containers. Service providers building on Nutanix can integrate Traefik Hub to offer Layer 7 services within their tenant catalogs.

These four platforms join more than 12 existing technology, cloud, and service provider partners in the Traefik Labs ecosystem. The articles provide no pricing details, rollout timelines, or customer counts for the new integrations. They describe the arrangements as already in place rather than as future plans. Any further deployments or availability changes would have to come from later company or partner announcements.

stories.Headline: AI-Written Complaints Swamp U.K. Public Bodies, Some Running 200 Pages
stories.Summary:
Complaints drafted with generative AI are overwhelming public bodies across Britain, according to a Guardian report published on November 9, 2026. Local councils, Parliament and the courts have all seen sharp rises in submissions written with chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude, with some growing roughly tenfold in length. Deborah Evans, chief executive of Lawyers in Local Government, said the average complaint once ran about two pages but now often reaches around 20, and the longest she has seen ran to 200 pages. These documents sometimes include irrelevant material or cite foreign laws and court rulings that do not apply in Britain. They can also contain so-called hallucinations, where the AI invents laws or rulings that do not exist, forcing officials to verify every claim.

The Information Commissioner's Office said some freedom-of-information requests believed to be AI-written are so long or repetitive that it is hard to tell what the applicant is actually asking. Errors alone do not allow a public body to ignore a complaint, which must still be reviewed and answered under the relevant procedures. Holly Weakens, a senior caseworker in a Labour lawmaker's office, estimated that about half the emails she receives were written with AI, a trend she said began rising in earnest in 2024. GMB, the union representing staff in lawmakers' offices, reported that casework volumes have more than doubled at some offices, with staff repeatedly working beyond contracted hours. Alessandro Georgiou, leader of Enfield Council in London, said more residents are using AI to challenge council decisions, and he described the rise in parking appeals as a serious problem.

Transport for London received 4,769 freedom-of-information requests in the 2025-26 fiscal year, the highest on record and about 5% above the previous peak set in 2023-24. TfL said appeals that appear to be AI-written have increased recently and that some contain technically complex or inaccurate claims. Government figures show about 14,000 new single claims were filed with employment tribunals between April and June this year, up 28% from a year earlier, though the article notes that whether AI is driving the increase has not been established. Several ombudsman offices are capping complaint lengths or redesigning online forms to limit submissions.

Wiltshire Council is considering using AI to summarize long emails and draft initial replies. The British government has issued guidance telling civil servants to verify information generated by AI tools, avoid entering personal data, and leave final decisions to people. The article also notes that AI can help citizens who previously struggled to write complaints gain better access to administrative procedures. Public bodies are now weighing how to protect the right to complain while coping with the surge in work.

stories.Headline: If You Don’t Know The Answer, AI Does
stories.Summary:
The articles don't describe a news event in the usual sense. The main piece, published by The Concordian on November 10, 2026, is an opinion column by writer Rita Kamel about an AI overview that appeared when she searched her own name. The overview contained personal details she did not remember sharing online, including her major, minor and dyslexia, along with a summary of her writing style. It also cited an article written by a colleague and mixed her résumé up with another person named Rita Kamel.

Kamel says she found the experience unsettling because she had no control over what was attached to her name online, yet the AI presented that material as fact. She writes that the information traced back to an interview she gave in her first year to help a classmate. She argues that AI can be useful but that speed does not guarantee accuracy, and she notes that many generative AI programs warn users to double-check what they produce. She says relying on AI alone risks spreading misinformation, and that AI should be a starting point for research rather than the final one.

Kamel also says she was already unhappy with the automatic AI summaries that appear in search results, fearing they will erode the habit of research she learned before the internet. She concludes that AI is now part of daily life and that people need to learn to use it properly, which she describes as AI literacy. The other items in the same feed are a newsletter signup notice, a French-language piece about innovation and privacy, a note on the deaths of four Canadian soldiers at CFB Wainwright ahead of Remembrance Day, and a content warning with a sexual violence helpline. These are unrelated to the AI column, and the articles do not say whether any follow-up or policy response to the AI overview has occurred.

Articles.Title: If You Don’t Know The Answer, AI Does

stories.Headline: Better expands AI use, eliminates jobs amid Q3 loss
stories.Summary:
Better Home & Finance Holding Co. has eliminated several management layers and its home lending associate role, saying the work will now be handled by artificial intelligence, as it reported a wider net loss for the third quarter of 2026. The company, a digital mortgage lender, disclosed the moves on Monday during its earnings call with analysts. Founder Vishal Garg, who regained control of the board and returned to a leadership role in early October after a proxy battle, said the cuts represent more than $3.5 million in annualized savings. The company reported a net loss of $36.5 million for the quarter, up from $30.6 million in the second quarter but slightly below the $39.1 million loss a year earlier.

Garg said the eliminated management responsibilities are now performed by AI agents and dashboards that report directly to senior executives. He described the cuts as permanent and said the roles would not return as the company scales volume. The home lending associate position, which handled early customer outreach and application preparation before handing off to a loan officer, is now handled by the company's AI system, called Betsy. Better also removed vice president and director titles, leaving executive leaders working directly with frontline staff. The company says it has achieved $30.4 million in annualized savings toward a $64.2 million cost-reduction target.

Garg attributed the weak quarter partly to interest rate pressure, rising oil prices, and uncertainty tied to the Iran war, which he said weighed on loan volume. He also blamed the prior board's proxy contest for lowering conversion and delaying partner launches. The company originated $1.4 billion in loans in the third quarter, representing 4,748 units and 15% year-over-year growth, and ended the quarter with $77.5 million in cash. The leadership fight began when activist investor Daniel Lewis replaced Garg on the board on August 3, and Garg later returned backed by shareholders holding 52% of voting power. Better spent $12.8 million on the contest and a related shareholder rights plan, and added board members Bing Gordon, Steve Sarracino, and Linda Yaccarino afterward.

The company's fourth quarter to date includes an AI-powered home equity line of credit product launched with a large partner and an expanded wholesale platform now covering 39 signed brokerages. Better expects fourth-quarter operating expenses between $45 million and $47 million. It is also finalizing the sale of U.K.-based Birmingham Bank, with the buyer having placed 10 million pounds in escrow, and expects that deal to close in the first quarter of 2027 subject to regulatory approval. Chief financial officer Loveen Advani said the transaction should generate about $65 million in additional cash.

Articles.Title: Better expands AI use, eliminates jobs amid Q3 loss

stories.Headline: TSMC Just Delivered the AI Growth Shock Wall Street Was Waiting For
stories.Summary:
TSMC, the Taiwanese company that is the world's largest contract chipmaker, reported that its October revenue jumped nearly 60% from a year earlier. The company posted NT$586.89 billion, roughly $17.8 billion, which beat its previous monthly record of NT$514.81 billion set in August. Revenue for the first ten months of 2026 reached NT$4.49 trillion, a 43.3% annual gain. The strong showing suggests that demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure is holding up despite recent swings in semiconductor stocks.

TSMC makes advanced chips designed by customers such as Nvidia, AMD and Apple, so its sales serve as a gauge of AI hardware spending. Management raised its full-year revenue growth outlook to about 44% in U.S. dollar terms, up from a previous forecast of slightly more than 40%. The company also expects fourth-quarter revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, and October's figures indicate it is on track for that range. Third-quarter revenue had already climbed 41.2% to $46.72 billion, and gross margin reached 66.4%.

The article presents these results as the work of TSMC's management, which set the outlook and reported the figures. It notes that the company's chips depend on its manufacturing capacity, which is why investors in Nvidia, Apple and other chip designers watch its numbers closely. Other coverage in the same feed described AI-linked stocks falling despite upbeat TSMC earnings, showing that investor concerns about excessive AI spending and high valuations persist. A separate Motley Fool discussion from the same week described how the market is now scrutinizing free cash flow and debt financing across large technology firms rather than rewarding spending alone.

Looking ahead, the article identifies TSMC's November revenue report, scheduled for December 10, as its next key data point. Investors will watch whether sales momentum is strong enough to support the upper end of fourth-quarter guidance. Progress in 2-nanometer production, AI accelerator demand and advanced packaging capacity will also serve as indicators. The article warns that slower spending by large cloud providers, capacity constraints or rising manufacturing costs could pressure profitability even as revenue grows.

Articles.Title: TSMC Just Delivered the AI Growth Shock Wall Street Was Waiting For

stories.Headline: Even Martin Scorsese uses AI for storyboards. Can the art survive?
stories.Summary:
Storyboard artists, the illustrators who sketch a director's first visual plans for a film, are facing a new threat from AI image tools, according to a Guardian feature by Lana Crowe published on 10 November 2026. The piece notes that Hollywood's biggest filmmakers are increasingly adopting the technology, with James Cameron sitting on the board of a generative AI firm, Steven Soderbergh using Meta-powered tools for animation in his John Lennon documentary, and Christopher Nolan calling the idea that AI will replace humans "nonsense" while conceding it could provide useful imaging tools. Martin Scorsese is also among them, having announced in June a partnership with an AI firm whose text-to-image model he used while storyboarding his next movie. The article frames storyboard artists as the canary in the coalmine, since text prompts can now produce illustrations that once required their work.

The article explains why that work matters beyond the pictures themselves. Storyboards are usually made collaboratively by a director, an artist and crew members such as cinematographers, editors and production designers, and they serve as a blueprint for how a scene will look and how a director's vision reaches cast and crew. Alex Clark, a British storyboard artist whose credits include Mickey 17, The Gorge and The Last House, says the process is as important as the finished drawings because it forces artists to think through how each detail will affect a scene. Denis Villeneuve, who worked with artist Sam Hudecki on Dune, described storyboarding as "a new way of writing" and the first step in creating a film's cinematic language. Clark also says storyboards often leave space for actors, set decoration, lighting and camera movement to build on them.

The article also places storyboarding in a longer history. Ferdinando Cocco, a film lecturer at Abertay University in Dundee, points to changes in Disney's Beauty and the Beast, whose late 1980s storyboards had a rococo-inspired look before the character of Gaston took on a more modern form. Disney's animators began using storyboards regularly in the 1930s, and live-action productions adopted them by at least 1939 with Gone With the Wind. Alfred Hitchcock's meticulous boards, including Saul Bass's sketches for the shower scene in Psycho, and Bong Joon Ho's self-drawn panels for Parasite show how the drawings have become works of art. Storyboards are also pinned up on set and sold in books, and a Milan exhibition last year displayed panels from filmmakers ranging from Ingmar Bergman to Scorsese.

Despite the pressure, the article suggests there is room for hope. Cocco has seen a return to analogue methods and argues that AI could be used in ways that expand rather than dilute the creative process, since the need to communicate with others widens an artist's vision. Clark predicts that as AI use grows, audiences will value films with a human touch, and he says hand-drawn storyboards carry a direct sense of that authenticity. The piece does not report any specific policy, contract or industry action in response, so what happens to storyboard jobs in practice remains unresolved.

Articles.Title: Even Martin Scorsese uses AI for storyboards. Can the art survive?

stories.Headline: AI/R Compass UOL Expands AI/Cockpit One to Support More Than 80 Providers and 600 AI Models
stories.Summary:
AI/R Compass UOL, a subsidiary of the technology company AI/R, announced on November 10, 2026 that it has expanded its AI/Cockpit One platform to support more than 80 providers and more than 600 artificial intelligence models. The platform places these models in a managed enterprise environment and pairs usage governance with an approval workflow. The company describes the expansion as a way for businesses to match model choice to specific needs. The announcement was made through a GlobeNewswire press release datelined San Francisco.

According to the announcement, companies can compare alternatives, send simple tasks to more efficient models, and reserve advanced models for harder work. The stated goal is to reduce reliance on a single vendor and make ongoing optimization of AI spending easier. Models are not enabled by default, and each one passes through an approval workflow that reviews the data policies of the provider's service. Only models meeting the security criteria are made available, and the company says these criteria include reviewing retention policies and requiring that corporate data not be used for training. The platform also tracks adoption, token consumption and costs by model and user, and it supports spending limits by team.

Cleyton Ferreira, Director of Technology and Products at AI/R, said that enabling models and governing their use inside a company is not enough, since exposure and leakage risks can also originate with providers. He argued that without a managed environment, each team picks its own provider and the company loses visibility into spending and where its data goes. The release also says the platform offers user, role and permission management, corporate authentication, SSO support, and audit events. The company's background is described as an Amazon Web Services Premier Partner with more than 1,900 AWS-certified professionals.

The release is a paid press release and was distributed by the company itself, so its claims about security and performance have not been independently verified. The articles do not say how many of the 600 models are enabled for any given customer, nor do they name the providers involved. They also do not indicate pricing or a timeline for further rollout. Further details are available in the official AI/Cockpit One documentation.

Articles.Title: AI/R Compass UOL Expands AI/Cockpit One to Support More Than 80 Providers and 600 AI Models

stories.Headline: Cribl acquires Tero to accelerate AI-native observability
stories.Summary:
Cribl, the San Francisco-based AI platform for telemetry, has acquired Tero, a developer of intelligence tools for observability data, as it looks to expand across monitoring and AI-native observability. The deal was reported on November 10, 2026. Tero's three co-founders, chief executive Ben Johnson, CTO Adam Cohen and COO Nihar Singhal, will join Cribl along with their engineering team. Johnson will become VP of observability and help lead the company's product strategy in that sector. He previously co-founded Timber, the company behind the open source Vector data pipeline, which Datadog acquired in 2021.

Tero's technology helps organisations judge the value of their telemetry data by identifying information that adds little to their observability operations. It shows engineering teams where low-value data is building up across their tools and helps them deal with it without changing existing workflows. At Cribl, the team will focus on host monitoring, application performance monitoring, federated observability and AI-native observability. These capabilities will be built on Cribl's existing open platform, which lets customers collect, route and refine telemetry data. The acquisition is Cribl's third in four months, following its purchase of CardinalOps in July and the addition of Radiant Security's AI security operations centre technology in August.

Cribl said Tero brings observability expertise, established customer and partner relationships, and engineering experience that should speed up product development. The company said the deal also supports its wider aim of combining observability and security products on one shared telemetry platform. Founded in 2018, Cribl describes itself as an AI platform for IT and security telemetry, and its infrastructure supports its own SIEM, observability and AI SOC products. Co-founder and CEO Clint Sharp said that the best builders in observability are choosing to build with Cribl, and that Johnson has spent a decade on the problem of helping engineers control their data. Johnson said Tero was started to help engineers understand their telemetry rather than simply collect more of it, and that joining Cribl was a way to build the product together rather than compete with it.

Articles.Title: Cribl acquires Tero to accelerate AI-native observability

stories.Headline: Closing the AI guidance gap in education
stories.Summary:
OpenAI published a report on November 10, 2026, titled "Closing the AI guidance gap in education," drawing on new research from ThinkYoung and lessons from its education partnerships across Europe, the Middle East and Africa. The company says AI is prompting a rethink of what schools should prepare students for, since as intelligence becomes easier to access, the key question becomes which skills will help people thrive in an AI-enabled world. Recent debates led by the OECD's Andreas Schleicher on PISA and AI support this view. The article argues that as AI grows more capable, the role of teachers becomes more important, not less.

The company is working with governments and education systems in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, among others, to explore how AI can support educators. These partnerships share three priorities: equitable access to frontier AI tools, jointly designed AI literacy programmes, and ongoing measurement and evaluation, all adapted to local languages, curricula and institutions. The ThinkYoung research highlights a clear guidance gap, with 79% of surveyed students reporting they use AI for homework or assignments but only 47% saying they were shown how to do so. The article says governments need to support educators and give students clearer expectations about the terms and conditions of use. It also reports that teacher adoption and self-reported time savings are encouraging early signs, though it says more sustained evaluation is needed to understand where AI strengthens knowledge, independent thinking and retention.

The report frames its findings as early experiences rather than a single model for other systems to copy. It identifies three lessons from Estonia, Greece and Slovakia: strong public leadership to set a clear direction, investment in teachers' skills and confidence, and practical support tailored to local curricula and classroom needs. The authors, Tom Duff Gordon and Leah Belsky, present these as a foundation for governments integrating AI responsibly, while noting that implementation will vary by country. OpenAI says it wants to contribute to the evidence base and learn openly from findings, including ones that challenge its assumptions, and it points to its OpenAI Learning Lab, which brings education researchers together to study when and how AI can support education systems. The company frames the wider goal as making sure every young person can build the skills to take part in a world increasingly shaped by AI.

Articles.Title: Closing the AI guidance gap in education

stories.Headline: House House Discloses AI Use For 'Under 0.1%' Of Big Walk's Code Following IGF Voting Controversy
stories.Summary:
House House, the studio behind the cooperative puzzle game Big Walk, has disclosed that it used generative AI for some coding work after a controversy over the upcoming Independent Games Festival. A group of IGF jurors signed a statement saying they would not vote for any game that used generative AI in any capacity, and the statement did not name Big Walk directly. Kyle LeClair, a four-time IGF judge and a juror for the upcoming festival, said the most-discussed game of the year had become dominated by its AI usage. Developer Bruno Diaz then confirmed on Bluesky that the game in question was Big Walk, and that the disclosure had been shared with judges because IGF rules required it.

House House's updated FAQ says that large language models were used sparingly in the final stretch of development to help with difficult technical problems and bugs. The studio estimates that well under 0.1 percent of Big Walk's code had anything to do with this usage, and it says generative AI was not used in any other context. One example it gives involves a Unity URP shadow-culling problem that made the game run 50 percent slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset, where a chatbot suggested a fix that the team heavily modified, producing roughly 10 lines of code. The studio says it did not disclose the usage on Steam because the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. It also says it posted the disclosure because the matter has become one of public interest.

House House states that its use of these tools is not an endorsement of AI, and it expresses concern that voluntary disclosures could normalize the technology. The studio says it supports those working to limit generative AI's harm to games and apologizes that Big Walk's usage may not meet their standards. It acknowledges that Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy and calls that lack of policy a failure, promising a more comprehensive policy going forward. Diaz argued that the distinction between consultative use and code generation makes no real difference, and he said he believes Big Walk is not non-compliant with Steam's AI disclosure requirements.

The dispute comes as the IGF is set to take place on March 3, 2027, and the jurors' statement asks the festival to adopt a strong anti-AI policy in future years that would disallow games containing any AI-generated work. The articles report internal disagreement among jurors, with some not signing the statement, and say the IGF has affirmed that judges may vote according to their own tastes and values. Diaz described many of the internal comments as disingenuous, disappointing, or dumb, but said he would not discuss them further. The articles do not report any decision by the IGF on how it will handle the controversy this year.

Articles.Title: House House Discloses AI Use For 'Under 0.1%' Of Big Walk's Code Following IGF Voting Controversy

stories.Headline: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
stories.Summary:
Google has introduced on-device automatic speech recognition and text-to-speech in its Google AI Edge Gallery, announced in a developer blog post dated November 10, 2026. The features let speech models run entirely on a phone or wearable, with no network connection needed, and they pair with small language models such as Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 so apps can transcribe speech as it is spoken and read replies aloud. According to the post, the system speech models in Android's ML Kit transcribe more than 100 languages at ten times real-time speed and begin speaking in about 100 milliseconds. The post also says the models add 0 MB to an app's package size, since they are built into the operating system.

For cross-platform apps, the post describes open-weight speech bundles in the .litertlm format, including Parakeet-TDT 0.6B, PocketTTS 100M, Kokoro-82M and Phonon 31M, that run through MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT. The company's showcase, called XR Language Teacher, lets a user point a camera at an object or menu, ask a spoken question, and hear an explanation in their own language with local pronunciation of the target-language phrase. The same voice features were also added to the AI Chat feature in the app, which offers dictation, read-aloud playback with sentence highlighting, and settings for choosing voices and language packs. The post says the code is open source and is available on GitHub for developers who want to adapt it.

Google's developer relations and Android teams are responsible for the release, and the post presents it as a way to make AI interaction more natural when networks are unavailable. The company says the speech models are managed through its AICore and speech services, which handle model updates and hardware acceleration on supported chips. It also names a range of performance figures, including a word error rate of 8.0% to 9.0% on the FLEURS benchmark, and says the text-to-speech model uses over 50% less power than traditional autoregressive models. The post names developers who contributed, and it points readers to an Android Dev Summit session on adapting the feature for smart glasses. The articles do not say when broader availability or further updates will arrive.

Articles.Title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery

stories.Headline: UDUUF to present ‘AI and the Human Spirit’
stories.Summary:
The Upper Delaware Unitarian Universalist Fellowship, known as UDUUF, will present a talk titled "AI and the Human Spirit: A Creative Partnership" on Sunday, November 15, in Narrowsburg, New York. The guest speaker is Daria Dorosh, Ph.D., who will show how she uses AI as a thinking partner to make new artwork, raise deep questions, and archive her life's work. The fellowship frames the event around a question about how an artist with a 50-year legacy can embrace the future. The service begins at 10:15 a.m. in Room 102 of the Narrowsburg Union at 7 Erie Ave., and everyone is welcome to attend.

The service is also available to join remotely on Zoom, using Meeting ID 937 630 1223 and passcode 123. The event is part of the fellowship's regular Sunday programming, which is organized by its members rather than by a professional clergy staff. The fellowship describes itself as a lay-led Unitarian Universalist congregation serving the Upper Delaware River valley. Its announcement was published on November 10, 2026, by the River Reporter. The article also notes, in a separate line, that according to researchers at the University of California, Riverside, a single 100-word AI prompt uses about one bottle of water.

Responsibility for the presentation rests with the UDUUF, which issued the announcement describing the talk and its speaker. Dorosh's role is to demonstrate her creative process with AI, and the fellowship's wording presents that work as a way of exploring what it means to keep creating across a long career. The articles give no further statements from the speaker or the fellowship beyond the event description. They also do not report any response to the talk or any follow-up event.

Articles.Title: UDUUF to present ‘AI and the Human Spirit’

stories.Headline: Sharona B. Ross Discusses Human-AI Collaboration and the Responsible Integration of AI in Surgery
stories.Summary:
Sharona B. Ross, a foregut and hepatopancreatobiliary minimally invasive surgeon at the University of South Florida, shared a post on X about her participation as a board member in the Institute for Surgical Excellence Consensus Conference, titled "Shaping Human AI Collaboration in Surgery." The gathering brought together representatives from the FDA, surgical societies, the surgical industry, and leading academic institutions working on artificial intelligence research. According to her post, the discussions centered on the idea that the future of surgery will depend less on how fast technology advances and more on how responsibly it is brought into patient care. The article is a social media post, so it does not report a specific date for the conference itself.

Ross wrote that artificial intelligence, robotics, and automation are changing her field, and that meaningful collaboration among surgeons, researchers, industry leaders, professional societies, and regulators is more important than ever. She said that bringing these groups to the same table, sharing expertise, challenging conventional thinking, and accepting a shared responsibility could help shape a strong future for surgery. She named patient safety, ethical innovation, and excellence in surgical outcomes as the principles that should remain central to every advance. The post does not describe any specific rule, guideline, or policy that the conference produced or that would now be required.

Ross presented these views in her own words as a participant and board member, and the article does not attribute any formal position or decision to the FDA or the other organizations present. The article also does not say what the conference concluded, whether it will issue recommendations, or when any follow-up discussions or outputs might appear. OncoDaily presents the piece as a short news item built around her post, which links to other coverage of artificial intelligence on the site. Beyond Ross's account, the available reporting offers no further details about the conference's agenda, participants, or next steps.

Articles.Title: Sharona B. Ross Discusses Human-AI Collaboration and the Responsible Integration of AI in Surgery

stories.Headline: eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents
stories.Summary:
eBay appears to have blocked AI agents, including Meta's Muse, from browsing its platform, according to a report published by The Verge on November 10, 2026. A reader told the outlet that for several weeks his Muse agent had been compiling a daily digest of watches for sale on eBay and other sites, with links, prices, shipping details and notes on condition. That weekend, however, Muse could not pull any links or details from eBay and reported that it had been blocked from the site. The Verge was able to recreate the problem with other searches, and in some cases Muse directed users to outside sites that mirrored eBay listings.

eBay had already updated its user agreement to ban "buy-for-me agents" and "LLM-driven bots" that place orders without human review. Until recently, agents like Muse could still browse the site and pull listings. The report notes that other retailers have taken different approaches: Amazon blocks external agents from browsing or shopping entirely, Target's rules allow some browsing but block it in other cases, and Shopify has opened a catalog of a billion listings to shopper agents. Retail sites are largely built for human shoppers, and The Verge had earlier shown that Muse could hold product listings hostage on The RealReal by repeatedly adding an item to a cart, a problem that site fixed after the outlet's reporting.

eBay spokesperson Sybille St. Arromand did not directly say whether eBay had recently imposed new limits on AI agents. In an email, she said eBay takes a selective approach to third-party access and has restricted agent access in certain cases, including unauthorized scraping and training on its data. She added that eBay is in ongoing discussions with potential partners and is evaluating how third-party agents could help new customers find its inventory, with a focus on preserving the trusted experience buyers and sellers expect. The report also points to limited real-world use of agent shopping: Uber said it fulfilled only four rides through third-party agents in the third quarter and about 500 Uber Eats orders during the week of Halloween, while DoorDash said it fulfilled "several hundred" such orders out of 993 million total orders last quarter. The Verge says it is unclear how widespread agentic commerce is, and the article does not say whether eBay will reverse the restriction or formalize partnerships with agent providers.

Articles.Title: eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents

stories.Headline: AI is supercharging Iran’s cyber threat, Dream CEO Shalev Hulio warns
stories.Summary:
Cheap, powerful Chinese AI models are helping Iran launch more sophisticated cyberattacks, according to Shalev Hulio, CEO and co-founder of Dream. He made the remarks on November 10, 2026, while speaking at Cyber Week at Tel Aviv University and later with journalists. Hulio said Iranian threat actors now use AI to find zero-day vulnerabilities and to move through compromised networks with little or no direct human involvement. He said these capabilities became available once Chinese models, which he described as nearly as good as American ones and far cheaper, could be used without strict safety limits.

Hulio said AI now supports every stage of an attack, from writing convincing phishing and social engineering campaigns to spotting software flaws. He also described attackers using AI to reverse-engineer security patches, study the fix, work out the underlying vulnerability, and then find systems that have not yet been updated. He argued that this has widened access to advanced cyber tools well beyond nation-states and elite hackers, since anyone with access to unguarded Chinese models can attempt sophisticated operations. He also said that small groups, and possibly individuals, can now carry out work that once required teams of specialists. In his view, traditional defenses built around known past threats are no longer enough.

Hulio said Israel remains a primary Iranian target, and he pointed to attacks on water infrastructure in Israel and the United States as evidence of a wider threat. He also cited campaigns against universities and private individuals whose personal data can be stolen and published online. In his words, Iran is trying to position itself as a global threat actor, which he described as a real risk. Beyond cybersecurity, he framed AI as a question of national sovereignty and urged governments to control their own AI stacks rather than depend on foreign providers for sensitive applications. He also predicted that Israel could lead the world in areas such as defense robotics, AI-powered intelligence, and cyber-AI integration.

Articles.Title: AI is supercharging Iran’s cyber threat, Dream CEO Shalev Hulio warns

stories.Headline: The AI Futures Project updates its AI timelines after METR's report on Anthropic R&D, saying it now expects a Superhuman AI Researcher to arrive in 2027 (AI Futures Project)
stories.Summary:
The AI Futures Project, a group that forecasts the timing of advanced AI, published a timelines update on November 10, 2026, saying it now expects a Superhuman AI Researcher to arrive at some point in 2027, assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown. Its authors, including Eli Lifland, Brendan Halstead and Daniel Kokotajlo, described the update as urgent and said they wanted to publish quickly. The group's main reason for the change was a recent assessment by METR, a research organization, of how much faster Anthropic's AI research was moving. Before that report, Kokotajlo had given roughly a 50 percent chance of such a system arriving before 2029.

The METR report estimated that Anthropic's progress was running at about twice its historical rate, with a plausible range of 1.3 to 3 times, and it guessed that perhaps about 80 percent of that acceleration came from AI. The authors calculated this as an AI-attributable speedup of about 1.7 times, which they said was roughly five months ahead of the pace in their earlier AI 2027 scenario. Their own model had assigned less than 4 percent to progress being sped up by at least that much in November 2026, so they called the result a surprise. They also gave a 35 to 65 percent chance that AI able to automate all white-collar work, which they call TED-AI, would arrive before 2028. Several simple extrapolations they ran pointed to a Superhuman AI Researcher somewhere between late 2027 and mid-2028.

The authors said the timeline makes it urgent to pause or substantially pace frontier AI development, ideally through an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement. They argued that companies are not on track to align such a system, and that a misaligned one used for recursive self-improvement would leave the world in a very bad position. They also warned that China could steal the training recipe and possibly the model weights if such a system were trained soon. The authors said the METR estimates depend heavily on evidence that Anthropic redacted, and they urged the company to release enough information for outside observers to judge the findings. They described their own analysis as highly preliminary, and they invited corrections to any mistakes.

Articles.Title: The AI Futures Project updates its AI timelines after METR's report on Anthropic R&D, saying it now expects a Superhuman AI Researcher to arrive in 2027 (AI Futures Project)

stories.Headline: CNCF Welcomes CoreWeave as a Platinum Member to Further Open Source AI Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation announced on November 10, 2026, that CoreWeave has upgraded its membership to Platinum. The announcement was made from Salt Lake City and distributed through PR Newswire. The upgrade reflects CoreWeave's push to build open source technologies that power production AI infrastructure. CoreWeave already participates in the Certified Kubernetes AI Conformance Program and contributes to Kubernetes, Kueue, and llm-d.

The Platinum upgrade is a step in a longer pattern of contributions by CoreWeave to the cloud native ecosystem.
