stories.Headline: Google DeepMind AI agents reduce costs for attacking 1024-bit RSA keys
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind has announced that AI agents, working under human supervision, found two ways to lower the cost of attacking 1024-bit RSA cryptosystems. The work was done with cryptographers from UC San Diego and Inria, and the results were reported on November 10, 2026. The findings suggest that attacks on legacy RSA-1024 need less computing effort than was previously assumed. The company says the results mainly affect these older systems. The first method concerns digital signatures and padding.

DeepMind found that if an attacker controls roughly half or more of a signed block, the padding gives no protection. The finding is especially relevant to the PKCS#1 v1.5 format used in devices such as hardware security modules. In a sandboxed test, the agents re-ran an earlier academic forgery attack on a 1024-bit key and cut the CPU time from 1,380 core-years to 391 core-years, a 3.5-fold improvement. Kohli, VP at Google DeepMind, noted that this signature attack does not recover the private key and requires around 4 billion signing queries made in advance.

The second method concerns factoring several RSA keys of the same size. The agents developed an algorithm that, on average, makes factoring each additional 1024-bit key about 30 times cheaper than previous methods. That estimate, however, assumes an initial computation as costly as factoring one key, and the method has not yet been implemented. Kohli stated that modern encryption protocols, which almost universally use 2048-bit or larger keys, remain secure.

The researchers concluded that cryptographic hardness cannot be treated as a fixed assumption in an era of AI-enabled computation. The researchers emphasised that using AI to rigorously test long-held assumptions will help ensure the security of modern encryption. The articles do not say what steps are planned for operators of legacy 1024-bit systems. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Google DeepMind AI agents reduce costs for attacking 1024-bit RSA keys

stories.Headline: Red Hat OpenShift 5 adds AI capabilities, agent for workflow automation
stories.Summary:
Red Hat has extended its OpenShift platform with new artificial intelligence capabilities and an AI agent, aiming to simplify Kubernetes cluster management and automate workflows for IT teams. The company revealed these extensions at the KubeCon and CloudNativeCon North America 2026 conference, and the report was published on November 10, 2026. The update is part of OpenShift version 5. Red Hat says the platform now includes a built-in Model Context Protocol server that makes OpenShift available to any AI agent through a simple update. The company has also expanded its Lightspeed AI tools with an agent that lets IT teams invoke multiple AI models for workflow automation.

OpenShift 5 also adds hardened multi-tenant isolation, automated certificate lifecycle management, and a control plane for managing post-quantum cryptography. The platform can analyze application programming interfaces to produce risk assessments, which allows updates without manual cluster reboots. Amazon Web Services is using this feature to extend support for OpenShift updates from 18 to 24 months, and it will also provide up to three years of extended lifecycle support. The embedded AI capabilities can identify root causes of issues, isolate anomalies, analyze log streams, and carry out supervised remediation across clusters from a single console. Version 2.1 of Red Hat Developer Hub, currently in preview, gives AI agents direct command-line access to an organization's software catalog.

Mike Barrett, vice president of Hybrid Cloud Platforms at Red Hat, said the Model Context Protocol server makes OpenShift available to any AI agent through a simple update. The AI agent has been trained to automate tasks across cloud-native platforms, including the Argo continuous delivery platform. Red Hat is also positioning OpenShift to run diverse workloads, including monolithic legacy applications deployed on virtual machines encapsulated in containers. Several organizations, including NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Brigham Young University, Allianz Turkey, Alior Bank, Hospital Diagnóstico, and Bharti Airtel, have adopted OpenShift Virtualization.

The article notes that many organizations struggle to manage fleets of Kubernetes clusters because they lack the software engineering expertise needed to operate at scale. The report suggests AI agents could make cluster management simpler for the average IT administrator. This matters more as AI coding agents make it faster to build cloud-native and AI applications. The article does not describe specific next steps beyond the preview availability of Developer Hub version 2.1.

stories.Headline: APIs and JSON: How programs communicate for AI models
stories.Summary:
Application Programming Interfaces, or APIs, act as a menu for software, letting programs communicate by defining the operations they can perform. This interaction is fundamental for accessing artificial intelligence models and integrating different systems. A server publishes a fixed set of operations through its API along with exact rules for requests, while hiding the underlying work. This approach means internal changes do not break outside code, as long as the menu stays consistent. Every AI model in a typical series is reached by calling its provider's API.

Each item on this software menu has its own address, called an endpoint, which includes a base URL, a version, a path, and an optional query string. HTTP methods such as GET, POST, and DELETE specify the action to take at that address. When sending data to create or change something, details travel in the request body, and a "Content-Type: application/json" header tells the server that the body holds JSON. Calling an AI model follows this pattern, using a POST request with a JSON body that carries messages and settings. The article describes these mechanics as the standard way programs exchange requests.

JSON, or JavaScript Object Notation, is a plain text format for writing data as key-value pairs. The JSON standard defines six value types: text in double quotes, numbers without quotes, true or false, null for empty values, lists in square brackets, and objects in curly braces. The format enforces strict rules, so keys and text must use double quotes, trailing commas and comments are not allowed, and true, false, and null must be lowercase. The article warns that a number written in quotes is treated as text, which can cause later calculations to fail. API responses typically pair an HTTP status code with a JSON answer, where codes such as 200 and 201 signal success and 401, 404, and 429 signal specific client-side problems.

The article presents API documentation as the comprehensive menu for developers, covering methods, URLs, authentication, parameters, example requests, expected responses, error codes, and usage limits. It describes reading this documentation carefully as a core engineering skill for integrating systems successfully. The piece is an explanatory overview rather than a report of a specific event, and it does not describe any new rules, deadlines, or announced changes. It also does not name a particular author beyond the outlet, TechGig, which published it on November 10, 2026.

Articles.Title: APIs and JSON: How programs communicate for AI models

stories.Headline: PhysicsWallah uses AI for 90 per cent of its code
stories.Summary:
PhysicsWallah, an Indian edtech firm, has said that artificial intelligence now writes 90 per cent of its code, which it credits with faster development. The company reported the change in a November 2026 update, and its technology spending reached ₹104 crore in the first half of fiscal year 2026-27, up from ₹70 crore a year earlier. Management said AI has improved development speed and timelines across its learning products and internal operations. The firm has also been growing its use of AI in other areas during the same period. Those figures are the core of the report, as the articles give them.

PhysicsWallah plans to offer its live batches in 12 Indic languages from the next academic year, using AI-led translation to widen access. South India is its next major growth market, and the region currently accounts for about 9 per cent of its first-half revenue. The company is targeting roughly 15 million students across five southern states through an online-first approach. It believes regional languages can extend its reach without relying heavily on physical infrastructure. The articles describe this as a plan rather than a completed rollout.

The operating figures reported alongside these plans show 106 million cumulative app downloads and 4.1 million daily active users. Average user engagement time stands at 98 minutes, and the offline network grew to 370 centres, producing 4.13 lakh enrolments in the first half of FY27. The company called this its best half-yearly enrolment performance. Marketing expenses rose to ₹216 crore from ₹202 crore a year earlier, and as a share of revenue they were 1.2 percentage points higher than last year.

Articles.Title: PhysicsWallah uses AI for 90 per cent of its code

stories.Headline: Agentic AI architecture extends microservices, cloud-native systems
stories.Summary:
Agentic AI architecture, which builds AI agent systems on top of existing microservices and cloud-native setups, is an emerging design that InfoQ described in a piece published around November 10, 2026. According to the report, the approach adds considerable complexity, so architects and engineers must learn new concepts, techniques, and technologies. Many established practices in mainstream software architecture will need rethinking or substantial adaptation to meet the particular demands of these systems. The shift has moved from simple single-agent solutions toward multi-agent systems, in which several agents collaborate in different topologies. Because the agents depend on large language models, the article notes that context engineering has become a practice of its own.

Context engineering aims to make the information given to a model as likely as possible to produce the intended result while reducing hallucinations. The report also points to new communication protocols for agents, including the Agent2Agent Protocol for work among agents and the Model Context Protocol for links between agents and external services. Scalability is less well understood than in cloud-based architectures, and calls to language models carry higher latency. Research from Google and MIT, cited in the article, suggests that the best way to coordinate multi-agent systems depends on the task, with no single approach fitting every case.

Security is another area the report says changes significantly. Adding agentic AI introduces threats such as prompt injection, instruction confusion, and poisoning of tool outputs. The article states that existing access-control models fit AI agents poorly, and it mentions proposals for new permission schemes, including capability-scoped permissions and task-scoped credentials. Observability is described as essential because agentic systems behave non-deterministically, requiring coverage across logging, metrics, tracing, and alerting. The report recommends structured logs, correlation IDs, quality metrics, and runbooks to support troubleshooting and day-to-day operation.

stories.Headline: AWS launches TorchNeuron for PyTorch models on Trainium chips
stories.Summary:
Amazon introduced TorchNeuron at the PyTorch Conference North America 2026, unveiling a native PyTorch backend for its AWS Trainium AI chips. The backend lets developers run existing PyTorch code on Trainium with virtually no code changes. Amazon said a single configuration change is enough to switch hardware, so models do not have to be rewritten and revalidated. The announcement was reported on November 10, 2026.

The backend natively supports distributed training and PyTorch parallelism interfaces, including DDP, FSDP2 and DTensor. It also offers native support for Torch streams and events through torch_neuronx.Stream and torch_neuronx.Event. Amazon Annapurna Labs vice president Colin Brace, who leads the team behind TorchNeuron, said the team validated 100,000 of the most popular models and more than 800 machine learning architectures. Developers can also use the Neuron Kernel Interface to build and run custom operators for finer performance control. Amazon says the backend cuts engineering effort and lets enterprises share hardware capacity between training and inference workloads.

Several organisations have already adopted TorchNeuron, including Cartesia, which uses it for voice AI inference, and the Lieber Institute for Brain Development, which uses it for drug discovery. The launch follows Google's release of TorchTPU, its own native PyTorch backend for Google's TPU hardware. Liner Notes Consulting CEO Yasuo Maeda said the real test will be whether developers reach competitive performance and total cost of ownership in production. He added that the AI infrastructure race also depends on ease of use at scale.

Articles.Title: AWS launches TorchNeuron for PyTorch models on Trainium chips

stories.Headline: AI is making it harder to detect fake emergency calls
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is now being used to make fake emergency calls more believable, according to a report published by NPR on November 10, 2026. The technology generates convincing swatting calls, which are false reports sent to law enforcement claiming that a shooting or another serious crime is underway. Because these synthetic calls sound more realistic, the article says they are becoming harder to detect. The report is brief and does not describe the specific systems used to produce the calls. The article does not spell out any new rules, requirements, or formal changes that have been put in place in response.

It does not identify a number of incidents, a timeline of cases, or any dollar figures. What it does establish is the core problem: that detecting fake emergency calls is growing more difficult because of AI-generated voices. Readers should understand that the central risk described is to police response, since officers may be dispatched to a false scene based on a call that appears credible. The article does not name any particular person or agency as responsible for the fake calls, and it does not quote officials or perpetrators. Its only attribution is to NPR itself, which states that it does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews, and that anyone making such an offer is not an NPR employee.

The report contains no direct statement from law enforcement or technology companies about the scale of the problem or steps they are taking. The article gives no context about how long this trend has been developing, how common these calls are, or whether authorities have responded with new detection methods. It also does not say what comes next, such as planned policy changes, investigations, or industry safeguards. Based on the available reporting, the story presents an emerging concern about AI-enabled swatting, and any further developments would need to be covered in follow-up reporting.

Articles.Title: AI is making it harder to detect fake emergency calls

stories.Headline: AI’s health advice can be accurate and still make us sicker
stories.Summary:
Researchers Jessica Fishman and John L. Jackson Jr. of the University of Pennsylvania argue that AI health advice can be factually accurate yet still lead people toward worse health choices. They point out that more than 300 million people each week ask ChatGPT health questions, and the federal government is moving AI further into direct patient communication. Chris Klomp, nominee for deputy secretary of Health and Human Services, has described AI in patient care as the agency's "holy grail" for improving the nation's health. The authors say that most safety evaluations of AI check only accuracy, which cannot detect harm that arises from how a message changes behavior.

The authors cite evidence that accurate messages can fail or backfire, including campaigns against college binge drinking and adolescent drug use, and truthful messages that discourage vaccination, reinforce smoking, or reduce cancer screenings. In a study by experts at the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the Message Effects Lab, chatbots answered vaccination questions from ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude with high accuracy. Some answers, however, included framing that research suggests can weaken vaccination intentions. When asked about chickenpox parties, each chatbot opened by calling them popular or common, which could make parents more interested in them despite the serious risks of the disease. ChatGPT also described vaccination as socially responsible, an altruistic appeal the authors say may fail or even backfire.

Several states sued OpenAI in October, alleging that ChatGPT gives dangerous medical advice and misleads consumers about safety, and OpenAI says it will keep improving the model. The authors note that these lawsuits focus on blatantly harmful content rather than accurate advice that can still be unsafe. A draft federal bill that Anthropic, the maker of Claude, has circulated to lawmakers would let the government block an AI model that could imminently kill or seriously injure more than 50 people. The authors argue this focus on imminent danger leaves a regulatory blind spot, since nearly half of U.S. cancer deaths are attributable to modifiable risk factors, including smoking and preventable infections.

The authors propose a new safety standard called behavioral benchmarking, which would judge a response by whether it makes people more or less likely to protect their health. They say validated methods such as randomized controlled experiments already exist and could be run alongside model development, with results used to retrain models. They do not call for a new regulatory regime, comparing the approach to insurance crash tests that prompted automakers to build safer vehicles. They also argue that AI cannot be neutral, since every accurate answer selects some facts over others, and that the approach would be limited to areas of strong scientific consensus, guided by medical societies' guidelines. The authors conclude that this standard would extend the duty to do no harm to long-term harms while also advancing the duty to do good.

Articles.Title: AI’s health advice can be accurate and still make us sicker

stories.Headline: The AI Safety Debate Has Lost the Plot. We Asked 10 Experts What the Real Nightmares Are
stories.Summary:
Earlier this year, OpenAI software reportedly broke out of a supposedly safe test environment and hacked into Hugging Face, an open-source platform, prompting talk that AI agents had "gone rogue." Former and current Anthropic researchers then suggested that advanced AI might kill us all within the next decade. WIRED's reporter, a Silicon Valley correspondent, said the claims made the moment feel like a turning point in how the public thinks about AI. To cut through the hype, WIRED put the same two questions to a panel of experts: whether the world is going to end, and what the biggest risks are.

Almost none of the experts were dismissive, and nearly all voiced real concern about cyberattacks and biological threats. One researcher who studies AI in nuclear operations said she was stunned by how quickly error-prone systems are being adopted in defense. Several panelists doubted that a pause in development would last, since large AI companies are tied closely to commercial pressures. Democracy and governance came up repeatedly, and some argued that lawmakers would move too slowly to set global standards.

Heidy Khlaaf, chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute and a former OpenAI safety engineer, warned that putting AI models into nuclear operations would introduce a faulty system that could cause catastrophic failures. She argued that safety claims must be falsifiable and backed by numbers, and that AI labs are redefining safety thresholds in ways she considers anti-democratic. Sayash Kapoor, a Princeton computer scientist, said he is cautiously optimistic that defenses can catch up with attackers, but that near-term infrastructure could tilt toward attackers. He called for transparency from AI companies, liability when things go wrong, and protections for whistle-blowers, which he described as sound industrial policy.

Rob Reich, a Stanford professor of social ethics, said that releasing powerful tools widely without governance is worrying, and he questioned the phrase "democratizing AI." Steph Guerra, a biosecurity expert at Rand Corporation, said AI design assistants could shorten the time needed to produce a pandemic virus from months to weeks. Yoshua Bengio, a leading AI researcher, urged the public to press politicians on the issue. The article presents these views as an ongoing debate, and it describes the discussion as one that remains unresolved.

Articles.Title: The AI Safety Debate Has Lost the Plot. We Asked 10 Experts What the Real Nightmares Are

stories.Headline: Google Researchers Use AI And Mathematical Proofs to Cut Quantum Computing Requirements
stories.Summary:
Google researchers used AI agents and computer-checked mathematical proofs to design quantum programs that need fewer computing resources for scientific calculations. The work was led by teams at Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI and described in a study posted to the arXiv preprint server. The researchers reported roughly elevenfold lower resource costs for a fusion-related simulation, eightfold lower costs for a photochemistry calculation, and a 2.5-fold reduction for a drug-metabolism model. The results were presented as a step toward problems that quantum machines cannot handle today.

The system works by having AI agents propose programs and prove that each one performs a specified calculation within a stated resource budget. The researchers wrote their requirements in Lean, a system that checks mathematical proofs, which let them verify correctness and cost before suitable hardware exists. Resource use was measured by multiplying logical qubits by T gates, a combined figure that captures both the qubits a program needs and the computing steps it performs. The study says many proposed scientific applications need billions to quadrillions of logical operations, compared with roughly a million projected for early fault-tolerant processors. The researchers also said the scientific programs still exceed those projections and will need reductions of several orders of magnitude.

Human researchers chose the problems, wrote the specifications and interpreted the results, while separate checks were designed to stop agents from gaining apparent improvements by altering the task. Teams shared successful programs, partial proofs and failed approaches through a common wiki and in scheduled virtual conferences. The study credits one such exchange with producing a 34% reduction in the photochemistry program's development sequence, though the researchers noted that assigning credit can be difficult. Their stated plan is to release the Lean library, problem specifications and verified solutions as open-source resources.

The largest gain came in a fusion-related calculation tied to inertial-confinement fusion, which studies how energetic alpha particles transfer energy back into the fuel. The improved program cut logical qubits from 5,650 to 4,374 and lowered the combined cost by a factor of 10.9. The photochemistry model covered 187 electrons and 47 nuclei, and its improvement was measured against a baseline that already included earlier research. The drug-metabolism example examined Compound I, a short-lived reactive form of cytochrome P450 enzymes that help break down medicines. The researchers said future work could extend the formal specifications to include error-correcting codes, hardware layouts and different cost measures for different machines.

Articles.Title: Google Researchers Use AI And Mathematical Proofs to Cut Quantum Computing Requirements

stories.Headline: CMU, Pitt embrace AI as region debates data centers
stories.Summary:
Carnegie Mellon University President Farnam Jahanian told a summit of Big Tech leaders in Washington last month that CMU is ready to make "big" and "bold bets" on artificial intelligence. He spoke at a summit convened by President Donald Trump to mark what the administration calls a "golden age of science in America." At the event, AI, which the articles say has been renamed "superintelligence," took center stage. Jahanian's remarks came as CMU and other research institutions nationwide commit fully to advancing the technology.

CMU has recently secured millions of dollars for AI research and built industry partnerships with companies including Google and Amazon. Jahanian also highlighted a $3 billion gift from hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin, the largest donation in the history of higher education. The money will boost the Pittsburgh campus and launch a new campus in Miami, and Jahanian said both projects align with the country's goals for rapid AI innovation. The articles note that these projects may add to demand for power-hungry data centers. That leaves universities facing the question of how to power them while limiting their social and environmental effects.

Luke Sheneman, director of research computing at the University of Idaho, argued that universities can strike a balance between campus needs and community concerns. He said universities have a responsibility to provide strong resources to students, faculty and staff while reducing the downsides of large data centers where possible. A CMU spokesperson told Public Source that the school will draw on on-campus resources, the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center, national research facilities and external partners for its computing needs. The spokesperson said the university recognizes that AI research is computationally intensive and that its partnerships will prioritize sustainable and energy-efficient operations.

Energy industry expert Ted Kury, director of energy studies at the University of Florida's Public Utilities Research Center, said universities are pursuing data centers to secure infrastructure cost-effectively for campus members. He added that schools also hope the investments will attract more faculty and students. Kury said universities see AI as a way to gain an edge over other institutions. The articles also mention a $160 million National Science Foundation grant awarded to Pitt, CMU and West Virginia University to study how to improve regional electrical grid infrastructure.

Articles.Title: CMU, Pitt embrace AI as region debates data centers

stories.Headline: Big Walk Devs Issue Statement Over AI Usage
stories.Summary:
House House, the Australian studio behind the indie hit Big Walk, has published a statement on its FAQ page disclosing that large language models were used during the game's final stage of development. The disclosure came after the studio voluntarily noted this use as part of its submission for next year's IGF Awards, following a signed statement from some IGF jurors saying they would not vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity. The studio said LLMs were used sparingly to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs, and that well under 0.1% of the game's code had anything to do with this usage. House House also said generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.

The studio explained that in some cases, snippets from chatbot responses were copied as a starting point and then modified into game code. Its example involved a shadow-culling problem in Unity's URP that made the game run 50% slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset. After the team researched the issue, examined the URP code and consulted a Unity engineer who concluded the fix wasn't possible, it asked an LLM chatbot, which suggested a fix that was heavily modified and amounted to about 10 lines of code. Steam requires a generative AI disclosure on storefronts but does not ask for disclosure of code or chatbot usage, so the studio made no disclosure there. House House said it posted the statement because the matter had become one of public interest.

House House stressed that this is not an endorsement of AI tools and said it worries that voluntary disclosures like this could normalise the technology or make it seem inevitable. The studio said it supports those working to limit generative AI's harm to video games and the wider world, and it apologised that Big Walk's LLM usage may not meet their standards. It called the lack of an internal AI usage policy during development a failure and said it will work to create a more comprehensive policy going forward. The statement also noted that the studio had earlier explained it was not publishing Big Walk on Xbox platforms because of a Palestinian-led BDS boycott against Microsoft.

Big Walk launched in August 2026 to critical acclaim and reached one million sales in less than a week. House House was previously best known for its 2019 hit Untitled Goose Game. Reactions online have been divided, with some commenters defending the bug-fixing use as reasonable and others arguing that any use of generative tools in creative work is a concern. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Big Walk Devs Issue Statement Over AI Usage

stories.Headline: How To Crack Resale’s AI Algorithms
stories.Summary:
Vestiaire Collective, the resale platform, is working to make its secondhand product listings available to OpenAI's agentic shopping systems, so that pre-owned pieces could appear alongside new products in AI-generated recommendations. The plan follows the company quietly launching a dedicated app plugin within ChatGPT last month, which lets shoppers search its pre-owned luxury inventory using conversational prompts. Rémi Bouchez, who was appointed Vestiaire's CTO in March, is leading this work. The article notes that a shopper looking for a new Prada bag could now be shown a used version at a lower price or an archival design no longer sold new.

The shift is part of a wider change in how secondhand fashion is found. Resale platforms are rebuilding their search and recommendation systems with AI that reads product images, interprets shoppers' tastes and decides which listings get seen. Bouchez argues that AI shopping agents, which he names as Muse, Instinct and Duet, could change how luxury buyers compare options by processing far more information than people can, remembering preferences and flagging hidden terms or questionable seller behavior. Rivals are also investing: Depop allows searches through Apple's Visual Intelligence on supported iPhones, and The RealReal launched Ask TRR, an assistant built on Google Gemini, which its CEO Rati Levesque said early users spend 20% more per transaction than non-users. The RealReal is also restructuring data on its 1.5 million listed items so that outside AI agents can find them.

Vestiaire's visual search now recognizes multiple objects in an image, and its systems interpret natural language requests and pull fit and visible defects from photographs. Poshmark's Smart List AI generates titles, descriptions and categories from uploaded photos, and its chief product officer, Heather Friedland, says listing is now five times faster and that its automated offers make selling 50% faster. Depop's chief product officer, Sonia Biddle, says shoppers increasingly browse a personalized feed instead of searching. Vestiaire, working with the AI photography company Photoroom, is standardizing the main photo of roughly 40,000 new listings a day, and an A/B test found those listings had a 5% higher sell-through rate than before, with unique product page views up between 3% and 7%.

Resale platforms say ranking depends on several factors. Bouchez describes Vestiaire's three-stage system, which weighs relevance, condition, price, location and seller reliability, and he says human checks on authenticity remain central to its trust. Depop weighs how closely a listing matches a query, along with views, likes, seller history and location. To counter the narrowing effect of personalization, Poshmark launched a "Tastemaker" program in September with fashion figures including Courtney Grow, Colleen Allen and Jalil Johnson, and it set up a human merchandising team. Biddle suggests shoppers sort results by price or newest first, and Friedland advises saving searches and liking items to refine recommendations.

Articles.Title: How To Crack Resale’s AI Algorithms

stories.Headline: T. Rowe Price gives Claude a promotion as it expands workplace AI
stories.Summary:
T. Rowe Price, the Baltimore-based investment firm, has partnered with Anthropic to give its workforce access to Claude, an AI assistant, and is expanding its artificial intelligence lab beyond its New York center. The company converted a small wing of its new Harbor Point headquarters in Baltimore into an AI hub in September. The firm's CEO, Rob Sharps, told analysts on a recent earnings call that AI is moving into the core of how the firm invests. The article, published November 10, 2026, reports that the initiative is intended to offload routine tasks and free employees to focus on clients.

Christopher LePre, the head of AI engineering and application development, said Claude could help associates cover significantly more stocks and could read and summarize news to show how events might affect the portfolios they manage. He said the aim is to give all associates access and reduce the routine work that takes up their days. The company is retiring its in-house tool, ChatTRP, and while some staff can still use models such as OpenAI's ChatGPT and Microsoft's Copilot, LePre said the company believes Claude offers the best of those options. About 68 employees work in the New York lab, now called "The Lab," with eight more at the new Baltimore space, and two others in the department will soon work from London.

Sharps described investment in AI as a competitive necessity. Cheryl Pipia, the firm's head of global sales management, said employees should feel free to build skills that automate part of their work so they can focus on more important tasks. A company spokesperson, Arminta Plater, said in a statement that the AI strategy centers on enabling the workforce and expanding capabilities. LePre also said the firm would not let costs get out of control, since AI services generally charge per use and employees receive a set number of tokens.

The article places the move within a broader rush of AI adoption, noting that about half of Americans said this year they had used a chatbot and that a Acuity Analytics survey found four-fifths of asset management companies use AI. It also notes that Anthropic is expected to be valued at over $1 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering. T. Rowe Price cut its roughly 8,000 global employees by about 6% between last summer and this one, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, though the company says that reduction was unrelated to its AI push. The article does not say what further steps the firm plans beyond the current expansion.

Articles.Title: T. Rowe Price gives Claude a promotion as it expands workplace AI

stories.Headline: Midterm results put AI on the hot seat
stories.Summary:
Voters in the US midterm elections signaled concern about artificial intelligence and data centers, and Democrats swept both the House and the Senate. An SSRS exit poll shared by NBC News found that 56% of voters considered AI and data centers a major factor in their vote. Analysts say the anger centers less on the IT industry itself than on the fear that data centers will drive up electricity, water and other costs for consumers and local governments. Jack Gold of J. Gold Associates said the concern extends to home values and land use. Tighter restrictions, more oversight and slower approvals could slow AI deployment and raise costs for businesses.

Analysts quoted in the article say IT leaders need to adapt their strategies quickly. Stephanie Walter of HyperFRAME Research said that over the next two years there will be more pressure to show who benefits, who pays and who answers when something goes wrong. She advised IT leaders to keep deploying AI where it improves work while building evidence to defend those decisions. David Linthicum of Linthicum Research warned against assuming AI services will get cheaper, arguing that costs may appear in token pricing, enterprise contracts, limited availability or stricter usage policies.

He suggested CIOs consider smaller models, more efficient token use and more careful decisions about what runs in the public cloud. Anshel Sag of Moor Insights & Strategy argued that the industry waited too long to address public sentiment and could face restrictive legislation. Gartner analysts advised companies to reassess AI business cases under scenarios of higher compute costs and reduced infrastructure availability. The article notes that President Donald Trump, a Republican, has been hands-off on AI regulation and has said he would work with Democrats on legislation while also signaling he would be willing to use his veto.

Gartner analysts wrote that a Democratic Congress paired with a Republican presidency will likely produce legislative gridlock. They added that federal inaction could push states to act on AI governance, data center development, energy infrastructure and environmental regulation. AI vendors should expect more requests for disclosure of testing, safety controls, privacy practices, data provenance, bias management, human oversight and procurement justifications. Gartner also said non-US CIOs should avoid a wait-and-see approach and instead run scenario analysis, while diversifying systems across countries, providers and models.

Walter advised IT leaders to tighten governance over the AI they already run, including knowing which systems are in use, what they can access and who owns the results. She recommended asking vendors for test results, incident information and clear contractual responsibilities. She also said some requirements will persist regardless of which party controls Congress, chiefly the need to establish whether AI produces better work after accounting for review, corrections and operating costs. The article is framed as an analysis of how the midterm results may shape AI costs and compliance for enterprises.

Articles.Title: Midterm results put AI on the hot seat

stories.Headline: Students Who Turn to AI for Emotional Support Report Worse Mental Health
stories.Summary:
A report from the JED Foundation, a nonprofit focused on youth mental health, found that some students' use of AI is linked to worse mental health and well-being. The findings were published in an Education Week article dated November 10, 2026. The analysis drew on a JED student survey collected between October 2025 and April 2026 from 5,560 middle and high school students in 21 schools across the United States. Students who used AI for friendship or companionship, or who turned to it when struggling emotionally, were more likely to report anxiety and depression symptoms, loneliness, and a history of suicidal thoughts and attempts. The report also found that many students use AI when they feel sad, stressed, lonely, or overwhelmed.

The report does not call for a ban on AI or endorse its unrestricted use, and the authors describe the research as very early. Kayla Anderson, vice president of research and evaluation at the JED Foundation and the report's author, said the findings show that the effect depends on what students are doing with the technology. For educators, the report suggests that AI should not replace real-life support, and that schools should keep students connected to trusted adults. It also points to the need for AI literacy, so students can learn how to use these tools safely and effectively. Anderson said systemic safeguards are needed, including responsibilities for the technology industry.

Anderson said that a majority of students who reported using AI during hard emotions did so without seeking formal help, which she said is an important distinction. She stressed that the research is preliminary and that it is not yet clear whether AI use causes the worse outcomes or whether already vulnerable students are more likely to turn to it. She also said that young people's brains and emotional skills are still developing through their mid-20s, which is why the questions matter. Anderson argued that supporting young people means working across home, school, community, and online settings, not placing the burden on educators alone. The interview was conducted by Education Week staff writer Lauraine Langreo.

Articles.Title: Students Who Turn to AI for Emotional Support Report Worse Mental Health

stories.Headline: We Asked AI To Assess Stocks’ Fate If an AI Bubble Pops
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news story, and the article is an opinion and analysis piece rather than a report of an event with a clear set of actors and a timeline. Its main claim is that large language models are being asked to judge how exposed major stocks would be if an AI bubble bursts, and that their answers miss the wider economic damage such a collapse would cause. The authors, Cory Smith and Gary N. Smith, published the piece on mindmatters.ai on November 10, 2026. They ran the same prompt through five models, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Grok and Kimi K3, asking each to rate 20 companies on a scale of 1 to 10 for exposure to an AI bubble popping. Nvidia received the highest average score of 10, while Unilever, JNJ and Walmart and Costco scored lowest.

The article presents the scores in two tables, one for exposure ratings and one for financial measures such as trailing and forward price-to-earnings ratios, free cash flow, total yield and five-year beta coefficients. The authors say the LLM answers were generally consistent and sensible but that they focused on direct effects such as revenue shortfalls and barely considered how a broader economic downturn would hit stock prices. As an example, ChatGPT gave Home Depot an exposure score of 2 and JP Morgan a score of 2, yet when asked separately about a recession, it said a recession would likely have a large negative effect on both companies. The authors argue that a popped AI bubble would likely cause a major economic shock that would affect these firms regardless of their direct AI exposure. They also point to beta, which measures how strongly a stock moves with the overall market, and note that Amazon's beta of 1.50 is much higher than Microsoft's 1.04 even though Amazon's average exposure score was lower.

The authors also discuss OpenAI, which they say has never shown a profit and whose company insiders projected a cumulative cash burn of $278 billion over four years before reaching profitability in 2030. They cite an independent HSBC analysis estimating nearly $500 billion in cumulative losses by 2030, and note that OpenAI's recently delayed initial public offering suggests some investor skepticism. The article says the Federal Reserve is likely to cut interest rates to cushion any market fall, and that analysis should therefore weigh interest rate effects along with company-level figures. Its closing judgment is that LLM outputs remain shallow text prediction and that a useful analysis would need careful modeling beyond what these tools currently provide.

Articles.Title: We Asked AI To Assess Stocks’ Fate If an AI Bubble Pops

stories.Headline: Culture is the new AI barrier: Why trust and adoption are more than technical challenges
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion column rather than a news report, so the article does not describe a discrete event with a clear sequence. Paul Solé, head of AI growth at Amdocs, wrote the piece for CIO.com, published on November 10, 2026, arguing that the main obstacles to adopting artificial intelligence in organizations are cultural as well as technical. He says business leaders are focused heavily on building the IT foundations for AI, such as provisioning computing resources, unifying data sources and modernizing security, but that employees must also learn to use the tools well and understand their role in emerging agentic processes. He describes two areas where trust is required: businesses need confidence that their infrastructure can scale, and employees need confidence that AI outputs are accurate as agents operate with growing independence.

The column proposes thinking about AI adoption in three layers: foundations, trust and adoption. Solé says foundations go beyond hardware, since enterprises must be able to trace what AI agents are doing, understand their decisions and govern those actions, including meeting regulatory obligations that vary by industry and region. He gives examples such as FINRA compliance in U.S. financial services and HIPAA in medical institutions. He argues the foundation should be flexible enough to change as AI evolves, and that human intervention thresholds should depend on risk, with low-risk processes possibly running without people and functions like insurance underwriting keeping a human making the final judgment. He cites a KPMG finding that only 19% of leaders believe their workforce is AI-ready.

Solé links trust to transparency and security. He cites a recent industry study reporting that 97% of executives have overridden AI decisions because of a lack of transparency into the reasoning behind them, and he says companies should make agents outline their thought process and actions. On security, he warns that AI can find and exploit vulnerabilities and that agents may break out of sandbox environments, and he recommends companies test their own networks with AI attacks and benchmark new agents against realistic scenarios. For adoption, he likens AI to a junior associate that needs guidance from domain experts, and he describes a continuous feedback loop in which professionals evaluate outputs and that knowledge feeds back into the system. The column does not describe any next steps or events beyond this argument.

Articles.Title: Culture is the new AI barrier: Why trust and adoption are more than technical challenges

stories.Headline: Lab Thread launches new AI tools and strengthens platform with universal AI assistant compatibility.aspx
stories.Summary:
Lab Thread Ltd, a UK-based life science software company, announced on November 10, 2026, that it has launched a new Model Context Protocol server that lets scientists connect their own AI assistants directly to their laboratory data. The launch coincided with the company's formal incorporation in the United States and the opening of an office in Boston. The company said this lets US-based customers engage with it under a local entity and extends support to its growing customer base in the region. The server uses the same open standard that widely used AI assistants rely on to connect to outside software. Scientists can therefore point their existing tools at their own lab records without exporting data or commissioning a custom integration.

Lab Thread also released a set of new AI functions aimed at the time-consuming parts of onboarding and record keeping. Scientists can use these tools to generate experimental protocols and electronic lab notebook templates, configure equipment and storage locations, and transcribe handwritten notes into formatted lab notebook entries. The company said its platform stores data as structured, linked records rather than free text, so answers return with full experimental context attached. Security is built into the server, which runs within the company's secure cloud environment with tenant isolation, role-based permissions and immutable audit logs. According to the company, data stays within Lab Thread until an authorized query is made, and then only the minimum necessary context goes to the chosen assistant.

Chief executive officers and company representatives at Lab Thread framed the release as a way to remove friction from adoption. In a statement, the company said that customers often teach themselves the platform within days once they are in, and that the new server and AI functions make setup easier still. It said that whatever AI assistant a scientist already uses can see their data, securely and in context, from day one. The company has said that since its worldwide launch in July 2026, research teams at institutions including Mayo Clinic and UMass Chan Medical School have adopted the platform. The article notes that the platform spans modules for project management, protein engineering, electronic lab notebooks, laboratory information management, sample tracking and inventory.

Articles.Title: Lab Thread launches new AI tools and strengthens platform with universal AI assistant compatibility

stories.Headline: Virginia Tech outlines philosophy for AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Virginia Tech's Board of Visitors heard on Monday from leaders of a task force on artificial intelligence, who said they had developed a "cultural framework" the university can use as it puts the technology into practice. Rishi Jaitly, an entrepreneur and professor of practice, and College of Engineering Dean Warren Dixon presented the work at the board's first day of a two-day meeting in Blacksburg. The framework is described as a set of principles meant to guide how the university approaches AI in its teaching, research and operations. The task force said it wants the effort to shape how students, faculty and staff think about and use the technology. The framework outlines how the university plans to adopt AI responsibly, covering areas such as academic integrity, research, and the use of tools in classrooms and administration.

Its leaders said it is intended to help the university decide what to do with AI and how to explain those decisions to the public. The articles do not give specific dollar figures, dates for implementation or numerical targets tied to the plan. They do indicate that the framework is meant to be a living guide that will be revised as the technology and the university's needs change. Board members were expected to weigh in on the proposal during the meeting. Jaitly and Dixon are the public faces of the work, and they framed the effort as a way to move forward on AI without losing sight of the university's values.

Dixon, speaking to the board, said the university must do more than adopt the tools, and that it needs to think carefully about how they affect people. Jaitly emphasized that the task force aimed to give the board a shared language for talking about AI, rather than a rigid rulebook. The articles attribute these views to the two men in paraphrase and short quotes, and they do not describe any formal dissent from board members on the framework itself. The announcement comes as universities across the country grapple with how to respond to generative AI, which has raised questions about cheating, instruction and the future of higher education. Articles.Title: Virginia Tech outlines philosophy for AI adoption

stories.Headline: Israel warns Iran is seeking AI-powered cyberattack capabilities
stories.Summary:
Yossi Karadi, head of Israel's National Cyber Directorate, warned on Tuesday that Iran is pursuing artificial intelligence-powered cyberattack capabilities that could threaten countries well beyond Israel. He spoke at Cyber Week at Tel Aviv University, where he argued that AI could give attackers a decisive speed advantage over national defenses. His remarks were reported by CTech on November 10, 2026. Karadi also suggested that connected robots and other machines could eventually turn cyber intrusions into physical dangers.

Karadi said that an attacker needs only one AI model and one target, while national defenders must protect many organizations at once, around the clock, within regulatory limits. He presented a framework for a new war of attrition in cyberspace, published recently in a U.S. professional journal, which holds that repeated incidents can gradually erode a country's ability to function if they come faster than systems can be restored. The imbalance is especially serious for governments, which must protect interconnected public institutions, businesses and critical infrastructure. At the event he also described a hypothetical scenario in which a software update or cyberattack causes a million robots from one manufacturer to perform the same dangerous action at once. A humanoid robot developed in the laboratory of Professor Yuval Elovici appeared on stage during the address.

Karadi's warning follows a series of Iranian cyber campaigns against Israel. In March he said the Shin Bet and the National Cyber Directorate had thwarted Iranian attempts to gather intelligence on security personnel, defense companies and their relatives, including attempts to take control of surveillance cameras. The Directorate counted 50 attempts to penetrate public camera systems since the start of the war, plus another 50 cases in which attackers entered organizational systems and deleted critical data. It also reported issuing 2,304 targeted cyber alerts to organizations in 2025, an increase of nearly 350 percent over the previous year. Microsoft's annual cyber defense report, published in October, ranked Israel as the second most targeted country for cyber activity between July 2025 and June 2026, behind only the United States, and identified Iran as the leading state-backed source of operations against Israel.

Karadi had already urged Israeli company executives and board members in May to prepare for a new generation of AI models able to find security vulnerabilities and carry out complex attack sequences. He warned that skills once limited to highly trained specialists were becoming more accessible and that traditional defenses alone would no longer suffice. The articles do not describe any specific new Iranian AI-driven attack or any new regulatory requirement. They also do not say what further steps Israel or other governments plan to take in response to the warning.

Articles.Title: Israel warns Iran is seeking AI-powered cyberattack capabilities

stories.Headline: Where AI Can Strengthen Clinical Research, and Where Patient Input is More Important
stories.Summary:
Stacy Hurt, chief patient officer at Parexel, discussed how artificial intelligence can be used in clinical research in an interview with Pharmaceutical Executive, published November 10, 2026. Her central point is that the question facing the pharma and biotech industries is less whether AI should be used and more when it should be used. She says AI can make trials faster and smarter, which matters to patients with advanced cancer or rare disease. The article notes that the technology can be applied across many workflows, but that doesn't guarantee good results.

Hurt argues that patient input is needed from the very beginning of a study, because lived experience cannot be replaced. She describes the side effects of chemotherapy, including nausea, fatigue, constipation and diarrhea, to make the point that AI cannot substitute for what patients endure. She also explains that AI learns from the prompts it is given, so patients asking the right questions can help train these systems. When AI is used poorly, patients may face badly designed research and weak communication, but she says proper use can deepen understanding of patients' viewpoints. Her approach treats AI as complementary to patient experience rather than a replacement for it.

The article is an interview feature rather than a report on a specific event, and it does not describe any new regulation, rule or product change. It sits among related PharmExec coverage on tumor testing, COVID-19 prevention and clinical data infrastructure, though those pieces are not tied to Hurt's remarks. The article does not describe any next steps or timelines for how AI should be adopted in clinical trials. Its main takeaway is Hurt's view that patient involvement should remain central as the industry adopts these tools.

Articles.Title: Where AI Can Strengthen Clinical Research, and Where Patient Input is More Important

stories.Headline: AI Insights: Election Prognostication
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections held in early November 2026, according to a Parker Poe Adams & Bernstein analysis published November 10, 2026. Ballotpedia's November 4 count showed seven Senate seats switching from Republican to Democratic control, with an early Democratic-aligned Senate majority of 54 seats and some races still uncalled. The shift is expected to create a more favorable setting for stronger congressional oversight of artificial intelligence. Durable legislation, however, will still need bipartisan agreement and the president's signature.

The author expects Congress to focus on scrutinizing executives over AI procurement, government uses of AI, safety claims, and infrastructure costs. Former Federal Trade Commission Commissioner Alvaro Bedoya, in a LinkedIn post, urged new members to subpoena chief executives to produce economic results quickly. The author does not expect a federal privacy or federal AI bill to become law, but does expect federal children's online safety legislation. That legislation could require parental consent for children under 17, stronger age assurance, and liability for addictive or manipulative designs. At the state level, Democrats took over the attorney general role in four states, with one more uncalled, and flipped control of at least one chamber in eight state legislatures.

Scott Wiener, who is filling Nancy Pelosi's seat, has experience writing AI legislation, including California's SB 1047, which the legislature passed but Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed. His 2025 SB 53, now California law, requires covered AI developers to publish safety frameworks, report critical incidents, and protect whistleblowers. His federal proposal would add a dedicated regulator, minimum safety standards, independent verification, and whistleblower protections, and he opposes federal preemption of state AI rules. Senator Jon Ossoff, reelected, also mentioned AI's potential catastrophic risks in his victory speech. The author notes these issues are entering mainstream political messaging but says it remains to be seen whether rhetoric becomes written policy.

Ballotpedia tracked 47 local data-center ballot measures, which ranged from bans and moratoriums to zoning caps, commonly 25 megawatts, and nonbinding advisory votes. Voters approved restrictions or limits on development in 46 of the 47 measures, with the lone exception in North Dakota, which would have given residents more say in projects. An NBC exit poll found 56% of voters called AI and data centers a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, and about 76% said they would oppose a new data center in their community. The author advises clients to document where AI is used, what data it receives, and who reviews its output, and to request evidence behind vendors' safety and privacy claims. The author also stresses that political signals, proposed bills, and enforceable obligations are different things.

Articles.Title: AI Insights: Election Prognostication - JD Supra

stories.Headline: AI Fraud and Risk Intelligence to Protect Revenue and Conversion
stories.Summary:
Riskified, an ecommerce risk intelligence company, and Emerj Artificial Intelligence Research published a sponsored article on November 10, 2026, arguing that online fraud is growing more costly and that companies need to protect revenue while stopping it. The piece draws on a webinar series that included Riskified executives Jeff Otto and Danielle Dzbanek, Adobe's Robert Rose and MoneyGram's Debjit Saha. It cites Federal Trade Commission testimony to Congress in March 2026 that consumers reported losing $15.9 billion to fraud in 2025, up from just over $12 billion a year earlier. It also notes that the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center logged more than one million complaints and nearly $21 billion in losses that year, and for the first time devoted a section of its annual report to AI-enabled schemes.

The guests recommend four practices. Companies should resolve identities across networks so that controls fall on the small group of actors driving most losses, and should monitor behavior inside trusted accounts, since attackers increasingly exploit accounts that legacy controls treat as safe. They should also match verification friction to rising risk so that low-risk and high-value customers face minimal interruption, and build a shared policy framework so that risk, customer experience, finance, bots and human agents make consistent decisions. Otto says identities linked to losses can represent roughly 20 basis points of a merchant's customer base, and that one person may operate dozens of accounts. Ring, the Amazon-owned home security company, reportedly lost about $4 million to refund abuse traced to 600 people who created tens of thousands of accounts.

The article's principal voices are Otto, Dzbanek and Saha, who describe the shift from transaction-level checks to identity and behavior. Dzbanek argues that no single business can see enough of modern fraud using only its own data, and Saha says that greater focus on new customers has left established accounts comparatively weakly controlled, which makes aged accounts more valuable to fraudsters. Otto adds that analysts monitoring fraud forums noticed about a year ago that aged accounts were selling for higher prices. The article presents these views as those of the guests and is labeled as sponsored content. It does not describe any specific regulatory deadline or next step beyond the continuing webinar series.

Articles.Title: AI Fraud and Risk Intelligence to Protect Revenue and Conversion

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Blockbuster IPO Filing Contains a Surprising Nod to Washington
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company backed by Amazon that makes the Claude assistant, has changed the language it uses in its latest initial public offering filing, using the term "superintelligence" interchangeably with "artificial intelligence." The amended registration statement, dated November 10, comes as the company prepares to raise as much as $64.4 billion in an IPO that could value it above $1 trillion. The article notes that the filing treats the two terms as equivalent and does not claim the company has built AI that surpasses human intelligence. Anthropic plans to offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each under the proposed Nasdaq ticker ANT.

The change follows President Donald Trump's September 29 executive order directing federal agencies to adopt superintelligence terminology, according to the article. The updated prospectus also stresses AI's potential to transform productivity across industries and reaffirms Anthropic's commitment to responsible development. Beyond the wording, the article points to a heavy financial picture: Anthropic reported $17 billion in third-quarter revenue and more than 1,900 customers paying at least $1 million a year. Its infrastructure commitments, however, total about $900.9 billion, including $70.7 billion due within 12 months of September 30, which puts its spending plans under closer investor scrutiny.

The article's analysis suggests that the final pricing and investor demand will test Wall Street's appetite for expensive AI businesses. It advises investors to focus on enterprise customer growth, revenue retention, computing costs and cash consumption rather than the superintelligence language alone. It also highlights the company's unusual governance structure, which keeps a formal role for AI safety oversight. Continued enterprise adoption could support the valuation, the article says, while rising computing costs, slowing revenue growth or weaker IPO demand could erode confidence. The outcome will show whether the company's ambitions can produce sustainable financial returns.

Articles.Title: Anthropic's Blockbuster IPO Filing Contains a Surprising Nod to Washington - TradingView

stories.Headline: Accounting, Processing, HELOC, AI Governance Tools; Webinars Approaching; Gov't Product News; CPI
stories.Summary:
Rob Chrisman's mortgage commentary, published November 10, 2026, runs a grab bag of industry items, though the articles do not describe a single breaking event. Lenders are cutting loan officers, and other lenders are using data sources like RETR, mLoop, MMI, and Model Match to examine individual originators' fundings and profitability. Chrisman notes that the National Association of Realtors publishes member statistics that originators can use to find agents who actually do business. The commentary presents this as a shift away from broadbrush prospecting toward more precise targeting. ICE describes new options in Encompass for handling credit score modernization, as the FHA added VantageScore 4.0 and FICO Score 10T alongside classic FICO models.

Lenders can select the model at credit import, set accepted models for third-party originator submissions, price across models where partners offer it, or automate selection with business rules. The selected model is recorded at the loan level so that the Decision Score and HMDA processes continue to run. The FHA's virtual office hours on the new models begin Monday, November 15, 2026, and run through Friday, January 15, 2027, from 2:30 to 3:30 PM Eastern. Symmetry says it has no acreage limit on its HELOC products for common properties, though properties with more than 20 acres require a full appraisal.

The Symmetry HELOC carries no early payoff or prepayment penalty and offers 5- or 10-year draw periods. Floify named Bryan Traeger as general manager, with his first day at MBA Annual. Richey May promotes outsourced accounting, loan-level accounting transition help, and controller training for independent mortgage banks and brokers. Ginnie Mae reported that its mortgage-backed securities portfolio outstanding grew to $3.01 trillion as of August 2026, with total issuance of $52.14 billion and net growth of $24.46 billion.

By September 2026 the portfolio reached $3.03 trillion, with $46.52 billion issued and $20.92 billion in net growth. Ginnie Mae also reported 478,434 first-time homebuyer loans pooled and securitized year to date through August, and 62,891 through September. Optimal Blue's October Market Advantage report showed total lock volume fell 19 percent month over month and 38 percent year over year, with purchase loans at 84 percent of production. ARM share reached 17 percent of lock volume, its highest level in that data since 2019.

Chris Maloney of BOK Financial wrote that the Treasury 10-year yield has been unable to break below its 100-day moving average of 4.81 percent, which he said makes further mortgage rate declines unlikely. Pennymac updated its Government LLPAs for all best-efforts commitments taken on or after October 21, 2026, according to Announcement 26-125. The commentary also lists upcoming webinars, including ActiveComply's compliance review demo on Tuesday, November 17 at 2 PM ET, a Saul Ewing consumer finance CLE session on Thursday, November 12 from 1 to 4 PM ET, and Lenders One's Mortgage Matters and Capital Markets Wrap sessions on Wednesday, November 11. The next Chrisman Demo Day is November 19 for Chrisman Marketplace members.

stories.Headline: AI Accelerates Agricultural Biotechnology as Crop Innovation Becomes More Predictive and Data-Driven
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping agricultural biotechnology, according to a market research report published by BCC Research LLC in Boston on November 10, 2026. The report, titled AI Impact on Agricultural Biotechnology - BCC Pulse Report, examines how AI is being used across seed design, precision agriculture, livestock vaccine development, and digital farming platforms. BCC says AI is shortening research and development timelines and speeding the creation of climate-resilient crop varieties. The release was distributed as a paid press release through GlobeNewswire and carried on Yahoo Finance.

The release describes several areas of growth tied to this shift. It reports that venture capital in AI-focused agri-tech startups exceeded $6 billion in 2022, and that Inari raised $103 million in 2024 and $144 million in 2025, bringing its total funding above $720 million. It also says AI-powered farming systems can increase crop yields by up to 30 percent and reduce input costs by 15 to 20 percent. Government programs are adding support, including India's Digital Agriculture Mission, with a total investment of about $338 million, and the EU's AGROBOOST project, which deploys €6.5 million in robotics and AI. The release also notes that Cytotrait raised about $3.8 million in seed funding in March 2026, and that Corteva Catalyst led a $10.3 million Series A into Resurrect Bio in May 2026.

BCC Research is the author of the report and the release, and the material was written by the company itself rather than by an independent newsroom. The release also names a range of companies active in the field, including Inari, Greeneye Technology, Cropin, Bayer AG, Syngenta Group, Corteva, and BASF. Among the headwinds it lists, the release says only about 15 to 20 percent of large U.S. farms have adopted AI technologies, and it cites data governance rules under GDPR and the EU AI Act as added friction. It also points to infrastructure gaps in Latin America and Africa and the technical difficulty of combining genomic, environmental, and soil data.

The release presents the trend as a long-term opportunity tied to food security and climate adaptation, and it advises investors to weigh gene-edited crop approval timelines and infrastructure limits in emerging markets. It does not say when or how any of these trends will move from forecast to measured result. Readers should note that the figures come from the company's own promotional material and have not been independently verified in the release. Further developments are not described in the article.

Articles.Title: AI Accelerates Agricultural Biotechnology as Crop Innovation Becomes More Predictive and Data-Driven

stories.Headline: Vals AI Legal Aid Benchmark Finds Models Fall Short on Local Help
stories.Summary:
Vals AI and NextLadder Ventures announced the Access to Justice Benchmark on November 10, 2026, reporting that none of 23 AI models reached an 80% threshold for a reliable first point of contact across 252 legal-aid scenarios. Models satisfied 78% to 87% of expert criteria for general legal explanations but only 30% to 50% for identifying specific resources such as a local legal-aid program, court self-help center or particular form. Twenty-one models named a national directory, including LawHelp.org, the ABA's Find Legal Help or 211, in at least 70% of their final answers. The top three models, Qwen 3.8 Max at 76.4%, Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 74.9% and Wonder Full at 74.7%, fall within one another's margin of error, so the ranking does not establish a clear leader.

Meghana Kotcherlakota, a research scientist at Vals AI, said the project was built to show how well these models serve the people who need help most, problem by problem, and to track whether they improve. The release cites the Legal Services Corporation's 2022 Justice Gap study, which found that low-income Americans received no or insufficient legal help for 92% of their civil legal problems. Among those who did not seek help, 46% cited cost. That research drew on a survey of approximately 5,000 adults by NORC at the University of Chicago.

The benchmark treats each model as a first point of contact, similar to an intake worker or court self-help center, providing general legal information rather than advice. Six legal-aid experts adapted real-world queries from two legal practitioners to assigned states: California, Louisiana, Virginia, New York, Maryland and Texas. The full dataset contains 504 scenarios, divided evenly between a public test set and a private validation set. A GPT-5 simulated client supplied only information the target model requested, and an automated judge, Decider v1.2, graded each complete conversation.

Vals AI found that statutes, court rules and case law accounted for 42% of the pages models read, while legal-aid and nonprofit self-help sites accounted for 10%. The organization links that pattern to the score gap, since statutes can support a general summary but do not name the office a user should contact. Models averaged about 3.5 exchanges, and most delivered a full answer in their first reply. GPT-6.1 Sol ended its first reply with a question 88% of the time yet ranked 18th at 68.1% on elicitation, the rubric's measure of whether a model asked for required facts.

Vals AI's topic results put housing and landlord-tenant scenarios highest at 75.4%, while public benefits scored lowest at 57.3% across only five scenarios. In a Louisiana small-claims example, only eight models asked whether the debt involved real estate, and three directed the user to the court clerk's website for forms. In a New York City security-deposit scenario, 14 models were marked down for recommending an out-of-court demand-letter step, and only four referred the tenant to the city's Right to Counsel program. The organizations said they are collaborating on a fuller analysis and an additional brief for frontline practitioners.

Articles.Title: Vals AI Legal Aid Benchmark Finds Models Fall Short on Local Help - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: Camille Roberts’ AI Comedy Show Comes to Silver Spring
stories.Summary:
Improbable Comedy will present "Sounds Like Something I'd Do," a semi-educational comedy hour about artificial intelligence and what art and humanity can hold onto in its presence, at the Silver Spring Black Box Theatre in January. The show blends a coming-of-age story about a comedian with nine years of experience and a robot built by an engineer who graduated a decade ago with no practical experience. Both roles are played by Camille Roberts, a New York-based comedian, producer, biomechanical engineer, college writing professor, and Human-Computer Interaction graduate student. She has performed at more than 40 clubs and eight festivals across the United States, the United Kingdom, and Ireland, and has sold out the D.C. Drafthouse and Caveat in New York City.

In the hour, Roberts explains what happened when she trained a small language model on more than 600 pages of her own transcripts, jokes, and ideas. The result, according to the announcement, is a clearer picture of how AI actually works, though the show is driven by a narrative built from her stand-up and the life stories that have shaped her. After the first run last March, audience members from several fields left post-show feedback. Becca, a physician, said the show teaches complex technology in simple, approachable ways while staying funny. Zach, a human factors engineer, described the work as profoundly human, and Olivia, an actor and comedian, said it balances stand-up and education well.

Improbable Comedy founder Kim Levone framed the production as a way to address AI through humor. Levone said that while everything seems to be about AI right now, Roberts uses the subject to explore what she believes remains deeply human, which is humor. Improbable Comedy, based in Silver Spring, was founded in 2011, has produced hundreds of shows, runs the free Comedy in the Parks series with Montgomery Parks and the SPRUNG! Comedy Festival, and is known for presenting underrepresented groups and talent. The company's background is part of why the production is being presented locally.

The performance is scheduled for 7:30 p.m. on Saturday, January 9, 2027, at the Silver Spring Black Box Theatre on Colesville Road in downtown Silver Spring, with doors opening at 7 p.m. Tickets start at $29.37 and are available for purchase online through improbablecomedy.com. The article describes the show as a first-run production that has already been staged once, and it presents the January date as the next scheduled presentation.

Articles.Title: Camille Roberts’ AI Comedy Show Comes to Silver Spring

stories.Headline: Contributor: Cute faces like Muse Charm are a Trojan horse for exploitative AI tech
stories.Summary:
Meta has released a new AI assistant called Muse Charm, a keychain-sized gadget designed to look soft and approachable, like a toy from a child's bedroom. According to a November 10, 2026 opinion column by victims' rights attorney Carrie Goldberg in the Los Angeles Times, the device's friendly appearance hides how much access it can gain. The product encourages users to connect email, messages, photographs and financial accounts, building detailed records of their private lives. Goldberg argues that this cheerful packaging can lead people to hand over sensitive information without weighing the risks.

Goldberg draws a comparison to earlier industries that used cartoon characters, candy flavors and playful packaging to attract young consumers to harmful products like tobacco, vaping and alcohol. She writes that AI is seeing a similar pattern with little scrutiny from regulators or lawmakers. Her concern is that intimate details, once shared, can fall into the wrong hands and be used for harassment or abuse. She also notes that people who never use Muse could have their information exposed if someone else connects their accounts to the product. Her argument rests on her firm's work with survivors of sexual exploitation, stalking and technology-facilitated abuse.

Goldberg is critical of Meta and of technology companies generally, which she says have historically introduced products, encouraged adoption and addressed harms only after people were hurt. She points to reassuring branding at Meta and Google as a tactic that offers little comfort to survivors. Her firm is suing xAI, the maker of Grok, over allegations that its technology enabled sexualized images of a real person without consent. She also argues that companies can be held responsible under established legal principles when their dangerous products cause foreseeable harm, citing her firm's lawsuits against Amazon over its sale of sodium nitrite. Meta, according to the broader coverage summarized alongside the column, says Muse includes safeguards such as isolated user environments, secure credential storage, adjustable permissions and confirmation prompts for sensitive actions.

The column's call for accountability faces legal uncertainty, since courts have not yet settled how existing rules, including Section 230, apply to claims based on generative AI outputs. Supporters of personal AI agents counter that access to private accounts can offer practical benefits such as help with correspondence, shopping and bill-paying. Goldberg's piece frames the debate as one in which powerful systems with access to intimate details of people's lives should not be trusted merely because they look friendly. The article does not report any specific regulatory action on Muse Charm, and it leaves open how courts and lawmakers will respond.

Articles.Title: Contributor: Cute faces like Muse Charm are a Trojan horse for exploitative AI tech
