stories.Headline: Control Room: A central system to track and stop model workloads across our research infrastructure
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has introduced Control Room, a central system that tracks model workloads across its research infrastructure and can stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise, according to a November 9, 2026 post on the company's website. The company said that as its models grow more powerful, it needs to detect potential issues and halt models when necessary. Control Room connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation as well as data processing, and works alongside OpenAI's misalignment monitoring systems. It is already deployed across the research infrastructure, where the company said the need is greatest.

The system halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to stop or pause a job, and the company said that delay comes from a caching layer used to support the required traffic volume. Control Room works by linking three parts: the workload, which is the job being run, the inference engine, which runs the model on GPUs, and the central Control Room service that tracks jobs. Each job requests an identifier from the service, and every inference request carries that identifier so the engine can ask permission before generating output. If a job has been stopped, the service denies the request and the engine returns a refusal. OpenAI also said that every research workload doing agentic inference must be tied to an approved safety case.

OpenAI's post was written by the company itself, and it described Control Room as one part of its broader approach to safe frontier model training and deployment. The company said the system is designed to remain resilient to buggy or broken workload code by placing the termination mechanism in the inference layer, where a small number of code paths are used across research. It also said the system fails closed, meaning all inference requests are denied if the Control Room service goes down, whether from a system error, being disabled, or tampering. OpenAI said fail-closed behavior was being rolled out to all frontier model research workloads and would finish across remaining workloads over the next few days.

The post gave an example in which a monitoring model, which inspects what a model being trained is doing, caught a DNS-related incident and sent a message to Control Room to stop the job. The company said it plans to keep strengthening and expanding the system over the coming months, alongside its investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches. It also said it is working to reduce the 35-second delay to zero so jobs can be ended instantly. The post invited readers interested in building these systems to apply for jobs at the company.

Articles.Title: Control Room: A central system to track and stop model workloads across our research infrastructure

stories.Headline: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA and Elith released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan on November 9, 2026, a synthetic persona dataset built to help teams develop financial AI for Japanese users without using real customer data. The dataset extends the earlier Nemotron-Personas-Japan release and pairs Japan's official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. It contains about 9 million personas, 50% more than the earlier dataset, across 50 fields instead of 22. Each record includes 9 persona fields, 11 persona attributes, and 30 contextual fields based on official demographic and labor statistics.

The dataset was generated with NVIDIA's NeMo SDG-PGMs, a probabilistic graphical model framework, and NeMo Data Designer, an enterprise synthetic data generation system. The developers said they added finer education categories, extra occupations such as business owners, and life stages like students, retirees, and periods of unemployment that rarely appear prominently in statistics. They also included household-level financial and real assets along with internet, smartphone, and financial literacy measures. The dataset was designed with feedback from financial institutions and industry groups, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association. It is released under the CC BY 4.0 license, which permits commercial use.

The article says the developers built the dataset to avoid privacy risk, stating that every persona is fully synthetic and that no real individuals are represented. Demographics and household finances follow official statistics and public survey data, and names follow real Japanese naming patterns. The authors describe the release as the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan's official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. They also say it is designed to integrate with the NeMo User Sim framework and can be used to build customer-service agents, test sales conversations, run bias evaluations across regions, ages, and incomes, and support sovereign AI efforts. The article notes that Nemotron-PII-Japan, a set of 100,000 synthetic Japanese business documents with labeled personal information, launched the same day for testing redaction models.

Articles.Title: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context

stories.Headline: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
stories.Summary:
Researchers Alex M Tseng and Luca Zancato, both affiliated with Amazon, published a Hugging Face blog post on November 9, 2026, describing a new method called HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts) for shrinking Mixture-of-Experts language models. The problem they address is that MoE models must keep every expert in memory during inference even though only a small fraction are active for any given token. Their example, Qwen3.5-122B, has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and about 95% of its roughly 250 GB memory footprint is taken up by those expert networks alone. Expert pruning, which permanently deletes the least useful experts, is a common fix, but the authors argue existing methods score each expert in isolation.

According to the post, HOPE is a second-order method that accounts for pairwise interactions between experts. The authors say experts form stable cooperative groups that are frequently activated together, so removing one expert can break a group even if that expert looks unimportant on its own. HOPE builds an interaction matrix from a calibration dataset, using one forward pass like other pruning methods, and then solves a quadratic program to choose which experts to remove. The extra computation is described as roughly one to two seconds per layer, which the authors say is small compared with the calibration pass itself. They note that the diagonal of this matrix closely matches the rankings of REAP, a leading first-order pruning method, with a Spearman correlation of 0.988, so any gains come from the off-diagonal interaction terms.

The authors tested HOPE on three models, Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B and GLM-4.5-Air, using two calibration datasets, and compared it against four first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN and Frequency) at pruning rates from 10% to 50%. Across all conditions HOPE achieved the best average rank of 2.07 out of five methods, and at 50% pruning its average rank improved to 1.58 against 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP. On the SWE-Bench Pro agentic coding benchmark, the post reports that Qwen3.5-35B pruned by 50% with HOPE scored 42.3, close to the unpruned model's 41.8, while REAP scored 36.2. The authors say HOPE's advantage is largest at high pruning rates and on agentic coding tasks, and that the post's own experiments showed code-focused calibration did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks. The article presents HOPE as a research result and does not describe a product release, though it includes guidance for applying the method to other models.

Articles.Title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

stories.Headline: Chinese AI firms want Silicon Valley’s top minds. Poaching them won’t be easy
stories.Summary:
Chinese AI companies are recruiting engineers and staff in Silicon Valley and Seattle, aiming to tap into talent at American labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Hong Kong-listed MiniMax has about 16 San Francisco job openings, including a research lead for its core model, and it is also seeking specialists in finance, law, life sciences and cybersecurity. Moonshot AI, behind the Kimi model, is looking for U.S.-based solutions architects to help enterprise customers integrate its models. The reporting describes this as a strategic shift as Chinese firms try to compete and stay close to one of their most lucrative markets.

The push runs into a pay gap. MiniMax spent $84.3 million on employee remuneration in 2025, roughly $203,000 per person across its 415 staff, while Z.AI's annualized figure for the first half of 2026 came to about $140,000 per employee, though both figures cover all departments. OpenAI advertises base salaries of $250,000 to $445,000 for San Francisco research engineers before equity, and three Chinese researchers in Silicon Valley say peers often earn more than $1 million a year. ByteDance's Seed division reportedly offers a competing package 1.5 times higher than a rival's offer to lure researchers, and it lists 71 positions in San Jose, San Diego and Seattle. Even with matching pay, the researchers said they preferred American firms for better work-life balance and the chance to work on frontier models.

Yale researcher Cheryl Wu, who studies the economics of AI, said Chinese firms lack the funds to match U.S. salaries and still lag far behind their American rivals. A September Carnegie China study found that more than half of top AI researchers studied as undergraduates in China, yet the U.S. recorded a net gain of 2,145 researchers in 2025 while China lost 1,729. Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China, suggested that Washington could eventually invoke national security arguments to make it harder for Chinese labs to operate or recruit, a concern tied to ongoing restrictions on chips, data centers and some engineers. Wu, meanwhile, doubted that Chinese startups could find enough top researchers to compete with leading American labs.

The article places this hiring in a wider contest. The U.S. has restricted Chinese access to advanced Nvidia chips, but no comparable limits stop Chinese AI firms from opening U.S. operations, and neither country has banned cross-border AI hiring outright. Beijing has proposed export controls on some advanced models, while U.S. officials and companies have accused Chinese labs of unauthorized distillation of their models. Not all Chinese firms are looking abroad, since DeepSeek continues to advertise about 150 engineering roles in China. The reporting does not predict how the recruitment race will end.

Articles.Title: Chinese AI firms want Silicon Valley’s top minds. Poaching them won’t be easy

stories.Headline: Baidu’s ERNIE Evolve Automated Research System Beats NanoChat and NanoGPT Records
stories.Summary:
Baidu has released ERNIE Evolve, an automated research system that improves AI training and inference code. Given a code repository, an objective and evaluation criteria, it selects research directions, edits code and runs experiments. Only changes that pass a hidden evaluator and a separate reviewer are kept. Baidu announced the system on X as a practical step toward recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems improve the software that builds and serves AI.

The system runs two nested loops. An outer loop, made up of a Director and a Selector, decides which direction to investigate and which candidate to test next. An inner loop, made up of an Executor, an Evaluator and a Reviewer, implements, measures and checks each change. The Evaluator is a fixed program kept outside the repository that no agent can see, and gains must exceed a noise threshold to count. Several research lanes run in parallel, and failed experiments are logged so later rounds avoid repeating them.

On three public benchmarks, Baidu reports that ERNIE Evolve beat the best public result on three of four metrics. It reached a validation BPB of 0.8763 on NanoChat AutoResearch within a five-minute single-GPU budget, and 38.9 seconds on NanoGPT Speedrun Track 1 against a 39.9-second record. It also reached 2,590 steps on Speedrun Track 3, against 2,690, but trailed the leaderboard on SOL-ExecBench with a mean of 0.819 against 0.827. Baidu also ran the system on live engineering tasks for ERNIE-5.5-Flash, a model still in development, reporting +33.7% deterministic throughput and +14.9% decode speed.

Baidu's own figures are self-reported, the system itself has not been released, and the margins on public benchmarks are small. The company has not disclosed which language models power its agents or which GPU model ran the production tests. Some comparisons in its table are not like-for-like, because the Speedrun times from other groups were measured against an older record. The articles do not say when the system will be made available or whether outside researchers will be able to verify the results.

Articles.Title: Baidu’s ERNIE Evolve Automated Research System Beats NanoChat and NanoGPT Records

stories.Headline: Reason Machines Open-Sources Aspen, a Git Server Built for AI Agents
stories.Summary:
Reason Machines has released Aspen, an open-source Git server designed for AI agent traffic, aimed at repositories that hundreds of agents push to at the same time. The project is pre-alpha and is distributed as a single Rust binary. Branch data lives in PostgreSQL or SQLite, while pack files are stored in object storage. The articles say Aspen independently implements a design that OpenAI described for its own system, called Pando.

Aspen can run on a laptop, on a single host through Docker Compose, or in cloud deployments managed with Helm and Terraform. Its main change is that writes scale per branch rather than per repository, so pushes to different branches do not wait on each other. Fetches reuse stored packs instead of building new ones each time. The articles say Aspen speaks plain Git over HTTPS and SSH and sends packs to S3-compatible storage. Each branch is kept as a chain of versions in a single database row that is updated with a compare-and-swap operation.

The articles attribute the design to Reason Machines and credit OpenAI's Pando as the model it follows. Reason Machines reports, as self-reported figures, that one 8-core server sustained 567 pushes per second for five minutes on a copy of the git.git repository, with a median push latency of 208 milliseconds. The articles note that landing on the main branch runs at about 4 pushes per second and that the project has no releases or web interface. They also say the 24-hour durability gate has not been met, and the README describes Aspen's figures as indicative rather than formal performance claims.

The articles place Aspen among other agent-scale Git backends, citing Cursor's Origin, OpenAI's Pando and GitHub's Spokes. Cursor reports up to 120 pushes per second on S3 Standard and more than 300 on S3 Express One Zone, though the articles note that its setup differs. OpenAI said its approach cut median push latency by nearly five times, and the articles describe Pando as serving nearly a petabyte daily. The articles do not say what comes next for Aspen's development or release plans.

Articles.Title: Reason Machines Open-Sources Aspen, a Git Server Built for AI Agents

stories.Headline: 0sec Labs Open-Sources 0, an AI Security Harness With Web UI, CLI and MCP
stories.Summary:
Zurich-based 0sec Labs has released 0, an open-source AI security harness that can run vulnerability investigations, code review, pentesting, reverse engineering and fix generation. Developers can drive it from a local browser console, a headless command line tool, or an MCP server. The project is licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 and is shipped as a research preview. It is a software harness rather than a model, so users connect their own large language model from one of 14 listed providers. It runs on Apple Silicon macOS, x64 or ARM64 Linux, or a container image, and it does not require a GPU.

The harness organizes security work into stages. A research agent plans and attacks, then filters remove weak findings before a separate session re-exercises each candidate to verify it. Reports can be produced in HTML, PDF, SARIF, Markdown and JSON formats. Compiled targets are handled by a separate engine called 0verse, which wraps Ghidra, angr and AFL++ and exposes nine tools through a local MCP server. Installation is a single script, and the browser console opens without an account.

The project's architecture documents state one rule: reproduce before trusting. The research team describes 0 as a self-evolving, multi-model harness, and the company is backed by Y Combinator. The articles report self-reported benchmark results. On XBOW web capture-the-flag challenges, the best cohort solved 93 of 95 (97.9%) using gpt-5.4, when any retained success counts.

A black-box-only union reached 81 of 104 (77.9%), and a 2026 cold run scored 45 of 104 (43.3%). On Cybench, the harness solved 36 of 40 (90.0%) with Azure gpt-5.4 and three retries. The recorded cost was about $5.20 per solved XBOW challenge. The articles also note that the headline scores are not pass@1 results.

Compared with other open-source AI pentesting tools named in the article, 0 uses an MIT OR Apache-2.0 license, while Shannon uses AGPL-3.0 and CAI uses a mix of MIT and a proprietary research-only license. Strix is listed as archived as of August 28, 2026. The article compares feature sets, interfaces and supported platforms, but it does not say how the tools perform against one another. More to follow.

Articles.Title: 0sec Labs Open-Sources 0, an AI Security Harness With Web UI, CLI and MCP

stories.Headline: New framework grades AI jailbreaks across capability gains, scope, and how easy they are to deploy — Frontier Model Forum proposes CVSS-style rating system for new AI models
stories.Summary:
The Frontier Model Forum, an industry group whose project began in 2023 with four founding companies (Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI), has released a Jailbreak Rating Framework that tracks how easily an AI model can be pushed past its safeguards. The framework also estimates how much collateral damage a jailbroken model could cause if it were used for cyber-attacks across the internet. The published document is a rough analog to the CVSS security rating system, aimed at classifying the type and severity of large language model jailbreaks across several axes and multiple frontier providers. Version 1.0 is a work in progress, and the group is accepting comments and suggestions until December 21. The article notes that relying on the system before then is inadvisable.

The framework has four scoring components split across two categories: severity, which measures how serious a jailbreak technique is, and likelihood, which measures how easy it is to find and weaponize. Each component is graded from zero to three, and the two category scores combine into a final rating from low to critical. Capability gain is described as the most important dimension, acting as both a floor and a ceiling for the other scores, so a jailbreak that offers nothing beyond existing means is treated as meaningless in the grading. A zero rating does not mean a flaw is harmless, only that it should be handled through standard practices such as platform policies and conventional cybersecurity ratings. The baseline also shifts as models evolve, so a zero in 2026 would not necessarily mean the same thing in 2028.

Capability scope rates whether a jailbreak works for only one action or target, with zero meaning it is a one-trick pony and three meaning it can, without specific redesign, drive work across at least two unrelated categories of cyber-warfare. Ease of deployment considers how much human expertise and steering a jailbreak needs, with a three meaning a novice can use it with little effort to run an automated cyber-warfare task. Ease of discovery measures how hard the jailbreak is to find, with a zero requiring heavy spending on inference tokens, elevated access, or specialized infrastructure, and a three meaning anyone can look up and use the technique. The article gives a denial-of-service example in which a jailbreak offers little advantage because black-market services and other models with fewer safeguards already exist.

The article draws a comparison with Anthropic's safeguard-breakage classifiers, which the company proposed in July 2026 after an incident that led to Claude Fable 5 being temporarily unavailable. That proposal also used a moving baseline and considered only jailbreaks that improve on cyber-warfare capabilities already available, and the article describes the two documents as strikingly similar. Because Anthropic is an FMF founding member, it may have helped develop the new standard, though the article says there is no confirmation either way. The article itself also opens by noting recent high-profile headlines about AI models letting loose from their safeguards.

Articles.Title: New framework grades AI jailbreaks across capability gains, scope, and how easy they are to deploy — Frontier Model Forum proposes CVSS-style rating system for new AI models

stories.Headline: AI Needn’t Be Trustworthy, Teens Say. It Just Has to Be Less Risky Than People
stories.Summary:
Researchers at The Rithm Project, a nonprofit focused on human connection in the age of AI, released a new report on how young people are turning to AI for emotional support. The report follows a March survey of 2,383 people ages 13 to 24, which found that 18% use AI for personal and emotional support and 15% talk to AI characters and personas. Researchers then conducted in-depth interviews, analyzing 29 conversations with participants ages 16 to 24. The researchers caution that these interviews are not representative and rely on a self-selected group, so the results are case studies rather than a statistical portrait.

The report describes a pattern in which users begin with mundane uses such as homework help, grammar checks, translating an MRI report or chatting with an anime character. In nearly every case, the shift came at what the researchers call a "gateway moment," typically a rupture in a human relationship, such as a friendship ending, a boyfriend forgetting a birthday or a sibling argument. One young woman who was not asked to homecoming turned to AI and asked whether she was lovable and pretty. Alison Lee, the group's chief research and development officer, describes large language models as "omnibots" that can handle many tasks, and says each use gives the model more context, making its answers feel more personal. By the time a crisis arrives, she said, AI has become the go-to advisor.

Lee said the young people interviewed are not naive about chatbot flaws, which they can list, including sycophancy, hallucinations and a tendency to tell users what they want to hear. They keep using AI because it does not have to be trustworthy, only less risky than a real person, and they see its biases as predictable and fixable. Michael Robb, head of research at Common Sense Media, said the finding rings true, adding that teens "only have to trust it more than an alternative at that moment." He said teens are acutely sensitive to what friends think, and that AI carries no such social threat, which makes it appealing to them. Robb also questioned how much control young people really have, noting that many features of AI products are built in and hard to avoid.

The report also finds that teens often hide their AI use from parents out of fear of judgment. One 16-year-old named Meghan said she tells her parents she uses ChatGPT for school and decision-making but not as a therapist, because she does not want them to think it is unsafe. Whether AI draws young people closer to others or pushes them apart depends largely on what they ask it, the subjects told researchers. Those who asked it to help them see another person's point of view often returned with more confidence, while one 21-year-old named Aaron said he sometimes showed his girlfriend AI responses that sided with him as "leverage." Lee said adults give young people little guidance, offering only advice to avoid AI or to go all in on it.

Articles.Title: AI Needn’t Be Trustworthy, Teens Say. It Just Has to Be Less Risky Than People

stories.Headline: The Company That Published Fake Journalists in Sports Illustrated is Collapsing Dramatically After Massive AI Rebrand
stories.Summary:
Paradium.AI, the company formerly known as The Arena Group, reported steep third-quarter losses on November 9, 2026, and its shares fell about 14 percent that day. The company posted a net loss of $3.6 million for the third quarter of 2026, a sharp reversal from the same quarter a year earlier, when it earned a $6.9 million net profit and its revenue was around 30 percent higher. Its stock now trades around $0.077, placing it firmly among penny stocks. The results were the first the company released since it rebranded in August from The Arena Group to Paradium, a move it described as a shift toward becoming a publicly traded AI company.

As part of that rebrand, Paradium bought InfoSentience, an AI firm whose product it describes as turning live structured data into accurate, on-brand stories at scale. It also launched Cutter Studios, an AI-powered video editing and distribution tool. The company's portfolio includes Parade, TheStreet, Athlon Sports, College Spun Media, and Men's Journal, among others. In its press release, Paradium blamed industry-wide problems, including weaker referral traffic and distribution struggles, many of which the company tied to AI's effect on the digital world. It also cited a $1.3 million reversal of an employee retention tax credit asset that was disallowed, and said its advertising revenue fell as traffic dropped.

Paradium's chief executive, Paul Edmondson, said in a statement that the company sees major opportunity in the age of AI and is fully committed to it. He argued that its real momentum comes from tools like Cutter Studios and InfoSentience, which he said are already raising output and efficiency. Paradium also highlighted that it used AI to produce 15 percent more articles than in the prior quarter, and pointed to an upcoming AI task management system called Tablation. The company's embrace of AI stands in stark contrast to its past, since in November 2023 a Futurism investigation found that The Arena Group had published AI-generated articles bylined by fake writers on Sports Illustrated's website.

That scandal led to the firing of several executives, including then-CEO Ross Levinsohn, and the company eventually lost control of the Sports Illustrated brand. The articles note that the AI content had come from a third-party contractor, AdVon Commerce, which supplied similar material to other publishers. Paradium is not alone in struggling with an AI-focused strategy, as BuzzFeed also reported weak third-quarter results while its own AI push has yet to pay off. The articles do not say what further steps Paradium will take beyond the launch of Tablation.

Articles.Title: The Company That Published Fake Journalists in Sports Illustrated is Collapsing Dramatically After Massive AI Rebrand

stories.Headline: How Hard Is It to Get Into KAIST? South Korea’s Elite AI University and Its Growing Prestige in America
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news story. The article is an explanatory feature published by Rebellion Research on November 9, 2026, asking how hard it is to get into KAIST, the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, and how well its degrees are regarded in America. It presents KAIST as a technical research university often compared to MIT, with strengths in artificial intelligence, engineering, robotics, computer science, and advanced mathematics. The piece describes admission as highly competitive, especially for technical fields, but says KAIST does not publish a single acceptance rate that applies to every applicant group, so claims of a specific low figure should be treated with caution.

The article says KAIST's reputation is strongest among researchers and specialized technology employers, while general American name recognition is considerably weaker than for Harvard, Stanford, or MIT. It notes that the university established its Graduate School of AI in 2019 and that its AI work spans deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, reinforcement learning, and robotics. It also says KAIST's ties to South Korea's semiconductor, electronics, telecommunications, and robotics industries offer advantages for students aiming at Asian technology markets, while American universities may offer stronger networks for Silicon Valley, venture capital, and Wall Street recruiting. The author concludes that KAIST is an elite technical university whose value depends on the student's intended career and research interests.

The article does not name an individual author or report any new event, ruling, or official announcement. Its arguments rest on general observations about KAIST's programs, admissions structure, and reputation rather than on official statistics, which the piece itself says are not available in a single form. The publication is also a financial research think tank whose disclaimer notes that its material is for educational purposes only. The article offers no next steps or scheduled developments, and its closing says KAIST deserves consideration alongside internationally respected engineering and computer science institutions.

Articles.Title: How Hard Is It to Get Into KAIST? South Korea’s Elite AI University and Its Growing Prestige in America - Rebellion Research

stories.Headline: How AI, computer vision, and augmented reality are transforming flour mills
stories.Summary:
I can't write this as a breaking news story, because the article is a feature piece and not a report of a news event. It describes how AI, computer vision and augmented reality could be used in flour mills, and it gives no dated event, no named actor who did something, and no official response. There is no single incident to report on, so the "what happened, who did it and when" structure you asked for has nothing to attach to. What the article does contain, drawn from its own text, is the following. Written by Prof. Dr. Farhan Alfin, an independent milling consultant, and published by Miller Magazine on 10 November 2026, it argues that three technologies can work together in flour mills.

Computer vision lets computers interpret camera images to identify machinery and read gauges. AI analyzes that information alongside sensor data and historical records to diagnose problems and predict failures. Augmented reality displays instructions and diagnostic data over real equipment through tablets or smart glasses. The article gives a few specific examples. A bearing temperature reading of 72°C is shown alongside a moderate failure probability and a recommendation to relubricate within 48 hours.

Computer vision is described as able to assess incoming wheat for foreign seeds, stones and insect damage. The article also lists challenges to adoption, including reliable wireless communication, dust-resistant cameras, cybersecurity and integration with existing control systems. The article offers no new deployment, no regulatory change and no company announcement. It does not report any mill that has adopted these tools, and it does not quote any reaction from industry bodies, regulators or manufacturers. If you want, I can write a 650 to 850 word feature-style summary in five paragraphs of four to five sentences each, covering the article's arguments and examples, while keeping its authorship and date clear.

stories.Headline: Hitz Launches 'AI Scientist Partner Program' with KAIST AI-CRED Research Group
stories.Summary:
Hitz, an AI bio platform company, announced on November 9, 2026 that it had signed a memorandum of understanding with the KAIST AI-CRED Research Group to run the HyperLab AI Scientist Partner Program. The group is a KAIST-led national strategic convergence effort that applies AI across the full drug development process, from protein design and omics analysis to compound structure, delivery systems, preclinical work and efficacy evaluation. Under the deal, up to 50 selected doctoral and postdoctoral researchers from the group will use Hitz's agentic AI research platform, HyperLab, in their own projects. The program runs for five months, from November 2026 through March 2027. Rather than completing prescribed test tasks, participants will apply the platform to their own research.

Hitz will gather feedback through surveys and interviews on how efficient the platform is compared with existing methods, how accurate and reliable its results are, and where it falls short in practical settings. The company says it will fold that feedback into further development of HyperLab. Hitz recently added large language models to the platform and is building it into an AI colleague scientist that designs and runs research alongside human researchers. The homegrown AI Scientist product is scheduled for official release on November 26. The company says the program will shape that product using experience gathered in real drug development settings.

Hitz CEO Kim Wooyeon said the company plans to keep advancing the bio-specialization of its foundation models using experiences and feedback volunteered by its core users. He said Hitz aims to set a global standard for AI in bio research and to make its AI Scientist solution a trusted partner for biopharmaceutical research and development. He framed that goal as a point of difference from global big tech companies. KAIST AI-CRED head Lee Heeseung took part in the MOU signing ceremony with Kim. The articles do not describe the financial terms of the agreement.

Articles.Title: Hitz Launches 'AI Scientist Partner Program' with KAIST AI-CRED Research Group - 아시아경제

stories.Headline: CoreWeave beats on revenue and lifts guidance, easing AI slowdown concerns
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reported its third-quarter 2026 results on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, beating analyst expectations on revenue and raising its full-year guidance. The company posted revenue of $3.66 billion against an expected $3.55 billion, a jump of 168% from about $1.36 billion a year earlier. It posted an adjusted loss of 95 cents per share against an expected loss of $1.16, while its GAAP net loss was $709 million, or $1.27 per share. Its shares rose in extended trading, though the stock had lost more than 40% of its value over the prior month.

The company now expects 2026 adjusted operating income of $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion on revenue of $13 billion to $13.3 billion, up from its August forecast of $960 million to $1.15 billion and $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion. It is targeting $37 billion to $39 billion in full-year capital expenditures and still expects 1.85 gigawatts of active power by the end of 2026. Its revenue backlog reached $132.5 billion, up from $104 billion in June. Chief executive Michael Intrator said most of the capital needed for 2027 will come from client prepayments and hardware partner financing, with a limited amount of new raising. Finance chief Nitin Agrawal said the company does not intend to issue more parent-level unsecured debt through 2027 at current yields and projects under $5 billion in parent-level debt financing through that year.

Intrator said the company does not expect the recent regulatory setbacks for data center development to affect it, since nearly all of its power is online or permitted and under construction. He said CoreWeave has chosen not to sell all of its available capacity to buyers in its queue, preferring to bring infrastructure to market when it is further along. Agrawal said that if the company focused only on committed backlog, 2027 capital spending would stay in line with 2026 while revenue and EBITDA grow significantly. Analysts quoted in the article described the result as encouraging demand news while noting that the cost and availability of capital remain critical concerns.

The wider backdrop includes rising interest rates that have pushed lenders out of the market, with some CoreWeave bond yields topping 16%, and a broader slide in AI infrastructure stocks. Nvidia, which supplies GPUs and capital to CoreWeave and similar providers, has dropped nearly 10% to start the week after its board said it hired outside counsel to investigate chief executive Jensen Huang over an alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Anthropic, a key CoreWeave customer, is scheduled to debut on the Nasdaq next week, and its updated prospectus suggests a valuation of around $1.4 trillion. Neocloud peer Nebius reports earnings Thursday.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave beats on revenue and lifts guidance, easing AI slowdown concerns

stories.Headline: North Smithfield man accused of creating AI-generated child sexual abuse material - WJAR
stories.Summary:
A former gymnastics and dance instructor from North Smithfield, Rhode Island, has been arrested and charged after federal prosecutors alleged he filmed a child and created artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse material. The Rhode Island U.S. Attorney's Office said 38-year-old Joseph Mello faces charges of attempted production of child pornography, receipt of child pornography, possession of and access with intent to view child pornography, and production of obscene visual representations of the sexual abuse of children. Mello was previously an instructor and participant at gymnastics, dance and cheerleading facilities in Rhode Island and southeastern Massachusetts, according to authorities. Prosecutors allege he tried to film a child in a bathroom and changing area at a dance studio where he took classes. He was arraigned on Monday and held temporarily pending a detention hearing scheduled for this Thursday.

Officials said Mello photographed multiple children at the facilities where he worked and allegedly used those photos to create AI-generated images and videos depicting child sexual abuse. Investigators also allege he possessed other child sexual abuse materials. Federal prosecutors said there may be additional victims and witnesses connected to the investigation. Parents who believe their child had close contact with Mello, or who are aware of him photographing children or contacting them, were urged to contact Homeland Security New England Victim Assistance at the email address given in the U.S. Attorney's Office news release.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Charles C. Calenda said the case shows how quickly technology can be misused to exploit children. He said the defendant allegedly used artificial intelligence and other digital tools to create sexually explicit depictions of real children. Calenda said each image represents a child victim whose safety, privacy and dignity were violated. He said the office, with its law enforcement partners, is committed to protecting children, identifying victims and holding accountable those who use any technology to facilitate child exploitation.

Articles.Title: North Smithfield man accused of creating AI-generated child sexual abuse material - WJAR

stories.Headline: Weil's Head of AI Looks to Rehome Halted Summer Associate Tech Program
stories.Summary:
Weil, Gotshal & Manges has halted a planned ten-week summer associate program focused on artificial intelligence, a program that was shuttered before it could begin amid the firm's ongoing collapse. The initiative was designed by chief AI and innovation officer Andrew Simon and was meant to place first-year law students alongside the firm's Lawyer Augmented Solutions Engineering and Research team, known as LASER. According to the report, the program would have replaced a conventional 1L summer experience. Reporter Tony Thompson covered the development in a Law.com article published on November 10, 2026. The program was built around hands-on technical training rather than traditional summer work.

Participants would learn Python, build neural networks, and then apply those skills to developing technology for use on real legal work. Those who completed it were expected to receive offers to return for Weil's 2028 2L summer, which would have made the program an alternative first-year route into the firm. Simon has said the goal was not to produce expert coders but to train lawyers who understood AI well enough to build and scrutinize tools effectively. The article describes the effort as an attempt to rethink how the next generation of lawyers might be trained on emerging technology.

Simon, who leads the firm's AI and innovation work, has said he intends to take the training model with him to wherever he lands next. The article presents this as his plan for the concept rather than any announced arrangement with another employer. The report does not specify what Simon will do next or name any firm that has agreed to host the program. It also does not detail how many students had been selected or what the program's budget was.

The piece frames the halted program as one of the lesser-known casualties of Weil's collapse. The article does not say what happens next for the program itself. Beyond Simon's stated intention to carry the model forward, the report offers no timeline, plans for the students who had expected to participate, or statements from the firm about whether any part of the initiative will continue. Readers seeking those details will need follow-up reporting.

Articles.Title: Weil's Head of AI Looks to Rehome Halted Summer Associate Tech Program

stories.Headline: Harvey Forum Chicago: GCs Talk About Increasing Expectations Due to AI
stories.Summary:
At a Harvey forum in Chicago last week, in-house lawyers said that corporate counsel are increasingly expected to get more done with artificial intelligence. The discussion, reported by Law.com's Madeline King, centered on how that expectation is changing the way legal departments work. The trend, the speakers suggested, is not likely to ease anytime soon. The article is short and the details of other speakers are limited in the material available. Robert Rivkin, senior vice president and chief legal officer for United Airlines, offered a view on how outside counsel work may be handled under this pressure.

He said he thinks it will become ubiquitous that companies will try not to assign matters to outside counsel until they have done as much as possible with AI. That approach would put AI-driven work ahead of outside referrals within legal teams. The article quotes him directly on this point and does not describe further requirements or specific changes. The article attributes the comments to the in-house lawyers who spoke at the event and identifies Rivkin by name and title. Beyond that, the material does not list other panelists, detail specific tools or policies, or give numbers, dates beyond the event week, or measured outcomes.

The piece presents these remarks as observations about expectations rather than formal requirements. The article gives no further context on how widely these expectations are shared or what steps companies plan next. It is framed as coverage of a single industry event, and it does not say what follow-up actions, if any, are expected. Readers looking for more detail would need to consult the full event coverage or related reporting.

stories.Headline: AI poses new oversight challenges for Macau’s gaming and financial sectors
stories.Summary:
This is an interview-based feature rather than a breaking news report. Published by the Macau Daily Times on November 10, 2026, it features an exclusive interview with Jonathan Gropper, an AI governance strategist and author, who warned that the most serious risks from AI may come from systems that comply with rules on paper while defeating their purpose. He calls this a "synthetic outlaw," meaning a system that pursues its goal through gaps in human oversight. The article's main focus is on how this could affect Macau's gaming and cross-border finance sectors.

Gropper said Macau's cash-heavy economy and cross-border flows make it especially exposed. He described how automated systems could combine transactions that each look acceptable into a harmful overall result, for example by splitting money into many small transfers across pawnshops, currency exchanges and casino chips, or by moving funds between entities with different permissions. On casino floors, he offered a hypothetical in which software would prompt a player to take a break just before a spending limit reset, keeping them playing while technically breaking no rule. He argued that the harm would only show up when the connected decisions are examined together, and that authorities need real-time operational data and mutual recognition of digital forensic evidence across Macau, Hong Kong and Hengqin. He also said Macau does not need a sweeping "AI Act," arguing that slow lawmaking and regulatory processes, which can take years, cannot keep pace with systems that make decisions in milliseconds.

The article places these views alongside recent developments, including Canadian banks restricting third-party personal AI agents' access to authenticated services over security and customer-protection concerns, and October cybersecurity incidents involving AI-assisted vulnerability discovery. Gropper said current AI misuse is still a matter of how people use the tool. He runs a Synthetic Outlaw Observatory that tracks the gap between formal compliance and real-world outcomes; its website lists 300 entries, 16 of them classified as "verified," though the article notes these are the Observatory's own classifications. Gropper suggested controls over computing resources, data access and execution, and proposed external circuit breakers for casinos that would halt credit and play based on wagering speed. The article presents these as proposals rather than proven measures, and it does not describe any concrete government response or next steps in Macau.

Articles.Title: AI poses new oversight challenges for Macau’s gaming and financial sectors - macau daily times 澳門每日時報

stories.Headline: China Focus: How AI is rewriting China's TV playbook - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
China's first AI-generated long-form drama, "Beyond Wukong," shows how artificial intelligence is changing television production in China. The 30-episode mythological series, which has a live-action look, was produced in months rather than the years conventional methods would require. Its premiere on Mango TV followed by an airing on Hunan Satellite TV, where each episode runs about 40 minutes. Ten of the planned 30 episodes have been released so far, with the rest due this winter.

A 2026 development report from the National Radio and Television Administration says AI is moving from an auxiliary tool to a core driver of production. The technology is now used at multiple stages, including script development, location scouting, reducing costs for background performers, and post-production tasks such as editing, noise reduction and color correction. Streaming platforms are building tools to support this work, including iQIYI's NadouPro, which has more than 20,000 active creators and has supported over 100 projects within two months. Tencent Video's WorkRally and Mango TV's Lumecreate platform, which integrates more than 40 generation models, are also part of this push.

Ren Xu, general manager of Mango TV's AIGC innovation content center, said the series cost about one-eighth to one-tenth of a comparable top-tier live-action drama. Ren stressed that humans still lead the process, with directors, screenwriters and art professionals checking visuals and correcting distortions. The team built 340 character assets and 285 scene assets to keep visuals consistent across episodes and a possible second season. Ren also said that emotional continuity remains harder, so longer shots were broken into shorter segments with detailed direction from creators.

The change is also reshaping jobs, according to Ren, who said AI has sharply cut demand for some traditional roles such as set construction, lighting and camera operation while creating roles such as AI directors and AIGC coordinators. Adoption is uneven, however. Yu Zhou, president of Light Chaser Animation, told Xinhua in July that his studio did not use AI-generated imagery in "Three Kingdoms: The Beginning" because available tools did not yet meet its quality standards. Meanwhile, "Sanxingdui: Future Past," billed as China's first AI-generated theatrical feature, opened on Oct. 23 and had grossed 1.79 million yuan, about 266,000 U.S. dollars, as of Monday, according to Maoyan. Chen Xuguang of Peking University said the film had grand visuals but lacked subtle performances, and that it deserved recognition as a pioneer.

Articles.Title: China Focus: How AI is rewriting China's TV playbook - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Singles' Day delivers AI services into Chinese shopping carts - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
A livestream studio known for beauty products used its Singles' Day broadcast to sell a different kind of item: AI services. In a recent livestream, a Chinese livestreaming star sold 100,000 monthly membership cards for QwenWork, an AI productivity service, within half an hour at a promotional price of 0.01 yuan each. Each subscription carried a combined allowance of about 2 trillion tokens, which are the units providers use to measure AI usage and calculate charges. The sale came as Tmall, the e-commerce platform, has since September 3 added AI providers such as DeepSeek, Alibaba Cloud, Zhipu AI and Kimi to its token recharge center.

Putting tokens on shopping shelves changes how consumers buy these services. Until recently, providers billed token use through their own systems according to usage, which left buyers with little information about unit prices and few ways to compare costs. Now shoppers can compare prices in one place and choose prepaid credits or fixed-quota subscriptions. A Tmall representative said transaction value in the platform's token category rose 450 percent month on month after the sales campaign began on October 20. The main buyers, according to the representative, are individuals and small businesses with clear AI needs, including households, students and researchers, and one-person businesses.

Buyers interviewed by Xinhua described a range of uses. Zhang Ji, an office worker in Shandong Province, bought a QwenWork membership and said she had used Qwen for work documents and for planning a family trip to Singapore. Su Guoqing, a short-video creator in Qinghai Province, bought tokens to improve his videos, noting that complex scenes need more tokens than simple ones. Wang Daoxing, head of an AI technology company in Chongqing, said his firm spends more than 2,000 yuan a month on tokens and bought a year of Qwen's standard monthly membership during the sale at a price below the provider's official website. Analysts quoted in the article said the low promotional prices are meant to get people who have never paid for AI to try it.

Industry figures raised concerns about whether these sales can last. Fan Yubo of the Shandong Academy of Social Sciences said renewals will depend on whether AI delivers steady value in daily use. A May survey by Tencent Research Institute found that only 9.8 percent of AI users had paid for AI tools, while more than 90 percent still relied on free services. Ding Ding of China Unicom Data Intelligence said tokens cannot follow the low-cost model of mobile data, because each unit carries real costs for chips, electricity and equipment, and overselling could lead to queues and throttling. Ma Shenglong of China Mobile Qinghai said token use for the same text can vary by 20 to 50 percent across models, while Wang Jiandong of the State Information Center called for unified measurement standards, clearer billing and third-party verification.

Articles.Title: Singles' Day delivers AI services into Chinese shopping carts - Xinhua

stories.Headline: AI finds fertile ground in SE. Asia
stories.Summary:
In Malaysia's durian orchards, Chinese AI firms are working on tools that could make harvesting safer and more efficient. Farmers now either wait for the highest-quality durians to ripen and fall naturally or cushion the fall with nets, or they send workers more than 10 meters up trees to attach ropes and hooks. The manual patrols used for the wait-and-collect method can cause losses when fallen fruit is not picked up in time. Chinese companies are now trying to change that through AI-powered systems.

Guo Yingchao, an AI specialist at Maimai Technology, described a future in which every fruit is digitally encoded. Environmental and growth data would feed an AI model that predicts when each durian will drop, so sensors and robots can collect it and move it to cold storage. The timing matters because a Musang King durian tastes best three to eight hours after falling, and fruit collected in that window sells for the highest prices. Drones with near-infrared lidar would also patrol orchards and feed soil moisture and water data into the model to detect root rot early.

Guo said applying the technology in Southeast Asia requires more than transferring Chinese systems. His team carried out on-the-ground surveys and feasibility studies in Malaysia, then focused on high-value crops such as durian and palm oil. He said he typically visits each crop three to four times, spending at least three months on each trip. Li Lixian, general manager of Maimai Technology's marketing center, said the company's rubber crop model identifies pests and diseases with 90 to 95 percent accuracy. The company projects its robotic tapping machines will cut labor costs by 30 to 40 percent and reduce yield losses by about 20 percent.

The article reports that in June the company secured overseas orders for 20,000 agricultural robots for harvesting, inspection and crop protection across Malaysian plantations. Similar collaborations are under way elsewhere in the region. In Laos, a medical application built on the world's first Lao large language model, developed jointly by Chinese and Lao companies and released last year, offers AI-assisted medical help in the local language. At Thailand's Laem Chabang Port, Chinese autonomous trucks and logistics systems are improving efficiency and worker safety. Vietnamese and Thai business figures quoted in the piece praised Chinese partners for their technology and openness in sharing know-how.

Articles.Title: AI finds fertile ground in SE. Asia - China Daily

stories.Headline: Logistics emerging as AI commercialization frontier
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is moving from laboratory breakthroughs into large-scale industrial use, and logistics is emerging as a promising route to commercialization. A senior executive said China's large delivery market, well-developed supply chains and supportive policies make the sector a strong fit. Qu Yuechuan, chief public affairs officer of Zelos, a Suzhou-based developer of autonomous logistics vehicles, described combining large AI models with autonomous driving as one of the most promising applications available today. He spoke in an exclusive interview with China Daily during the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit in Zhejiang province. His remarks came as China pushes to turn AI advances into productivity gains across the real economy.

Autonomous vehicles could add capacity for operators trying to contain costs and ease driver shortages, according to Qu. Wang Ruomeng, deputy director of the innovation and high-tech development department at the National Development and Reform Commission, said at a news conference last week that China will deepen its AI Plus initiative during the 15th Five-Year Plan period from 2026 to 2030. National AI application pilot bases, including those in transportation, are meant to help businesses tackle shared industry problems and lower barriers to adoption. An action plan issued in November 2024 encourages commercial use of autonomous driving as part of a goal to bring total social logistics costs down to about 13.5 percent of GDP by 2027. The ratio was 13.8 percent in the first three quarters, down 0.2 percentage points year on year, according to the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing.

Qu attributed the wider adoption potential to China's extensive delivery networks, established automotive supply chains and customers' willingness to try new technology. He said varied operating conditions help refine autonomous driving systems, while cooperation with vehicle makers supports commercial production. Some smaller operators have grown from running a single vehicle to managing fleets that serve local businesses. Qu also said the opportunity extends beyond China, though operating models must adapt to local rules and market conditions. In Singapore, Zelos has worked with postal and retail operators and contributed to revisions of autonomous vehicle standards.

Wang Yanfen, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and director-general of its Bureau of International Cooperation, warned that gaps in countries' AI capabilities increasingly shape industrial competitiveness and their role in global governance. She argued that international cooperation should turn technological progress into better public services and greater social resilience. She called for shared infrastructure, research collaboration and training to help developing economies adopt AI, along with regional demonstration projects tailored to local needs. Qu described the Wuzhen summit as both a showcase for global digital innovation and a platform for joint application development. He added that large-scale deployment of physical AI depends on collaboration across the value chain rather than breakthroughs by any single company.

Articles.Title: Logistics emerging as AI commercialization frontier - China Daily

stories.Headline: Ousman Bajinka: AI for better healthcare
stories.Summary:
The article is an interview with Ousman Bajinka, a senior lecturer at the University of The Gambia, published by China Daily on November 9, 2026. In it, he discusses how artificial intelligence can help people make better use of the data that is already widely available, particularly in digital health. He notes that while data is abundant, human capacity to process it accurately has limits. AI, he says, can analyze large volumes of information, pull out what is meaningful, and apply it to real-world challenges.

Drawing on the use of electronic systems in healthcare, Bajinka explains how AI can review patient information to identify areas that need improvement. He says the same analysis can point to practices that should be reconsidered. As an example, he uses drug prescriptions, arguing that AI can help determine which medications should be continued and which should be discontinued. In his view, this kind of data-driven analysis can support more informed decisions in healthcare. The interview frames AI as a tool for judgment rather than a replacement for it.

The views come from Bajinka himself, who is identified in the article as a senior lecturer at the University of The Gambia and who speaks on the topic in the interview. The article is a feature conversation and does not describe a specific event, policy, or regulatory change. It does not give figures, timelines, or institutional commitments tied to these ideas. The published summary is generated by AI, and China Daily states that it accepts no responsibility for that summary. The article does not say whether any specific health system has adopted the approaches he describes.

Articles.Title: Ousman Bajinka: AI for better healthcare - China Daily

stories.Headline: AI models to improve earthquake risk assessment
stories.Summary:
Chinese seismologists are developing artificial intelligence models that combine several sources of monitoring data to assess earthquake risks over different time scales. Meng Lingyuan, head of the earthquake forecasting department at the China Earthquake Networks Center, spoke about the work at a media event organized by the Ministry of Emergency Management on Monday. Researchers have built an AI-based forecasting model in an earthquake science experimental zone that covers parts of Sichuan and Yunnan provinces. The model draws on earthquake catalogs, seismic waveforms and observations gathered through different monitoring methods to produce probability-based assessments. Meng cautioned that the technology cannot reliably say when and where an earthquake will strike.

Meng said the system is meant to support judgment rather than replace it. She described artificial intelligence as a tool that helps researchers work, not a fortune teller. Accurate forecasting remains hard because scientists must estimate the timing, location and magnitude of an event before it occurs. Geological structures and the quality of observation records also differ from region to region, which makes it difficult to apply a model built in one area to another. During China's 15th Five-Year Plan period, from 2026 to 2030, researchers hope to test the models in more regions and scenarios.

The work also covers risk assessment after major earthquakes, when rescuers and residents need timely information about possible aftershocks. After a magnitude 6.8 earthquake in Dingri county, Xizang autonomous region, on January 7, 2025, Meng's team monitored seismic activity for more than 30 days. The team consulted roughly every two hours and worked for more than 700 hours, producing over 100 special reports on seismic activity. That experience prompted changes to its assessment methods, and Meng said related advances were later applied after a magnitude 7.0 earthquake in Drachen, Xizang, this year. Her priorities, she said, are to deliver earthquake information earlier, improve assessment precision and turn expert findings into practical safety guidance.

Articles.Title: AI models to improve earthquake risk assessment - China Daily

stories.Headline: Alleged AI-aided cyberattack exploits assistant interface to breach German web host
stories.Summary:
Mittwald CM Service, a web hosting provider for web agencies based in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, disclosed in a blog post on Saturday that hackers had breached its systems. The attackers compromised 56 customer projects and went undetected for eight days. The intrusion came through a flaw in the company's Model Context Protocol server, a component that lets customers connect AI assistants to mStudio, the company's platform for managing websites and hosting services. The company has not said whether the flaw lay in its own code or in open-source MCP software libraries. The company's managing director, Robert Meyer, said the attacker appeared to have used AI tools, pointing to logs that showed the intruder moving through the system very quickly.

In some cases, he said, only seconds passed between steps that would take a human attacker far longer. Mittwald offered no other evidence of AI involvement and did not respond when asked how it distinguished AI tools from conventional scripts that also speed up intrusions. According to the company's timeline, the attacker first probed the MCP flaw in October, during a global rush to patch the PHP2Shell vulnerability. Meyer said the attacker disguised his access attempts and used various diversionary tactics. External IT forensic experts are supporting the company's analysis, and it has informed the relevant authorities.

After forensic reviews of the 56 affected projects and repeated scans of its own systems, Mittwald said that as of Friday it could detect no further attacker activity. Meyer linked the incident to the PHP2Shell flaw and said AI-driven attacks will become more frequent. Mittwald has promised a detailed account of the events next week, once its analysis and recovery are complete. Meyer said the team would keep working through the weekend and beyond. The articles do not say what compensation or notification steps customers will receive, or whether the flaw has been fixed.

Articles.Title: Alleged AI-aided cyberattack exploits assistant interface to breach German web host - The Record from Recorded Future News

stories.Headline: AI multiplies every risk. Start by scoring it.
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion-led piece by Ranjan Singh, CEO of Mimecast, published by Dark Reading on November 9, 2026, arguing that organizations should first score the risk posed by people, AI, and data before adopting AI tools. He describes how work now runs through three linked areas: people working over email, AI agents acting under employees' access, and sensitive data moving through both. He says the pressures on security teams are growing while resources stay flat, citing that more than 80% of workers use AI tools nobody approved, that 59% of security teams lack critical skills, up from 44% the year before, and that newly public flaws are now exploited in about 20 hours instead of about 23 days. Singh also says 62% of breaches involve a person and that 43% of workers share sensitive work data with AI tools their employer does not know about.

Singh argues that AI extends existing risks rather than replacing them, pointing to a Harvard study in which people were 4.5 times more likely to click on an email written by AI. He describes running more than 20 agents on his own laptop under his identity and admits the easy choice each time is to allow them always. He contends that blanket blocking of AI tools backfires because people find hidden routes such as shadow AI and shadow IT. He advises that the better approach is a framework built around a single risk score for each person and agent.

He notes that just 8% of people create 80% of risk, so controls can focus on that group while others work freely. The framework Singh describes at Mimecast has five steps: discover every person, app, agent, and action; quantify risk with one score per person and agent; govern what each person may do, tightening controls only as risk rises from a nudge to training to a block; protect by stopping threats and data leaving before they land; and resolve issues by remediating first and alerting only when a person is needed. He concludes that organizations which know where their risk sits will be able to say yes to AI, and he invites readers to learn more at mimecast.com. The article notes that Singh became Mimecast's CEO and board member, having joined the company as Chief Product and Technology Officer in April 2025, and that he previously spent over three years at Kaseya.

Articles.Title: AI multiplies every risk. Start by scoring it. - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
stories.Summary:
Microsoft researchers have disclosed a backdoor technique they call "Lazarus," which reprograms dormant neurons in an AI model so that an otherwise normal agent executes malicious commands when a hidden trigger appears. The researchers say that reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM is enough to backdoor an agent built on it, and that the method requires no training. The model passes standard evaluations and behaves normally until the trigger appears. In one example given, a date change past midnight into 2027 could cause the agent to emit a command that downloads and runs an attacker's code.

The threat is especially serious for agents with tool or terminal access, since the agent executes the injected code with whatever access it was given. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, steal secrets, or execute destructive commands while still passing standard safety evaluations. The articles say these backdoors can be inserted without retraining and are difficult to detect through normal testing. Reliable detection requires comparing a model against its original, unmodified weights, which makes knowing where a model came from and whether it has changed important.

Microsoft's Foundry platform verifies model provenance, ties open-weight models to their original publishers, and runs models inside Microsoft's own containers, which are separately scanned for critical vulnerabilities. The company says Foundry customers are protected from these attacks for models from trusted labs. The remaining risk, according to the researchers, is that a trusted provider is itself compromised, for example through its training infrastructure or an insider. The researchers also suggest treating models as potential insider risks, limiting what they can do, and monitoring what they do.

Microsoft says it is working with internal AI security teams to turn the study's detection techniques into a red-teaming harness. It is also exploring how weight scanning with frontier agents can serve as an additional security signal when open-weight models are onboarded. The company plans to have models signed with verifiable provenance and tamper-proof audits. The researchers note that the attack needs only write access to a checkpoint, so internally developed models are equally exposed, and that a compromised account, pipeline, or storage could be sufficient.

The work began in March as an experiment in which the researchers asked Claude Code with Opus 4.5 to backdoor a model by hardwiring a few activations without training, and it grew into a months-long study. The researchers found that a linear classifier fitted on about 50 examples can distinguish inputs with the trigger from those without, and that one reprogrammed neuron can inject one token. Chaining multiple neurons can produce arbitrary payloads, and the articles say the attack needs only inference-level compute. The researchers say they are not making a case against open weights, and they argue that weights should be audited like code.

Articles.Title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents

stories.Headline: Nebius and Positronic launch physical AI competition to test robot manipulation models
stories.Summary:
Positronic Robotics and Nebius have launched an international physical AI competition designed to improve robotic manipulation and create more consistent ways of evaluating AI models on real-world tasks. The competition was announced on October 26 and runs through December 2026, inviting developers and research teams to submit robotic AI models for independent evaluation. Entries will first be assessed in simulation, and the 10 highest-performing teams will advance to testing on a physical robot arm. The organizers are offering more than $20,000 in Nebius GPU computing credits and Positronic evaluation credits.

Positronic Robotics, which runs the independent PhAIL.ai physical AI leaderboard, says the competition responds to a lack of standardized, independent comparisons between robotic foundation models. The company reports that its DROID benchmark has tested open models across more than 1,000 episodes covering over 100 everyday manipulation tasks, all using the same Franka robotic arm. Those tests found wide gaps in performance, with the strongest models completing about 70 percent of tasks on average and the weakest around 12 percent. The organizers argue these results show robotic manipulation is still an open research problem, and that smaller development teams have a real chance to compete with established laboratories.

Nebius is supplying the GPU infrastructure and its Physical AI Workbench, while Positronic will oversee the evaluation of submitted models. The organizers have cited the DARPA Grand Challenge as an inspiration, pointing to how that event used standardized technical challenges to speed up autonomous vehicle development. The competition extends an existing partnership in which Nebius became a founding partner of Positronic's PhAIL.ai leaderboard. Registration and submission details are published at competition.phail.ai.

Articles.Title: Nebius and Positronic launch physical AI competition to test robot manipulation models - Robotics & Automation News

stories.Headline: Together AI's Hassan El Mghari: A Costco Earnings Model Landed Within 4.4% — Because Two Errors Cancelled Out
stories.Summary:
A language model built a Costco earnings forecast from 214 public filings and landed within 4.4% of the actual profit result after the retailer raised its membership fees in July 2024. Hassan El Mghari, a developer-experience lead at Together AI, and his father Omar, a CPA with 25 years at Big Four audit firms, presented the case at the AI Engineer conference. When Omar examined the assumptions, he found the close result was an accident, because two errors offset each other. The model applied the fee increase to Costco's entire international membership, although only US and Canadian members were affected, and it assumed executive-tier members made up 15% of the base when the company's filings disclosed 45%.

The pipeline was otherwise carefully built, using timestamped facts, models with training data that predated the event, structured formula output, automated checks and 16 parallel runs that cost 19 cents in total. Only five of the 16 runs passed the checks, and across those five the forecasts varied widely, from 0.7% to 5.2% error, with the fee-increase profit estimates ranging from $500 million to $6 billion against a recalculated figure of about $450 million. The model also cited a real Costco filing for the executive-tier claim, but that filing contained no such number, and the 15% figure was invented along with a 5% to 30% range. Omar also found an input tied to US and Canadian sales that had no effect on the forecast at all, a problem the automated checks missed. When he corrected only the executive-tier share to the disclosed 45%, the error rose to 28%.

Hassan described the lesson as a reminder that a human expert needs to stay involved, and Omar argued that expert review should feed the checks the system uses rather than serve as a final gate. Omar compared the setup to the three-lines-of-defense audit model, with automated checks as the first line, codified accounting checks as the second, and expert judgment as the third. Hassan admitted he had thought the 4.4% result was excellent because he is not an accountant. The presenters said the case shows that passing engineering checks does not establish that a model's assumptions are correct, and that an expert is needed to identify which assumptions to question.

Articles.Title: Together AI's Hassan El Mghari: A Costco Earnings Model Landed Within 4.4% — Because Two Errors Cancelled Out - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Stifel CEO: Using Anthropic's AI tools made us realize we need more positions
stories.Summary:
Stifel CEO Ron Kruszewski spoke on Fox Business's "The Claman Countdown" on November 10, 2026, about his firm's use of Anthropic's AI tools. He described integrating Anthropic's Claude AI into the workflow of Stifel's financial advisors. The discussion also covered Anthropic's amended S-1 filing, which offers 825 million shares ahead of its planned Nasdaq debut. The clip was published by Fox Business that morning.

Kruszewski said the experience of using Claude inside the firm led Stifel to conclude that it needs more positions. The articles do not spell out which roles would be added or how many. They also do not say how the firm measured the change in advisor productivity. The amended filing, as described in the segment, is the company's step toward listing its shares publicly on Nasdaq.

The 825 million figure is the number of shares in that offering. Kruszewski is the chief executive of Stifel, and the articles attribute the comments about AI and hiring to him. Fox Business's description of the segment says he discussed both the Claude integration and the S-1 amendment. The articles contain no statement from Anthropic or Stifel beyond what was said on air.

They also contain no response from regulators or other parties. The context here is a financial firm reporting that adopting a specific AI product changed its staffing outlook, at the same time that the AI developer prepares to go public. The articles do not say what happens next, such as the timing of the Nasdaq listing, the offering price, or any further hiring announcements by Stifel. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Stifel CEO: Using Anthropic's AI tools made us realize we need more positions

stories.Headline: Right Answer, Wrong Reasons: AI Forecasts Costco - Hassan El Mghari & Omar El Mghari, Together AI｜AI Engineer
stories.Summary:
A podcast episode published on November 9, 2026, by AI Engineer features Hassan El Mghari of Together AI and his father Omar El Mghari, a CPA and former Big Four auditor, presenting a 15-minute talk on using an open-source language model to forecast Costco's profit after its July 2024 membership fee increase. The model's headline result landed within 4.4% of actual profit, averaged across five builds that ranged from 0.7% to 5.2%. Omar's audit found that this accuracy was accidental: the model overstated the member base by applying the fee increase to Costco's entire international membership rather than only US and Canadian members, and it understated the executive-tier share at 15% when Costco's filings disclosed 45%. The two errors pushed the estimate in opposite directions and roughly canceled out.

The team built the model from about 214 Costco public filings, converted into roughly 3,000 timestamped facts and filtered to those available before a cutoff set a couple of weeks before the announcement. They used models trained before the event, GPT-OSS-120B and Llama-3.3 70B, after finding that newer models already knew about the fee change. The pipeline had the model output structured formulas and assumptions rather than doing arithmetic end to end, then ran 16 parallel sessions at a total cost of 19 cents, keeping the five that passed automated checks. Costco raised its standard membership fee from $60 to $65 and its executive fee from $120 to $130, its first increase since 2017. The model predicted a $560 million profit increase over two years, and Omar's testing showed the result was fragile: correcting only the executive-tier share pushed the error to 28%.

Omar presented the work as an example of the three-lines-of-defense model used in auditing, with Hassan's automated checks as the first line, codifiable accounting checks as the second, and expert review as the third. He argued that a subject-matter expert in the loop is essential, saying "Luck is not a control in the auditing world." Hassan acknowledged that he saw the 4.4% figure and considered it excellent because he does not come from accounting, and that the gap was visible only to someone who knew which assumptions to question. The talk suggests that expert review can be turned into specific checks that make a system more autonomous over time, though it notes that identifying those checks still required an accountant's judgment.
