The same attorneys also represent Eight Mile Style, the publisher that administers songs by Eminem, which filed a separate copyright suit against Suno the same day in the same court. That complaint accuses Suno of training on copyrighted works and using copyrighted lyrics in its outputs. Earlier, in late October, Elvis Presley Enterprises had sued the AI developer Anthropic over alleged direct copyright infringement. The article does not say how the court will rule on these claims or when any hearings are scheduled.

Articles.Title: Elvis Presley rights holders sue AI music generator over licensing, copyright violations

stories.Headline: AI-assisted atomic models reveal how protective shells regulate aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Tohoku University have used a newly developed AI agent, called MLP Copilot, to build atomic models that show how protective oxide shells control the oxidation of aluminum nanoparticles. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on October 15, 2026, and the team's findings were reported on November 9, 2026. Aluminum nanoparticles store a large amount of chemical energy, but the thin oxide shell on their surface can limit how quickly they react with oxygen. Understanding how that shell changes could help future efforts to control oxidation and the release of energy.

The framework learns atomic energies and forces from quantum calculations, and the resulting models make larger simulations feasible. Across roughly 80 active-learning iterations, the team assembled 88,833 atomic configurations, with uncertain cases guiding additional quantum calculations and model training. Before using the model in oxidation simulations, the researchers checked it against reference results, thermodynamic properties and independent cluster tests. The coordination methods can be reused across other materials systems, with calculations, training data and validation adjusted for each application. Throughout the workflow, AI agents organized project knowledge and retrieved evidence, while computational tools kept datasets, model versions and evaluation reports.

The lead researcher, Hao Li, a distinguished professor at the Advanced Institute for Materials Research at Tohoku University, said the framework is meant to make materials science more efficient while keeping humans in control. The authors of the paper include Yiming Lu and colleagues. According to the researchers, human scientists still decided which models to accept, where to use them and how to interpret the results. Li compared the system to an autopilot that eases the work of pilots without replacing them.

The simulations found two behaviors in particles with an existing oxide shell. At moderate temperatures within the study, temporary nanoscale pathways let oxidation continue while limiting material transport, a behavior the team called a "breathing mode." At higher temperatures, the shell ruptured, exposing the aluminum core to oxygen and speeding up oxidation. The analyses pointed to outward aluminum transport as the dominant pathway under the conditions studied. The researchers also said that this kind of workflow could support future research into recursive self-improvement, though that idea remains a possibility rather than a demonstrated result.

Articles.Title: AI-assisted atomic models reveal how protective shells regulate aluminum nanoparticle oxidation

stories.Headline: AI used to predict cavities
stories.Summary:
Researchers from New York University and several Brazilian universities used artificial intelligence to identify groups of people at high risk for tooth decay, and published their findings in the journal Caries Research on November 9, 2026. The team, led by Fernando Neves Hugo, chair of the Department of Epidemiology and Health Promotion at NYU College of Dentistry, analyzed existing data from the Brazilian Oral Health Survey, a national study coordinated by the Brazilian Ministry of Health. The data covered 23,726 people who took part in the 2023 survey, including children, adolescents and adults. The researchers ran several machine learning models on this data, which captures demographic details, social factors such as wealth, household density, private dental insurance and water source, behaviors such as time since the last dental visit, and clinical exam results for tooth decay.

The traditional analysis found that wealth and household density were the strongest predictors of cavity risk, with non-white populations at higher risk in every age group. Private dental insurance and recent dental visits were protective, and water source mattered a great deal: 62.5% of 12-year-olds without access to fluoridated water had cavities, compared with 35.5% of those who had fluoridated water. The AI models were able to predict cavity risk and severity by age group by weighing how much each factor contributed. Hugo said the approach can flag individuals whose profiles signal elevated risk that would otherwise be hidden inside community averages. The article does not describe any change to clinical practice or policy that the study requires.

Hugo said the tools could help target resources and preventive care to the groups that would benefit most, and he framed the approach as a way to make better use of limited public health funds. The researchers caution that the findings may carry over to other middle-income countries, but that local factors such as access to dental care and benefits would likely change which variables matter most elsewhere. Their stated goal is to repeat the analysis with factors specific to other countries. Hugo and his colleagues are preparing a similar analysis using data from the United States National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Additional authors are Jessye Melgarejo do Amaral Giordani, Orlando Luiz do Amaral Júnior and Maria Laura Braccini Fagundes of the Federal University of Santa Maria, and Juliana Balbinot Hilgert of the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul.

Articles.Title: AI used to predict cavities

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang is living proof that AI’s rockstar CEOs are also a hidden risk
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board said on Sunday, November 8, 2026 that it is investigating reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair with an executive who, according to reports, was working with Chinese intelligence, and US officials reportedly suspect that person passed intelligence to China and helped smuggle advanced AI chips into the country. Huang said he was unfaithful, that his conduct hurt his wife and children, and that he takes full responsibility and accepts the criticism that follows. He also said he supports the board's investigation, and he did not name the other person involved.

The article's central point is that the fortunes of many leading AI companies depend heavily on a single leader, a risk often called "key man risk." Analyst Dan Ives told CNN that such powerful CEOs are both a blessing and a curse, and Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld said these companies have built a "solar system model" of leadership that can be problematic and needs deeper bench strength. Sonnenfeld noted that Nvidia has no obvious board succession plan, and that Huang has bragged about having 60 direct reports. The article contrasts this with JPMorgan Chase, which has built a deep roster of talent behind Jamie Dimon. Nvidia's annual filing says the company is "highly dependent" on its executive team and acknowledges that failure to ensure effective succession planning could hinder its long-term success.

The article describes Huang as central to Nvidia's rise into a company valued at $4.5 trillion, and as the industry's most prominent voice in Washington and abroad. It cites his role at a White House meeting in September 2026 on AI safety, his help in assembling a $500 billion plan to keep money flowing into AI chips, and his promotion of "sovereign AI" in European capitals. Nvidia disclosed $99 billion in equity investments across the AI ecosystem in September, up from $2.2 billion two years earlier. Sonnenfeld estimated only a 50/50 chance that Huang keeps his job, given the multiple investigations from the board and congressional committees, and suggested the board could move him into a symbolic role or bring in an experienced outside leader such as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. The article's account ends there, so the outcome of the investigation is not yet known.

Articles.Title: Jensen Huang is living proof that AI’s rockstar CEOs are also a hidden risk

stories.Headline: Dot-Com lessons for the AI bubble
stories.Summary:
Chi Onwurah, a Labour Party member of the U.K. Parliament and chair of the House of Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, published an opinion piece on November 10, 2026, in The Korea Times, distributed by Project Syndicate, arguing that the current artificial intelligence investment boom may be a bubble and that the late-1990s dot-com crash offers warnings. Drawing on her own experience as an engineer at a telecoms infrastructure company that collapsed in the early 2000s, she describes how that boom ended with the loss of her job and visa. She notes that firms such as Global Crossing and WorldCom filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, while Nortel Networks and Lucent lost about 99 percent of their stock value. She says the infrastructure providers of that era relied heavily on debt and on "vendor financing," in which suppliers helped their own customers pay for products, and she sees similar circular arrangements in today's AI sector.

Onwurah points to specific examples of this circularity. She cites Anthropic buying compute capacity powered by Nvidia chips from a company in which Nvidia is a major investor, and Microsoft investing more than $13 billion in OpenAI while also selling it cloud services through its Azure division. She also writes that justifying the trillions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure would require more than $2.5 trillion in annual revenue by 2030, and that this revenue would likely have to come from customers cutting costs, mainly salaries. Her view is that such cuts could cause societal upheaval, and that a financial crash could follow either from that process or from markets concluding that AI firms cannot repay their debts. She argues that today's scale of debt is far larger than in 2001 and closer to the run-up to the 2008 financial crisis, and that the technology, media, and telecommunications sector now accounts for nearly half of the broader U.S. large-cap equity market, up from one-fifth during the 2008 crisis.

Onwurah says booms end when lenders stop funding them, pointing to American Express suspending her former company's credit cards months before its bankruptcy filing. She asks whether money withdrawn from AI could flow into productive investment elsewhere, such as in Newcastle or in youth unemployment, or instead into safe assets like gold, and says she does not know the answer. She concludes that with the U.K. placing AI at the center of its ambitions during its 2027 G20 presidency, the country's agenda should include security, standards and planning for a possible crash. The article does not describe any formal government action or response to her arguments.

Articles.Title: Dot-Com lessons for the AI bubble

stories.Headline: Enticed by massive GPU sales···The AI chip ‘backdoor’ market reexamined amid the Jensen Huang affair
stories.Summary:
Reporting from Korea's Kyunghyang Shinmun on November 10, 2026, describes how an adultery scandal involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has drawn renewed attention to a practice in which China has reportedly obtained advanced AI chips through Southeast Asia despite US export controls. The woman involved, Alice Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm suspected of illicitly exporting graphics processing units. According to industry sources cited in the article, Megaspeed has grown into the largest buyer of Nvidia GPUs in Southeast Asia. Bloomberg reported that from 2023 through November 2025 the company procured at least 4.6 billion dollars in Nvidia equipment and leased computing capacity to Chinese companies, including Alibaba.

The article also reports that the US Commerce Department had been investigating allegations that Megaspeed illegally exported GPUs, citing the New York Times. In August of last year, Nvidia's top legal officer reportedly asked to meet Commerce officials and said he had secured the approval of a deputy secretary, after which the inquiry was halted. This has prompted allegations that Nvidia tried to influence the probe to protect its GPU sales. US short seller Culper Research estimated in May that more than 20 percent of Nvidia's computing revenue in fiscal 2026 came from Chinese demand routed through Southeast Asia and other regions, and its founder, Christian Lamarco, said he had identified at least six more firms with similar warning signs. Separately, Bain & Company reported that data center capacity in Southeast Asia rose 45 percent in half a year, from 4 gigawatts at the end of last year to 5.8 gigawatts in the first half of this year, and the Institute for Progress estimated that about 75 percent of AI compute Chinese firms access remotely from overseas is concentrated in the region.

The article explains that US policy has largely allowed remote leasing of chips while blocking physical smuggling. The Biden administration's AI Proliferation Rule, which would have restricted exports to places such as Malaysia and Singapore, was rescinded by the Trump administration two days before it was to take effect after industry objections. More recently, Nvidia has required overseas cloud providers to sell at least 51 percent of their services to customers outside China, and on the 4th it emerged that Oracle, under US government pressure, canceled a GPU leasing deal with Tencent. On the 9th, Republican Representative Jim Banks and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren called for tougher export controls on AI chips bound for China, and supporters of a Chip Security Act pressed for mandatory location tracking of GPUs overseas. A domestic AI industry source quoted in the article said that chip purchases through routes such as Malaysia had long been an open secret, and that confirmed violations could cause serious damage to the industry.

Articles.Title: Enticed by massive GPU sales···The AI chip ‘backdoor’ market reexamined amid the Jensen Huang affair

stories.Headline: AI-interpreted echocardiograms comparable to human reports, cardiologists' time cut by about 50%
stories.Summary:
An AI tool that drafts echocardiogram reports was tested against reports prepared by ultrasound technicians and cardiologists, and the researchers found the AI-assisted reports were comparable in accuracy. The study was presented on Monday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago, and it was described as new, independent, preliminary late-breaking science. An echocardiogram is a heart ultrasound, the most widely used type of heart imaging. Normally a sonographer acquires the images and a cardiologist reviews them and writes the report. The trial was reported as the first randomized trial testing an AI tool to write a full echocardiogram report, including interpretations and measurements.

In the trial, an AI tool, a sonographer and a cardiologist each prepared preliminary reports for the same 1,200 echocardiograms that had been obtained during routine care. Cardiologists then reviewed and finalized these drafts without knowing which source had produced each one. Cardiologists made substantial changes to 50.6% of the AI-generated drafts, compared with 49.7% of the human-prepared drafts, which met the study's criteria for noninferiority. Cardiologists spent an average of 4.6 minutes per scan reviewing AI drafts, compared with 8.5 minutes to write reports without AI help, a saving of about 46%. The AI-assisted reports were also more consistent with historical reports in the medical record, and reviewers could not tell which drafts came from the AI.

The lead investigator, Keane K. Lee, a cardiologist at Kaiser Permanente Santa Clara Homestead Medical Center, said the team expected strong accuracy but was surprised by how much time the tool saved. Lee said that saving a few minutes per scan could add up over a day and could mean faster results and more time with patients. Lee also said that AI cannot replace the human team, and that the cardiologist remains responsible for the interpretation and for certifying the final report. The article notes that a July 2026 study in the Journal of the American Heart Association projected a national shortfall of about 7,000 cardiologists by 2036, which the authors cited as a reason to strengthen the workforce.

The study drew on 1,200 exams performed over two weeks in March 2025 at 21 medical centers across Kaiser Permanente Northern California, with patients averaging 69 years of age. Nine sonographers and 20 cardiologists took part. The article lists several limitations: the study did not test whether AI-assisted interpretation improves patients' long-term health, and cardiologists knew they were in the study and may have changed their usual habits. The article says more research is needed to see how the tool performs in everyday clinical settings at larger scale. The findings were published in the Journal of the American Heart Association.

Articles.Title: AI-interpreted echocardiograms comparable to human reports, cardiologists' time cut by about 50%

stories.Headline: Trump Shares AI Video of Dana White Berating Reporters Days After Violent Cartoon Post
stories.Summary:
On November 9, 2026, President Donald Trump posted two AI-generated videos on Truth Social showing a fake version of UFC CEO Dana White acting as White House press secretary. The first clip layered White's likeness over years-old footage of rapper Lil Yachty performing on a Chicago festival stage in 2021, and it showed White dancing and rapping at a podium bearing the presidential seal. Minutes later, Trump posted a second, 13-second video in which the fake White angrily scolds reporters, one of whom holds a microphone labeled "FAKE NEWS." The videos followed a cartoon Trump had posted the day before, on November 8, depicting White sending UFC fighters to attack journalists. Those posts came just after Trump said he had only been joking when he offered White the press secretary job.

The videos were published as Trump continued a running joke about White and the role, which has been largely vacant since Karoline Leavitt left the White House in August. Trump had brought White into the briefing room that afternoon for an impromptu press conference, where he said the UFC president loved the idea and would do a good job. White flew to Washington after UFC fights in London on November 8, and he told TMZ that he was heading to the White House to have Trump sign a trading card commemorating the UFC Freedom 250 fights held on the president's 80th birthday in June. He said he has "less than zero political aspirations" and that the press secretary idea came from Trump, who put it out publicly. The articles do not describe any formal change in policy or any consequence arising from the videos.

White has said he will leave the decision about the job to Trump and is not going to respond with disrespect, while stating that he has many other jobs and is busy with obligations in several states. He told reporters in the briefing room that the past 24 hours had been insane and that he had no interest in politics. Trump, for his part, described White as someone who would be good in the role and said he was only kidding when he first offered it. The articles frame the episode as part of a pattern of Trump posting satirical and AI-generated content, though they do not report any response from the press corps beyond the scripted lines within the video itself.

Articles.Title: Trump Shares AI Video of Dana White Berating Reporters Days After Violent Cartoon Post

stories.Headline: Hitjis and Jenus music videos will be created through an AI video contest
stories.Summary:
MindSpark is running the generative AI video contest "The 3rd Korea AI Advertising Awards," accepting entries from November 9 through midnight on November 30. This year's biggest change is a music video category that uses unreleased new songs from two idol groups, the five-member girl group Hitjis, who debuted in April of last year, and the five-member boy group Jenus, who debuted in April of this year. Entrants can pick a track from either group and make a music video with generative AI. MindSpark will choose one standout work per track and give each winner 1 million KRW.

The category is meant to ease a real burden on rookie idols, since sets, filming crews, and equipment quickly push production costs up. Several creators can interpret the same song through different videos, letting Hitjis and Jenus review multiple versions of a music video for one new track. Entrants also get hands-on experience making videos for newly debuted idols. The organizers present it as a chance to see how far AI video can extend beyond advertising into music content.

Alongside the music category, the contest is running brand advertising briefs from 14 companies across finance, beauty, food, and robotics. Samsung Securities wants ads that make pension products approachable for younger audiences, while JB Financial Group seeks ads that present its group image with an MZ-generation sensibility. Entrants may submit a horizontal AI Video Ad (16:9, 30 seconds) or a vertical AI Short-form Video (9:16, 30 seconds to 1 minute), with one work per category and the option to try several brands. Anyone aged 14 or older can enter individually or as a team, and a new corporate division has been added for production companies and studios.

The contest has grown quickly, with entries rising from 725 in the first edition in May last year to 999 in the second in December, a 38% increase in seven months. The total prize pool has also grown from 47 million KRW to 50 million KRW and now 53 million KRW this year. According to a Ministry of Science and ICT report, 44.5% of people have used generative AI, up 11.2 percentage points in one year. Judging is 80% expert panel and 20% public YouTube vote, and some winning works will be shown on the M-CITY billboard at the Euljiro-ipgu Station intersection in Seoul. A MindSpark representative said AI advertising is no longer an experiment but a production method that brands actually use.

Articles.Title: Hitjis and Jenus music videos will be created through an AI video contest

stories.Headline: AI analysis of ECG data measured by smartwatch may help detect reduced heart pumping function
stories.Summary:
An AI model analyzing electrocardiogram recordings taken by smartwatches may help flag a hidden heart condition known as left ventricular systolic dysfunction, according to preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago, held November 6 to 9. The condition, which the study defined as a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% or less, can occur without symptoms and can lead to heart failure if left untreated. The researchers examined whether the software could identify people who might need a traditional screening test, such as an echocardiogram, to check how well the heart pumps. The results varied between watch brands and across recordings, so the findings remain early and exploratory.

In the largest group, 2,211 adults scheduled for an echocardiogram at an outpatient cardiology clinic in South Korea had ECGs recorded on both an Apple Watch and a Samsung Galaxy Watch during the same visit. The AI model distinguished people with and without the condition about equally well on both watches. However, when the same score cutoff was applied to both devices, 200 participants, or 9%, were classified as positive on one watch and negative on the other. A separate group of 146 adults recorded ECGs at home, and requiring positive results on at least two of three consecutive days cut false positives from 18 to nine among the 70 participants without the condition. That rule also missed two cases compared with a single-positive-day rule, and the researchers tested several repeat-testing rules.

Lee, a cardiologist and chief medical officer of Medical AI Co., Ltd., which developed the model, said some people have reduced pumping function without noticeable symptoms. He said the study explored whether smartwatch analysis could help identify people who may benefit from additional screening. Lee also noted that a single smartwatch ECG is a snapshot and that repeated recordings can give different results. He said larger studies are needed to determine how best to use these results to guide further evaluation.

The study was conducted at Incheon Sejong Hospital, with the first group enrolled from July 2023 to May 2024 and the second from July 2024 to December 2025. Because participants were patients referred for echocardiography, many already with known heart failure, the results may not apply to the general population, and the researchers adjusted their estimates for lower prevalence. The study did not determine whether using these AI results leads to earlier treatment, fewer hospitalizations or improved survival. Its limitations include the single hospital setting and the small number of participants in the repeat-testing analysis.

Articles.Title: AI analysis of ECG data measured by smartwatch may help detect reduced heart pumping function

stories.Headline: Goldman CEO Solomon says AI financing remains strong despite market jitters
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon told CNBC on Monday that demand for financing artificial intelligence infrastructure remains strong, even as investors have grown uneasy about the massive spending on AI. He said Goldman has been "very active" in AI capital markets deals in recent weeks and expects that activity to continue over the next two months. The comments came after AI-related stocks, including chipmakers and neocloud providers, had sold off in recent weeks as investors questioned whether the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into AI infrastructure will earn good returns. That selloff began before the U.S. midterm elections and deepened after Democrats won sweeping victories on Tuesday, raising fears that political opposition could slow the industry's expansion.

Solomon said shifts in the political environment will create recalibrations and ups and downs, but he remains firmly convinced of AI's long-term power to drive productivity in the economy. He also defended data center construction against political resistance, arguing that the infrastructure is essential to the U.S. economy and can be built responsibly. He warned that if it is not built in the U.S., the demand for computing power will push it to places outside the country. Goldman is among the banks leading the process for a potential initial public offering by the AI model lab Anthropic, which could become one of the biggest tests yet of public market appetite for AI companies. Solomon declined to discuss the IPO in detail, saying only that the market environment remains fairly constructive.

A separate analysis from Barron's, published by Mint, painted a more cautious picture of the same period. It said the Democratic victory had produced a sharp rally in stocks, a pullback in Treasury yields, and a steep drop in oil prices, but that the AI trade had become a major source of doubt. The article noted that nearly every major local ballot measure opposing data centers was winning or leading, with North Dakota the only exception, which casts doubt on a quarter of next year's buildout and the 96 gigawatts of capacity expected for 2028. It reported that the Nasdaq Composite fell more than 1,300 points on Thursday, that the PHLX Semiconductor index dropped 11% that day, and that Nvidia fell 9.2% to $181.64. The Cboe Volatility Index rose nearly 50% to 24.47, its highest level in seven months.

Taken together, the two accounts show a sharp split between the banker's view that AI financing is still strong and the market's growing concern about the buildout's future. Solomon's comments came from a Monday interview, while the Barron's piece describes the market's reaction later in the week. Neither article says what the next steps will be for the Anthropic IPO or for the local data center fights. Solomon's view rests on continued deal activity and long-term growth, and the Barron's analysis suggests the outcome will depend on whether the political changes meaningfully alter the fundamentals behind AI spending.

Articles.Title: Goldman CEO Solomon says AI financing remains strong despite market jitters

stories.Headline: The AI Trade Looks Like It's Falling Apart. AMD's Earnings Delivered a Reality Check.
stories.Summary:
The AI trade has been under heavy pressure over the past month, with stocks falling after the U.S. midterm results, which saw Democrats win several key states while campaigning against AI data centers. Against that backdrop, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) reported its quarterly earnings, and the article describes them as a reality check amid the bearish wave. The company's data center segment sales almost doubled year over year, driven by record sales of graphics processing units and central processing units. AMD generated $13.4 billion in third-quarter revenue, which exceeded the high end of its guidance. The results also showed rising profit margins, with AMD reporting 95% year-over-year net income growth.

The article argues that demand for chips is still strengthening, and that AMD hinted at a stronger fourth quarter. Because GPUs require liquid cooling, AI racks, memory chips, and optical cables to come online, the article suggests that strong chip sales will drive spending on those other components as well. Nvidia reported similar results for its fiscal second quarter of 2027 and is set to report its third-quarter results on November 17. The author, Marc Guberti of The Motley Fool, says the fundamentals remain strong even though the stock market has reacted negatively. He points to financing concerns and the midterm results as sources of investor anxiety, and he notes that the market is rushing to the sidelines.

He also cites a projection from tech bull Dan Ives that Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta Platforms will exceed $1 trillion in capital expenditures in 2027. He adds that Micron expects its fiscal 2027 to be better than its fiscal 2026. The article also reports that CNN's Fear and Greed Index shows a "Fear" rating, which signals prolonged selling pressure. The author says that news cycles dominate short-term thinking, while fundamentals prevail over the long run. The piece does not say what the stock market will do next, and it notes that the next key data point is the U.S. CPI report due November 10, 2026, at 8:30 AM EST.

Articles.Title: The AI Trade Looks Like It's Falling Apart. AMD's Earnings Delivered a Reality Check.

stories.Headline: Findrix Launches AI Search Platform for Marketing Agencies
stories.Summary:
Findrix, an AI search visibility platform, announced on November 9, 2026 the launch of a platform built for marketing agencies. The product lets agencies offer their clients generative engine optimization, which means getting a brand named and recommended in AI answers, and run that work from a single Findrix account. The announcement was distributed as a paid press release through ACCESS Newswire from Wilmington, Delaware. The platform tracks each client across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode, asking buyer questions several times per engine and attaching a confidence band to each rate. It converts the gaps it finds into website fixes, pages to write and correction letters to sites that state wrong facts.

Agencies can send client reports under their own name and logo and can work with client data inside ChatGPT and Claude through the Findrix MCP server. The company says agency packages are available through its team at findrix.ai/for-agencies. Yosif Merman, co-founder of Findrix, said clients often read falling traffic as a broken SEO strategy when buyers are instead getting answers from AI tools and not clicking through. Tom Wells, an AI search researcher and Findrix's Lead Research Advisor who developed the measurement method, argued that week-to-week swings in AI answers are often normal noise and that a niche baseline lets a brand be judged against its market. The launch adds a benchmark layer: Findrix measures each client against the brands in its own niche, and public benchmarks already cover about 64,000 businesses in 395 categories and cities through AI Rankings Australia, and 1,736 brands in 74 markets through Findrix Radar.

The release supports its case with outside figures. Pew Research Center found that users click a traditional result in 8% of visits when Google shows an AI summary, compared with 15% without one. A 2026 AgencyAnalytics survey of 494 agency professionals found that 66% said AI search is the top service clients ask them to add. The articles do not report independent results for the platform, and they do not say how many agencies or clients currently use it.

Articles.Title: Findrix Launches AI Search Platform for Marketing Agencies

stories.Headline: AI has made applying for jobs impossible—and it’s harming us all
stories.Summary:
Brian McConnell, a longtime San Francisco tech worker, published an opinion piece on 48hills.org on November 9, 2026, arguing that AI has made job applications nearly futile. He describes how automated application bots flood employers with mass submissions, while applicant tracking systems powered by AI filter candidates out before any human reads their resumes. He says he has applied to more than 200 jobs in the past year without a single conversation with a person, that a colleague has sent around 500 applications without a callback, and that his only two interviews were conducted by AI bots. He also points to a Workday lawsuit alleging that its filtering algorithms exclude candidates based on age, race, and disability.

McConnell proposes a low-tech fix: companies would stop accepting online applications and require mailed or in-person submissions instead. He argues that this added friction would make mass automated applications economically unviable while showing employers that a candidate is a real person willing to make an effort. He suggests that some Bay Area employers could test the idea and publish the results, perhaps by mailing verification codes the way banks mail PINs. He says the change would not be costly for the system to adopt. He also notes that a Netflix localization role drew about 2,000 applicants from LinkedIn alone, and that by his math well over 90 percent of those were likely fake or poorly targeted.

McConnell places the problem within the wider history of the tech industry, which he says was once run by inventors and has since been taken over by financial engineers, with the AI boom centered in the Bay Area. He compares the current excitement over AI to the dot com boom, though he says the sums involved are far larger. He also argues that older workers, whom he describes as those over 45 in tech, face the greatest exposure and that friends' advice to simply "get a job" is unhelpful. The article does not describe any formal response from Workday or any employer, and it does not describe any plan by companies to adopt the proposed mail-in system.

Articles.Title: AI has made applying for jobs impossible—and it’s harming us all

stories.Headline: When AI writes, what remains human?
stories.Summary:
Philippe Jaenada, who was named winner of France's Prix Goncourt on November 3, 2026, has admitted using AI three times while writing his prize-winning novel, "L'inconnue du quai de Javel." The admission came amid a wider dispute in France over AI in literature, which the opinion piece links to the removal of Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien from the shortlist in September after allegations of AI use. Orélien denied using AI, while Jaenada acknowledged his actions voluntarily. Social media critics have questioned whether Orélien, a writer of color, was treated more harshly than Jaenada, a white man.

Jaenada said he had inserted a ChatGPT-generated sentence to "play with the reader" and included an AI-generated section to show how unreliable the tool could be on technical questions. The author of the column says his explanations are hard to judge for sincerity. The dispute has also produced a new literary award, the Pascal Prize, which accepts only works created with AI and requires applicants to submit a technical dossier naming the large language models used and the prompts that started the work. Its jury is chaired by futurist Jacques Attali. The organizers first proposed a Goncourt AI Prize, but the Goncourt rejected that idea, saying it honors books written by humans, not machines.

The column draws two lessons for Korea. First, the Goncourt remains France's most prestigious literary award, so an AI controversy there carries real weight. Second, the French debate has split into acceptance of the technology on one side and insistence on purely human authorship on the other, and the writer argues Korea would gain little by copying that rigid division. Publisher L'Observatoire plans a label called "Sanctuaire" to certify fully human-authored works, which the column presents as part of that polarization.

The column argues that AI use is already spreading through Korean writing, translation and research faster than these debates are moving. Lee Eun-hye, head of the publisher Geulhangari, wrote on Facebook that she has received noticeably more translation proposals from master's and doctoral candidates, and that some of the samples are suspiciously polished. She told the columnist she strongly suspects some of those samples were prepared with AI. The column also cites Kim Seong-woo's 2024 book, which describes how AI can let researchers write while relying on machine summaries instead of reading the original papers. The author ends by asking what distinguishes human intellectual work once machines can write, summarize and translate, and says it is time to reconsider what it means for writing to be entirely human.

Articles.Title: When AI writes, what remains human?

stories.Headline: Calif. hospital system loses nearly $3M in elaborate AI fraud scheme
stories.Summary:
A California hospital system lost $2,968,497 in December 2024 to an international fraud scheme in which scammers allegedly used advanced artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys. Federal prosecutors announced the case on Friday, November 6, 2026, with the hospital system unnamed in the public filings. The unsealed indictment says the hospital was one of many companies worldwide defrauded of more than $129 million between 2024 and 2026. Other victims included a Missouri hospital system that lost $4.8 million, a Rhode Island bank that lost $2.7 million, and a British financial technology company that lost $11.6 million.

Three men, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, are accused of using AI-generated voices and images to pose as chief executives and lawyers, persuading employees to wire millions of dollars. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain in June and August, and Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. All three face seven federal charges, including wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering, and extradition requests are still pending. The scheme reportedly began with fraudulent emails, sometimes sent through platforms such as DocuSign, asking staff to sign nondisclosure agreements for confidential transactions.

Prosecutors say the stolen money moved through accounts in nine countries, including China, Spain and the United Arab Emirates, before being converted into cryptocurrency. U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald, in a statement, said the technology offers tremendous potential but that some people seek to use it for criminal goals. McDonald said the defendants abused advanced AI to impersonate real people and deceive corporate executives. Soall allegedly scripted a call he called "Lawyer Call," posing as a British attorney and discouraging victims from discussing the transactions with colleagues.

Prosecutors also allege Hazan helped launder the money and boasted of laundering more than $400 million over three years. The case shows how AI tools can make impersonation schemes more convincing to the employees targeted, and the charges reflect the government's effort to hold the alleged participants accountable across borders. The articles do not say whether the hospital system has been identified publicly or whether any of the stolen funds have been recovered. Next steps include the pending extradition requests and the court proceedings on the seven federal charges.

Articles.Title: Calif. hospital system loses nearly $3M in elaborate AI fraud scheme

stories.Headline: Kolmar Korea's AI lip maker wins top CES beauty award
stories.Summary:
Kolmar Korea, a South Korean beauty company, has won three innovation awards at CES 2027 for two AI-powered devices, including the top Best of Innovation Award in the beauty tech category. The honor went to ChromaFlow, a system that creates personalized lip colors in about one minute. The company's skin care device, LumiJet Pro, also earned an Innovation Award in the artificial intelligence category. The Korea Herald reported the news on November 10, 2026.

ChromaFlow uses AI sensors to assess a user's lips and determine a customized color based on their natural lip tone. The system then blends pigments from seven color cartridges according to an AI-generated formula. LumiJet Pro analyzes skin condition and thickness before delivering skin care ingredients through its NanoJet technology, which sprays ultrafine particles onto the skin. The device also uses specific wavelengths of light to help disperse those ingredients.

Kolmar Korea developed the nanoparticle formulation used in the device. The recognition marks the second consecutive year that Kolmar Korea has won the top Beauty Tech award. At CES 2026, its AI-powered Scar Beauty Device, designed for scar care and makeup coverage, received the same honor. A company official said the win recognizes its data-driven manufacturing technology, which connects the entire cosmetics production process through AI.

The official added that the company will keep developing its beauty tech platform using accumulated data. Kolmar Korea plans to build a beauty tech data platform using skin and color data collected through ChromaFlow, the Scar Beauty Device and Caiome, an AI-powered scalp analysis system. The platform is intended to connect skin analysis, personalized cosmetic formulation and manufacturing, allowing the company to expand its data-driven beauty services. The company will showcase ChromaFlow and LumiJet Pro at CES 2027, scheduled for January 6 to 9 at the Venetian Expo in Las Vegas.

Articles.Title: Kolmar Korea's AI lip maker wins top CES beauty award

stories.Headline: AI Model Accurately Estimates Pediatric Chest Circumference From Single Frontal Photographs
stories.Summary:
An artificial intelligence pipeline can estimate the chest circumference of children with microtia from a single frontal photograph, according to a single-center observational diagnostic-accuracy study published in the European Journal of Medical Research. The article reports that the approach combines keypoint detection with a geometric model to produce the measurement without contact. Researchers from the study team tested the method on a group of 500 children, split evenly between boys and girls, and compared its estimates with reference measurements taken by trained personnel. Accurate measurement of the subxiphoid chest circumference is needed for clinical assessment and treatment planning in children with microtia.

Conventional tape measurement requires an in-person visit and can suffer from site errors when untrained caregivers perform it. The researchers used a YOLO11-pose model to locate bilateral chest points in one frontal photograph, then applied a Ramanujan ellipse model that sets chest depth at 0.75 times width. A lateral view was used only to check chest depth. The cohort was divided into 400 cases for development and a locked test set of 100 cases.

In the locked test set, the pipeline reported a mean absolute error of 0.938 cm, a root mean squared error of 1.193 cm, and a median absolute error of 0.80 cm, with a mean bias of −0.127 cm. Estimates fell within 2 cm, 3 cm, and 5 cm of reference values in 93.0%, 99.0%, and 100% of cases, and the Pearson correlation was 0.935. At a 60-cm threshold, sensitivity was 87.3%, specificity was 100.0%, and overall accuracy was 90.0%. Error was somewhat higher in overweight or obese children, at 1.025 cm, than in normal-weight children, at 0.897 cm.

The authors, led by X. Li and colleagues, state that automated landmark detection reduces site error by non-medical users. They cautioned, however, that all photographs were taken under controlled conditions, so the reported performance may not carry over directly to in-home use, and that larger cohorts are needed for further validation. The article does not describe any clinical rollout or next steps beyond that validation. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI Model Accurately Estimates Pediatric Chest Circumference From Single Frontal Photographs

stories.Headline: DEEPX's AI chip built on Samsung's 2-nanometer foundry process wins CES award
stories.Summary:
DEEPX, a South Korean neural processing unit developer, said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that it had won a CES 2027 Innovation Award in the artificial intelligence category for its next-generation AI semiconductor. The winning product is the DX-M2, an ultra-low-power chip built on Samsung Electronics' 2-nanometer foundry process. The company said the chip is designed to run inference on large language models and vision-language models. Its design allows generative AI applications on robots and industrial devices without depending on cloud computing. The chip is meant to support on-device generative AI inference, which reduces reliance on cloud services, and it draws around 5 watts of power.

DEEPX completed the chip's tape-out earlier in November. Initial mass production is scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2027, with full-scale production slated to begin in 2028. The article notes that the picture accompanying the report shows the DX-M2 chip. DEEPX's announcement was made through a company statement reported by Yonhap News Agency, and the article attributes the award and product details to the company. The article does not include comments from Samsung Electronics or from the CES organizers beyond identifying the award's name and category.

It also does not describe the award's selection process or the chip's performance against competing products. The report places the chip within the broader push toward AI hardware that runs locally rather than in the cloud, a shift the company frames as its core aim. The article does not say whether the chip has customers or partners beyond its foundry relationship with Samsung. It also gives no further timeline beyond the mass production and full-scale production dates.

Articles.Title: DEEPX's AI chip built on Samsung's 2-nanometer foundry process wins CES award

stories.Headline: New AI malware ranks victims by how much they're worth
stories.Summary:
New malware called VOLTA-AUTODOXER, uncovered by researchers at Cisco Talos, steals data from Windows computers and then uses artificial intelligence to rank victims by how valuable they might be to criminals. The malware collects saved browser passwords, payment card details, login sessions, cryptocurrency wallet information and certain work-related credentials. It also gathers saved Wi-Fi passwords, screenshots and information from applications such as Microsoft Outlook and Slack. The findings were reported in an article published on November 9, 2026, by Fox News.

The stolen information is sent to an AI model through a platform called OpenRouter, which is instructed to act like an intelligence analyst. The model is asked to produce a section titled "WHAT THEY'RE WORTH," assigning low, medium or high rankings to valuable information. A second section, "THEIR OPSEC," examines the victim's security habits, including password practices. The malware can also search Gmail receipts and order histories from services such as Uber Eats, DoorDash, Grubhub, Amazon and Walmart to help confirm a victim's home address. Researchers say the AI analysis is optional, and the malware can still send the data to attackers if that step fails.

Cisco Talos found that the malware uses Anthropic's Claude as its default AI model, with Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash as fallbacks if a model refuses the request. The resulting assessment can be sent to criminals through Telegram. The article notes that researchers identified these capabilities by analyzing the malware's code and have not established that criminals have used the AI rankings to choose real-world victims for further attacks. The malware can also delete its main executable after finishing, though it may leave a diagnostic file called volta_debug.txt behind that records what was collected and whether the AI analysis succeeded.

Articles.Title: New AI malware ranks victims by how much they're worth

stories.Headline: AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3B in 8 months
stories.Summary:
Nominal, a four-year-old Austin-based startup that makes an AI platform for engineering and testing complex hardware such as aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has tripled its valuation to $3 billion. The company announced on Monday that it raised a $240 million Series C, led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners. The round follows a $155 million Series B extension announced in March at a $1 billion valuation, led by Trae Stephens of Founders Fund. That earlier deal was a preemptive offer, meaning the investor initiated it rather than the startup. Other backers include Sequoia, General Catalyst, and Lux Capital.

Nominal says it counts 80 commercial and government organizations as customers, including Anduril, the defense company co-founded by Stephens. In October, the U.S. Air Force selected Nominal for a $71.2 million Strategic Funding Increase, known as STRATFI, a program that requires matching funds from outside the Air Force. The article does not say what the matching funds must total or how that requirement will be met. The funding is aimed at helping the company expand its work with the military and other large buyers of complex hardware. The article does not provide further details on how the money will be deployed.

Nominal's chief executive and co-founder, Cameron McCord, is a former U.S. Navy submarine officer who previously worked at Anduril. The company's rapid rise in valuation reflects strong investor interest in AI tools for building and testing physical systems, a category that sits alongside software for defense and industrial customers. The article does not describe any plans for future rounds, public offerings, or product launches. It also does not indicate whether the valuation increase signals changes in the company's revenue or headcount. The story was reported by TechCrunch's Julie Bort, and the information comes from the company's announcement and the investors involved.

Articles.Title: AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3B in 8 months

stories.Headline: Essential Reading in an Era of AI Doomsaying
stories.Summary:
Shannon Vallor, a professor of ethics of data and artificial intelligence at the University of Edinburgh, published a reading list on Nautilus on November 9, 2026, recommending ten books as a response to what she calls the current wave of AI doomsaying. She describes doom predictions as everywhere, spreading from the media into everyday conversation and shaping how people think about the future. The list is organized as five pairs of fiction and nonfiction titles, each chosen to offer a vision of how broken situations can be repaired rather than how the world ends. Vallor says the books are meant to help readers think about the future and technology with more love, courage and wisdom.

Vallor is clear that she does not dismiss the risks. She says today's AI technologies are dangerous to human agency, to self-understanding, to relationships, to people's ability to think for themselves, and to prospects for living sustainably. Her case rests on the distinction between doomsaying and calls to action. Doomsaying, she argues, produces decision paralysis, apathy and resignation, while calls to action restore a sense of agency, purpose and moral urgency. She notes that her own book, The AI Mirror, published in 2024, comes from the same concern that reasonable fears cannot be avoided by looking away from them.

The selections include Imagining AI, edited by Stephen Cave and Kanta Dihal, which gathers essays on AI from many regions, and Becky Chambers's A Psalm for the Wild-Built, a gentle story about humans and machines learning when to stop. Vallor pairs Adam Becker's Everything Forever with N.K. Jemisin's The Fifth Season, and Carissa Véliz's Prophecy with Samuel Butler's Erewhon. Other picks include Ruha Benjamin's Imagination, Ursula K. Le Guin's The Lathe of Heaven, David Karpf's Vaporware, Inc, due in 2027, and Neal Stephenson's The Diamond Age. Vallor characterizes Karpf's book as a critique of "digital futurism," a pattern of promised technological abundance that she says keeps failing to arrive.

Articles.Title: Essential Reading in an Era of AI Doomsaying

stories.Headline: SPH Media looks to plug into AI channels without losing its place in the news
stories.Summary:
SPH Media, the Singapore publisher, is seeking a place in the channels through which people increasingly find news rather than trying to resist artificial intelligence, according to executive chairman Chan Yeng Kit. He has voiced concern that publishers could lose their role between reporting and audiences if AI services become a main route to information. The article, published on 9 November 2026 by Tomorrow's Publisher, frames this as part of a wider shift in which news organisations have depended on technology platforms for distribution. Earlier reliance on search and social media left publishers exposed when platform priorities changed, and AI services that summarise journalism may add to that pressure. The risk is that readers take in information without visiting or recognising the outlets that produced it.

SPH Media's response includes a partnership with Google meant to extend the reach of its journalism through Google's channels. The partnership also aims to strengthen newsroom capabilities in areas including generative AI verification and AI-enabled workflows. The two companies have named talent development and audience engagement as areas of cooperation. The article stresses that these are stated aims, and that their practical effect on publisher control and sustainable revenue remains uncertain. Alongside this, the Chinese-language publication Lianhe Zaobao has launched an English-language website using AI-assisted translation with human proofreading and editing.

The initiative is meant to reach younger readers and other language communities while keeping its Chinese-language edition. Malay and Tamil offerings are expected to be considered progressively as the operation develops. Chan has argued that technology can extend the audience for existing journalism but that reporting still depends on people's ability to build trust, draw out personal accounts and make editorial decisions. The article cites the Associated Press, whose standards say AI may assist newsroom work but does not replace journalists' responsibility for gathering and assessing facts.

Staff must verify AI-generated material and remain accountable for published work. ProPublica is also quoted as saying AI-assisted journalism must receive human review and meet the newsroom's usual editorial standards. The article notes that the tools and their effects are still developing, leaving publishers to balance access to new distribution systems against the risk of becoming less visible to audiences. SPH Media presents its approach as adaptation, alongside investment in a range of products and the fundamentals of journalism.

Articles.Title: SPH Media looks to plug into AI channels without losing its place in the news

stories.Headline: Apple Makes Major AI Pricing Move as New Revenue Opportunity Emerges
stories.Summary:
Apple has introduced paid usage packs for subscribers who go past their monthly AI limits in its Creator Studio applications. The company, which is based in the United States and makes the iPhone, is trying to turn artificial intelligence into a direct source of revenue. The move was reported on November 9, 2026, by GuruFocus and republished by Yahoo Finance. It marks one of Apple's earliest attempts to charge directly for AI use inside its software.

The AI features cover several creative and productivity apps, including Keynote, Pages, Numbers, Pixelmator Pro, Freeform and Logic Pro. They include image and shape generation, presentation creation, image enhancement and AI help for music production. Subscribers on the entry-level allowance can generate 50 images, 250 shapes and 50 presentations each month, along with presenter notes covering 700 slides. Customers who go beyond those limits can buy additional intelligence usage packs for $49.99. Apple said the feature is available to active Creator Studio subscribers in eight countries, including the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Germany and India.

Apple confirmed the change itself, and the article describes it as part of the company's broader AI strategy. The article also notes that Apple works with outside AI providers, including OpenAI and Google, to support some of these capabilities. Apple has not said how much revenue it expects from the packs or how many subscribers are likely to exceed their monthly allowances. The article links the change to the company's Services segment, which brought in $31.57 billion in its latest reported quarter.

The article presents the move as a test of whether customers will pay extra for AI features that competing software platforms increasingly offer. It says AI features carry computing and infrastructure costs, so the new revenue will only improve profitability if pricing covers those expenses. Investors are advised to watch Creator Studio subscriber growth, uptake of the usage packs and their contribution to Services revenue. The article does not say what Apple will do next beyond these existing plans.

Articles.Title: Apple Makes Major AI Pricing Move as New Revenue Opportunity Emerges

stories.Headline: Shanghai to create AI test base for shipping and logistics
stories.Summary:
Shanghai has begun building an artificial intelligence test base for shipping and logistics, according to a Smart Maritime Network report by Rob O'Dwyer dated November 10, 2026. The facility is being developed by Shanghai International Port Group, known as SIPG, together with academic and industry partners. It is meant to support testing of AI applications across port handling, cargo transport and multimodal logistics. Work on the infrastructure is already underway, and 54 business AI agents have been registered for testing and deployment.

The base will supply computing, data storage and security infrastructure, along with industry-specific datasets, AI models and an agent management platform. Its work will focus on three operational areas: port cargo handling, port hinterland transport and multimodal transport. The aim is to give AI applications a route from development into day-to-day use in shipping and port operations. The article describes this as the purpose of the initiative rather than setting out any separate legal or regulatory requirement.

The facility was announced alongside a new action plan from the Shanghai Municipal Transport Commission for integrating AI into the transport sector. The plan covers ports and shipping, aviation, rail and road transport, autonomous driving, postal services and logistics. It names three core development areas: transport large language models and AI agents, high-quality industry datasets, and computing infrastructure. Planned applications include autonomous port hinterland transport and AI-based government transport services, and the city also intends to set up a trusted data space for transport and mechanisms for data sharing.

The same event saw the establishment of a Yangtze River Delta regional centre for the Transport Large Model Innovation and Industry Alliance, with its secretariat in Shanghai. The centre will coordinate technical development and applications across Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Anhui, including sharing operational environments for testing transport AI. The article does not describe any further timetable or next steps beyond these announcements. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Shanghai to create AI test base for shipping and logistics

stories.Headline: Deux revives late Kim Sungjae's voice with AI for new album
stories.Summary:
Legendary Korean hip-hop duo Deux is set to release a full-length album, "4th Deux," on November 21, 2026, and will use artificial intelligence to recreate the vocals of the late Kim Sungjae. The album arrives more than 30 years after the duo's previous record, "Force Deux," which is widely regarded as one of the best albums in K-pop history. The pair split barely three months after that release, and each went on to a solo career. Kim was found dead in a Seoul hotel room in November 1995, one day after his solo debut, and the case remains unsolved.

The upcoming album has nine tracks, and Lee led its production and wrote "The Future," one of two focus tracks. The other main track, "I Want You," features Dynamic Duo, another well-known hip-hop pair. Lee described the song at a pre-listening session in Seoul on Saturday, saying it sounds like what Deux might have produced had it taken a new jack swing number a step further. Under Lee's wishes, a portion of the album's proceeds will go to Kim's family. The articles do not say how the AI was used or how the vocals were produced.

Lee is the person the article ties most directly to the project, as he led production and wrote the focus track. The article reports his remarks at the pre-listening session and his request that proceeds go to Kim's family. It gives no further statements from the duo's partners or from Kim's family. The article also notes that the two musicians parted ways after their last album and later released two albums, a live recording and a best-of set, in 1995 and 1997. It does not report any further developments beyond the album's release plans.

Articles.Title: Deux revives late Kim Sungjae's voice with AI for new album

stories.Headline: Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records
stories.Summary:
Palantir, the US data analytics company co-founded by the billionaire Peter Thiel, lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI software into NHS GP records, according to messages obtained by Foxglove, a tech equity campaign group, under the Freedom of Information Act and shared with the Guardian. The exchanges, which span July 2025 to March 2026, appear to be between Palantir's UK boss, Louis Mosley, and the former health minister Zubir Ahmed, with the push in February this year. The company argued via a direct WhatsApp channel that joining up primary and secondary care data was "unarguable" and that its software was "ideal" for the job. This came despite GP data being expressly ruled out of the scope of Palantir's existing £330m contract with NHS England to run its federated data platform.

The lobbying matters because it would stretch the company's reach into patient records that doctors and campaigners say should stay out of its hands. The British Medical Association and other groups have argued that bringing GP data into the platform would undermine patient trust and the doctor-patient relationship. When the previous Conservative government announced the deal three years ago, it stated that GP data would not be part of the national platform. Palantir's messages suggested the minister should "get out ahead of" likely political opposition from doctors and critics such as the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, and the Your Party led by Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana. The firm also told Ahmed that its software could bring faster GP access and more targeted management of frail patients, while keeping control of data local.

Foxglove's director of advocacy, Donald Campbell, said the messages showed Palantir lobbying to take in more sensitive personal data and that the company knew how sensitive the request was. The BMA council chair, Dr Tom Dolphin, warned of "scope creep" and of patients worrying about who could access their information. Marc Farr, chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytical Officer Network, said Palantir appeared to be bidding to widen its work beyond what ministers and NHS leaders had said, which would require legislative change. Palantir responded that it has long argued data sharing can improve the NHS, that it is for government to decide how the software is rolled out, and that the exchanges reflect those points. The Department of Health and Social Care declined to comment.

The disclosure comes as ministers reportedly stopped short of ending the Palantir contract soon, despite campaigners and two House of Commons committees calling for it to end as early as spring. Health secretary Yvette Cooper told parliament that a review was ongoing and spoke of the long-term benefit of developing UK sovereign AI, which suggests a British replacement may be sought when the contract reaches its next end point in 2029. The articles also report that Tom Watson, a Labour peer hired by Palantir as a full-time lobbyist in September, wrote to Cooper urging her to keep the contract going. The articles do not say whether the lobbying changed any policy, and the status of GP data in the platform remains unresolved.

Articles.Title: Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records

stories.Headline: Sakana AI may go public in 2027
stories.Summary:
Sakana AI, a Japanese artificial intelligence company, may go public in 2027, according to media reports. Nikkei broke the news, saying the firm is weighing a listing on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, Nasdaq, or both for its initial public offering. The company's market value could exceed that of Mercari, which is valued at ¥680 billion ($4.3 billion), and would put Sakana AI among Japan's most valuable startup listings. Goldman Sachs has reportedly been hired as an adviser for the process.

Sakana AI responded in an X post on Monday, saying it has no near-term plans for an IPO. The company said its priority is building a generational AI company that serves as Japan's national AI champion. The reports come as AI companies worldwide face problems with valuations, local resistance to data centers, and doubts about how useful the technology is. AI shares fell sharply after the U.S. midterm elections, as investors worried a Democratic-controlled Congress would tighten AI rules and slow data center construction. The Nasdaq is about 9% below its all-time high, partly because of the retreat in AI stocks.

The company has raised ¥32 billion ($200 million) in Series B funding from backers including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Google and Citi, and Nvidia took part in an earlier Series A round. Earlier this year, Sakana AI introduced Sakana Namazu, its first large language model, which was built on Kimi 2.6, an open-weight model from China's Moonshot AI. Concerned about overreliance on Chinese and U.S. models, Japan has made developing its own language models a priority, and it has reportedly invested $6 billion in an AI effort through Noetra, a consortium that includes Sakana AI, SoftBank and Sony. On Oct. 26, Sakana AI said it was training its own model from scratch, and its planned Sakana Sawara series will include a large and a small model.

Articles.Title: Sakana AI may go public in 2027

stories.Headline: Apple is now offering additional AI access via one-time $50 "intelligence usage packs" when monthly usage caps are met, starting in its Creator Studio apps (Ryan Christoffel/9to5Mac)
stories.Summary:
Apple has begun selling one-time "intelligence usage packs" that give users more access to its AI features once they reach their monthly usage limit. The first of these packs arrived on November 9, 2026, tied to the Logic Pro update within Apple Creator Studio. Users reach the purchase option by choosing Logic Pro from the menu bar, then "Intelligence Features," then "Show Usage," where a "Buy More Usage" option appears. The only offering is a one-time purchase priced at $49.99.

According to Apple's website, the packs cannot be shared through Family Sharing and work only with the Apple Account used for iCloud at the time of purchase. Unused usage rolls over from month to month and expires 12 months after purchase. Additional usage is consumed only after a user has reached the monthly limit for the relevant features. The articles say Final Cut Pro, Pixelmator Pro, and the iWork suite are expected to offer the packs as the rest of the announced Creator Studio updates arrive later in the month. The articles do not identify who set these terms beyond Apple's own published conditions, which are linked in the report.

Apple had previously said it would eventually charge for expanded use of select AI features, and this launch marks its first step in that direction. The articles note that most other AI services rely on subscriptions rather than one-time purchases, which makes Apple's approach at least initially different. The reporting also says all Apple Intelligence features had been free on Apple devices until now. The articles suggest the same model could extend to other server-based features such as Siri AI, Image Playground, and Photos editing tools, but they describe this as a likely future development rather than an announced plan.

Articles.Title: Apple is now offering additional AI access via one-time $50 "intelligence usage packs" when monthly usage caps are met, starting in its Creator Studio apps (Ryan Christoffel/9to5Mac)

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang's affair shines a spotlight on Nvidia's weak board and opaque succession planning at what has become the world's most important company (Semafor)
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang faces questions about his future after admitting to an affair with a woman suspected of spying for Chinese intelligence, a revelation that has drawn attention to the company's governance. Shares fell about 5% in afternoon trading on November 9, 2026, wiping out more than $200 billion in market value. The article reports that Huang's position now rests with a board that lacks the experience and stature typically found at a company of Nvidia's size. Huang has led the company since he co-founded it in 1993, and he has built it into the center of the AI boom.

The board has allowed a leadership structure with little precedent in corporate America, in which Huang has more than 50 direct reports. Nvidia has never publicly named a successor, has no president or chief operating officer, and its latest annual report does not use the word "succession." Analysts quoted in the piece say a replacement would likely have to come from outside, with chipmakers such as AMD and Broadcom mentioned as sources of candidates. The average board member has served almost 15 years, and none are current or former S&P 500 chief executives or have national-security experience. Huang and two other directors have been on the board since the company was founded.

Former SEC chair Gary Gensler said Huang appeared to have misled the public, given earlier company and Huang denials that his dealings were normal. Gensler said the stock drop could make the matter material to a court. The SEC declined to say whether it would investigate. Nvidia's board has said it still has confidence in Huang and that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. President Donald Trump has also expressed confidence in him.

Governance experts quoted in the article describe a board that may have struggled to check a celebrated chief executive, and they note the company's internal investigation and likely congressional hearings will determine whether any secrets were exposed. The company could also face more shareholder litigation if it is found to have misled investors. The scandal arrives alongside other pressures, including a Democratic Congress that could slow the buildout of AI infrastructure. The article does not say when the board's investigation will conclude.

Articles.Title: Jensen Huang's affair shines a spotlight on Nvidia's weak board and opaque succession planning at what has become the world's most important company (Semafor)

stories.Headline: India's electronics firms face PCB squeeze as AI demand drives up costs
stories.Summary:
India's electronics manufacturers are facing high costs and supply constraints for printed circuit boards as an increasing share of capacity is captured by booming demand for artificial intelligence hardware. Nikkei Asia reporter Ananta Agarwal reported the story from Bengaluru on November 10, 2026. Printed circuit board makers worldwide are diverting more production toward advanced and specialized boards for demanding AI applications. That shift is squeezing India's traditional users in the electronics industry, which rely on more ordinary boards. The article says that prices for these materials have risen by as much as 350 percent.

Manufacturers in India are passing those higher costs on to their customers. The article gives no further figures on the size of the increases or on the period over which they occurred. The article does not name a specific company or official who is responsible for the squeeze. It describes it as a result of market forces, with global board makers choosing to put their output into AI-related work.

The article gives no statement from any named industry figure, government body or board maker on the situation. The article does not describe any policy response or a timeline for relief. Its headline frames the squeeze as the outcome of rising AI demand, and the body text points to the same cause. The piece gives no outlook for how long supply will stay constrained.

Articles.Title: India's electronics firms face PCB squeeze as AI demand drives up costs

stories.Headline: Integration among ASEAN, China, Japan, South Korea boosted by AI boom
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence boom is accelerating economic integration across Southeast Asia, China, Japan and South Korea, according to Yasuto Watanabe, director and CEO of the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO). He made the remarks in Bangkok on Nov. 10, 2026, as reported by Nikkei Asia. He said the technology will boost trade and investment within the region. The report centers on his outlook for regional ties. Watanabe's comments came at a time when the private sector is driving closer links among these economies.

The article says AI demand is pulling companies into deeper cooperation across borders. It does not give specific figures on trade volumes or investment totals in its excerpt. Nor does it set out any new policy requirements or formal agreements tied to his remarks. Watanabe, who leads AMRO, is the source of the outlook described in the report. The article attributes the bullish view to him and does not report any dissenting official view.

He is quoted at an event held during the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings, which the article places in Bangkok on Oct. 14. The photo caption describes him speaking at that gathering. The surrounding coverage points to a region where AI and related supply chains are reshaping business ties, though the excerpt provided does not spell out the details. Other stories listed alongside the article cover electric vehicle competition, chip-related supply chain pressures and regional trade frictions. The articles provided do not say what steps AMRO or governments will take next.

Articles.Title: Integration among ASEAN, China, Japan, South Korea boosted by AI boom

stories.Headline: Y/N (YC S23) is hiring a growth lead to distribute superhuman A.I. storytelling
stories.Summary:
Y Combinator has posted a job listing for a Founding Growth Marketer at Y/n, a San Francisco startup from its S23 batch, with the listing appearing on November 9, 2026. The company describes itself as building interactive stories, where people play a character in a book and their texts shape the plot. Its stated mission is to build a superhuman A.I. storyteller and distribute it to billions of people. The posting says the company has already seen more than one billion messages sent on its platform.

The hire would be the company's first growth employee, and the listing calls for someone who can find marketing channels that work and then own them from start to finish. Responsibilities could include running ads and the creative pipeline across Meta, TikTok, or Google, or building creator partnerships with BookTokers, YouTubers, and a user-generated content program. The listing pays between $130,000 and $300,000 a year, offers equity of 0.30% to 2.00%, and says the company will sponsor visas. Candidates would take two team interviews and a paid day-long work trial, and the role is full-time and on-site in San Francisco.

The company is led by founders Gabriel Birnbaum and Eric Meier, and the listing says Y/n has raised $14 million from top investors and has a team of four. The founders say story quality determines the company's success, and they describe the culture as commercially minded, with a focus on measuring results and cutting what does not work. The posting also predicts that by 2030 playing stories will become the dominant form of entertainment. The articles do not describe any further hiring plans beyond this role or any timeline for the company's growth.

Articles.Title: Y/N (YC S23) is hiring a growth lead to distribute superhuman A.I. storytelling

stories.Headline: Show HN: STE80 Humanizer – de-AI text by writing 80% of the way to ASD-STE100
stories.Summary:
The article describes a GitHub project called STE80 Humanizer, posted to Hacker News as a "Show HN" under a headline that uses the phrase "de-AI text." The repository, published on 9 November 2026 at 06:00 UTC by the account Dodaios, is an agent skill that removes common signs of AI-written prose and rewrites text to be closer to ASD-STE100, the controlled English used in aircraft maintenance manuals.
