The article notes that Conductor's local application will keep receiving model support and critical bug fixes until early next year, but the company has not committed to longer-term support beyond that.

The shutdown means enterprise teams could lose more than their code, according to Jeet Pattanaik of Glokal AI, who is quoted in the article. Teams may also lose agent configurations, instructions, task assignments and work histories, and must rebuild and validate their agent coordination, review and testing workflows if they move to other platforms. Rebecca Wettemann of Valoir advises enterprises to negotiate contracts that allow data export at any time, at no extra cost, in open formats, along with penalty-free termination, refunds for prepaid fees, at least 90 days' notice of discontinuation, and transition help. Meta's acquisition is part of its wider AI ecosystem, which the article lists as including its Enterprise Platform, Muse personal agent, Muse API, Muse Code and Muse Wonder and Wonder Full models. Meta's Superintelligence Labs unit will oversee Conductor and its technology.

The article reports that Meta has not disclosed the financial terms of the deal or explained how Conductor's technology will fit with its developer tools. Conductor, founded in 2024, had said in a March funding update that dozens of engineers at companies including Google, Meta, HubSpot, Amazon and Spotify used its platform. The article contrasts Meta's handling with OpenAI's plan to acquire Pierre Computer, announced the same day, under which Pierre Code Storage customers could keep using the service and its open source projects would stay open. Pattanaik and Wettemann both urge companies to plan exits before adopting AI tools, such as by testing data exports and keeping prompts, agent logic and tests in company-controlled systems. The article does not say what Meta plans for Conductor's technology after the shutdown.

Articles.Title: Meta’s Conductor deal puts enterprise AI coding workflows on deadline

stories.Headline: Microsoft Starts Limiting Copilot Chat Usage For Users Without Paid Licenses
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has begun limiting some Copilot features for users who lack Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses, with the restrictions taking effect for larger organizations today. The company started applying the limits to organizations with 2,000 or fewer Microsoft 365 seats on Nov. 2, according to an online post from the Redmond, Wash. technology giant. Microsoft calls these "fair use" limits, though the articles note the term does not carry its copyright-law meaning. Chat remains included in Microsoft 365 subscriptions, and solution providers do not have to take any administrative action.

Administrators cannot view or adjust the limits, and Microsoft does not publish specific thresholds because they can vary throughout the day and change as the product evolves. When a user hits a limit, they receive a message about Microsoft 365 Copilot, Microsoft 365 Copilot Business, or other Copilot capabilities they can upgrade to. Most organizations will see an option in that notice to request a license from administrators, who can approve or deny the request through the Microsoft 365 admin center. Organizations can also allow direct purchases from the notification, and administrators can turn that off for each product.

Responses already in progress are not interrupted when a limit is reached, and the message tells users when the features will be available again. The limits apply to commercial tenants using Copilot Chat on the web, desktops, and mobile apps. Microsoft has also said that usage-based billing will be on by default for new Microsoft 365 Copilot Business subscriptions bought through Cloud Solution Provider partners between January and March 2027. Microsoft itself is the party setting and managing these limits, and the vendor has recommended that admins tell their help desk staff and review license request settings.

Dawn Sizer, CEO and co-founder of 3rd Element Consulting in Mechanicsburg, Pa., said she would like visibility into users approaching the limit so clients can plan and control spending. Microsoft has told partners that users who reach limits show real demand and make strong upgrade candidates, and it suggests "Copilot in 30" trial offers for eligible users. Microsoft's Nicole Herskowitz said in September that the limits are meant to ensure most people never reach them. The articles also note that Microsoft's Satya Nadella described a model combining a basic allotment of compute under a license with metered charges for more advanced AI use.

The articles do not say whether the limits will expand beyond organizations with 2,000 or fewer seats, and CRN reported that it had reached out to Microsoft for comment. Solution providers can use Microsoft's AI Business Solutions and Security Partner Experience dashboard to see which clients have users hitting limits. Resellers with Partner Center access can review that dashboard or contact their distributor for more information. The shift reflects Microsoft's broader move toward consumption-based AI pricing, and the articles indicate that further pricing changes are expected as the economics evolve.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Starts Limiting Copilot Chat Usage For Users Without Paid Licenses

stories.Headline: AMD Launches Epyc SP7, Helion as AI Rack Demand Rises
stories.Summary:
AMD said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that its sixth-generation Epyc SP7 server processor is now generally available and that hardware makers have begun shipping servers powered by the chip. The company also said the first Helion racks for agentic AI, which hardware vendors build from an AMD blueprint, will become available throughout this month. The SP7 supports up to 256 cores and is the first of four sixth-generation Epyc CPUs to become available. AMD said the other three are expected in 2027. The broader family, much of which is code-named "Venice," is designed for enterprise, cloud, high-performance computing, and AI workloads.

AMD said it is seeing strong demand for the new chip. During the company's third-quarter earnings call last week, AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su said early demand for Venice is the strongest AMD has seen for any new generation of Epyc processors. Su said AMD began revenue shipments of Venice during the third quarter and that hardware makers have committed to more than 240 Venice platforms, 20% more than the number committed for Turin, AMD's fifth-generation Epyc chip. Su also said Venice delivers significantly better performance per watt, per core, and per dollar than any other x86 or Arm server CPU. AMD said systems based on the SP7 deliver up to 3.7 times the performance of an Nvidia Vera CPU-based system and up to 2.2 times the performance of an Intel Xeon 6980P system.

AMD is working to capture more market share in CPUs, GPUs, and overall AI infrastructure as it competes with rivals amid surging AI demand. It is directly challenging market leader Nvidia in GPUs and rack-scale systems, while Nvidia is taking on AMD with its own CPU. Arm has also introduced an Arm-based CPU to compete with Intel and AMD's x86 processors. Cloud providers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure have built their own custom AI accelerators and Arm-based CPUs. AMD introduced Helion in October as an open rack-scale design for agentic AI, with partners that include Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Lenovo, Supermicro, and Cisco.

AMD said Helion will come in three versions. Helion Liquid is a CPU-only, liquid-cooled rack designed to operate side by side with a Helios rack for large-scale agentic AI deployments. Helion Air is a CPU-only rack designed to expand agent capacity within existing air-cooled data centers. AMD Helion Air Inference is an air-cooled rack that combines CPUs and GPUs for inference. The article notes that Helion racks are built for agentic AI and differ from AMD's Helios racks, which are designed for large-scale inference, frontier model training, and fine-tuning.

Matt Kimball, vice president and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said Venice is an important launch for AMD and for enterprises. Kimball said enterprise CIOs have fixed power budgets and need infrastructure that supports traditional workloads today and agentic AI in the years ahead. With up to 256 cores, Venice lets companies run traditional workloads on fewer servers, freeing up space for AI infrastructure. Kimball also said that servers running sixth-generation Epyc processors are well suited to future agentic workloads because of the CPU's high core count and large cache and memory. AMD also said Meta is preparing to deploy sixth-generation Epyc platforms at scale and that Microsoft Azure's HDv2 service for AI data processing is in preview.

Articles.Title: AMD Launches Epyc SP7, Helion as AI Rack Demand Rises

stories.Headline: CodeRabbit scales agentic software development and ships 20x more
stories.Summary:
On November 9, 2026, OpenAI published a customer story about CodeRabbit, a North American startup in the technology sector that builds an AI-powered governance and control platform for AI-generated code. The article describes how CodeRabbit uses OpenAI models to review and trust code produced by agents, and Codex to speed up its own software development. According to the company's co-founder and CEO, Harjot Gill, the platform is used by over 20,000 organizations and more than 150,000 open-source projects. The article presents these claims as coming from CodeRabbit and OpenAI, not as independently verified results.

The story centers on the productivity gains CodeRabbit reports. Harjot says the company has shipped roughly 20 times more software over the last six months without adding engineers, and he personally estimated pushing 2,500 to 3,000 pull requests in the 30 days before the interview. Reaching that pace meant rethinking the delivery process, including streamlining releases, reconsidering where human approvals belong, and letting CodeRabbit automatically ship low-risk changes. The company also built a Codex-powered Slack bot that triages production incidents, messages, and support tickets, and it manages some marketing work, such as Google Ads, through pull requests. Lower-cost OpenAI models, named in the article as GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6 Astra, let the company run more subagents, with the cheaper model handling much of the work and the other handling planning and orchestration.

CodeRabbit's security product, CodeRabbit Secure, uses OpenAI's Daybreak with Codex models to find and fix vulnerabilities. The article says that over the past two weeks the company ran a promotional offer covering $1 million in free deep scans, which found more than 43,000 security vulnerabilities across 13,000 deep scans, and that thousands of these have already been fixed by customers. Earlier, CodeRabbit used OpenAI's Cyber model through Daybreak for internal penetration testing and said it found multiple vulnerabilities in its own platform. The article also says that, on CodeRabbit's internal benchmark, GPT-6 Astra caught 50 percent of the known issues at the time of the interview, which the company described as the top result among models it tested.

Harjot Gill credits OpenAI's reasoning models with steadily improving CodeRabbit's ability to find issues at scale, and he said each new model release has brought large gains. He also said the company's review benchmark keeps changing as agents make new kinds of mistakes. Looking ahead, the article says CodeRabbit is expanding toward agentic software development, with the goal of helping teams validate, prioritize, explain, secure, and verify agent-generated code. Harjot expects teams to need more help deciding which agent-made changes to take to completion as background agents begin responding to alerts without a person starting each task. The article does not describe any further announcements or timelines beyond this.

Articles.Title: CodeRabbit scales agentic software development and ships 20x more

stories.Headline: Cisco Live Melbourne: AI agents will break today’s enterprise network, and Cisco wants to rebuild it
stories.Summary:
At Cisco Live APJC in Melbourne, Cisco Asia Pacific, Japan and Greater China president Ben Dawson said agent token consumption passed human consumption for the first time in February, and agents now consume tokens at roughly seven times the human rate. He said each agent generates far more traffic and data than a human doing the same task. Cisco's focus at the event shifted from GPUs, AI factories and data centers to the campus, the branch and the network that connects everything. Speakers argued that networks built for people will not hold up when thousands of agents work around the clock. The keynote framed the problem as a need to rebuild enterprise networking for agent behavior.

Jeff Schultz, Cisco's SVP of portfolio strategy and marketing, explained that agents still send heavy north-south traffic to reach models and context. They also generate large volumes of east-west traffic as agents talk to other agents across desktops, campuses, branches and data centers. Schultz said the architecture for campus and branch networking needs to be fundamentally reimagined. Dawson said AI will place new demands on wired infrastructure, making it more critical. Cisco's chief sales officer, Oliver Tuszik, cited IDC data showing only 9% of organizations in the region believe their networks are fully ready for new AI and digital initiatives.

He also cited research indicating 85% of organizations globally are experimenting with agents, but only 5% have deployed them to production. Cisco's product announcements covered the data center, campus and operations. Schultz highlighted 102.4 Tbps systems based on the Silicon One G300 for scale-out, and the deep-buffered Silicon One P200 for connecting data centers across metro, long-haul and transcontinental distances. Cisco is integrating ThousandEyes into its Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 access points at no extra cost for customers with eligible Networking Essentials and Advantage licenses. Schultz admitted ThousandEyes has been difficult to license and deploy.

Cisco Cloud Control, the company's unified operations layer, combines cross-domain telemetry, purpose-built models and both Cisco and third-party agents. Schultz said no new Cisco product will ship unless it is integrated with Cloud Control. Cloud Control is currently available only for US-based infrastructure. Cisco scheduled Australia, the EU and the UK for February 2027, followed by Japan, India and Canada in May. Schultz said the line between observing an agent and securing an agent is beginning to blur, citing an agent that suddenly deleted 10,000 files.

Cisco AI Defense is adding Anthropic's Claude Mythos to its adaptive red-teaming engine, limited to targets customers own and have registered. The model will be available to select enterprises soon, with broader availability for qualified customers later. Splunk's Tokenomics feature enters private preview in December, with general availability on AWS Marketplace in early 2027. Customers described their own deployments at the event. John Kelvie, chief digital and information officer at Asahi Beverages, described a Melbourne head office for about 1,000 employees built on Cisco's SD-Access architecture.

Asahi has since brought operational technology on its production floor onto a single IP network. Kelvie said his biggest obstacle is data, not people or technology. Yessie Yosetya, CIO of Indonesian operator XLSmart, inherited two networks after a merger, with security maturity scores of 3.2 and 1.6 on a NIST-based scale. She redesigned around five areas and reduced the company's security tools from 54 to 14. XLSmart put eight agents into production for red, blue and purple teaming, then found it could not scale them without standardization.

Articles.Title: Cisco Live Melbourne: AI agents will break today’s enterprise network, and Cisco wants to rebuild it

stories.Headline: 10 Generative AI Companies to Know
stories.Summary:
Built In published a roundup on November 9, 2026, titled "10 Generative AI Companies to Know," which lists firms shaping the generative AI industry. The article describes generative AI as a field that creates new content, such as text, images, music, video and computer code, by learning patterns from large datasets. It traces the mainstream rise of the technology to the November 2022 debut of ChatGPT, which drew one million users in less than a week. Since then, the article says, a competitive global race has pushed investment beyond chatbots toward multimodal, reasoning and open-weight models.

The roundup names OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Microsoft, Anthropic, Nvidia, xAI, Amazon, Prosodica, Mistral AI and Meta as the companies to know. Each profile highlights a distinct approach. xAI, founded by Elon Musk, trains its Grok models on a Memphis facility the article says holds 200,000 liquid-cooled GPUs. Microsoft's Copilot, according to the article, now writes an average of 46 percent of code across user programming files on GitHub.

Meta's Llama models have passed 470 million downloads on Hugging Face, and the article notes that Meta AI reaches more than one billion monthly active users across its apps. The article does not assign responsibility for any single event, since it is a list rather than a news report on one incident. Each profile attributes its figures to the companies themselves or to their public statements, such as Microsoft's reported GitHub number and OpenAI's claim that more than 92 percent of Fortune 500 companies use its products. Anthropic's design goal, described as "constitutional AI," is presented as the company's own stated training approach.

The piece does not offer independent verification of these claims. The article places these companies within a broader, fast-moving industry, noting that Nvidia makes about 80 percent of the processors used in data centers. It frames the sector as one where cloud providers, chipmakers and model developers are all racing to deploy AI into products and enterprise operations. The roundup does not describe any specific next step or pending decision, so beyond continued competition and new product releases, the article leaves the future unspecified.

Articles.Title: 10 Generative AI Companies to Know

stories.Headline: At Northern Trust, finance experts and Microsoft engineers partner to move faster on AI
stories.Summary:
Northern Trust, the Chicago-based bank, worked with Microsoft Frontier Company this year to test whether AI could speed up client onboarding, a process that can take weeks. The bank wanted an AI agent that could convert years of transaction history and cash flows from multiple investments and formats onto its in-house platform quickly and accurately. Microsoft's forward-deployed engineers worked alongside Northern Trust's finance experts to build a library of rules for the agent to follow. The teams trained the model on business vocabulary and anonymized data from several earlier onboardings, and ongoing feedback from the bank helped expand those rules.

The agent's first-pass quality score reached 96.5 percent, and the remaining 3.5 percent of items the agent could not categorize go to a human reviewer. Northern Trust kept that human check deliberately to avoid passing on wrong information. Before going live, the company still runs its usual reconciliation to confirm its books match those of the previous administrator. Northern Trust measured the change and found that mapping transaction data for new clients fell from about two and a half weeks to three days. The bank says all client data stays within Northern Trust and is not used to train outside AI models.

Pete Cherecwich, the bank's chief operating officer, credited Microsoft's engineers with getting the project to market faster than the bank could have on its own. He said the faster process means quicker revenue and happier clients. Vik Singh, a corporate vice president at Microsoft Frontier Company who leads the engineering team on the project, described the work as a true collaboration in which each side needed the other to get the agent's accuracy right. Singh suggested it could serve as a model for AI in regulated industries. Cherecwich also said the bank will not let AI make large payments on its own anytime soon.

The article places the project within a wider push at Northern Trust, which has trained all 23,000 employees on Microsoft Copilot. Staff have built more than 15,000 Copilot agents, and the bank ran a contest with a cash prize for the best one. Cherecwich addressed worries about jobs by saying roles will change and workers will need new skills. The bank is now examining how AI agents could be used with other products and services. The article does not say what other uses are planned or when they might arrive.

Articles.Title: At Northern Trust, finance experts and Microsoft engineers partner to move faster on AI

stories.Headline: Alice Huang boasted about Nvidia AI chip access to investors, told them Alibaba would be a client for the
stories.Summary:
Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, pitched a multimillion-dollar artificial intelligence infrastructure project to investors in early 2025, according to a Financial Times report published around November 9, 2026. She and her business partner Kang Wei sought funding for a Southeast Asian data-centre project estimated to be worth hundreds of millions of dollars. During the pitch, the pair reportedly said they had no problem securing Nvidia graphics processing units, a key component for building and running AI systems. They also named Alibaba as a prospective client, according to an investor familiar with the discussions.

The claims raise questions about how advanced Nvidia chips could reach Chinese businesses through infrastructure located outside mainland China. US export controls bar Chinese companies from owning certain advanced AI chips, but Chinese firms can lease computing capacity from overseas data centres, subject to applicable restrictions. The FT reported that access to Nvidia GPUs was central to the investment proposal. Documents the FT reviewed showed Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries in 2024, and people familiar with the company described Alibaba as its anchor customer and largest client.

The pitch comes amid allegations that Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to build a relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and possibly influence his position on US restrictions on advanced chip exports to China. US intelligence officials reportedly believe she was connected to such an espionage effort. These allegations have not been independently established. Beijing has rejected the espionage claims, and Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing related to chip smuggling. Jensen Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair and apologized to his wife and family.

Nvidia's independent directors have launched an investigation into whether Jensen Huang was targeted in a foreign intelligence operation. The company has said it has no reason to believe its national security interests or confidential information were compromised. The article does not say what the investigation will find or when it will conclude. The allegations have nevertheless drawn fresh attention to Nvidia's business dealings in China and the security implications of its global AI chip supply chain.

Articles.Title: Alice Huang boasted about Nvidia AI chip access to investors, told them Alibaba would be a client for the

stories.Headline: The GIGABYTE AI TOP ATOM 64 GB is now available and expands the possibilities of AI development on desktop PCs
stories.Summary:
GIGABYTE has made a 64 GB version of its AI TOP ATOM desktop AI system available as of November 11, 2026, alongside the existing 128 GB model. The announcement was distributed through PR Newswire from Taipei. Both memory versions are built on the NVIDIA DGX Spark platform and share the same compact chassis design. The 64 GB version is offered with either a 1 TB or a 2 TB NVMe M.2 SSD using PCIe 4.0 connectivity, so buyers can match storage to their needs. The system is intended for local AI development, giving developers dedicated AI compute in a desktop form factor.

It supports local model inference, prototyping, data analysis, and application validation in offices, labs, and educational settings. Users can run models and process project data within their own IT environment. For supported distributed AI workloads, up to four AI TOP ATOM systems can be linked into a cluster using the built-in NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking and NVIDIA Sync's Cluster Assistant. The announcement says this can add storage and compute resources, depending on the application and software setup.

GIGABYTE also bundles its AI TOP Utility software, which supports downloading supported models, running inference, and retrieval-augmented generation for building question-answering tools on a user's own documents. GIGABYTE's announcement says availability, sales channels, pricing, and memory configurations may vary by region. More information is available on the company's AI TOP ATOM product page. The release also notes that GIGABYTE has recently expanded its local AI lineup with the AI TOP AERO, a separate desktop built on NVIDIA's RTX Spark platform.

Articles.Title: The GIGABYTE AI TOP ATOM 64 GB is now available and expands the possibilities of AI development on desktop PCs

stories.Headline: S-1: Nvidia plans to invest ~$10B in Anthropic after its IPO, or ~10% of the total new cash Anthropic is expected to raise in November, including in its IPO (Cory Weinberg/New York Times)
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the maker of AI software tools, began courting investors on Tuesday for an initial public offering that could value the company at up to $1.4 trillion. The filing shows that Nvidia, the chipmaker that has become the financial engine of the AI boom, plans to invest about $10 billion in Anthropic immediately after the IPO. That sum would amount to roughly 10 percent of the total new cash Anthropic is expected to raise in November, including through the offering. The deal was reported by Cory Weinberg of The New York Times, based on the investor prospectus. Anthropic said Nvidia would be among a group of AI companies investing alongside the offering.

The arrangement ties together two companies that had long kept their distance from each other despite operating in closely connected parts of the industry. For years they grew into some of the most valuable firms in the world without doing much business together. Their chief executives also publicly sparred over how the U.S. government should regulate AI technology. The new investment changes that picture, since Nvidia is now set to hold a direct financial stake in Anthropic.

Kevin S. Xu, chief investment officer of Interconnected Capital, which invests in publicly traded AI companies, said the two companies' futures are now more intertwined than ever. The article describes the timing as notable, with one company preparing for its public debut while the other faces what it calls a prolonged corporate drama that has shaken the AI industry and left investors on edge. The article does not detail the nature of that drama. It also does not say what conditions, if any, attach to Nvidia's planned investment, or how the stake would be structured beyond the roughly $10 billion figure.

Articles.Title: S-1: Nvidia plans to invest ~$10B in Anthropic after its IPO, or ~10% of the total new cash Anthropic is expected to raise in November, including in its IPO (Cory Weinberg/New York Times)

stories.Headline: FORGE Lab uses agentic tools to identify memory safety issues in Rust
stories.Summary:
The Microsoft Security Blog published an article on November 9, 2026, describing research by its FORGE Lab into memory safety issues in Rust's standard library. The team used agentic tools, including Hyenas, its research version of the codename MDASH AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system, to find cases where the standard library's unsafe code could trigger undefined behavior, including in code written entirely in safe Rust. The researchers reproduced the bugs, assessed their security impact, and reported them to the Rust issue tracker, where maintainers responded quickly and fixes are in progress or under review. The article notes that two of the reported issues remained open at publication.

The findings are grouped into three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code. The first is trusting code not to panic, illustrated by a panic safety bug in the MapWindows::clone function, where a buffer's destructor could run over uninitialized memory if a user-supplied clone call panicked. The article also points to allocator unwinding as a related hazard, noting that the stabilization of the Allocator API, shipping in Rust 1.100 on November 12, instead requires implementors never to unwind from the trait's methods or from drop. The second pattern is trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, where safe but inconsistent comparators, iterators or trait implementations can lead to problems, and the article contrasts Rust's approach with C++, where such misuse can be undefined behavior. The third pattern concerns trusting the underlying system.

The authors state that Rust's safety guarantees matter more as the language spreads into software that billions of people use daily. They cite Microsoft's adoption of Rust as a Tier-1 internal language alongside C++, C# and TypeScript, GitHub's rewrite of the Copilot agent runtime in Rust, and moves by Bun, Android, the Linux kernel and Cloudflare. The authors describe the work as a continuation of their earlier Rudra analyzer from 2021, which searched the Rust ecosystem for memory-safety bugs. The article presents the findings as a discussion of what Rust does and does not guarantee rather than a claim that Rust is unsafe. The article also asks readers who are interested in an open issue to comment only with genuinely new information or real-world use cases.

Articles.Title: FORGE Lab uses agentic tools to identify memory safety issues in Rust

stories.Headline: Northern Trust and Microsoft Frontier Company collaborate to transform client onboarding through AI
stories.Summary:
On Monday, November 9, 2026, Northern Trust and Microsoft announced an expanded collaboration to speed up AI adoption across the bank. It starts with a new AI-powered client onboarding agent for clients on Northern Trust Asset Servicing's Front Office Solutions platform. The agent was built jointly by Northern Trust and the forward deployed engineering teams of Microsoft Frontier Company. Its job is to turn years of client data and transaction history into a standard format that works in Northern Trust's reporting environment.

The agent cut data preparation time by 83 percent, from two and a half weeks to three days, based on measurements of real client onboarding cases. It also reached a 96.5 percent F1 first-pass quality score, a common AI measure that blends precision and recall. That score came from controlled testing on seven representative cases using anonymized historical client transaction workbooks, with the agent's output compared against analyst-prepared references. The remaining 3.5 percent, items the agent cannot categorize with confidence, goes to a human reviewer. The agent runs on Microsoft Azure and Microsoft Foundry and connects with tools such as Excel and SharePoint, so analysts can review, refine and approve its work.

Pete Cherecwich, Northern Trust's chief operating officer, said the agent combines the bank's asset servicing expertise with Microsoft's AI to get clients running faster while keeping the oversight clients expect. He added that working with Microsoft's engineers got him speed to market for a project that might otherwise have been put aside, and that revenue now arrives sooner and clients are happier. Bill Borden, a Microsoft corporate vice president for worldwide financial services, said the work shows how AI can amplify human expertise in regulated industries, with governance and human oversight built in. Vik Singh, who leads the engineering team on the project, called the effort a true collaboration and a model for AI in regulated sectors.

Northern Trust says the problem is common in its industry, since 57 percent of asset owners it surveyed named consolidating data from scattered sources as their biggest challenge. Microsoft tuned the agent using only anonymized data, so client data stayed under Northern Trust's control and is not used to train outside AI models. Before the process, the bank's analysts and the engineers built a library of rules for the agent to follow. Northern Trust is now looking at using agents for other products and services. It has offered Copilot training to all 23,000 employees, who have built more than 15,000 Copilot agents.

Articles.Title: Northern Trust and Microsoft Frontier Company collaborate to transform client onboarding through AI

stories.Headline: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
stories.Summary:
Evan X. Merz, a software developer, published an essay on his blog on November 7, 2026, arguing that heavy reliance on AI coding tools produces fragile codebases. He wrote that he was laid off from Meta in May, though he could only speculate that his resistance to adopting AI tools as quickly as some peers played a part. In his final months there he generated at least 90 percent of his code with AI, the minimum for a decent rating, but he said the tools did not multiply his output and that the code his AI-reliant colleagues pushed was brittle. He now works at another large tech company and generates all of his code with AI, which he describes as the current expectation.

Merz names four failure modes. He says AI writes shallow tests, mostly trivial get and set checks and end-to-end tests that cover only already-tested paths and a single type of user, which leaves gaps that line coverage metrics do not reveal. He says AI writes overly complex code, using several helper methods where one would do and applying rules like DRY to excess. He argues that a growing reliance on AI reduces how well human developers understand the codebase, leaving them unable to spot poor abstractions. Finally, he says AI produces pull requests faster than humans can review them, so reviewers skim and small quality problems accumulate into long-term technical debt.

As symptoms of such a codebase, Merz lists more incidents over time, longer recovery times because engineers are working in unfamiliar code, errors that surface only for real users rather than in tests, and a poorer user experience. He concludes that software serving human customers needs human judgment and that the most expensive, well-regarded products will continue to be developed mainly by people. The essay is his opinion and offers no measured data on incident rates or any company's practices. It does not describe any next steps beyond his prediction that many people will come to see AI-heavy development as unsustainable.

Articles.Title: AI usage generates a fragile codebase

stories.Headline: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy
stories.Summary:
Apple appears to be developing a new Mac app called Harbor, which is designed to make running local AI models simple. The app was discovered by the leaker Aaron Perris, who shared details in a post on X on November 10, 2026. According to the post, Harbor turns a Mac into a private AI inference server that runs open-weight models on Apple silicon, so data stays on the user's hardware and does not reach the cloud. The report says Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple's Claris brand.

Harbor is described as offering several features aimed at ease of use and scale. It detects devices connected over Thunderbolt 5 and forms a cluster automatically, without manual configuration or command-line work. Users can browse, download, and load open-weight models from inside the app, which handles model management. Two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Macs can also be connected so that their unified memory is pooled into a single inference resource, allowing larger models or more concurrent requests than one machine could handle alone.

The information comes from Perris's discovery and his public post, and the article does not report any statement from Apple about the app. The report places Harbor within a wider trend in which the Mac has become more popular as a tool for running AI models locally on machines such as the Mac Studio and Mac mini. The article notes that budget-friendly models like the MacBook Neo have also contributed to that growth. It suggests Apple may be leaning harder into this use case, and it expects a public launch in the weeks or months ahead, though no date has been confirmed.

Articles.Title: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy

stories.Headline: Celestica Stock: Is AI Growth Worth the Risk in a Retirement Portfolio?
stories.Summary:
Celestica (TSX: CLS), which designs and manufactures networking and computing equipment for data centres, is drawing attention from investors weighing its exposure to artificial intelligence. The Motley Fool Canada analysis, published November 10, 2026, asks whether the stock's growth is worth the risk in a retirement portfolio. The article reports that the stock closed at $330.24 on the day of publication after falling about 9.2% that day. It notes that Celestica's October results showed third-quarter revenue rising 83%. Celestica's 2026 free-cash-flow outlook was reduced from US$600 million to US$460 million, while management lifted its sales outlook.

The company attributes the reduction to working-capital investment for faster growth ahead, including more inventory and receivables. The article explains that free cash flow is money left after the company's defined adjustments and capital spending. It also notes that the company has raised its 2026 revenue outlook to US$20.5 billion, according to a related Motley Fool headline. The author, Amy Legate-Wolfe, writes as a Motley Fool Canada contributor and states she has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. Her view is that Celestica suits a patient, long-term growth role rather than income.

She suggests an initial allocation of 2% of an otherwise diversified retirement portfolio, not a centrepiece holding. She also advises keeping near-term withdrawals in cash or suitable guaranteed investments. The article presents its illustrations as arithmetic, not predictions. It shows that a 40% share-price decline would reduce a whole portfolio by 0.8% at a 2% weighting, 2.0% at 5%, and 4.0% at 10%. It adds that holding the stock inside a Tax-Free Savings Account can generally shelter Canadian tax on gains, provided there is contribution room.

The article also says that Motley Fool's Stock Advisor Canada list of top TSX stocks for 2026 does not include Celestica. The article does not describe any next event for Celestica or set out a timeline for future results. It offers no forecast for the share price. The author's stated conclusion is that customer orders turning into cash would earn her confidence more than another ambitious outlook.

Articles.Title: Celestica Stock: Is AI Growth Worth the Risk in a Retirement Portfolio?

stories.Headline: In age of AI, human touch still matters
stories.Summary:
Prime Sarmiento, a China Daily correspondent based in Hong Kong, wrote a first-person column published on November 10, 2026, after covering the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank in Bangkok, which he reached on October 12. He had expected the event to focus on the IMF's World Economic Outlook, interest rates, inflation and the energy shock, but he found that artificial intelligence came up in most discussions across the week. Some sessions were devoted to AI, including a popular panel featuring Jack Clark, co-founder of the United States company Anthropic. Participants, he wrote, felt a mix of optimism about AI's benefits and unease that its costs could outweigh the economic gains it was expected to bring.

The IMF's World Economic Outlook, released during the meetings, projected global growth of 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 percent in 2027, but the gains are unevenly spread. Economies tied into the AI supply chain are better placed to absorb external shocks, while energy-importing economies outside that chain face higher import bills, exchange rate pressure and tighter fiscal room, and many of them are low-income or vulnerable countries. At a fireside chat with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh gave no clear signal on US interest rates and instead focused on AI, including its potential to fundamentally transform monetary policy and its still-uncertain effect on jobs. Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, noted that since ChatGPT's launch, job postings requiring emerging AI skills have grown, roughly twice as fast in occupations highly exposed to the technology.

The author, who said he has used AI to transcribe interviews, do research, process data and copy edit, argued that AI cannot conduct interviews, build relationships with contacts or produce truly in-depth stories. He acknowledged that AI-generated content is widespread online and that producing a news report with a language model is one thing, while whether that report is worth reading is another. He concluded that only human journalists can verify questionable data, supply the context that makes facts meaningful, demand accountability and build understanding with audiences. He wrote that journalists remain relevant and have become more important in the age of AI, though the article does not describe any formal policy or institutional change arising from these discussions.

Articles.Title: In age of AI, human touch still matters

stories.Headline: SGLang RCE Exploit Breaches NEAR AI, Steals Data From 18 Agents and About 100 Users
stories.Summary:
An attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, an open-source inference engine, and ran code on one of NEAR AI's inference servers last Sunday. The attacker could also have seen requests processed on that server that day, including requests sent in confidential mode. That mode runs requests inside a trusted execution environment meant to keep them private even from the company. The company said that environment does not protect against flaws in the software running inside it, and SGLang runs there. The attacker then moved further into the company's systems.

The attacker reached an internal system behind Private Chat, a product the company had already deprecated, and downloaded account details for about 100 users, including email addresses and names. For some accounts, plan and balance information was also taken, though the company found no sign that stored conversations or uploaded files were accessed. The attacker also reached 18 AI agents on an older NEAR AI Agents deployment that did not run inside the company's trusted environment, taking chat history, settings and logs. Two customers' NEAR AI Cloud API keys were exposed in logs, and the company has revoked both. After detecting the attack, the company revoked all active sessions and administrator credentials, replaced all agent tokens, and took Private Chat offline.

NEAR AI said it deployed a fix for the SGLang flaw on all its inference servers, rotated remaining credentials, and completed a full forensic review, according to its incident report. It has restored access to its NEAR AI Cloud service and reported the flaw to the SGLang project. The company has not given a CVE number, named the affected SGLang versions, or said whether the project has released a fix. It contacted affected users directly from its security address and advised them to be wary of unexpected messages about their accounts or balances. In a follow-up post, it said users who have not heard from it need take no action.

The company has not said whether people whose requests passed through the affected server last Sunday were among those contacted. Brave, the browser maker, said in an October 15 technical write-up that its Leo assistant runs chats with one model inside a trusted environment operated by NEAR AI. NEAR AI has not said whether the affected server handled any of those chats. The articles do not say whether further disclosures are planned.

Articles.Title: SGLang RCE Exploit Breaches NEAR AI, Steals Data From 18 Agents and About 100 Users

stories.Headline: PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery
stories.Summary:
David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate on the technical staff of the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic's Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem in quantum computing, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture. The reporting was published on November 10, 2026, by TechCrunch. The solution concerns whether quantum computers can solve certain problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the researchers who posed the problem, said he does not fully follow the proof but believes it is correct because it was autoformalized in Lean and checked by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared it.

The result appears to rule out one route quantum computers could take to solve some hard problems quickly, though not all of them. PSI held the result until Anthropic's model was nearly ready for release, which gave it time to share the work with relevant experts. Turturean said the academic community will expect him to explain the result. Aaronson wrote that he was surprised the problem was missing from a recent OpenAI batch of solved problems.

PSI CEO Matt Pines said the company's model relies on specialized harnesses, tools, memory systems and simulation infrastructure to tackle scientific problems across breadth and depth. For now, the company earns revenue by using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating heat, power, water and sound. Its longer goal is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into real technologies, which Pines acknowledged has not yet happened. He noted that AI has claimed solutions in mathematics and computer science, where results can be expressed in validated code, but physics is harder because nature has the final say.

Jim Halverson, a Northeastern University professor who advises PSI, said transparency and contacting experts are emerging best practices, and he will attend an MIT summit next week where leading physicists will discuss the new pace of science. Pines said PSI focuses on validating computational results with experiments as efficiently as possible. The startup Discovered Materials recently released a $1 million grand challenge for AI-driven research on problems such as superconductivity and heat dissipation. Participants in these new "neolabs for science" are still working out what standards will govern this work.

Articles.Title: PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery

stories.Headline: Taco Bell Put AI in 900 Drive-Thrus — Here’s What Happened to Sales
stories.Summary:
Taco Bell has put voice AI to work taking drive-thru orders at more than 900 of its locations, and the company reports that these stores are seeing a sales lift. According to Restaurant Business, those locations have seen about a 1.5% increase in sales from larger checks. The article says the same technology has also helped the parent company, Yum! Brands, report a 6% rise in drive-thru satisfaction and better crew retention.

Taco Bell has plans to expand the system to more than 1,500 restaurants by the end of the year. The AI system is credited with prompting customers to add items, since it always offers a side or drink, even during busy periods. KFC, also owned by Yum! Brands, is making its own changes with a new kitchen display system at its U.S. locations.

That system has made drive-thru service 8% faster and cut refunds by 12%. Delivery drivers now wait 20 fewer seconds for their orders. The article quotes Yum! Brands CFO Ranjith Roy, who said the company expects AI to be transformative to the business.

The rollout has not been without problems. Last year, the system drew attention after a customer tried to order 18,000 cups of water, a moment that spread widely online. The article's author, Jonathan Small, is an Entrepreneur staff writer who reports on the results. The article does not describe any further steps beyond the planned expansion to more than 1,500 restaurants.

Articles.Title: Taco Bell Put AI in 900 Drive-Thrus — Here’s What Happened to Sales

stories.Headline: Georgia students raise privacy concerns over AI smart glasses
stories.Summary:
Georgia students are voicing worries about Meta's AI-powered smart glasses, which can translate conversations, send texts, take calls and record video. The glasses look like ordinary eyewear, and an LED light is meant to show when recording is underway, but students told WSB-TV that they cannot easily tell whether someone is filming them. Georgia Tech student Gia Pisicchio said that without a visible camera she never knows whether she is being recorded. Another student, Hufsa Qidwai, said unwanted recordings, including some involving sexual harassment, have become a concern on campus. The reporting by Tom Regan was published on November 10, 2026.

Earlier this year, University of Georgia police investigated complaints from students who said people wearing smart glasses secretly filmed them on campus. One interaction involving a student's appearance was later posted to social media. Kade Crockford of the ACLU said people still expect some privacy and anonymity in public spaces. Under Georgia and federal law, recording people in public is generally legal because there is no expectation of privacy there. Recording in private places such as restrooms, locker rooms or homes can bring criminal or civil consequences.

Misuse has also appeared beyond Georgia and in the state itself. In Boston this summer, a registered sex offender was charged with using camera-equipped sunglasses to record children changing at a playground. In June, Milton police arrested Christopher Hall on felony eavesdropping and surveillance charges after a mother found smart glasses on her car pointed toward her 13-year-old daughter's bedroom window. Hall's friend told Channel 2 he believed Hall may have gotten drunk at a party and left the glasses behind. A Georgia law that took effect this year bans smart glasses and other personal electronic devices in schools.

Superintendent-elect Dr. Lydia Powell warned that students could photograph tests and post them online or record classmates in restrooms. Privacy advocates are also worried that facial recognition could be added to the glasses, which the ACLU says could let wearers covertly identify people and store that information. Meta says it is exploring the technology but has not made a final decision. According to Meta, the recording light cannot be turned off or disabled, and if it is blocked, such as with tape, the camera will not work. Questions remain about how images and other data collected by the glasses are used.

Articles.Title: Georgia students raise privacy concerns over AI smart glasses
