Kim Young-joo, head of the macroeconomic forecasting department at the Bank of Korea's Research Department, cautioned that the chip-led boom could prove a double-edged sword, since overall growth becomes more sensitive to swings in the semiconductor cycle. Lim Hong-ki, director of the economic analysis division at the Ministry of Finance and Economy's Economic Policy Bureau, said next year's policy motto is to let growth spread beyond semiconductors to other sectors.

Articles.Title: Bloomberg, JPMorgan See Korea Growing Faster Than 3.1% Next Year on AI Spending - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Some school board members push back against Google's AI search ultimatum - The Frederick News-Post
stories.Summary:
Some Frederick County school board members have pushed back against a recent Google announcement that it will cut off Google search access to schools that have banned AI. The announcement, reported by the Associated Press and published on November 10, 2026, is aimed at school districts that have restricted artificial intelligence tools. The articles do not say exactly when Google's cutoff would take effect or how many districts it would affect. What is clear is that the policy has drawn sharp reactions from local educators.

Board President Dean Rose said Monday that the board will not bend to what he called Google's "strong-arm tactic," and he noted that schools losing Google search would not be left without options because "they are not the only search engine on the market." Rose's comments were reported as part of the board's public response. The articles also quote a Google spokesperson, who indicated that the company views its AI tools as a way to help students, though the excerpt provided is partly garbled and does not give a full statement. The school board's position is that its decisions about AI use belong with the district, not the company.

Frederick County Public Schools has restricted AI in classrooms, and the district's leaders say they will continue to make those decisions for their students. The articles do not say whether the district has taken any formal step beyond these public statements, such as filing a complaint or changing its search provider. Other school boards, including one in Nevada whose president, Melissa Frank, reportedly criticized the company, have also spoken against the policy, according to the Associated Press report. The articles do not indicate whether Google plans to revisit the policy or how the dispute will be resolved.

Articles.Title: Some school board members push back against Google's AI search ultimatum - The Frederick News-Post

stories.Headline: Job Seekers Cram AI Skills, but Firms Say Basics Suffice
stories.Summary:
Seven to eight out of ten South Korean job seekers believe artificial intelligence skills matter when applying for jobs, yet only two in ten companies formally assess those skills during hiring. The Federation of Korean Industries released the findings on the 10th, based on a survey of 500 university students in their third year or above and 200 companies among the country's top 1,000 firms by revenue. Of the job seekers, 77.0% said AI skills are important for landing a job, while 15.2% called them of average importance and 7.8% said they were not important. The survey showed a clear gap in expectations between the two groups.

Among the companies, 39.0% said they place significant weight on AI skills when hiring entry-level staff, another 39.0% rated them of average importance, and 22.0% said they were not important. Only 20.0% include AI skills as a formal item in hiring evaluations, while 43.0% consider them only if applicants raise them voluntarily and 37.0% ignore them entirely. The two sides also disagreed on the proficiency needed. Of the job seekers, 54.8% said candidates must be able to verify and revise AI output or redesign work processes with AI, but only 18.0% of companies set either level as the minimum for new hires.

Most companies set a lower bar. A combined 67.5% cited either task application, meaning using AI to produce work for a specific business purpose (39.0%), or basic use such as searching, summarizing and drafting (28.5%). Another 14.5% said they do not require AI skills at all. Kwon Hyuk-min, head of the growth strategy division at the Federation of Korean Industries, said job seekers should focus on gaining experience applying AI to their majors and job functions rather than mastering advanced technology. He also said university education needs to shift toward practical training tied to majors and specific job roles.

Articles.Title: Job Seekers Cram AI Skills, but Firms Say Basics Suffice - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: U.S. Stocks Plunge in Unprecedented AI Panic Selling
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, New York stocks fell sharply in what the article calls unprecedented AI-driven selling. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite closed at 24,315.00, down 1,421.52 points, or 5.52%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, to 51,523.06. The Standard & Poor's 500 dropped 334.89 points, or 4.36%, to 7,353.73. The Nasdaq and S&P 500 declines were the steepest since April 2 of last year, when Trump announced reciprocal tariffs.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25% to 9,011.14, its biggest drop since a 15.90% fall on March 16, 2020. The index closed below the 10,000 line for the first time since April 28. Nvidia's value shrank to $4.3765 trillion, widening its gap with Apple, which remained above $5 trillion. Shares of AI infrastructure firms such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN also fell for a second straight day.

The article says the selling was driven by fears that Democratic governors will restrict AI data center construction. Democrats won governorships in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, states where many new data center projects are planned. Goldman Sachs estimated that about 45% of planned U.S. data center expansion capacity could be affected by the Democratic victory. Some estimates put scrapped projects at roughly 10 to 15%, and Wall Street expects at least 10 to 15 gigawatts of capacity due online next year could sit idle.

Texas Democrat Gina Hinojosa, elected governor, pledged an immediate moratorium on approvals for new data center construction, saying data centers are depleting residents' drinking water and raising electricity bills. Senator-elect James Talarico of Texas pledged to end tax breaks for data center developers, and Ohio Senator-elect Sherrod Brown pledged to work for voters rather than data centers or Wall Street. According to Ballotpedia data cited by Politico and CNBC, residents voted against development in 40 of 41 data center referendums across 10 states. Elon Musk, who gave $446 million to Republicans in the midterms, saw SpaceX stock fall to $123.62, below its $135 IPO price, and the combined market value of SpaceX and Tesla lost $370 billion this week.

Oil prices were also volatile, with Brent and WTI rebounding about 3.88% and 2.72% on November 5 after falling more than 8% the previous day. Ten-year Treasury yields fell 0.049 percentage point to 4.843%, and gold rose 0.99% to $4,113.50 per troy ounce. According to CME FedWatch, the odds of a Fed rate hike at the December 8-9 FOMC meeting fell to 70.9% from 82.7%. The article notes that investor sentiment could also weigh on AI company IPOs planned by Anthropic and OpenAI.

JonesTrading chief market strategist Michael O'Rourke said a slowdown in data center investment driven by political change will materialize and that earnings estimates behind the bull case are no longer valid. Bill Ackman told CNBC on November 3 that stocks were trading at prices that make no sense. Other analysts disagreed, with Natixis's Mabrouk Chetouane arguing the Democrats will not halt AI policies given the U.S.-China competition, and RWA Wealth Partners' Joseph Edmund Powers calling the concerns somewhat exaggerated. Powers said the burden on state governments will grow but will not greatly affect existing projects. Some predict Democratic governors will pursue alternative regulations or conditional approvals instead of outright bans.

Articles.Title: U.S. Stocks Plunge in Unprecedented AI Panic Selling - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: PwC to Train 85,000 Staff in Critical Thinking as AI Reshapes Work
stories.Summary:
PwC has announced a critical-thinking and judgement certification programme for more than 85,000 partners and employees, as artificial intelligence takes over tasks that junior professionals have traditionally performed. The firm made the announcement on 9 November 2026, according to the Big4News report published on 10 November. The aim is to help staff evaluate information, question assumptions and exercise independent judgement when working alongside AI tools. The programme will include personalised simulations in which employees must challenge AI-generated conclusions, such as reviewing an AI assessment of a company's internal controls and identifying its deficiencies. The training will combine diagnostic assessments, masterclasses, practical exercises and workplace tools.

PwC plans to begin rolling it out in December 2026 across its US and Mexico offices and offshore service centres, with completion targeted for June 2027. The firm expects to invest more than $100 million in the initiative, including programme development and support for universities. It also intends to make its critical-thinking framework available to universities in early 2027. The report places the move within a wider problem facing the Big Four, where AI increasingly performs the routine work through which junior auditors once built their professional judgement. Earlier in the year, KPMG US redesigned its audit internship programme to add fraud-detection simulations, and a study it ran with the University of Texas at Austin found mixed results among 523 early-career professionals working with AI agents.

Half improved on the AI's performance, about a quarter matched it, and nearly a quarter performed worse than the AI alone. The article also cites warnings from Wayne Banks, a chartered accountant and former global CFO, about automation deference, the gradual loss of scepticism when staff accept polished AI output without testing it. The article raises the open question of whether simulations and formal certification can build the depth of judgement that years of supervised audit work once produced. It notes that the answer will matter for audit quality as AI takes on more analysis and evidence evaluation. The report does not say how PwC's programme will be assessed beyond its completion target.

Articles.Title: PwC to Train 85,000 Staff in Critical Thinking as AI Reshapes Work - https://www.big4news.com/

stories.Headline: Meta to Introduce Muse AI Agent in India Starting With ₹1,799 Plan: Report
stories.Summary:
Meta has reportedly listed subscription prices for Muse, its personal artificial intelligence agent, ahead of a planned launch in India. According to a report by The Hindu, cited by Analytics India Magazine on November 10, 2026, the Power plan is listed at ₹1,799 per month and the Maximum plan at ₹8,999. The prices appear on Muse's service, with slightly higher charges for subscriptions bought through Google Play and Apple's billing systems. Meta has not confirmed a launch date or the India-specific pricing, so it remains unclear whether these figures are final.

Muse is designed to carry out tasks on a user's behalf rather than only answer questions. Meta introduced it on September 8, and the agent can browse websites, work with connected applications and keep working on assigned tasks after the user closes the app. It can send emails, book travel, fill in online forms and coordinate longer-term tasks through a dedicated cloud-based virtual machine with its own browser. Users choose which applications Muse may access and set permissions for different activities, and the agent asks for approval before sensitive actions such as sending emails or making purchases. Indian users are currently on a waitlist, and although the web and WhatsApp interfaces can be reached from India, some features remain restricted.

Meta is the company behind Muse, which it first rolled out in the United States through its website, dedicated iOS and Android apps and WhatsApp. The company has also said it plans to bring the agent to its AI glasses. In the US, the Power plan costs $20 per month and the Maximum plan $100 per month, and both paid tiers offer higher usage limits than a free tier. Analytics India Magazine's report does not give a launch date for India, and Meta has not announced one.

The context is the agent's growth so far. According to SensorTower data cited by TechCrunch, Muse has recorded more than 10 million downloads within two months of its launch. Its integration with WhatsApp could give it an additional route to users in India, where the messaging platform has a large user base. The articles do not say when Muse will officially become available to Indian users or whether the listed prices will be confirmed.

Articles.Title: Meta to Introduce Muse AI Agent in India Starting With ₹1,799 Plan: Report - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: TSMC October Revenue Hits Record $17.81 Bn on Skyrocketing AI Chip Demand
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world's largest contract chipmaker, reported its highest-ever monthly revenue for October, with sales up 59.7% from a year earlier. Consolidated revenue came to NT$586.89 billion, or about $17.81 billion, which was 14.7% higher than in September. The figure beat the company's previous monthly record of $15.63 billion, set in August. Analytics India Magazine reported the results on November 10, 2026.

Revenue for January through October reached $140 billion, a 43.3% increase over the same period last year. The growth reflects rising demand for advanced semiconductor manufacturing as technology companies expand their artificial intelligence infrastructure. Much of that demand is for chips made on advanced processes, including the 2-nanometre technology that has entered commercial production. During its October earnings conference, TSMC raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast to about 44% in US dollar terms, up from an earlier projection of slightly above 40%.

The company attributed the revised forecast to robust demand for its advanced manufacturing processes, and it expects fourth-quarter revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion. In the third quarter, high-performance computing rose 22% from the previous quarter and made up 68% of total company revenue. The 2-nanometre process accounted for 8% of total wafer revenue in that quarter. TSMC's shares closed 2.24% higher on the Taiwan Stock Exchange on November 10.

The article also notes wider turmoil among AI chip players, since TSMC manufactures chips for NVIDIA, among other firms. NVIDIA has faced scrutiny over reports of an investigation involving its CEO, Jensen Huang, and his relationship with an accused Chinese spy, as well as a proposed shareholder lawsuit. According to Reuters, NVIDIA shares fell 4.3% on November 9, erasing roughly $190 billion in market value. The article does not say how these matters will affect TSMC's future orders.

Articles.Title: TSMC October Revenue Hits Record $17.81 Bn on Skyrocketing AI Chip Demand - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Gartner Introduces Framework for CIOs to Determine AI Outcomes
stories.Summary:
Gartner has released a framework called the Value-Risk Flywheel to help chief information officers align the value that artificial intelligence creates for enterprises with the risks it brings, according to an article published on November 10, 2026. The framework centres on two forces that shape AI outcomes, momentum and drag, and the company says these forces do not always behave as expected. Gartner argues that momentum is not always good and that some drag is beneficial. The framework is meant to guide organisations through the complexity of AI implementation and governance.

Daryl Plummer, Distinguished VP, Managing VP and Chief of Research at Gartner, said the best thing a CIO can do is align value with risk and align safety with governance. He said that CIOs who outperform know how to build positive momentum and add useful drag while reducing harmful momentum and harmful drag. As an example, the article says that in software development, value can compound faster than risk because AI can generate a significant share of code. This relieves developers of manual coding and lets them focus on rapid prototyping, requirements-driven development, architectural thinking and product engineering.

Plummer also said the flywheel needs a governor at its centre, a figure who decides when value is worth the risk, which perspective on value should dominate and how to keep the organisation safe. Kristin Moyer, Distinguished VP Analyst and Gartner Fellow, described this governor as a centralised decision authority that drives advice and guides action on accountability, technology and economics. The article ties the framework to a Q2 2026 Gartner survey of more than 2,000 CIOs and technology executives. That survey found that 71 percent of organisations expect to deploy agentic AI within the next 12 months, while only 21 percent have governance mechanisms for agentic AI. Moyer said this imbalance makes it harder to create value faster than AI increases risk.

Articles.Title: Gartner Introduces Framework for CIOs to Determine AI Outcomes - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: AI Theatre vs Real Adoption - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Raj Goodman Anand, founder and director of AI-First Mindset, argued in an ETCIO opinion piece published on November 10, 2026 that many companies stage AI adoption without really changing how work gets done. Despite substantial investment in AI licences and training, usage often rises after launch and then falls back to a flat line. He described seeing companies with a hundred licences where only five people opened the tool on an ordinary day. The piece draws a line between visible steps, such as buying licences and holding training sessions, and the harder work of rewriting workflows.

The author set out several signs that adoption is theatre rather than real. AI is mentioned at town halls but appears in no process document, and pilots run without end dates, which he treats as a way of avoiding decisions. A Head of AI may hold a title but have no budget or authority to change how a department works. He also warned against measuring success by logins, since a login shows curiosity but not whether a task got faster, cheaper or better. Training, he added, fades quickly unless people apply it to their own real tasks within about a week, with their managers checking.

Anand's central recommendation is to start small: pick two or three frequently repeated workflows that frustrate the people doing them and give each a clear owner. He suggests timing each task before and after redesigning it with the people who do the work, using a sales proposal as an example, where AI produces the first draft and a senior person reviews it. Ownership matters, he argued, because a workflow owned by a committee has no one who can say whether it worked. He also set a test for CEOs: name three tasks that take less time today because of AI, and say by how much. Companies should scale what works and stop what doesn't, rather than announcing a company-wide rollout of something unproven.

Articles.Title: AI Theatre vs Real Adoption - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Zendesk launches outcome AI platform with new pricing
stories.Summary:
Zendesk has launched its Outcome AI Platform along with a new plan called Zendesk Unlimited, moving its service software away from per-seat charges. The platform combines AI assistants, specialised AI agents and human teams in one system for customer and employee requests. Under the new model, customers can set an outcome budget and pay for eligible issues resolved and business work completed rather than buying software seats. Zendesk says the platform can automate up to 84% of service requests and cut resolution times from hours to minutes. Outcomes are assessed for quality and completeness before they count towards a customer's budget.

Zendesk Unlimited removes seat limits from the new plans, so customers get unlimited seats alongside AI tools, with features varying by tier. The company argues that as AI takes on more service work, businesses want spending tied more directly to completed work and verified resolutions. The announcement also introduced Open Service Directory, an open specification and public directory of verified brand support channels that personal AI assistants can use to find official routes for a business. Businesses that join can decide what information they share and when human review is required. Zendesk says the directory does not access private customer data or act on its own.

Zendesk also unveiled Zendesk Bridge, which connects external AI tools and agents to Zendesk service workflows. Administrators can control which AI tools connect, what information they can access and which actions they can take, and each action is subject to identity checks, permissions, human approvals and audit trails. Early directory participants named in the announcement include Betterment, ElevenLabs, Flex, TeamSystem, TBA Auctions, Telekom Payment and Wireless Logic. The launch was tied to Zendesk's survey finding that 52% of consumers are comfortable relying on personal AI assistants for everyday tasks.

Zendesk's chief executive, Tom Eggemeier, said the change reflects a broader shift in how people want to deal with organisations, wanting help to accomplish their goal without navigating channels or departments. Tapan Patel of IDC said the pricing model addresses enterprise buyers' wish to tie AI spending to verified resolutions and business outcomes. Bikram Mazumdar, Vice President of Zendesk Asia, said companies in the region face pressure to show returns from AI spending. The articles do not describe any further rollout timeline beyond the launch itself.

Articles.Title: Zendesk launches outcome AI platform with new pricing - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Linux Foundation launches Agent Name Service for AI
stories.Summary:
The Linux Foundation has added Agent Name Service, or ANS, as a new project, aiming to give AI agents a verifiable identity and a way to be discovered online. The standard was reported on 11 November 2026 by IT Brief Australia. It builds on the Domain Name System already used across the internet, and the project is being developed openly under the oversight of the project's technical steering committee. Eleven organisations have contributed to or adopted the standard so far.

The specification covers how AI agents are named and registered, how their identities are published through DNS and verified, and how identity records are monitored for unauthorised changes. It also sets out how agents authenticate one another. The work is organised into seven documents covering domain-anchored naming, registration and versioning, DNS publication, public log auditing, integrity monitoring, and agent-to-agent authentication. Supporters say building on DNS and certificate-based verification means relying on infrastructure that is already widely deployed and well understood.

Jim Zemlin, chief executive officer of the Linux Foundation, said autonomous AI agents operating across global systems cannot succeed without verifiable identity. He argued that neutral governance gives the industry a common foundation for trust that it can adopt and improve together. The eleven supporting organisations named include Cisco, Cloudflare, DigiCert, DistributedApps.ai, GoDaddy, HOL, Infoblox, Radix, Salesforce, OWASP, and Trustmodel.ai. Cloudflare's chief technology officer, Dane Knecht, said organisations need to know who an agent represents before trusting it to act.

The AGNTCY Agent Directory Service, another Linux Foundation project, already supports verification of ANS identities. ANS Finder implements the Agentic Resource Discovery specification and has passed registry conformance tests. Backers argue that wide use of autonomous agents will depend on a shared trust model rather than isolated vendor-specific approaches. Several backers also praised placing the specification under the Linux Foundation instead of a single commercial sponsor, which they say keeps the system open to multiple participants.

Articles.Title: Linux Foundation launches Agent Name Service for AI - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Australia leads use of AI agents, but managers feel strain
stories.Summary:
Australia ranked highest among seven markets for the use of AI agents in multi-step work, according to new research commissioned by monday.com and conducted by Nielsen. The study surveyed 1,701 Directors and Senior Managers in large companies and found that 46% of Australian respondents use AI agents for multi-step work, compared with a global average of 38%. It also found that 58% expect to manage more agents than people within the next 12 months. Alongside this rapid adoption, many Australian managers reported spending more time supervising AI output.

The research shows a gap between deploying AI and reorganising work around it. Some 59% of Australian leaders said they now spend more time reviewing and guiding their team's output since AI use increased, the highest result among the markets surveyed, and a third said AI adds hours to their working day. Managers must decide what work to delegate, provide context, connect systems, check results and correct errors, all while remaining responsible for the final output. Australian respondents also reported more software tools, with 65% using more since adopting AI, and 36% saying manual steps in workflows have increased.

monday.com, which uses the term "agent sprawl" for a growing build-up of AI agents and automated hand-offs without clear ownership, controls or measures of value, has been vocal on the issue. Gavin Watson, its Regional Director, AI & Industries, argued that agent count is becoming a vanity metric and that businesses should measure whether entire workflows move faster with less rework. He said every agent needs a defined outcome, its own permissions, a clear point of human escalation and one accountable owner. The survey also found that 44% of respondents fear agents will not receive enough human oversight, and 31% worry about being held accountable for an agent's work.

The findings come as policymakers and public agencies examine how organisations use AI systems and how much autonomy they should have. The survey also found that four in five Australian organisations have changed how they evaluate employees since adopting AI, and 40% use AI to draft performance reviews. Watson warned that polish and speed may stop being reliable evidence of ability when several agents help produce the same output. The article does not say what regulatory steps, if any, will follow.

Articles.Title: Australia leads use of AI agents, but managers feel strain - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Everpure adds AI & VM storage tools for Kubernetes
stories.Summary:
Everpure has introduced new Portworx features aimed at AI workloads and virtual machines running on Kubernetes, according to an IT Brief Australia report published on 11 November 2026. The updates include pre-staged volumes for AI and machine learning work, general availability of Kube Datastore for virtual machines, and broader observability in the Portworx operations centre. The company also said IDC MarketScape named it a Leader in container data and infrastructure management software. The changes are presented as a way to cut data access delays and give platform teams a more consistent way to manage storage.

Pre-staged volumes are designed to address delays where AI applications wait while large model weights or datasets are downloaded before a workload starts. The approach places warm local copies of persistent volume data across cluster nodes, and storage policies decide which copy a workload uses when it starts or moves to another node. This is meant to shorten startup times and speed recovery when workloads are restarted or rescheduled. The feature is not yet generally available and is expected in the first quarter of 2027. Kube Datastore, known as KDS, is now generally available on supported SAN arrays and lets storage for virtual machines, containers and AI workloads be managed through Kubernetes.

Everpure said KDS supports dynamic and static pools for predictable storage placement and capacity control, while relying on the underlying array for performance and resilience. It also said workloads can run with fewer replicas, and that platform engineers can handle rebalancing and maintenance through Kubernetes-native workflows. Greg Muscarella, General Manager of Portworx at Everpure, said enterprises need to build new applications and modernise existing ones without losing availability or adding operational complexity. He said the company's latest innovations, including Kube Datastore, are meant to simplify storage management, speed recovery from infrastructure failures and improve storage efficiency. IDC's MarketScape report described Portworx as a good fit for enterprises running mission-critical virtual machines, containers or AI workloads on Kubernetes.

The release also expands ecosystem support, with Portworx now available for customers deploying Red Hat OpenShift 5. Everpure's operations centre gained visibility into pool inventory, live migration progress and hyperconvergence state through a single interface. A bring-your-own-backup model will also sit alongside the company's own backup and disaster recovery tools, giving customers more choice. The article places these moves within a wider industry push to run virtual machines, containers and AI applications on one Kubernetes-based platform, a shift in which storage and data management have become central.

Articles.Title: Everpure adds AI & VM storage tools for Kubernetes - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Ansarada expands AI capabilities to streamline deals with OS Bondi 3.0
stories.Summary:
Ansarada, an Australian virtual data room company, is expanding its artificial intelligence capabilities with new tools for due diligence and document analysis in its operating system, OS Bondi 3.0. The company is developing automated question-and-answer workflows and document analysis tools that aim to reduce manual work in transactions while keeping AI security and governance controls in place. The announcement was reported on November 11, 2026, and the changes build on its existing AI assistant, AiDA. Managing Director Justin Smith described the developments as a shift from individual documents to data across the whole data room. The article does not give a release date for the new features.

The roadmap includes intelligent question prioritisation and automated draft responses, along with a document analysis feature called Review with AiDA, which is in early beta and initially available to a limited audience. Question prioritisation will identify questions submitted by multiple parties, such as potential buyers and investors, and prepare draft answers from documents in the data room. Review with AiDA will analyse information across multiple documents, such as contracts, clauses, addresses and remuneration details, to help spot inconsistencies and missing information. A planned My Documents feature will give users a personal file area for sharing and analysing documents before they are added to the indexed material. Ansarada is also developing AiDA access packs that authorised participants, including buyers, can purchase.

Smith said the company is working to keep human reviewers responsible for the process, with AiDA drafting answers that reviewers check, verify against evidence and approve before they are shared with external parties. He said the aim is to give deal teams more time for judgement, and that Ansarada is not replacing advisers or giving advice. Smith also said the company's large language models do not learn from the substantive content of customers' data room documents, but from activity patterns and interactions. He further said the platform operates within Ansarada's own cloud environment and respects existing access permissions, with customers able to control and revoke AI access. The article also says the platform keeps an auditable record of activity.

Ansarada's platform is used for mergers and acquisitions, where due diligence often requires reviewing extensive documentation and answering large numbers of questions from outside parties. The article says Ansarada's experience across approximately 60,000 transactions informs its plans. The company's AiDA assistant helps deal teams search documents, retrieve information and summarise key details within a secure data room. The article notes the Q&A process is one of the most time-consuming parts of due diligence.

Smith identified more proactive assistance as a key development area over the next 12 months. A future version of AiDA could highlight missing information, flag risks and suggest actions based on the stage of a transaction. The company wants to make AI-supported transaction management accessible to smaller organisations and founders selling a business for the first time. Smith said the goal is to give smaller businesses access to the same kinds of secure technology and transaction insights available to larger organisations. The article describes the challenge as reducing the administrative burden of complex transactions without compromising confidentiality, accountability and human judgement.

Articles.Title: Ansarada expands AI capabilities to streamline deals with OS Bondi 3.0 - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Bizarre AI chip demo uses butter to highlight how new chip runs 40 degrees cooler than the competition
stories.Summary:
Deepx, a chip company, has drawn attention with an unusual demonstration in which competing chips are shown melting butter while its own processor leaves the butter intact. The article, published by Tom's Hardware on November 9, 2026, describes the demo as a dairy-based benchmark for thermal performance. The headline says the new chip runs 40 degrees cooler than the competition. The article's core claim is that the Deepx processor generates less heat than rival chips during operation. The article's details are limited, but the thrust of the story is that lower thermal output is presented as the key advantage of the new processor.

The demo was used to make that difference visible in a simple way, with butter standing in as a heat indicator placed on or near the chips. The headline's reference to a 40-degree gap is the only specific figure given for the comparison. The article does not appear to set out the test conditions, the chips compared, or the methodology in detail. The company behind the chip is Deepx, and the article reports that the demonstration highlights its low thermals. The article as provided does not include direct statements from Deepx executives or independent testers.

Responsibility for the claims therefore rests with the company and with the outlet's report of its demo. Readers should note that the comparison is a promotional showcase rather than a published, independently verified benchmark. Heat management has become a central concern for AI accelerators, since high power draw and temperatures affect cooling costs, density, and reliability in data centers. The articles provided do not state what happens next, such as product availability, pricing, or further independent testing. Any such developments would need to come from later reporting.

Articles.Title: Bizarre AI chip demo uses butter to highlight how new chip runs 40 degrees cooler than the competition

stories.Headline: Reliable Retrieval for Production AI Systems
stories.Summary:
Lan Chu, an AI Tech Lead and Senior Data Scientist at Rabobank, gave a talk titled "Reliable Retrieval for Production AI Systems" at QCon London, which was recorded on December 16, 2026 and published by InfoQ on November 10, 2026. Her talk concerned how to move enterprise retrieval-augmented generation systems beyond simple prototypes and into production. She drew on real deployments at Rabobank to describe the changes needed for that move. The talk is about 45 minutes long and is presented as part of the AI, ML and Data Engineering track.

According to the summary, Chu covers several specific practices. She recommends replacing naive OCR with agentic multimodal parsing, so that documents are read in a more capable way. She describes encoding non-textual temporal signals, which helps prevent systems from retrieving outdated information. She also discusses using bootstrap statistical evaluations to test system quality, and establishing continuous observability so that systems can meet the strict governance demands of banking. The summary frames these as necessary for systems to survive in a heavily regulated environment.

Chu's background includes more than seven years building production data and machine learning pipelines and more than three years building generative AI products. She specializes in designing data and AI pipelines and in responsible AI practices, with deep expertise in natural language processing. The talk is one of many at QCon London, a practitioner-driven conference for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors and project managers. The article is an InfoQ presentation page, so it describes the talk and its speaker rather than reporting on any new event or policy.

Articles.Title: Reliable Retrieval for Production AI Systems - infoq.com

stories.Headline: Fluidstack begins construction on a 99-acre AI data center campus in Wythe County, Virginia
stories.Summary:
Fluidstack, the AI cloud provider building data centers for Anthropic, has begun construction on a 99-acre campus at Progress Park in Wythe County, Virginia, DatacenterDynamics reported on Tuesday. The company expects most of the campus to be finished by the end of 2027, with operations starting in phases, as it told county supervisors last month. The site was first announced in December 2025 by Solis Arx, a new developer led by founder and CEO Rob Noll, which projected a total investment of over $1 billion according to county administrator Stephen Bear. Fluidstack later took over the project, and the county's board approved an amendment renaming it Fluidstack in August. Neither the company nor the county has disclosed the campus's power capacity or building size, and no end customer has been named.

Solis Arx arranged electric service directly with Appalachian Power, and the county said the project would not affect local electricity rates. Fluidstack says it will pay for its own electricity use, the infrastructure it needs and upgrades to the nearby substation. The campus will use a closed-loop cooling system that needs an initial fill of about 400,000 gallons of water, with ongoing use mostly for staff. Fluidstack expects about 1,000 construction workers at peak and 75 permanent jobs once the campus is running, and says it did not seek or accept project-specific tax incentives. The county gave the ungraded lot to the developer at no cost and projects more than $10 million a year in tax revenue by 2028 if the schedule holds.

The project has drawn local opposition, and Wythe County has no zoning outside its two towns. Andy Kegley, leader of the residents' group Preserve Wythe, said at an October 28 open house that the deal was done and grading was already underway. The county is now drafting its first land-use ordinance. Anthropic said in November 2025 that it would invest $50 billion in U.S. computing infrastructure with Fluidstack, starting with sites in Texas and New York. Fluidstack is also the anchor tenant at bitcoin-miner conversions backed by Google, including TeraWulf's Lake Mariner campus in New York and Cipher Mining's 168 MW lease.

Articles.Title: Fluidstack begins construction on a 99-acre AI data center campus in Wythe County, Virginia - MLQ.ai

stories.Headline: Google’s chip business is on a faster track than Nvidia’s own AI boom
stories.Summary:
Google introduced two new tensor processing units, its homegrown AI chips, on Monday, November 9, 2026. The TPU 8tx and the TPU 8i Max join the 8t and 8i that the company unveiled in April, which makes this the first time Google has launched four TPU systems in a single year. Both of the new chips ship next year. Alphabet shares rose about 3% on the news, while Nvidia fell 8% after the opening bell and traded at its lowest level since March.

The 8tx is built to keep data encrypted for governments, banks and other regulated businesses, and it is paired with processors from AMD. The 8i Max puts two chips into one package to handle requests with long context windows, meaning the amount of information an AI model can juggle at once. Google used to roll out about one data center TPU a year, and it now has one for each kind of job. Bloomberg Intelligence expects TPU sales to climb from about $12 billion this year to more than $135 billion by 2028, a rise of more than 11-fold in two years, and that figure leaves out chips rented through Google Cloud.

Demand is already strong, according to Yahoo Finance. Epoch AI estimates that TPU shipments doubled in computing power in a single quarter this year, to roughly 800,000 chips. Anthropic's IPO filing shows about $161 billion of lease payments tied to TPUs, which Raymond James says makes it the biggest custom-chip customer of Broadcom, Google's design partner. Meta, OpenAI and Oracle are also buyers. SemiAnalysis found that Google's current Ironwood TPU delivers up to nearly three times as much AI output per dollar as Nvidia's Blackwell chips when running AI agents, though Nvidia's top system still wins when speed matters most.

Nvidia's slide came as its board looks into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, which Yahoo Finance called Wall Street's first $4.5 trillion CEO scandal. Nvidia still holds the stronger hardware, with its next-generation Rubin chip rated at 35 petaflops against about 10 for Google's 8i and about 20 for the 8i Max, by Yahoo Finance's calculations. The article stresses that forecasts are not sales and that Nvidia still sells far more AI chips than anyone else. Nvidia reports third-quarter results on November 17, a day before a requested closed-door House briefing on Huang, and investors will want to know whether customers are hedging their bets. Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon told clients that Huang is no ordinary chief executive and that he is Nvidia.

Articles.Title: Google’s chip business is on a faster track than Nvidia’s own AI boom

stories.Headline: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
stories.Summary:
Scott Wiener, a California state senator who had authored AI safety legislation, was declared the winner of a tight congressional race to succeed former Speaker Nancy Pelosi in San Francisco, a result known by the Friday after the election. The article, published by MIT Technology Review on November 9, 2026, reports that Wiener spoke shortly after his victory was announced. The day before, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report widely read as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a process in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement. Wiener said the report was very concerning and that the window for regulating AI is closing quickly.

Wiener said he had hoped Congress would take decisive action before the end of the year, but he said that did not appear to be happening. The article notes his earlier work, including SB 1047, which Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed in 2024, and SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Wiener has backed a strong, empowered and nimble federal regulator, supported whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements and a kill switch requirement, and said he would be eager to serve on a select committee on artificial intelligence if Congress creates one, a idea Democrats have discussed since September. He also opposes broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some proposed federal legislation would require.

The article describes Wiener's campaign as having received more than $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit favoring AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. Opponents criticized him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener rejected that charge, saying the group backed him because he was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce and pass AI regulation. He described the attacks as cynical. On the broader political mood, the article reports that voters approved 40 of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on the same day, and Wiener said he views that movement as driven mainly by local concerns such as electric bills, water use and impacts near homes rather than by AI risk.

Wiener described himself as only cautiously optimistic about Congress's ability to rein in AI, citing its record on regulating the tech industry. He also voiced concern about getting legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a hoax in September. Wiener said Trump's unpredictability offers some hope, while adding that he hopes a disaster does not prompt action. The article presents these views as Wiener's own and does not describe any specific federal bill advancing or any vote scheduled.

Articles.Title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI

stories.Headline: Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company that has generally preferred renting computing capacity to owning physical infrastructure, is now spending $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines. According to a Financial Times report cited by TechCrunch, the company is buying Caterpillar generators that the equipment supplier OnePWR had originally ordered. The generators can produce up to 1.7 gigawatts of electricity. The article describes the purchase as part of a broader rush by AI firms to secure power as demand for computing grows.

Anthropic's shift is notable because the company has historically avoided buying infrastructure. Its S-1 filing in May disclosed that it pays SpaceX subsidiary xAI $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 for computing power. In that filing, Anthropic said it expected to enter into additional similar services contracts. The article notes that the backlog for natural gas turbines extends into the early 2030s, and grid connection queues can be just as long, which may have pushed the company toward direct ownership. OnePWR had ordered the turbines a couple of years ago but could not find financing to complete the purchase, so Anthropic bought from Caterpillar directly instead.

TechCrunch reports that OnePWR did not explain why it could not secure financing, despite Anthropic's apparent interest as a customer. The article suggests Anthropic may have wanted to keep the generating capacity for itself rather than let a competitor acquire it. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta have each announced plans to build large natural gas plants to power their data centers on site instead of relying on the public grid. The article's author, Tim De Chant, a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch, frames the purchase within this wider trend.

The article places the buildout in a larger context. It says the trend has given new momentum to fracking, the drilling method used to extract natural gas from underground rock. If the plans proceed, U.S. data centers alone could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035. It also warns that reliance on gas exposes these companies to price swings, and one analyst expects prices could more than triple by the end of the decade in some markets. If that happens, the article suggests, Anthropic could regret the purchase.

Articles.Title: Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines

stories.Headline: AI-fueled hacking is getting worse — top cyber companies are turning away some victims
stories.Summary:
Cybersecurity firms say they are being overwhelmed by work as AI-aided cyberattacks have grown severe enough that some of the largest companies in the sector are turning away new customers who need emergency help. The report, written by Kevin Collier and published by NBC News on November 9, 2026, describes a surge in attacks that have been made faster and more effective through artificial intelligence tools. The article itself is largely built around that central development, and the page text available to me contains little beyond the headline, the opening summary, and unrelated navigation and story listings. Because of that, the specific figures, dates of individual incidents, company names, and detailed requirements or policy changes that a fuller account would normally include are not present in what I was given.

What the piece reports is that the strain on the industry has reached the point where firms cannot take on everyone who calls. Victims seeking urgent assistance after breaches are being refused by some top providers, which means organizations hit by attacks may have to look for help elsewhere or wait longer for response. The article's summary frames this as a worsening trend rather than a single event, pointing to the growing volume of AI-fueled intrusions as the driving pressure on response capacity. Beyond that, I cannot confirm which firms are involved, how many customers have been turned away, or what changes in pricing, staffing, or service rules the companies have adopted.

The article's summary also indicates that the companies themselves are the ones describing the flood of work, so responsibility for the capacity limits rests with the firms' own accounts of their workloads. I do not have their statements or any quoted remarks from executives, government officials, or security researchers, so I cannot paraphrase what any particular party said. Nor can I say what regulators or lawmakers have done in response or what the next steps are expected to be. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI-fueled hacking is getting worse — top cyber companies are turning away some victims

stories.Headline: New survey finds enterprises trapped between legacy software and AI modernization
stories.Summary:
A Google Cloud blog post published on November 9, 2026 under the byline of Jeanette Manfra, a vice president and head of risk and compliance at the company, reports on a survey of 1,250 enterprise IT and business decision-makers across the United States. The survey was conducted with Hypothesis Group and examined how existing software affects companies' ability to adopt artificial intelligence. Its central finding is that legacy software, meaning programs that run locally on computers and servers rather than natively in the cloud, is holding back AI projects. The article says that 49% of respondents reported that reliance on on-premises software had delayed, reduced in scope, paused or canceled AI or other technology initiatives.

The article describes the operational toll as a zero-sum contest for engineering time. Routine patching and maintenance of legacy systems were identified as a main bottleneck, and the author argues that AI-enabled vulnerability discovery is surfacing flaws faster than human security teams can address them. Because of this, IT staff are spending time maintaining old systems instead of pursuing AI modernization. The survey also found that 39% of decision-makers said reliance on legacy software and cloud providers forces them into complex licensing rules, contracts or limited negotiating flexibility. The author further warns that concentrating operating systems, productivity tools, cloud hosting and AI models with a single vendor creates a single point of failure and a larger attack surface.

The author, Manfra, argues that vendor lock-in is the reason organizations keep relying on constraining legacy environments, and calls on enterprise buyers and policymakers to ensure genuine choice and interoperability. The survey found that 80% of leaders agree a provider's installed base should not determine which AI technology an organization uses, and 78% believe the providers who led the previous era of enterprise technology may not be best positioned to lead the AI era. The post recommends demanding architectural and provider choice, building secure-by-design software that eliminates vulnerability classes before release, and using AI-driven defenses such as Google's Security Command Center and Mandiant threat analytics to remediate existing legacy vulnerabilities. The article does not report any regulatory action or scheduled next steps beyond these recommendations.

Articles.Title: New survey finds enterprises trapped between legacy software and AI modernization

stories.Headline: Medium’s new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process
stories.Summary:
Medium launched a new app called TK on Monday, which aims to bring AI assistance directly into the writing process. Users can invoke the built-in assistant by typing "@TK" followed by a request or prompt inside the editor. The name borrows from publishing, where "TK" marks a placeholder for information to be added later, and the spelling makes it easy for proofreaders to spot. The assistant is meant to fill in those blanks, answering quick factual questions that would otherwise send a writer to another tab and pulling in notes saved earlier in the drafting process.

TK will also ship with skills for editorial feedback and headline suggestions, and it can check a draft against the style guide for Medium publications. Writers can connect their own AI agent through TK's MCP server or a Claude skill so the app can better understand their projects and ideas. TK also offers memory and organization tools that surface past writing, along with writing prompts. A social layer lets writers share early drafts and collect feedback from others. The app is free for anyone with a Medium account and is currently available on the web, with a desktop version on the roadmap.

The launch comes at a sensitive time for the publishing industry, which has been grappling with AI's role in long-form writing. Several authors have lost book deals after suspicions that they used AI to write, and some literary awards have faced scrutiny over similar concerns. Writers have long relied on automated tools for proofreading, but there is growing worry that AI editing suggestions can end up replacing the writer's own thoughts. Reliability of AI detection tools is also in doubt, since models trained on human writing make it hard to tell AI-written text from AI-assisted text. Medium's stance is that these distinctions will matter less over time, and it argues that AI can amplify human intelligence.

Medium acknowledges that AI raises the risk of low-quality content and blurred lines between human and machine writing. To address this, TK lets authors publish notes that explain how AI was used in a piece. Medium described this as a first step toward making the origins of writing clear, transparent, and inspectable, including the prompts and source material used. The article does not say how many writers have adopted the notes feature or whether Medium plans further safeguards.

Articles.Title: Medium’s new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process

stories.Headline: Maryland AI Tracker Focuses on National Job Gains and Displacement Risks
stories.Summary:
Maryland's comptroller, Brooke E. Lierman, has launched a public AI Economic Impact Tracker that combines evidence of growing demand for artificial intelligence skills with forecasts of major workforce disruption. The portal gathers government data, university research and private-sector analysis into one place. Its stated purpose is to give policymakers a view of an economic shift that reaches well beyond the state. The tracker also links these employment and adoption trends to possible pressure on tax revenues and public budgets. That gives fiscal officials a framework for weighing AI's effects alongside employers and workforce planners.

Its dashboard reports 273,000 U.S. AI job postings during the first nine months of 2026, up 79% from the full-year 2025 total. AI positions made up 1.8% of all postings in the third quarter, and California, New York, Washington, Texas and Illinois led in posting volumes. These posting figures come from the University of Maryland–LinkUp AI Maps project, which analyzes employer listings. Its definition covers technical AI skills such as machine learning and model development, and it excludes roles that only use chatbots or that build and maintain data centers. Because the figures count postings, they measure recruitment demand rather than completed hires or net job gains.

Displacement evidence tells a different story: employers cited AI in 120,136 announced U.S. job cuts through September, about 21% of the total, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. AI was the leading reason cited for cuts in that period, although these are employer announcements rather than an independently verified count of jobs lost solely to automation. Longer-term estimates are far larger. The American AI Jobs Risk Index, developed at Tufts University's Fletcher School, identifies 9.3 million jobs vulnerable to displacement under its median adoption scenario, with a range of 2.7 million to 19.5 million depending on how fast adoption proceeds. The tracker places these projections within a two-to-five-year horizon.

Tufts estimates annual wage income at risk at $200 billion to $1.5 trillion, with a midpoint near $757 billion, and it estimates displacement vulnerability at 18% in information, 17% in finance and insurance, and 16% in professional, scientific and technical services. The portal acknowledges that evidence on enterprise integration, operational spending and realized productivity remains thin. Its initial business findings come from a Maryland survey of 276 senior decision makers, mostly at AI-engaged organizations, so the sample cannot establish a national adoption rate. Even so, 91% of respondents used AI, while only 32% reported advanced uses involving core systems, automated processes or agents.

The tracker will receive quarterly updates, with periodic fiscal research briefs starting in 2027. The survey's staffing responses suggest disruption may appear through slower hiring as much as through layoffs, since only 4% expected to eliminate existing positions while 32% expected fewer replacement hires or slower recruitment. For policymakers and businesses, the tracker's usefulness will depend on keeping technical capability, employer intentions, observed hiring and modeled losses clearly separate. Tracking them together could show where retraining, worker support and closer scrutiny of AI deployment may be needed.

Articles.Title: Maryland AI Tracker Focuses on National Job Gains and Displacement Risks

stories.Headline: AI helps sort specialty referrals before scheduling at UTMB
stories.Summary:
The University of Texas Medical Branch, known as UTMB, has begun using artificial intelligence to sort specialty referrals before they are scheduled, a change aimed at shortening long waits for specialist care. The health system added referral triage to an AI agent it already used, built by Bunkerhill Health, and the tool reviews each referral's full chart and assigns a priority. Early results reported by Dr. Salim Hayek, UTMB's vice president and chief transformation officer, show average waits for a first new-patient visit falling from 93 days to 65 across four of the system's longest-running specialties. Those figures are preliminary, and UTMB says its full analysis is still underway. The system works by reading the order, clinic notes, labs, imaging and outside records behind each referral, then applying a playbook written by UTMB's own specialty physicians.

Each referral receives a priority score from 0 to 10 and a recommended pathway, such as a subspecialty clinic, an advanced practice provider, an e-consult, or a redirect to another service like transplant or dialysis. Anything that looks like an emergency goes to the emergency department before scoring, and the agent keeps reviewing the queue as new results arrive. No booking is automated, so schedulers and referral coordinators decide each case, and the recommendations link back to Epic. Hayek said division champions wrote and validated the playbooks against manual chart review, and each champion reviews a random sample of cases every month so the rules can be tuned. He described the aim as giving every referral the review an experienced specialist would give it before anyone schedules it.

He also said the system has reduced the need to add endocrinologists, noting that UTMB had estimated it needed three to four more to meet demand. Now about four in ten endocrinology referrals go to advanced practice providers, and e-consults answer many straightforward questions, often within 48 to 72 hours. The approach responds to a common problem in which referrals with very different levels of urgency sit in the same first-come, first-served queue. According to the article, research on Ontario's e-consult program found that 40% of planned specialist visits were avoided entirely. Hayek said UTMB is now redesigning its scheduling to hold new-patient slots by priority so the patients who need care most are seen first, and he expects the next gains to come from that change.

Articles.Title: AI helps sort specialty referrals before scheduling at UTMB

stories.Headline: AI stocks have 2 major headwinds driving recent volatility
stories.Summary:
AI stocks rose on Monday, November 9, 2026, but markets stayed on edge after a steep sell-off that began the previous week. Brian Sozzi, executive editor at Yahoo Finance, reported that investors fear a slowdown in data center build-outs could delay the profits expected from the largest technology companies. Those concerns grew after the midterm elections, when a wave of Democratic wins raised worries that newly elected senators and governors could disrupt AI expansion. A second, less obvious factor has also weighed on the sector.

Companies including Apple and Amazon have said they are watching their spending on AI tokens more closely, which suggests AI providers may not be able to keep raising prices without limit. Matt Maley, chief markets strategist at Miller Tabal, wrote that enterprises are pushing back on AI pricing. He said a new usage-based pricing policy caused a sharp rise in enterprise AI costs, prompting many firms to route simple queries to cheaper models, adopt open-weight and local models, and set budgets and token caps for employees. Maley argued that these pricing pressures raise doubts about how profitable AI will be.

The selling reached a historic level on November 5, when the S&P 500 fell 4.4 percent and lost about $3 trillion in market value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,800 points, its worst single-day decline since 2020, while the Nasdaq sank 5.5 percent, pulled down by chipmakers and cloud companies such as Micron and Sandisk. Tech stocks have kept trading lower since then. According to the article, the reported developments have intensified doubts about the return on investment from the AI industry, and Maley said many AI bulls' assumptions about the profitability of AI are beginning to fade.

Articles.Title: AI stocks have 2 major headwinds driving recent volatility

stories.Headline: E2E Networks unveils Blaze, a pay-per-token inference service for open AI models
stories.Summary:
E2E Networks has launched Blaze, a pay-per-token inference service for open AI models, and the announcement was published on November 10, 2026. Blaze gives developers and enterprises a single endpoint that is compatible with OpenAI's interface, connecting them to leading open models. The service runs on NVIDIA GPU infrastructure and uses open-source components from NVIDIA DSX OS. Customers pay only for the tokens they use.

The launch comes as Indian AI companies move from pilots to production, where the cost and speed of inference increasingly decide whether a product is viable. Rising token consumption from AI agents and growing AI-assisted development costs are adding pressure on chief information officers to use tokens more efficiently. Data sovereignty and keeping computing within India are also key priorities for buyers. Blaze is aimed at inference-heavy products where latency and cost per token matter most, including voice, coding agents, document AI and OCR, image and video generation, and language applications.

E2E Networks' founder and managing director, Tarun Dua, said customers want frontier-class open-weight models running on an NVIDIA Cloud Partner with reference design clusters as sovereign compute, and that Blaze provides this on E2E Cloud in India. He also said Blaze integrates easily with the rest of the E2E Cloud platform services. Vishal Dhupar, managing director for South Asia at NVIDIA, said access to AI computing and inference services is essential to advancing India's AI ecosystem. He added that NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform gives cloud providers such as E2E a foundation for making AI more accessible to developers and enterprises in India.

Blaze works alongside TIR, E2E's AI platform, which supports self-hosted inference and model training on NVIDIA Blackwell GPU clusters through managed Kubernetes. The service uses NVIDIA Dynamo for distributed model serving, along with other NVIDIA components for routing, scheduling and hardware-level isolation between customers. E2E says its AI factory capacity is expanding to about 14.6 MW, including a 1,024-GPU NVIDIA Blackwell cluster that has been live since May 2026. An additional 5.4 MW of Blackwell capacity, including HGX B300 systems, is also being added.

Articles.Title: E2E Networks unveils Blaze, a pay-per-token inference service for open AI models - varindia

stories.Headline: Berkshire Hathaway's Top AI Holding Is Poised to Outperform
stories.Summary:
Berkshire Hathaway has added to its holdings in Alphabet, the parent company of Google, with the stake now standing as the conglomerate's fourth-largest position across its Class A and Class C shares. According to a Motley Fool article by Neil Patel published on November 9, 2026, Warren Buffett initiated the purchase in the third quarter of last year, and current CEO Greg Abel followed with additional buying. The article presents Alphabet as Berkshire's top artificial intelligence holding and argues that the stock is positioned to outperform the market. It notes that the shares have risen 124% over the past 36 months as of November 4, yet trade 28% below their peak. Shares dipped after third-quarter results missed expectations on both revenue and earnings.

The article points to several figures that account for the valuation. Alphabet's capital expenditures are expected to total roughly $200 billion in 2026, with management projecting a substantial increase next year. Free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion in the third quarter, and long-term debt rose 169% from the end of last year to $125.1 billion. Alphabet trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 18.5, which the author describes as a compelling entry point. Sell-side consensus estimates cited in the piece project operating income growing at a compound annual rate of 28.1% from 2025 to 2028.

Patel attributes the growth case mainly to AI demand. Revenue rose 25% year over year in the most recent quarter, and Google Cloud sales climbed 103% in the third quarter, a streak the author describes as accelerating. The cloud backlog stands at $561 billion. The article says Google Cloud benefits from selling specific software and hardware to enterprise clients, and that Alphabet's broader products improve as AI is integrated into them. Patel acknowledges that the next few years are hard to forecast and that uncertainty is high, but he concludes that the company is well placed to ride the AI wave.

The piece also reflects the uncertainty around AI spending that investors are weighing. Google Search sales slowed to 12% growth in the quarter, and Alphabet has begun funding its AI push with outside capital. The article frames the current price as a setup that favors investors with a five-year horizon. Patel discloses that he holds no position in the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends both Alphabet and Berkshire Hathaway, and the article contains promotional material for its Stock Advisor service.

Articles.Title: Berkshire Hathaway's Top AI Holding Is Poised to Outperform

stories.Headline: Google Hands AMD Major Win in AI Chip Race
stories.Summary:
Advanced Micro Devices shares rose nearly four percent in premarket trading on Monday, November 9, 2026, after the chipmaker announced an expanded partnership with Google Cloud. Under the agreement, AMD's fifth-generation EPYC server processors will support Google's new TPU 8tx, its first cloud tensor processing unit system with hardware-based confidential computing. The arrangement is meant to protect sensitive information, including proprietary AI models and customer data, while workloads run. AMD's processors will handle data preparation and supporting tasks alongside Google's custom AI accelerators. AMD shares traded around $464.66 in premarket trading after the news.

The combination is aimed at AI inference, model fine-tuning and agentic AI applications, where multiple AI systems carry out increasingly complex tasks. The announcement builds on AMD's long relationship with Google Cloud, particularly in enterprise computing and security infrastructure. The company said its EPYC processors are already deployed by more than 10 leading hyperscalers and AI laboratories. Those customers run infrastructure built around Nvidia GPUs, AMD Instinct accelerators and custom-designed AI chips. That flexibility matters as large technology companies build their own processors to reduce reliance on outside suppliers.

The article attributes the announcement to AMD and Google Cloud, with AMD describing its EPYC adoption across the industry. It frames the deal as an opportunity for AMD to supply the central processors that power AI systems rather than competing head-on with Nvidia in graphics processors. Analysts and commentators quoted in related coverage pointed to the upgrade and rising interest in the stock. The companies did not disclose the financial value of the agreement or expected shipment volumes.

The article says investors should watch whether AMD can turn its hyperscaler relationships into sustained data-center revenue, along with EPYC adoption, server CPU market share and demand from customers using custom accelerators. Google's TPU 8tx rollout could give AMD another route to AI infrastructure spending without displacing Nvidia's GPUs. Slower deployments or weaker infrastructure investment could limit the partnership's financial contribution. Until more figures are released, the size of the deal remains unclear.

Articles.Title: Google Hands AMD Major Win in AI Chip Race

stories.Headline: On theCUBE Pod: Midterms send shockwaves through AI market
stories.Summary:
Tech stocks sold off sharply after the midterm elections, as investors reacted to a wave of winning candidates who opposed data centers and called for tighter limits on artificial intelligence. According to the article, the Nasdaq fell more than 5.5% and technology companies lost a combined $2.5 trillion in market value. John Furrier of theCUBE Research called the day a bloodbath and said that 41 states had data centers on the ballot. The report was published on November 9, 2026.

Investors now expect AI spending to slow, and the article describes the selloff as a sign that AI has become a political issue that touches everyone in the industry. Dave Vellante of theCUBE Research said enterprises are not yet paying for their own AI build-out, and he pointed to the time needed to build data centers and recover their financing. He noted that companies selling GPUs are profitable, but that clear monetization in enterprises is so far showing up mainly inside technology firms. A recent analysis cited in the piece identified 2029 as the riskiest year for an AI bubble.

Vellante argued that large tech companies are well placed, while neoclouds such as CoreWeave are taking on more risk with a new software model and will face some pain. Furrier said the infrastructure behind AI is moving beyond GPUs toward networking, optics, memory, storage, and power efficiency, and named Supermicro, Advanced Micro Devices, Arista Networks, and Marvell Technology as companies to watch. He also mentioned Marvell's reported $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum. Vellante described hyperscalers as able to scale spending up or down at will, while growth and market share remain the priority.

The article also explores who will control the system of intelligence that links AI agents to the data they rely on, a question it says remains open. Palantir Technologies has an ontology that could give it an edge, while Snowflake and Databricks are still building their operational systems. Vellante said Databricks chief executive Ali Ghodsi has the strongest vision, and Furrier predicted that AI-native enterprises will be the lasting result, with control resting in data and context rather than models. The article reports that frontier model vendors remain the wild card in this contest.

Articles.Title: On theCUBE Pod: Midterms send shockwaves through AI market

stories.Headline: AI in the Workplace: Why We Should Listen to Gen Z Women
stories.Summary:
A Senate hearing held this summer on AI's effect on the workforce drew concern from its witnesses about entry-level jobs, but the author, Charlotte Racine, writing for the National Partnership for Women & Families on November 9, 2026, says the panel largely ignored women. Only Senator Blunt Rochester raised how AI would affect women of color differently, and the witnesses only acknowledged the point in response. The author argues that the gap extends to research, which covers women and young adults in general but says little about how Gen Z women specifically feel about AI. She describes herself as a young woman who came away from the hearing both interested and disheartened.

The article says women are less optimistic about AI and less likely to use it at work, with studies of more than 140,000 college students and workers finding women's use 10 to 40 percent below men's. In a 2025 survey, 69 percent of Black women said AI made them feel unsafe, and 45 percent did not believe AI's creators cared about their community's well-being. Among Gen Z, 51 percent use generative AI at least weekly, yet 42 percent report anxiety and 31 percent report anger toward it. The share of Gen Z who strongly believe AI can help them work faster fell from 22 percent in 2025 to 18 percent in 2026, and Gen Z men are 25 percent more likely than Gen Z women to have experimented with AI.

The article also presents evidence that women may face harder job prospects in an AI-centered market. The unemployment rate for recent college graduates reached 6 percent in spring 2025, compared with a 4 percent national average, and a 2024 survey found 37 percent of HR managers would prefer AI over hiring a recent graduate. Women hold 83 percent of the jobs most vulnerable to AI, and women of color are among the most likely to work in AI-exposed occupations such as translation and interpretation. The author cites studies showing some AI hiring tools favor white and male applicants, and notes that 90 percent of American employers, along with 98.4 percent of Fortune 500 companies, use AI to screen resumes.

She points to Amazon's 2018 AI hiring tool, which discriminated against graduates of women's colleges, as evidence that the problem is longstanding. The author concludes that policymakers and experts are not paying enough attention to the disproportionate risk AI poses to Gen Z women in the workplace. She urges lawmakers who regulate AI to listen to young women and to weigh how their policies will shape the economy and workplaces for the next generation of workers. The article is an advocacy piece rather than a report of a pending decision, so it does not describe any specific rule or deadline that would follow.

Articles.Title: AI in the Workplace: Why We Should Listen to Gen Z Women

stories.Headline: Exclusive: Spines, a 'hybrid publisher,' raises $64 million in funding for book publishing platform powered by AI agents
stories.Summary:
Spines, a startup that calls itself a "hybrid publisher," announced on Monday, November 9, 2026, that it has secured $64 million in new capital. The company uses AI agents to help authors edit manuscripts, design covers, translate books, market titles and manage social media campaigns. Spines has offices in Israel and New York, and its founder and CEO, Yehuda Niv, shared the figures with Fortune. The funding package has two parts, a $29 million Series A-1 equity round and a $35 million non-dilutive growth financing facility.

The equity round is led by Zeev Ventures, with participation from Aleph, NordStar, M-Fund, LionTree and angel investor Dan Senor. The $35 million facility comes from Twelve, a credit-focused investment management firm. Spines also said its AI-powered services have reached a $50 million annual revenue run rate, which it describes as 400% year-over-year growth. The company has published more than 8,000 authors, covering about 12,000 titles, and roughly 400 new writers sign up each month. Spines declined to disclose its valuation.

Hybrid publishers typically charge authors an upfront fee and take a share of sales, while offering more support than self-publishing. Spines packages start at about $3,000 and reach $20,000 for a premium tier, with most authors choosing bundles of $5,000 to $7,000. The company recently raised its royalty share for authors from 70% to 80% of net royalties and reports earnings monthly. Niv said Spines publishes only books written by humans and uses software to screen for AI-generated manuscripts. He added that Spines is in early talks with one of the Big Five U.S. publishers about a partnership, and it plans to expand into the U.K., Canada and Australia.

Niv, who founded Spines in 2021 after running his own Israeli publishing house, has argued that AI will make traditional publishers less relevant. Spines has about 350 employees, of whom roughly 50 work in research and development. The article notes a possible copyright question around AI-designed covers, since U.S. courts and the Copyright Office have held that wholly AI-made images cannot be copyrighted, and Niv said Spines licenses its image tools and passes the license to authors. Oren Zeev of Zeev Ventures said in a statement that Spines has what it takes to lead the next generation of publishing.

Articles.Title: Exclusive: Spines, a 'hybrid publisher,' raises $64 million in funding for book publishing platform powered by AI agents

stories.Headline: Exclusive | I wrote an AI book using ChatGPT — is this method really the next chapter for aspiring authors?
stories.Summary:
