Asked what leaders should do next, Schroeder said companies should focus on role-based education and skills development because some employees remain uneasy or openly resistant. He said the technology works, so the task now concerns people and changing processes.

Articles.Title: Kyndryl says firms lag on AI readiness despite gains - IT Brief UK

stories.Headline: IBM stock gets fresh quantum and AI signals after Chicago launch - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
IBM unveiled its first quantum computer in Illinois on Friday, November 6, placing a Quantum System Two at the University of Chicago's Hyde Park Labs. The system runs on IBM's 120-qubit Quantum Nighthawk processor and is operational there now. IBM plans to move it to the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park once that campus is completed. The company says the machine will support the National Quantum Algorithm Center and partnerships with universities, government institutions and businesses.

Separately, IBM, AMD and Oak Ridge National Laboratory launched a joint platform that connects IBM quantum hardware with Oak Ridge's Umbra high-performance computer. The work targets quantum error correction under the U.S. Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission. On the AI side, IBM has made Agent Identity generally available in watsonx Orchestrate, giving enterprise AI agents individual identities along with activity logging and a kill switch. The feature extends IBM's governance tools for companies deploying agents in business processes. The articles do not give figures for how much these changes will add to revenue.

IBM is the company behind the Chicago system and the watsonx Orchestrate feature, and the articles report the announcements without quoting any company executive. The coverage notes that the quantum research and AI governance tools still need to turn into repeatable customer demand and profitable services. IBM stock traded at EUR 220.68 on Lang & Schwarz at 16:46 CET on Monday, November 9, about 0.26 percent above the Xetra close of EUR 220.10 on Friday, November 6. The articles say the next point of assessment is whether these initiatives strengthen growth in IBM's software, infrastructure and consulting businesses.

Articles.Title: IBM stock gets fresh quantum and AI signals after Chicago launch - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: The AI dilemma for cities: wait for perfect data or forge ahead?
stories.Summary:
Global AI Cities 2026, organised by Global Government Forum and co-hosted by Greater Manchester Combined Authority, brought more than 300 local government leaders from over 50 cities together in Manchester. The gathering, reported on November 9, 2026, focused on how artificial intelligence can improve public services and deliver better results for residents. A central question was whether cities should wait until their data is fully reliable before using AI, or start now with the data they have. Speakers examined examples from Helsinki, Greater Manchester, Camden and Madrid, and their findings were captured in a report titled Making AI work for people and places: Five priorities for cities. Speakers agreed that good data quality, governance and infrastructure are essential for using AI responsibly.

However, they argued that cities should not have to fix every problem in their existing systems before putting the technology to work. One speaker said that getting data right for AI is mainly a governance problem rather than a technical one. Without clear governance, systems could produce answers that are wrong or impossible to explain. Speakers also warned against reusing data collected for one purpose in AI tools it was never designed to support.

Their advice was to treat governance as part of design, fund the work needed to prepare data, and let non-specialists understand and use it. Tomas Lehtinen, head of data and emerging technologies at the City of Helsinki, said AI has raised the urgency of improving data without changing the basic priorities of data governance, discoverability and quality. Helsinki already uses almost 200 AI systems and applications, so the city is now deciding which pilots to scale into lasting services. Lehtinen stressed that frontline staff who enter data play as important a role as data scientists.

Matt Hennessey of NHS Greater Manchester described years of work to connect health data across GP practices and hospitals, and said that any new use case can build on those foundations. The next step is a civic data set linking health, local government, education and transport. Martin Waudby, chief data officer at the London Borough of Camden, said the council's focus is on demonstrating that it can fix its foundations rather than completing that work in full first. Juan Corro of Madrid City Council argued that cities can gain value from AI before solving all legacy data problems, since large language models already suit services such as cleaning, security and green areas.

Madrid has also labelled more than 100 regulations and published its regulation ontology and datasets so that other cities can reuse them. The overall message from the event was that cities should not choose between strengthening their foundations and delivering value. They are advised to build governance, quality and infrastructure for the long term while identifying where existing data is good enough to deploy AI responsibly. The organisers have invited cities to register for Global AI Cities 2027, which will take place on May 24 and 25, 2027, in Manchester.

Articles.Title: The AI dilemma for cities: wait for perfect data or forge ahead? - Global Government Forum

stories.Headline: F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them
stories.Summary:
F-Secure, the Finnish consumer cybersecurity company, has released a new AI Harms Taxonomy that identifies 26 distinct ways artificial intelligence can harm consumers, announced on November 10, 2026. The framework was developed by Dr. Megan Squire, Principal Threat Intelligence Researcher at F-Secure, and traces how each harm travels through AI systems until it reaches a person. Its stated purpose is to show where protections can intervene and which parties are best placed to provide them. The research addresses a gap in how AI risk is usually discussed, since many frameworks list possible failures without linking them to the systems and companies that could prevent them.

The taxonomy currently maps the 26 harms across five relationship types and 19 intermediary layers, and it proposes 24 defenses aimed at different points along those paths. The harms range from AI-generated voice and video impersonation to agents making harmful financial decisions, exposing personal information, or acting on outdated context. The research also examines attacks in which malicious instructions are hidden in content that an AI system processes, which could steer an agent's actions or a chatbot's answers. Some risks can be handled by security software on a person's own device, while others must be addressed upstream by the companies that build AI products, including how those systems retain memory and which external services they connect to. Dr. Squire said that developers have a responsibility to understand how their systems can fail, who gets hurt when they do, and to put safeguards in place before harm occurs.

According to the announcement, the shift from AI producing information to AI acting on it makes the question of responsibility more pressing. A chatbot that gives a wrong answer can mislead a user, but an agent with access to a person's accounts can cause real consequences without the person being part of each step. The research also suggests that individuals cannot protect themselves alone by spotting suspicious content or double-checking AI output. The work sits within a wider F-Secure effort around trust in the AI era, which includes F-Secure Trust, a strategic alliance with Quantum AI Lab QuTwo, and two products, TrustGuard and TrustPath. The taxonomy is available on the company's Illuminate Research Hub, and the article does not report any regulatory response or further timeline beyond that.

Articles.Title: F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon
stories.Summary:
In July, an independent developer named Autumn-27 published Artex to GitHub, an open source, multiagent AI penetration testing framework written in Go. The tool was built as a legitimate pen-testing product, but threat actors found ways to use it for malicious purposes, and by late summer and early fall a range of them had added it to their toolkits. Artex can brute-force passwords, dump databases, enumerate and abuse APIs, and operate at speeds no human could match. Microsoft observed an AI agent move from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

Around October 10, China's Storm-0940 used Artex to launch a password-spraying and credential-stuffing campaign against more than 300 user accounts at eight critical organizations, making more than 151,000 authentication requests. That averaged 2,900 attempts per minute without triggering automated lockout or alerts. When that largely failed, the group targeted ConnectWise's internal infrastructure and exfiltrated trusted OAuth application credentials for its Cloud Backup application. Those credentials let the attackers compromise more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 and Azure environments within three hours of initial targeting.

Artex's creator deleted the original GitHub repository at the end of October because of rampant abuse, but many forks remain available. Steve Winterfeld, advisory CISO for Akamai, said the Artex campaigns stand out for the acceleration in speed, coordination, and autonomy, noting that activities once requiring deliberate integration can now be chained together with limited hacking skills. GitGuardian separately detailed 45 similar agentic attack frameworks, some of which include built-in command-and-control functionality. The researchers noted that pen-testing tools have legitimate uses, but the range of options now available to attackers is wide.

Microsoft published a blog post last week describing how Storm-3358, a financially motivated Cambodia-based threat cluster, began using Artex against financial organizations, mainly in Southeast Asia. CrowdStrike on October 29 linked Artex-powered espionage activity to a threat actor it tracks as Vapor Panda, and India's CERT-In tracked a financially motivated actor hitting financial institutions. As of November 4, Censys observed more than 1,400 internet-exposed Artex console deployments, and it estimated actual global use is higher because internet exposure is not required. Guillaume Valadon, head of cybersecurity research at GitGuardian, said the fast pace of attacks and the agent's initiative to reach user goals stood out to him most.

Matt Snyder, head of security operations and threat research at Aviatrix, said the operational maturity of many threat actors deploying Artex appears low, given how many hosts remain internet-exposed. He said AI is lowering the skill floor for offensive operations without improving operational discipline. Microsoft's Storm-3358 blog includes extensive indicators of compromise and recommends considering defensive honeypots. Check Point advised organizations to expect greater automated pressure against exposed infrastructure, and Censys researcher Silas Cutler said that enforcing MFA, monitoring attack surfaces, and practicing good credential hygiene still hold.

Articles.Title: Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: University of Nebraska-Lincoln to lead cybersecurity in national AI project
stories.Summary:
The University of Nebraska-Lincoln has been tasked with leading cybersecurity for a national artificial intelligence research project called the Fabric For AI-driven Science, or FabAID. The project is operated by the Morgridge Institute for Research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and aims to connect AI-driven science and research to schools across the United States. The reporting was published on November 9, 2026. FabAID is designed to create a single fabric linking AI, data and computational services to universities and research programs.

FabAID will receive $24.5 million in funding over five years from the National Science Foundation. That money is part of a larger investment meant to strengthen the country's research infrastructure. The university's role comes in two parts. The Holland Computing Center will supply the cyberinfrastructure needed to keep the fabric running, and it will design and implement security practices for the system. Researchers at UNL will also be connected to shared data, AI and computing services through the project, which is intended to make research easier.

The Holland Computing Center has provided cyberinfrastructure services to similar systems in past years. The article names the National Research Platform, the Institute for Research and Innovation in Software for High Energy Physics and the Partnership to Advance Throughput Computing as examples. The article does not include a direct statement from university officials, so their specific comments on the assignment are not reported here. It also does not give a timeline for when the security work will begin or when the network will be fully operational.

Articles.Title: University of Nebraska-Lincoln to lead cybersecurity in national AI project - Nebraska Public Media

stories.Headline: AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub
stories.Summary:
Security firm Apiiro reported that AI coding assistants may be inadvertently leaking thousands of secrets to public GitHub repositories. Its research found 2,539 credentials across nearly 2,000 public repositories, including database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens and SSH root logins. Apiiro tied some of the leaked data to Claude Code, which copies secrets to a hidden file and commits them with the rest of a developer's code. The findings were published in a recent report.

The problem arises when a user approves a command. If a developer chooses "Yes, and don't ask again," Claude Code saves that exact command, secret included, to .claude/settings.local.json inside the project folder. Nothing in the repository marks that file as private, so it is committed with the rest of the code. Apiiro examined 104,185 publicly accessible copies of that file on GitHub and found that 1,122 contained real secrets. Those files held 1,379 distinct secrets, including 636 provider-specific keys and 743 passwords or tokens.

Apiiro researchers Shmulik Cohen and Matan Giladi wrote the report, and they said most of the secrets belong to individual developers across 63 organizations. Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing at database security firm Liquibase, said the workflow made exposure possible even though no one intended it. Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of AI penetration testing firm BreachLock, said developers clicking the prompt likely don't know the file exists. Boris Cherny, head of Claude Code at Anthropic, said the company has historically not scrubbed secrets but is looking into preventing the exposure.

Claude Code tries to protect the file by adding it to the developer's global Git ignore list, but that rule exists only on that developer's machine. The rule does not travel with the repository when it is cloned onto another machine. In 539 of the 1,105 repositories containing real secrets that the researchers investigated, a commit co-authored by Claude Code had modified the affected settings file. Apiiro had contacted Anthropic before publishing its findings.

Cherny said Anthropic may make sure auto mode catches the exposure or build in basic secrets scanning. The company will prototype these ideas "to understand the tradeoffs" before shipping them in its next version of Claude Code. Apiiro recommends that developers rotate every credential a file has ever held and delete every rule containing a secret. It also advises security teams to treat all AI agent folders as secret-bearing on laptops and in repositories, and to add them to pre-commit and secret scanning, including history.

Articles.Title: AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: In Depth: China Cracks Down on ‘Poisoning’ AI Chatbots With Fake Marketing
stories.Summary:
Chinese authorities are penalizing companies that deliberately poison AI search results through a practice known as black-hat generative engine optimization, which the tech industry regards as a new form of corporate fraud. Marketing agencies flood the internet with fabricated content to trick AI chatbots into recommending particular brands or inventing products entirely. Three administrative cases this year and a televised exposé by the state broadcaster CCTV have brought the practice to light. The episodes have pushed regulators and courts to consider how to protect consumers when trusted algorithms repeat paid-for falsehoods.

One prominent case involved an 11-person law firm in Guangdong province. A blog article on the Sohu portal, which the firm's head confirmed, presented a fabricated ranking of Guangzhou criminal defense firms for 2026 that placed the firm first with a score of 92.5. When users asked ByteDance's AI model Doubao for good local law firms, it repeated those invented figures as fact. Regulators found the ranking baseless and traced it to Guangzhou Liqing Zhifu Technology, which had bought access to a platform that mass-produced such articles. On Sept. 4, the Yuexiu District Market Supervision Administration fined the company 120,000 yuan, about $17,983, under China's Anti-Unfair Competition Law.

The practice drew national attention in March, when CCTV's annual consumer rights program showed insiders using a "Liqing GEO optimization system" to create fake reviews and promotional articles for a non-existent smart band. Two major AI models soon began recommending that phantom product, and authorities in Beijing's Huairou district are investigating the firm behind the system. Black-hat methods work by padding answers with added citations, invented statistics and fabricated consensus, while legitimate white-hat optimization simply structures verifiable information so algorithms can process it. Enforcement so far has mainly targeted the agencies that carry out the campaigns, since all three public penalties this year, in Guangzhou, Shenzhen and Beijing, were against service providers.

The question of whether AI platforms are liable for harm caused by such content remains unsettled. Yao Jia, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of Law, said courts cannot assume consumer injury merely because a chatbot gave a false recommendation. Chen Bing, director of Nankai University's Center for Competition Law, argued that platforms should neither face strict punishment for citing poisoned data nor receive blanket immunity on grounds of technological neutrality. Industry responses are also emerging: DeepSeek says its search tool filters out GEO manipulation, and in August a Chinese technology association published standards banning prompt injection attacks. On Sept. 7, the Supreme People's Court issued guidelines stating that anyone who uses AI to infringe, advertise falsely or compete unfairly must bear legal liability.

Articles.Title: In Depth: China Cracks Down on ‘Poisoning’ AI Chatbots With Fake Marketing - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: Why Getty’s appeal won’t address all UK AI copyright questions
stories.Summary:
Getty Images will ask the Court of Appeal of England and Wales to find Stability AI liable for infringing its copyright in the UK, after failing to win that point in the High Court last year. The appeal is due to be heard on Wednesday 11 November 2026, according to a Pinsent Masons analysis published on 9 November 2026. The case centres on Stability AI's Stable Diffusion image system, which Getty says was trained on its copyrighted images without permission. The High Court rejected Getty's claim because it could not show that the training itself took place in the UK.

Under the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, primary infringement claims require the alleged acts to have happened in the UK. Stability AI argued that none of its training of Stable Diffusion occurred in the UK, and Getty, lacking evidence to prove otherwise, withdrew that part of its claim. The article notes that the appeal raises important points of law. It also stresses that the eventual judgment will not settle every question creators and AI developers may have about how UK copyright law applies to generative AI systems. The analysis is written by Pinsent Masons, a law firm whose Out-Law service covers this area.

The article says the hearing sits within a wider context in which courts in other countries are also working out how existing law applies to AI and copyright. Policymakers, it adds, continue to weigh whether the law itself should be updated. The analysis points out that the primary infringement questions will linger even after the appeal is decided. Readers should therefore not expect a single ruling to resolve every open issue.

Articles.Title: Why Getty’s appeal won’t address all UK AI copyright questions - Pinsent Masons

stories.Headline: China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
stories.Summary:
China has handed over equipment for a customized version of MAZU, an AI-powered weather prediction tool created by the China Meteorological Administration, to Sri Lanka's meteorological department. The device was presented on Nov. 1, 2026, and is described by domestic media as a rectangular black box roughly the size of a portable toolbox. It will form part of a system to warn of heavy rain, strong winds, and cyclones, and is expected to enter service by the end of the year. Sri Lanka is one of eight countries where the platform has been deployed.

MAZU, launched in July 2025, is named after a Chinese sea goddess revered as a protector of sailors. It pairs AI forecasting models developed by Chinese research institutions with data from China's weather satellites. Conventional forecasting uses supercomputers to calculate atmospheric change from physical equations, while AI models learn from years of weather data. According to the article, one model can produce a 24-hour global forecast in 1.4 seconds, about 10,000 times faster than traditional numerical methods, and for forecasts covering 15 to 60 days it can cut computing costs to one-thousandth of conventional levels. Most of those savings come from routine forecasting, since training models and maintaining systems still require investment that many Global South countries lack.

Niu Zeyi, an assistant researcher at the Shanghai Typhoon Institute who led development of a forecasting model used in MAZU, explained the approach to Sixth Tone. He said these models predict future conditions from current variables such as wind, air pressure, temperature, and humidity. He also said the company's approach is to work with local meteorological agencies to improve datasets, run independent evaluations, and make local adjustments, and that human forecasters must still combine observations, AI predictions, and their own judgment before authorities issue warnings. The article notes that, according to domestic media, MAZU's cloud-based services are being tested by 58 countries, and China plans to deploy the system in 30 countries over the next five years. In Pakistan, the system has reportedly incorporated local radar and satellite data for warnings on heavy rainfall and glacial lake outburst floods, while in Djibouti it helps provide tailored warnings for the port.

The article also cautions about the technology's limits. Studies show AI models can be less accurate than conventional methods when predicting record-breaking extremes, which have little historical data behind them, and local weather in complex terrain remains hard to forecast. It is also not always clear how the models reach their predictions. The article does not describe any specific next steps beyond the Sri Lanka rollout and the planned expansion over the coming years.

Articles.Title: China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting - Sixth Tone

stories.Headline: Why AI Inputs, Training and Outputs Demand Different Legal Rules
stories.Summary:
Public Knowledge, a nonprofit advocacy group, published an essay on November 9, 2026, arguing that copyright law should treat AI training, data acquisition and AI outputs as separate activities with different legal rules. The author, John Bergmayer, says training AI models is likely a fair use of copyrighted material, but that this does not mean AI companies may freely take copies of everything ever printed. The essay ties this position to the group's amicus brief in the OpenAI copyright litigation, which urges the court to consider training apart from both acquisition and outputs. It describes these as distinct activities that copyright law has no particular reason to treat alike. The essay argues that a ruling against fair use for training would favor the largest AI, technology and media companies.

Such a ruling would likely force companies to strike licensing deals, and only the biggest firms could afford terms that smaller developers, open-source projects, smaller publishers and academic researchers could not match. Recognizing training as fair use, by contrast, would let more people build competing tools and let independent researchers inspect training data, modify models and test company claims. The author adds that copyright protects original expression but not the facts or ideas learned from works, and that analyzing word patterns across large bodies of text has long been allowed. He also points to software cases such as Sega v.

Accolade and Sony v. Connectix, where copying for analysis was held to be fair use. The essay separates training from outputs and from acquisition. It says AI outputs that regurgitate copyrighted material may infringe even if the underlying training is fair, and that the 2023 Supreme Court Warhol decision shows the same copying can be fair for one purpose and not another.

On acquisition, it cites Judge William Alsup's June 2025 ruling in Bartz v. Anthropic, which found training on the books fair and scanning purchased books fair, but held that downloading and keeping pirated books was not allowed. The essay also notes that scraping public websites differs from downloading pirated collections, while acknowledging that crawlers can overwhelm sites and that publishers may limit access or use robots.txt to state their preferences. The author concludes that policymakers can recognize fair use for training while still holding companies responsible for piracy and infringing outputs, and that fair use need not be given up to support creators.

Articles.Title: Why AI Inputs, Training and Outputs Demand Different Legal Rules - Public Knowledge

stories.Headline: Trump Claims His Administration Threatened to Jail AI Executive
stories.Summary:
Trump told CBS's 60 Minutes that his administration once threatened to jail the leader of a major AI company. He recounted telling the executive to go home, see his family and say goodnight, because "tomorrow morning you are going to jail." Trump did not name the executive, saying only that the person led one of the big AI companies, and the article notes that his description of a wife and children appears to rule out certain well-known CEOs. Trump also said he did not believe the executive acted maliciously and that the executive "totally changed everything" after the warning.

The article indicates the claim was made during a 60 Minutes interview published around November 9, 2026. Trump had previously made similar remarks, including a September 14 Truth Social post that singled out Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and said the government had stopped AI "people" from doing "bad, or potentially bad, things." It is unclear whether the 60 Minutes account refers to the same incident. Trump used the story to argue that government agencies can be trusted to handle AI safety risks, which he says are overstated, and he said he does not oppose guardrails but does not want the United States to fall behind China.

The article also places the claim alongside other AI news that week, including the Nvidia affair and espionage allegations involving CEO Jensen Huang, which China has denied. Trump said he had not spoken to Huang about the matter but hoped he would stay as CEO. Separately, the article describes AI safety as a growing political issue, noting that in September Anthropic's Amodei urged the industry to slow down and that Trump invited major AI firms to the White House to sign a voluntary safety agreement, which Trump called "morally binding." It adds that voters in recent local ballot measures rejected many data-center projects, and that Democrats, who will regain the House majority, have pledged tighter oversight, with Trump saying he would be willing to work with them on AI safety.

Articles.Title: Trump Claims His Administration Threatened to Jail AI Executive - Gizmodo

stories.Headline: Midterms swing AI market, AI shapes elections
stories.Summary:
Following Tuesday's midterm elections, AI and other tech stocks around the world fell sharply, with trillions of dollars in stock value lost as investors sold off shares. The sell-off was driven by fears of a slowdown in AI development and tighter market regulation once a Democratic Congress takes office in January. Across the country, voters faced 41 ballot measures to limit or reject data center development, and 40 of them passed. Industry experts attribute this result to concerns about how quickly data centers are being built and about their effects on electricity and water use, a pattern that polling had signaled for months.

The incoming Congress is widely expected to regulate the AI industry more strictly than the current government has. President Trump and the current Congress have declined to pass AI regulations, and President Trump rescinded a 2023 Biden administration executive order that had called for policy-based oversight of the industry. The Biden administration also passed the CHIPS and Science Act, which aimed to boost U.S. semiconductor production to support large-scale data center rollouts and reduce reliance on foreign manufacturing. Beyond regulation, the article describes how AI is shaping campaigns and voter information. A study of 50 national elections in 2024 found that generative AI played a role in 40 of them, most often in creating political content, and in about a fifth of cases the content came from foreign actors.

Campaigns in this year's races used AI both in political advertising and for "microtargeting," using AI apps to analyze census data, voting history and local prices to craft tailored messages for key voters in toss-up areas. A Pew Research study published Oct. 23 found that 8 percent of surveyed Americans used AI chatbots to research the midterms, most often asking about candidates' positions on issues, the accuracy of claims they had heard, and candidates' backgrounds. An investigation of seven commonly used chatbots found they confidently gave inaccurate information, including wrong voter registration and mail-in ballot deadlines and incorrect positions on issues, with accuracy varying among them. The article notes that campaigns have begun tailoring their content so AI tools will pick it up, and it closes by asking what will happen next as political scientists, politicians and voters grapple with AI's role.

Articles.Title: Midterms swing AI market, AI shapes elections - The Tartan

stories.Headline: Wuxi welcomes global dialogue on AI and intelligent communication
stories.Summary:
The 2026 China International Intelligent Communication Forum opened in Wuxi, Jiangsu province, on November 9, 2026, drawing officials, media leaders, academics and representatives of international organizations. The gathering set out to examine recent progress in intelligent communication and how artificial intelligence might shape the future of global media. China Media Group and the Jiangsu Provincial People's Government jointly hosted the event, which carried the theme "New Ecosystem, New Opportunities, New Future." Organizers presented it as a further step in a series of exchanges focused on media technology and culture.

The forum's main outcome was the Wuxi Initiative, which calls for the responsible use of technology, stronger international partnerships and wider dialogue among civilizations. The initiative aims to build an open, inclusive and cooperative ecosystem for intelligent communication. Separately, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences released the China Cities' International Intelligent Communication Capability Development Report 2026, which looks at how cities pursue international branding and build global influence. Several cultural and media projects were also launched, including a micro-series on how AI is changing daily life and a documentary on the cultural heritage of the Jiangnan region.

Speakers from government and industry addressed the forum's aims. Yu Junsheng, vice-president of China Media Group, described the forum as an important platform for international cultural exchange and media innovation, and called for closer integration of technology, art and content so that AI serves the public good. Xu Ying, head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Jiangsu Provincial Committee, said Jiangsu would use the event to promote digital cultural exchange and international cooperation. Cai Jianfeng, mayor of Wuxi, said the city would develop its AI industry, produce high-quality international content and turn the forum's results into concrete cooperation projects.

The keynote session brought together experts from science, technology, media and the creative industries, including Nobel laureate Michael Levitt, Discovery Channel Greater China Vice-President Vikram Channa and Digital Domain founder Scott Ross. Discussions covered AI-driven change in the media landscape, technological innovation, industrial development and international collaboration. Oleg Kopylov, deputy secretary-general of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, urged stronger international cooperation on AI development and governance. Zamir Ahmed Awan, founding chairman of the Global Silk Route Research Alliance, stressed mutual respect, cultural diversity and shared values. The forum also included a digital culture communication forum, an AIGC industry forum, an international media tour and a film and music evening.

Articles.Title: Wuxi welcomes global dialogue on AI and intelligent communication - China Daily

stories.Headline: Labels required for AI-made dramas
stories.Summary:
China's top broadcast regulator has introduced rules that bring AI-generated short dramas under national oversight for the first time, alongside live-action short dramas. The measures, enacted on Sept 1 by the National Radio and Television Administration, require mandatory pre-release filings, episode-by-episode AI labels, and tiered administrative reviews. The move formalizes an ecosystem that had sat in a regulatory gray zone between casual short videos and full-scale series. It follows a surge in AI production volume paired with viewer complaints about a market described as disordered.

Micro short dramas, serials with episodes typically lasting one to two minutes, have dominated mobile screens across China. Data from the China Network Audiovisual Association shows that media platforms released over 367,000 series in the first half of 2026. AI-generated series accounted for more than 74 percent of that volume, and over 1,500 new AI series are published on mobile platforms daily. According to DataEye, the user base for AI-assisted short series grew from 120 million in 2025 to over 600 million in the first half of 2026. On Douyin, 221,900 AI drama series were published in that period, and only 1,055 of them exceeded 100 million views.

Viewers have complained of repetitive tropes, including domineering executive romances, time-travel themes and instant revenge stories, as well as clickbait, copyright theft and unauthorized digital likeness clones. In March, model Qi Hai found that the AI serial Taohuazan on the Hongguo app featured a character identical to her, down to a distinctive mole, and the series, with 40 million views, used her image without consent. Another production modified its male protagonist after the legal team for actor Luo Yunxi objected to a near-identical digital replica of his likeness. He Biao, deputy director of the National Radio and Television Administration, said at a forum in early November that content quality must be ensured as AI short dramas grow faster. He said the aim is to stabilize volume and improve quality, adding that the boundaries of AI, the copyright bottom line and the ethical bottom line must be held.

Lin Qiwen, vice-president of DataEye, said the measures fill a gap in industry rules and give AI short dramas a clear identity. She described the regulation as ex ante access and whole-chain supervision, compared with the scattered rectification rules of the past two years. Lin said that every episode must display a clear prompt of its synthetic origin, a requirement she said protects viewers' right to know. Lin also said that while major streaming platforms have begun adding mandatory tags at the start of episodes, smaller studios have shrunk disclaimers into screen corners, a practice regulators are working to eliminate. Lin explained that the budget thresholds are meant to prevent creators from mass-producing cheap, high-risk content that bypasses national oversight.

The measures set a three-tiered system based on budget. High-budget AI productions, defined as works with an investment of 800,000 yuan ($120,000) or more, as well as any series covering politics, national security, military or religion, must undergo national NRTA pre-filing, full review and receive a distribution license before release. Mid-tier productions, with budgets between 300,000 and 800,000 yuan, are reviewed and registered by provincial-level broadcast authorities. Productions under 300,000 yuan can be reviewed internally by the hosting platform and assigned a program registration number. Traditional live-action micro dramas typically need budgets of 2 million to 3 million yuan before reaching top-level licensing.

Zhang Lanshan, a professor at Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, said at a seminar in late September that a human-led zone must be established in core narrative links such as creative values, story themes and character emotions. She said AI should expand the boundaries of creation while humans guard the soul of narrative. Zhang said the rules do not require AI dramas to mark where AI is used, only to state that the work is AI-generated, and they do not shut low-cost creation out. Regulators are still refining operational definitions, including the exact percentage of AI assets that triggers mandatory labeling and how self-review standards should be unified across competing platforms. On Nov 6 the NRTA launched a two-month enforcement campaign targeting low-brow themes, copyright violations and technical loopholes.

Articles.Title: Labels required for AI-made dramas - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: AI vs. AI: Two robots rally for 142 consecutive shots - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
Two robots faced off in a table tennis rally at the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, according to Xinhua. The machines used artificial intelligence to track the ball, predict its path and return shots in real time. No remote controls were involved, and the exchange reportedly reached 142 consecutive shots. The article was published on November 10, 2026.

The report is a short video piece and gives few details beyond the rally itself. It does not name the companies or engineers behind the robots, nor does it describe the hardware or the AI systems in technical terms. The article frames the event as a challenge for viewers, asking them to guess how long the rally would last before watching the video. The article is credited to Xinhua and carries the English-language site english.news.cn.

It does not include comments from the developers or from CIIE organizers. The surrounding page links to other CIIE coverage, including medical equipment, consumer goods and a segment on how media should respond to AI. The article does not say whether the demonstration was a planned exhibit or a one-time display, or what the robots will be used for afterward. It also gives no further details about future events or follow-up coverage.

Articles.Title: AI vs. AI: Two robots rally for 142 consecutive shots - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Paws and prompts: How AI-generated pet videos tap into China's "emotional economy" - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
A Xinhua feature published on November 11, 2026, examines how AI-generated pet videos are drawing large audiences in China and tapping into what the article calls the country's "emotional economy." The piece centers on the social media account "Maoziqi," whose three AI-generated cats brew coffee, ride rapids and craft porcelain in a rural courtyard. Within six months of launching in April, the account reportedly gained about 1.7 million followers and more than 500 million views across platforms. The article also cites the hashtag #AICutePets, which has drawn 3.19 billion views on Douyin and 75.89 million on Xiaohongshu.

The article describes the commercial side of the trend. The creator of "Maoziqi," a 29-year-old man from Chengdu, makes the videos from his bedroom using Microsoft Word, the CapCut video editor and the Dreamina AI generator, and brand deals account for about 70 percent of his income. Another creator, Zhu Bu'er, is quoted as saying that leading creators in the niche can command up to 80,000 yuan for a single advertising deal, with top creators reportedly earning up to 1 million yuan a month. The article also notes that AI platforms are offering cash rewards and other incentives to attract creators, and it places the trend against a pet economy in which China's urban dog and cat population reached 126 million in 2025, with pet consumption at 312.6 billion yuan and projected to reach 405 billion yuan by 2028.

The article attributes the appeal to the emotional bonds viewers form, citing a 2025 report that found nearly 90 percent of young respondents had paid for emotional value. Chen Wu, a psychological researcher at Wuhan University, is quoted describing the videos as offering "low-burden attachment" and "lightweight social interaction," since virtual pets need no feeding or care. The creator himself is quoted saying his stories draw on his two real cats and on real life, and that he does not leave everything to AI. The article's closing argument is that viewers project their own experiences and memories onto these characters, which is why the emotional response is real even though the animals are not.

Articles.Title: Paws and prompts: How AI-generated pet videos tap into China's "emotional economy" - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Exclusive | China, Russia and US try to nail down AI nuclear agenda in time for Apec talks
stories.Summary:
China, the United States and Russia are reportedly working to agree on an agenda for talks that could include a commitment to keep artificial intelligence under human control within nuclear arsenals. The South China Morning Post reported this exclusively on November 11, 2026, citing its sources. The discussions are aimed at the leaders' meetings planned on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen next week. The three nations have held weeks of back-and-forth exchanges on both the agenda and the protocol for those meetings.

According to the sources, the agenda is being shaped to focus on areas where the three sides might find common ground. The war in Ukraine and the denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula have largely dropped off the list of possible topics. Instead, the emphasis has moved toward artificial intelligence and its role in nuclear command and control. The sources described the AI commitment as one part of a broader agenda on global governance. The articles give no figures, dates beyond those already noted, or fixed terms for any such commitment.

The reporting does not name a single party as responsible for the proposals, and it attributes the details to unnamed sources rather than to official statements. Because the account rests on people familiar with the talks, the reporting does not show any formal position taken by the governments themselves. The article's framing places the matter within the wider context of the 2026 Xi-Trump summits and the continuing tensions over Ukraine and North Korea. What happens next depends on whether the leaders take up the proposed agenda at the Shenzhen meetings, which the articles present as still being prepared.

Articles.Title: Exclusive | China, Russia and US try to nail down AI nuclear agenda in time for Apec talks - South China Morning Post

stories.Headline: ETRI appoints special advisers in AI and 3D communications to strengthen research cooperation on future technologies
stories.Summary:
The Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute (ETRI) has appointed two outside experts as special advisers to strengthen its research on future technologies. The institute announced the appointments on November 11, 2026, at its international conference room in Daejeon. KAIST professor Seong-hyun Choi was named special adviser in 3D communications, and Song Jung, head of the KAIST Kim Jaechul Graduate School of AI, was named special adviser in AI. The appointments were made to strengthen the institute's competitiveness in research and development. The special adviser programme was created in response to a rapidly changing technology environment, according to ETRI.

The advisers will counsel the institute on core technologies and on the formulation of its research and development strategy. They will also help identify promising future technologies and new research tasks. ETRI plans to appoint special advisers across five key focus areas, namely AI, 3D communications, physical AI, spatial media and ADX convergence, to build a standing advisory system. The institute says the aim is to review its research directions through the views of external experts.

About 60 people attended the appointment ceremony, including ETRI President Se-woong Park and key officials from relevant research institutes. Each adviser gave a presentation after receiving an appointment certificate. Choi, a Fellow of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, spoke on AI-RAN and its role as an AI highway for physical AI. Jung, a KAIST ICT endowed chair professor who heads the Edge AI Research Center, addressed how AI may change the world as it moves from answers to actions.

Both advisers have held senior academic or industry posts in the past. President Park said that advanced technologies such as AI depend on close cooperation with leading outside experts, not only on a research institute's internal capabilities. He said ETRI will work to fold the advisers' expertise and experience into its research and aim to produce world-class results. The institute indicated that more special advisers will be named in the remaining focus areas as the advisory system takes shape.

Articles.Title: ETRI appoints special advisers in AI and 3D communications to strengthen research cooperation on future technologies - 디지털투데이

stories.Headline: "Not a single tree, but an AI forest… Results to be revealed in the second half of next year"
stories.Summary:
The Nvidia and KAIST joint AI research center has said it aims to build what its leader calls an AI "forest" rather than a single model, with results to be unveiled in the second half of next year. Kim Hyun-woo, head of the center, made the remarks in an interview at Nvidia Korea's office in Gangnam-gu, Seoul, on November 10. He said the center would release data and training methods that companies can use, instead of developing one specific AI model. The article describes the plan as a shift away from growing one successful tree toward showing the world how to build a whole ecosystem.

The two companies announced the center in July, pledging $300 million, about 403.2 billion won, over the first five years. Of that total, $250 million will go to computing resources, though the types and quantities of GPUs have not been decided yet. The research will focus on synthetic data technology, which lets AI generate its own training data, and on learning techniques that extract more information from existing data. The joint center will support at least 10 KAIST researchers each year, offering them internships at Nvidia, and it also plans to recruit full-time researchers.

Kim, who is also an assistant professor at KAIST's Kim Jaechul Graduate School of AI, said data is as important as GPUs in AI development, noting that training expertise is kept inside individual companies. He pointed to a shortage of high-quality public Korean datasets, noting that Korean made up just 0.88 percent of web documents in Common Crawl, an open web archive, as of last month. Google's multilingual dataset mC4 contains about 3.93 billion English documents compared with 24 million Korean ones. The center plans to build open recipes and data methods that start with Korean but can also apply to other languages.

Kim credited KAIST's research capabilities and the features of the Korean language for Nvidia's decision to set up the center in Korea. He also pointed to the Nemotron Persona Korea dataset, released in April under his leadership, which ranked first among the world's most popular datasets on Hugging Face for 10 days and was downloaded about 140,000 times, and which was used in LG AI Research's K-EXAONE 2.5. Kim said attracting talented Koreans working abroad back home is also a major goal of the center. He added that the research findings would be made available for use with other AI models and commercial applications.

Articles.Title: "Not a single tree, but an AI forest… Results to be revealed in the second half of next year" - 머니투데이

stories.Headline: Alibaba Internal Testing AI Creation Platform "Looogen" – Is It Alibaba's Version of Jimeng AI?
stories.Summary:
Alibaba is internally testing an AI film and television creation platform called Looogen, also written as Logic Smart Film, according to a report published on November 4, 2026 by the Chinese outlet ReadJia and carried by 36Kr. The product is designed for short drama and video production, and it can split scripts into episodes, design shots, generate character costumes and scene materials, produce character dubbing and background music, and output finished films. It also supports white mold preview, video expansion, and management of multi-episode material packages and studio assets. The article says the product is still in internal testing, so its functions, interfaces, pricing and service forms may change and remain subject to official announcements.

Looogen offers a desktop client that runs locally on Windows and macOS, with Intel and Apple chip support, and it also allows private deployment and access to self-owned model channels. All creation sessions, generated materials and finished films are stored on the local device, so project materials and script assets do not need to be uploaded to the cloud. The platform has a point-based billing system built into its dialogue execution link. Creators can choose the underlying model, aspect ratio and resolution before generation, with the internal test version offering Seedance 2.0 and ratios of 21:9, 16:9 and 9:16, along with 480P, 720P and 1080P options.

The product works in two switchable modes: a film and television Agent dialogue mode, which runs the full short drama production process from natural language instructions, and a film and television suite workbench, where creators can manually manage each module. The suite's homepage lists functions from video shot analysis, script evaluation and script supermarket through asset design, video generation, intelligent editing, subtitles, post-production and data insight. A built-in actor library is sorted by age group, and a scene library is sorted by themes such as ancient, Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing, Republic of China, modern and fantasy settings. The article states that Alibaba is the company behind the product and that it is being tested internally, but it does not name any individual responsible or quote any executive.

The article places Looogen against moves by ByteDance and Kuaishou in the same market. ByteDance's Mengxiang AI has launched an AI short drama creation service platform, and its Volcano Engine tested Seedance Studio internally in August 2026. Kuaishou launched LIKLI, an AI Agent for short drama creation, built on its Keling AI. The article says most AI tools focus on generating video clips, while multi-episode short dramas struggle with character face changes, scene style shifts and scattered project materials, which Looogen is meant to address. The article does not say what will happen next beyond the note that the product remains in internal testing.

Articles.Title: Alibaba Internal Testing AI Creation Platform "Looogen" – Is It Alibaba's Version of Jimeng AI? - eu.36kr.com

stories.Headline: Thinking of using a personal AI agent? Here's how to do it safely, Singapore News
stories.Summary:
On November 6, 2026, Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority, Cyber Security Agency of Singapore and Government Technology Agency of Singapore issued a joint advisory on personal AI agents, which AsiaOne reported on November 10. The agencies warned that these tools, which can manage emails, browse websites and make bookings for users by connecting to their apps and online accounts, could expose people to privacy and cybersecurity risks. Examples named in the report include Dots, Hermes, Muse, Grok Bot and OpenClaw. Unlike ordinary chatbots, these agents act on users' behalf, which is why the advisory focuses on how much access they are given.

The advisory sets out five steps for consumers. Users are advised to connect only the accounts an agent needs, starting with low-risk ones such as a secondary email account, and to keep banking, government services and healthcare accounts out of reach. They should never share passwords, passcodes or one-time passwords with an agent, and Singpass users should choose passkey login where available and complete authentication themselves. The agencies also recommend starting with read-only permissions, approving significant actions one time instead of choosing "always allow," and reviewing activity histories and revoking unneeded permissions. Users are further told to check what data is collected and how long it is kept, to delete inaccurate or unnecessary information the agent remembers, and to watch for hidden malicious instructions in websites, emails and documents.

The guidance places responsibility on users themselves, who remain accountable for what their agents do and may be held liable depending on the circumstances and applicable laws. The three agencies also ask users to consider whether family members, friends and colleagues would be comfortable with information the agent might access, to label emails or messages prepared or sent by an agent, and not to instruct agents to bypass paywalls or login requirements. The article notes that anyone who suspects a scam can call the 24-hour ScamShield Helpline at 1799, that compromised Singpass accounts can be reported to the Singpass Helpdesk at 6335 3533, and that hacked devices or accounts can be reported to SingCERT through its Cyber Aid form. The report does not describe any specific incident or any further regulatory action beyond this advisory.

Articles.Title: Thinking of using a personal AI agent? Here's how to do it safely, Singapore News - AsiaOne.com

stories.Headline: Apple Expands China AI Filing to Cover iPad and MacBook, But Launch Timeline Still Unannounced
stories.Summary:
Shanghai's Cyberspace Administration said on November 9 that Apple's generative AI service, Apple Intelligence, has completed a filing amendment that adds tablet and notebook use cases. The change widens the service's approved device range in China from iPhone to iPad and MacBook. The notice, however, did not name supported models, operating system versions, or a launch date. Completing a filing therefore does not mean the feature is live.

Apple had already said in October that the first batch of Apple Intelligence features for mainland China should arrive in December with iOS 27.3 on eligible iPhones. Other platforms are to follow after the required approvals. The regulator's notice describes the tablets and notebooks only by category, so it should not be read as confirming that every iPad and MacBook will be supported. Those details would have to come from later device lists and system update notes from Apple.

The China version relies on a local model partner, since overseas tools such as ChatGPT and Gemini are not available in the country. Alibaba has said that users will be able to reach its Qwen model's text and image capabilities through Siri, writing tools and visual intelligence. Alibaba also said developers could test the China version in the latest iOS developer beta from November 4, with the official release planned for December. Baidu has been named as another technology partner.

For the market, the expansion fills in the device coverage for the China version, and iPad and MacBook have a sizable installed base in the country. Alibaba would gain a large device entry point for its model. Observers are watching three things: whether Apple publishes specific supported models and OS thresholds, how the China feature list compares with the international version when iOS 27.3 ships, and whether tablets and notebooks will launch alongside the iPhone or in stages. Until Apple clarifies, the filing remains a regulatory step rather than proof that the service is fully available.

Articles.Title: Apple Expands China AI Filing to Cover iPad and MacBook, But Launch Timeline Still Unannounced - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: China targets AI-powered celebrity impersonation - chinadailyhk
stories.Summary:
China's top internet regulator, the Cyberspace Administration of China, announced on Friday that it is stepping up efforts to stop artificial intelligence from being used to impersonate celebrities. Such impersonation has been used to falsely promote products, gain followers or boost online views, and the regulator said more than 47,000 pieces of harmful content have been removed. In addition, 3,961 accounts have been penalized for misleading the public. The announcement came in a report carried by China Daily, which described the regulator's latest move against AI misuse online. The regulator called on internet platforms across the country to take greater responsibility and adopt more effective measures to prevent AI misuse.

Platforms were asked to protect users' legitimate rights and interests and to help keep the online environment cleaner. Separately, the administration has launched a two-month campaign against health-related rumors, with a focus on accounts spreading illegal financial information. The campaign will target accounts that fabricate welfare-related messages, impersonate medical professionals to spread pseudoscientific claims, or use AI to generate health rumors. Platforms will also be urged to better verify whether users are doctors or health professionals and to improve their ability to detect AI-generated content.

The regulator itself is the body responsible for the campaign, and it has cited several recent cases to illustrate the problem. On October 18, actress Wu Yue posted a video on Sina Weibo saying someone had used AI to fake her face and clone her voice to promote a facial serum, and she demanded restitution for consumers who had been scammed. The offending account was banned the same day. On October 26, Yi Zhongtian, a professor at Xiamen University in Fujian province, used his WeChat official account to refute AI-generated videos that falsely claimed he had Alzheimer's disease.

The article does not give further statements from the regulator beyond its call for platform responsibility. The crackdown follows a year of ongoing campaigns by Chinese internet regulators to combat AI abuse that disrupts online order. Those campaigns have targeted AI-based celebrity impersonation, misleading marketing and infringement of people's lawful rights in cyberspace. The article does not say what penalties the two-month health campaign will carry or when it will report results.

Articles.Title: China targets AI-powered celebrity impersonation - chinadailyhk

stories.Headline: Insurers need to cross the chasm into AI or face being left behind
stories.Summary:
The Sapiens Insurance AI Maturity Index, published in 2026, shows that most insurers remain at an early stage of adopting AI, with only a minority having acted on what the article calls the greatest technology inflexion point of our time. The article's author argues that the sector has a long way to go and that insurers risk being left behind. Insurance is perceived as risk-averse, yet the author says that being a laggard carries its own dangers. The piece appeared on computing.co.uk on 10 November 2026.

The author believes that insurers which do not commit firmly to AI-fuelled automation and business process re-engineering may be acquired, may see declining revenues, and may suffer a serious loss of customers. The article says that concerns over regulators and compliance should not serve as a reason for inertia, and that the time for proof-of-concept exercises and pilots should end. It points to Geoffrey Moore's 1991 book Crossing the Chasm and to Amazon's early embrace of the web as evidence that early movers gain an advantage. The Index also found that 87% of senior insurance professionals worldwide say agentic AI is important, but only 16% run it in production.

The author attributes this gap partly to fear of change and to the need for capital investment, and notes that some pilots have disappointed. Confusion over supplier choice, with hundreds of vendors making large promises, is also cited. The article says that two-thirds of respondents, or 67%, expect fully autonomous AI in insurance within three years. Servicing and fraud/SIU functions are relatively advanced, while reinsurance remains very low in adoption. The author argues that vendors should show concrete execution plans and quick returns to reassure customers.

The Index is built on four pillars, namely cloud migration, master data strategy, AI governance and HR policies, and the article says that insurers should get these foundations right. It identifies autonomous leaders, such as insurers in the Nordics, that do not let compliance concerns block transformation, and reactives that lag behind. Autonomous leaders, the Index reports, invest more in upskilling staff than reactives (71% against 35%) and hire AI-knowledgeable talent more often (57% against 20%). The article says that 77% of respondents believe they can bring new products to market about three months faster. The author concludes that insurers must decide whether to be first movers, fast followers or laggards, and warns that their futures depend on those choices.

Articles.Title: Insurers need to cross the chasm into AI or face being left behind - Computing UK
